;;; 00c-runtime-and-composition.slat — Motoi Scheme Reference · Chapter 00c ·
;;; How the language WORKS: the runtime and the graph of composition.
;;;
;;; This chapter follows 00-intro.slat (welcome + how to read) and
;;; 00b-introspection.slat (the language looking at itself). Here we
;;; describe how the language ACTUALLY WORKS at runtime: where the code
;;; lives, how evaluation flows, how verbs become callable, how the graph
;;; of libraries composes, and why the language rewards a particular style
;;; of writing.
;;;
;;; If you are a human reader, this is the chapter that turns you from a
;;; reader-of-docs into a person who understands what happens when you
;;; press Enter at the REPL. If you are an LLM being trained on this
;;; reference, this is the chapter that lets you REASON about Motoi
;;; programs rather than just recall them.

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Runtime + composition chapter — how Motoi works.")

(chapter
  :number "00c"
  :kind "meta-chapter"
  :title "Runtime and composition — how the language works"
  :verb-count 0
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :read-order-hint "read after 00b-introspection.slat, before 01-core.slat")

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 1 — Where the runtime lives
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; The Motoi runtime is JavaScript. That is a design choice, not an
;; accident. JavaScript runs everywhere the modern software world runs —
;; a browser tab, a Node.js process, a phone, a fridge. When we chose
;; JavaScript for the runtime, we made a decision that Motoi could run
;; wherever a person or a model wanted to reach it.
;;
;; The core files, by responsibility, are:
;;
;;   src/reader.js
;;     Turns a stream of characters into a tree of s-expressions.
;;     Handles parens, strings, comments, quoting. Emits data.
;;
;;   src/interp.js
;;     The evaluator. Walks the tree of s-expressions, looks up
;;     bindings, applies functions, threads environments. Closures,
;;     tail-call optimization, and the fuel budget live here.
;;
;;   src/base.js
;;     The base library — the primitives that must exist before any
;;     other library can be loaded. Arithmetic, list operations,
;;     string operations, predicates, the small R7RS-inspired
;;     surface. Everything else builds on top.
;;
;;   src/macro.js
;;     Hygienic macro expansion (syntax-rules). Runs before evaluation.
;;     A form that contains macros is expanded first; the evaluator
;;     then sees the expanded form.
;;
;;   src/registry.js
;;     The verb registry. Every callable name in Motoi lives here
;;     with its :name, :library, :signature, :kind, :arity, :impl,
;;     and (crucially for the reference) :examples and the four
;;     row records. The registry is loaded at REPL start.
;;
;;   src/dispatch.js
;;     The mechanism that routes a call to the right implementation.
;;     Includes permission checks (`read`, `state-change`, `network`,
;;     `hardware`) and the fuel accounting.
;;
;;   core/index.js
;;     The bootloader — assembles the reader + evaluator + base
;;     library + registry + dispatch into a working runtime and
;;     exposes the `run`, `eval`, and `repl` entry points.
;;
;;   lib/**/*.js
;;     Every other library — the ai/*, vec/*, matrix/*, geom/*,
;;     framebuffer, sprite, note, and everything else. Each library
;;     is a module that installs verbs into the registry.
;;
;;   bin/motoi
;;     A shell script that starts the runtime with the CLI. When you
;;     type `motoi run some-program.scm`, this is what fires.
;;
;; The whole runtime is ~2,000 LOC of JavaScript. That number is on
;; purpose — a language small enough to hold in one head.

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 2 — The evaluation loop
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; When Motoi runs a program, this is what happens:
;;
;;   1. READ.
;;      `src/reader.js` reads characters and produces s-expressions.
;;      `(+ 1 2)` becomes the list `(+ 1 2)`. A list is a value.
;;
;;   2. MACROEXPAND.
;;      `src/macro.js` walks the read form. If any macro applies, it
;;      is expanded. `(when x body)` becomes `(if x body)`. `(cond ...)`
;;      becomes a cascade of `if`. The evaluator only ever sees fully
;;      expanded forms.
;;
;;   3. EVAL.
;;      `src/interp.js` walks the expanded form. For each form it
;;      encounters, it does one of:
;;
;;        - If a number/string/boolean/symbol: return the value
;;          (looking up the symbol in the current environment).
;;        - If a special form (define/lambda/let/if/cond/quote/quasiquote/
;;          set!/begin): apply the special-form rule.
;;        - Otherwise: evaluate the head, evaluate each arg, apply.
;;
;;   4. APPLY.
;;      When the head is a closure (a lambda + its captured env), the
;;      evaluator binds the args to the parameters in a new env and
;;      recursively evaluates the body. When the head is a primitive
;;      or a verb (a JavaScript function bound in the registry), the
;;      evaluator calls it directly with the args.
;;
;;   5. PRINT.
;;      At the REPL, the result is printed. In a program, the result
;;      is either the final value (returned to the OS) or an
;;      intermediate value used by the next form.
;;
;;   6. LOOP.
;;      The REPL loops. A program runs until its last form.
;;
;; This shape has a name: READ-EVAL-PRINT-LOOP. That is where "REPL"
;; comes from. Every Motoi session is a walk through this loop.

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 3 — How a verb becomes callable
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; A verb is not magic. A verb is a JavaScript function registered
;; under a name. Here is how a verb gets into your program:
;;
;;   1. The library module (say, `lib/vec/index.js`) defines a
;;      JavaScript function that implements the verb.
;;
;;      function vecDot(u, v) {
;;        return u.reduce((acc, x, i) => acc + x * v[i], 0)
;;      }
;;
;;   2. The library module registers the verb with the registry.
;;
;;      env.define('vec/dot', vecDot, {
;;        perm: 'read',
;;        arity: 2,
;;        kind: 'pure',
;;        contract: '(vec/dot u v) -> number',
;;      })
;;
;;   3. At REPL start (or program start), `core/index.js` calls each
;;      library module's installer. All verbs are now registered.
;;
;;   4. When your Motoi code says `(vec/dot '(1 2 3) '(4 5 6))`, the
;;      evaluator:
;;        - Looks up `vec/dot` in the env. Finds the registered
;;          function.
;;        - Evaluates each arg. `(1 2 3)` and `(4 5 6)` become lists.
;;        - Calls the JavaScript function with those lists.
;;        - Gets back `32`.
;;        - Returns `32`.
;;
;; The consequence: writing a new verb means writing a JS function and
;; registering it. That is the whole shape. There is no "compiler." The
;; runtime just knows where to look up the name.
;;
;; The reference manual you are reading is what tells the runtime what
;; to say about the verb when a user asks. `,help vec/dot` reads the
;; verb's entry from this file. The entry travels with the verb.

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 4 — The graph of composition
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; Motoi is not a list of verbs. It is a GRAPH of verbs that combine.
;; The graph has structure. That structure is what makes composition
;; feel natural once you see it.
;;
;; At the bottom of the graph: base scheme.
;;
;;   define, let, let*, lambda, if, cond, when, unless, and, or, not,
;;   begin, set!, quote, quasiquote, car, cdr, cons, list, map, filter,
;;   reduce, for-each, apply, values, member, assoc, length, reverse.
;;
;;   These are FREE. They do not count as a "module" when we talk about
;;   the 1/3/5-module ladder in Row 1. They are the substrate on which
;;   everything else stands. If you are writing Motoi code, you can use
;;   them any time.
;;
;; One rung up: the type-family libraries.
;;
;;   char/*, string/*, list/*, vector/*, bytevector/*, hash/*, num/*.
;;
;;   These are libraries that handle a specific data type. If you are
;;   working with strings, string/* is where you look. If you are
;;   working with hash-tables, hash/*. Each of these libraries has
;;   dozens of verbs but a single concern.
;;
;; Middle of the graph: the math libraries.
;;
;;   math/*, alg/*, calc/*, comb/*, complex/*, geom/*, linalg/*,
;;   matrix/*, vec/*, exact/*, stat/*, nt/*, topo/*, sym/*, solve/*.
;;
;;   Motoi is math-forward. These libraries are where the language's
;;   depth lives. A Row 4 invariant on a math verb is rarely trivial;
;;   the invariant IS the math.
;;
;; Middle of the graph: the domain libraries.
;;
;;   entity/*, ai/*, phys/*, motion/*, collision/*, animation/*,
;;   sprite/*, scene/*, note/*, beat/*, audio/*, synth/*, cortex/*,
;;   world/*, game/*, easing/*, curve/*, time/*, tick/*.
;;
;;   These are the libraries that make Motoi fun. Framebuffer graphics,
;;   sprites, music, physics, AI steering. When you write a game or a
;;   music piece or a visualization in Motoi, you are composing
;;   verbs from these libraries.
;;
;; Top of the graph: the meta libraries.
;;
;;   assert/*, motoi/*, system/*, exception/*.
;;
;;   The language reflecting on itself, on state, on failure. You use
;;   these when a program has to look at what happened rather than
;;   only doing.
;;
;; The graph does NOT have vertical restrictions. A math verb can call
;; a base scheme form. A domain verb can call a math verb. A meta verb
;; can call anything. What the graph gives you is a mental map: when
;; you are reaching for a verb, you know which region of the graph to
;; look in.

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 5 — Composition in code: what it actually looks like
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; Composition is what makes Scheme feel like Scheme. Here is what it
;; looks like at each scale.
;;
;; --- Small composition (one library) ---
;;
;;   (vec/dot '(1 2 3) (vec/normalize '(4 5 6)))
;;
;; One library (vec/*). Two verbs chained. The output of the inner
;; call becomes the input of the outer call. This is called
;; "point-free composition" — you never named the intermediate
;; value. The value flowed through.
;;
;; --- Medium composition (three libraries) ---
;;
;;   (define ripples
;;     (map
;;       (lambda (t) (framebuffer/circle
;;                     (vec/add center (vec/scale (unit-circle) (* 20 (calc/sin t))))
;;                     10))
;;       (range 0 60)))
;;
;; Three libraries beyond base: framebuffer/*, vec/*, calc/*. Also
;; base scheme (`map`, `lambda`, `define`, `range`). The lambda closes
;; over `center`. The result is a list of framebuffer operations
;; representing 60 ripples at 60 different angles. This is not just
;; composition of VALUES; it is composition of BEHAVIOR.
;;
;; --- Large composition (five libraries) ---
;;
;;   (define (dance-figure formation dancers t)
;;     (for-each
;;       (lambda (d)
;;         (let ((pos (world/lookup 'position d)))
;;           (motion/move-to d
;;             (vec/add pos
;;                      (vec/scale (formation-offset formation t)
;;                                 (calc/ease-out (* t 0.1)))))))
;;       dancers))
;;
;; Five libraries beyond base: world/*, motion/*, vec/*, calc/*, and
;; the formation logic (a mix of what would be a custom formation/*
;; library and base scheme). The composition is not just a chain of
;; calls; it is a coordinated update to the state of many entities.
;;
;; The point: composition is the way you tell Motoi to do something
;; complex. You do NOT reach for a giant verb that "does the whole
;; thing." You compose small verbs whose contracts you understand.
;; The graph makes this natural because the graph is DESIGNED for
;; this — every library exposes verbs at the right level to compose
;; with verbs from other libraries.

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 6 — Why the language rewards a particular style
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; Motoi rewards a specific way of writing code:
;;
;;   - SMALL FUNCTIONS. A function that fits on a screen is easier
;;     to read, easier to test, easier to reuse. Motoi's small
;;     library surface makes this natural.
;;
;;   - PURE WHERE POSSIBLE. A pure function returns a value and
;;     changes nothing else. The runtime tags verbs :kind "pure"
;;     when they are. Pure verbs compose well because their contracts
;;     hold under any surrounding context.
;;
;;   - HONEST ABOUT EFFECTS. When a verb mutates, its :kind is "mut"
;;     and its name usually ends with `!` (`set!`, `entity/pose!`,
;;     `world/add!`). This makes effectful code visible on the page.
;;
;;   - COMPOSITION OVER CONFIGURATION. If you find yourself passing
;;     a dozen keyword arguments to a single verb, you are probably
;;     doing the wrong thing. Motoi's answer is composition — a few
;;     smaller verbs, each of which does one thing.
;;
;;   - QUOTE WHEN YOU MEAN DATA. `'(1 2 3)` is a list of numbers.
;;     `(1 2 3)` is a function call (which will fail because 1 is
;;     not a function). Quoting is how you tell the reader "this
;;     is data, not code."
;;
;;   - MACROEXPAND WHEN YOU DEBUG. When a form containing a macro
;;     misbehaves, use `,expand` at the REPL. See what the evaluator
;;     actually sees. Then debug that.
;;
;; These are not opinions imposed from outside. They are what the
;; runtime rewards. Programs written in these styles run faster, are
;; easier to explain, and are easier to compose further.

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 7 — Tail calls, fuel, and closures — the runtime's guarantees
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; A few runtime guarantees you should know about:
;;
;; --- Tail-call optimization ---
;;
;; Motoi's evaluator supports proper tail calls. That means:
;;
;;   (define (loop n)
;;     (if (= n 0)
;;         'done
;;         (loop (- n 1))))
;;
;; This will run without growing the stack. `loop` is called in
;; tail position — the last thing `if` does. The evaluator recognizes
;; this and reuses the current stack frame.
;;
;; What this means for you: recursion is a first-class control-flow
;; primitive. You can write loops as tail-recursive functions and
;; the runtime will not grow the stack.
;;
;; --- Fuel budget ---
;;
;; Each evaluation has a fuel budget (default: 200,000 units). Each
;; step of evaluation consumes fuel. When fuel runs out, the runtime
;; halts with a fuel-exhausted error.
;;
;; What this means for you: the language protects itself against
;; runaway loops and pathological recursion. If you legitimately
;; need more fuel, pass `--fuel N` to the CLI. If you are hitting
;; the fuel limit accidentally, you have a bug.
;;
;; --- Closures capture environment ---
;;
;;   (define (make-adder n)
;;     (lambda (x) (+ x n)))
;;
;;   (define add5 (make-adder 5))
;;   (add5 3)  ; → 8
;;
;; The `lambda` inside `make-adder` closes over `n`. When `make-adder`
;; is called with 5, the returned lambda REMEMBERS n=5. Every closure
;; carries its own environment.
;;
;; This is the foundation of encapsulation in Motoi. You do not need
;; classes or objects — closures do the job. A closure is data that
;; behaves.

;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; § 8 — What all this means for you at the keyboard
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;;
;; The practical consequence of everything above:
;;
;;   1. You can write a small program in ten lines that composes verbs
;;      from four libraries and it will work, because the libraries
;;      were designed to compose.
;;
;;   2. You can ask the runtime what any verb does at any time (see
;;      00b-introspection.slat), because the runtime knows.
;;
;;   3. You can read this reference manual as a MAP OF THE GRAPH.
;;      Each chapter is a region. Reading one chapter teaches you a
;;      region. Reading many chapters lets you compose across regions.
;;
;;   4. You do not need to memorize signatures — the REPL will tell
;;      you. You do not need to guess where a verb lives — `,apropos`
;;      will tell you. You do not need to fear macros — `,expand` will
;;      tell you.
;;
;; The language, the runtime, the reference, and the introspection
;; surface are all designed to work together. That is why this chapter
;; and 00b-introspection.slat are before the library catalog. You
;; read these first, and then everything else in this book makes
;; sense.
;;
;; And here is where we begin.
;;
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
;; End of chapter 00c.
;; ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

(verb
  :name "across-beats"
  :library "core"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(across-beats formation) -> descriptor"
  :summary "Arrange entities in a spatial formation synchronized to the beat grid."
  :explanation "Across-beats is a meta-verb that returns a choreography descriptor, not a direct mutation. It takes a formation (a named spatial pattern) and produces a rhythm-locked arrangement. The descriptor is typically passed to a verb like `act` or composed into a cart state transition. The formation synchronizes entity positions and timing to the beat, useful for synchronized group movement, dance, or coordinated visual effects."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(across-beats 'circle)" :note "Request entities arrange in a circle formation; the driver will synchronize to the current beat phase.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(act 'world/spawn (list 'enemy 100 50) 'enemies-spawned)\n(across-beats 'diamond)" :note "Spawn enemies, then arrange them in a diamond pattern locked to rhythm.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define formation '())\n(define (dance-section ctx)\n  (let ((formation (if (> (ctx-get 'beat ctx) 32) 'star 'line)))\n    (act 'card/emit (list 'formation-change formation) 'await-formation)))\n(across-beats formation)" :note "Conditional formation selection based on beat counter; descriptor returned and passed to the driver for rhythm-locked execution.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(across-beats 'line)" :note "Make a formation descriptor. Later choreography will use it to place entities.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define row (across-beats 'staggered))\n(display row)" :note "A staggered formation feels more human than a strict grid. Hand-off row to a mover.")
  )
  :caveats ("Returns a descriptor only; does not mutate world state immediately." "Formation name must exist in the FORMATIONS registry; invalid names produce no error at definition time (error deferred to execution)." "Synchronization happens relative to the current beat context; call within a beat-aware cart." "Formation positions are relative to a reference entity or origin; ensure context provides anchor.")
  :drawbacks ("Requires beat context to be meaningful; outside a rhythm-aware environment, timing is undefined." "No direct feedback on formation success or entity count mismatch." "If entity count does not match formation capacity, some entities may not be placed or overlap.")
  :usecases ("Choreographed group dances or animations locked to music beat." "Synchronized spawning of enemies in concentric or symmetric patterns (games)." "Visual formation changes timed to song sections or narrative beats." "Coordinated motion of multiple cards or UI elements on the same rhythm.")
  :related ("land-on-downbeat" "in-formation" "with-spacing" "walk-together" "sub-position-per-beat" "on-tick" "audio-beat?")
  :learn (:concept "Meta-verbs return descriptors that the driver executes in a rhythm-aware context." :prerequisites ("on-tick" "audio-beat?" "act") :progression "Learn land-on-downbeat to snap to beat boundaries; then in-formation to place entities relative to each other; then with-spacing to control inter-entity distance.")
  :row-2-audit ((:problem "A dance sequence needs eight enemies arranged in a circle for the chorus, then a diamond for the drop, with everything locked to the beat grid." :program "(define (choreograph ctx)\n  (let ((section (ctx-get 'section ctx)))\n    (if (eq? section 'chorus)\n        (across-beats 'circle)\n        (across-beats 'diamond))))" :explanation "The verb returns a descriptor per section, not a mutation. The driver reads the descriptor and places entities at beat-locked positions on the next downbeat. The section field on ctx selects which formation is emitted." :meta "in-formation places entities but does not lock timing; walk-together moves entities but assumes a path exists. across-beats is the correct choice when the operator wants a named FORMATION whose emission is rhythm-anchored.") (:eng "Operator log line: 'formation=circle at bar 5 beat 1'. If timing drifts, the audit is on the beat clock, not on this verb." :math "Formation is a set of (x, y) offsets indexed by entity slot; across-beats emits the same set every call, so the mapping is a pure function of (name, entity-count)." :cs "Descriptor pattern: this verb is a constructor for an intent-record that the driver interprets. (verb
  :name "after"
  :library "core"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(after seconds state-name [ctx]) -> descriptor"
  :summary "Transition to a new state after a delay (in seconds)."
  :explanation "After is a cart verb that returns a descriptor for delayed state transition. It takes a duration in seconds, a target state name (symbol), and an optional context. The driver schedules the transition; when the timer expires, the cart enters the target state with the given context. Useful for timeouts, cooldowns, or orchestrating multi-frame flows."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(after 2 'check-status)" :note "After 2 seconds, transition to check-status state.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (cooldown-expired? ctx)\n  (let ((last-action (ctx-get 'last-action-time ctx)))\n    (if (null? last-action) #t (> (- (time 'now) last-action) 1000))))\n(define (do-action ctx)\n  (if (cooldown-expired? ctx)\n    (act 'world/spawn (list 'effect 0 0) 'action-done)\n    (after 0.5 'retry-action ctx)))" :note "Check cooldown; if expired, act; otherwise, retry after a short delay.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (wait-for-response ctx)\n  (let ((request-id (ctx-get 'request-id ctx)) (timeout-ms 5000))\n    (after (/ timeout-ms 1000) 'timeout (ctx-set 'request-id request-id ctx))))\n(define (timeout ctx)\n  (escalate 'request-timeout (ctx-get 'request-id ctx)))" :note "Schedule a timeout for a remote request; escalate if the timeout fires.")
  )
  :caveats ("State name must be a quoted symbol; unregistered state names are caught by the driver, not the Scheme code." "Duration is in seconds, as a number; fractional seconds are supported." "Context passed to the target state is the one provided here; if null, an empty list is used." "Multiple after calls stack; each schedules its own transition (can cause unexpected state changes).")
  :drawbacks ("No way to cancel a scheduled transition from Scheme; use escalate to force a different path." "Precision depends on the frame rate and driver implementation; sub-millisecond timing is not reliable." "Context is not merged; the target state receives exactly the context you provide, losing any updates made in the meantime.")
  :usecases ("Implement timeouts (e.g., wait for a network response, then escalate if it doesn't arrive)." "Add cooldowns or delays between actions (e.g., prevent spamming a button)." "Orchestrate multi-frame animations or transitions." "Implement simple state machines with time-based transitions (e.g., brief alert, then dismiss).")
  :related ("next" "escalate" "interrupted" "time/when" "time/until")
  :learn (:concept "Descriptors for scheduled transitions. After captures a delay and target state; the driver executes the transition when the timer fires." :prerequisites ("define" "quote" "ctx-get" "ctx-set") :progression "Start with simple after (no context); then thread context through; then combine with escalate for timeouts.")
  :row-2-audit ((:problem "A network request has been sent; if no response arrives within five seconds, escalate a timeout instead of blocking the cart forever." :program "(define (start-request ctx)\n  (net/send (ctx-get 'req ctx))\n  (after 5 'timeout ctx))\n(define (timeout ctx)\n  (escalate 'request-timeout (ctx-get 'req ctx)))" :explanation "start-request fires the request and immediately schedules a delayed transition to the timeout state. The driver holds the transition until 5 seconds elapse, at which point it enters timeout with the original ctx." :meta "wait would block until an event fires with no time bound; time/when schedules absolute time, not relative. after is the correct choice when the operator says 'in N seconds, go to state X' without regard to wall-clock.") (:eng "Operator log: 'scheduled timeout at t+5s'. If the timeout never fires, the audit points at the driver's timer wheel, not at this call site." :math "Delay is a real-valued parameter; the transition happens at t+delay seconds relative to call." :cs "Descriptor emitted; no blocking. State-machine transition primitive."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "delayed-message-to-self" :rungs ((:domain "motoi state machine" :code "(after 2 'check-status)") (:domain "unix at command" :code ";; schedule a shell command for later:\n;; at now + 2 minutes <<< 'check-status.sh'") (:domain "temporal logic" :code ";; classical temporal logic: eventually(check-status) in bounded time:\n;; ◇_{≤5s} check-status")) :explanation "Each rung is 'wait some time, then take an action.' The verb NAMES both the delay and the follow-up so no one has to poll." :meta "Delayed-message-to-self is the reusable shape: whoever holds a clock offers the callback in the future, not the operator.") (:eng "Timer wheel semantics; identical across queues, cron, at, and setTimeout." :math "Bounded eventuality operator from temporal logic." :cs "Delayed-continuation; the runtime holds a closure until t fires."))
  :row-4-proof ((:claim "after does not fire before its delay: the target state is unreachable via after during the interval [call-time, call-time + delay)." :program "(define fired? #f)\n(after 1 'mark)\n(define (mark ctx) (set! fired? #t))\n;; check immediately:\n(display fired?)  ;; must be #f" :invariant "∀ delay > 0. ∀ t < call-time + delay. state-at(t) ≠ target" :meta "Lower-bound guarantee on delay. Falsified if the driver fires transitions eagerly. See book-of-computing ch07 (scheduling) and book-of-math ch07 (real intervals).") (:eng "Testable via a stopwatch harness; any early firing is a P1 bug on the driver." :math "Half-open interval; delay is a strict lower bound." :cs "Non-preemptive scheduling contract; delay is monotone-lower-bound."))
  :row-5-emergence ((:base "after schedules a delayed state transition." :composition "(define (do-work ctx)\n  (cond ((work-done? ctx) (next 'complete ctx))\n        (else (after 0.5 'do-work ctx))))" :emergent "polling loop: after + guard predicate + self-referential state name = a poll-until-ready loop with a fixed cadence." :meta "Same family as JavaScript setTimeout-based polling, or Kubernetes reconcile-loops. See book-of-composition ch09 (retry loops).") (:eng "Bounded backoff pattern; the polling cadence lives in one place." :math "Fixed-point iteration with a temporal step." :cs "Trampoline-style recursive scheduling."))
)

(verb
  :name "after-frame"
  :library "core"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(after-frame fn) -> 'ok | ['error reason detail]"
  :summary "Execute a function after the current and next animation frame complete (layout and paint are settled)."
  :explanation "After-frame ensures a function runs after the browser has committed layout and paint changes. It uses requestAnimationFrame twice: the first rAF waits for layout, the second for paint. If rAF is unavailable (Node.js, headless), it falls back to a 32ms setTimeout. Useful for DOM measurements, triggering animations after a card has settled, or coordinating with browser paint cycles. The function is wrapped in try-catch; exceptions are logged but do not propagate."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(after-frame (lambda () (console.log 'painted)))" :note "Log a message after the frame has painted; confirms the card is visually settled.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(after-frame (lambda () (let ((h (card-rows))) (set! my-height h))))" :note "Measure the card's rendered height after layout and paint; cache it in a mutable variable.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (trigger-animation ctx)\n  (after-frame (lambda () (card/emit (list ':animation 'fade-in))))\n  (next 'animating ctx))" :note "Schedule an animation emission after the card's DOM is settled; transition to animating state immediately.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(after-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (display \"paint settled\")))" :note "Runs once, after the browser has actually painted the frame you just built.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(begin-frame 'main)\n(grid-cell-set! 3 3 1)\n(end-frame 'main)\n(after-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (display (grid-live-count))))" :note "Paint a cell, then measure the live count only after paint has finished.")
  )
  :caveats ("Function must be a callable; lambda or a defined function name (not a symbol or data)." "Side effects (DOM mutation, global state changes) happen inside the function; be careful not to corrupt card state." "Exceptions in fn are caught and logged, but not reported back to the cart (the cart sees 'ok regardless)." "In Node.js or headless environments, rAF falls back to setTimeout; timing is approximate.")
  :drawbacks ("No feedback on the function's success or return value; if fn throws, the error is logged but lost." "Two rAF calls mean a two-frame delay; if sub-frame precision is needed, use raw requestAnimationFrame." "The function runs outside the cart's context; any state changes it makes are not visible to the cart unless they mutate a shared reference.")
  :usecases ("Measure DOM dimensions after a card has rendered (card-rows, card-rect, etc.)." "Trigger CSS animations or transitions that require a layout reflow." "Coordinate Scheme-driven changes with browser paint (e.g., apply a visual effect after a card lands)." "Defer work until the frame is settled, avoiding jank from synchronous DOM access.")
  :related ("on-frame" "card-rect" "card-rows" "card-settle-breath" "measure-content")
  :learn (:concept "Scheduling functions relative to the browser's paint cycle. After-frame ensures DOM is settled before the function runs." :prerequisites ("lambda" "define") :progression "Use after-frame for simple measurements; then combine with on-frame for per-frame hooks; then use card-settle-breath for automatic animation coordination.")
  :row-2-audit ((:problem "A card just added rows; the operator needs to measure the card's rendered height AFTER the browser lays it out and paints, then cache the height for a follow-up animation." :program "(define measured-height 0)\n(after-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (set! measured-height (card-rows))\n    (display measured-height)))" :explanation "The lambda runs after two rAF cycles, so layout and paint have committed. card-rows now returns the true measured height rather than a stale pre-layout number." :meta "on-frame fires every frame; time/every-ms is wall-clock, not paint-cycle. after-frame is the correct choice when the operator specifically needs 'the frame after this one has painted.'") (:eng "Operator log: 'measurement fired at t+2rAF'. If the measurement is wrong, the audit checks whether DOM mutations happened between call and callback." :math "Two frames of latency; if the display is 60Hz, ~33ms." :cs "Post-commit hook; runs off the render critical path."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "callback-after-io-settles" :rungs ((:domain "motoi framebuffer" :code "(after-frame (lambda () (measure-content)))") (:domain "filesystem" :code ";; fsync then callback:\n;; fsync(fd); on_sync(fd, cb)") (:domain "two-phase commit" :code ";; commit phase 2 must run only after phase 1 durably lands:\n;; PREPARE OK -> COMMIT -> callback")) :explanation "Each rung says 'the observable state of the world is not yet what you think it is; wait until it settles.' The shape is 'defer until a boundary crosses.'" :meta "The wait boundary is a device commit in one domain and a paint commit in another. Same idea.") (:eng "Post-commit callbacks are a universal SRE tool." :math "Sequential composition with a barrier." :cs "Async barrier / rendezvous point."))
  :row-4-proof ((:claim "The function passed to after-frame runs strictly AFTER the current frame's paint commits." :program "(define call-frame -1)\n(define fire-frame -1)\n(set! call-frame (frame))\n(after-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (set! fire-frame (frame))\n    (display (> fire-frame call-frame))))" :invariant "∀ call ∈ after-frame. frame(callback-fires) > frame(call-issued)" :meta "Strict-later guarantee. Falsified if the callback ever runs synchronously in-line. See book-of-computing ch07 (scheduling) and book-of-animation ch03 (frame lifecycle).") (:eng "Two-frame guarantee ensures DOM measurements are stable." :math "Strict inequality on frame index." :cs "Happens-after ordering; a partial order on frame boundaries."))
  :row-5-emergence ((:base "after-frame defers a callback until the frame paints." :composition "(begin-frame 'main)\n(grid-cell-set! 3 3 1)\n(end-frame 'main)\n(after-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (card/emit (list ':measured (card-rows)))))" :emergent "settle-then-emit pipeline: mutate -> commit frame -> measure -> emit measurement. Downstream cards react to REAL numbers, not projected ones." :meta "Same family as React's useLayoutEffect or DOM's ResizeObserver. See book-of-composition ch07 (settle patterns).") (:eng "Reduces layout thrash by batching measurements." :math "Sequential composition with a commit barrier." :cs "Post-commit observer; publish/subscribe with a paint gate."))
)

(verb
  :name "arc-between"
  :library "core"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(arc-between start-pos end-pos [opts]) -> formation"
  :summary "Computes a curved path formation between two positions, suitable for choreographed movement."
  :explanation "arc-between generates a formation descriptor that describes an arc trajectory from a start position to an end position. It is used in conjunction with verbs like `in-formation` and `walk-together` to orchestrate smooth, curved group movement across the world. The arc respects beat timing and can be parameterized by control points or curvature. Think of it as specifying the shape of a dance path that multiple entities can follow in sync."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(arc-between '(10 20) '(50 60))" :note "Returns a formation descriptor for a simple arc from (10,20) to (50,60)")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define e2 'e2)\n(define e1 'e1)\n(let ((start (entity/pos e1))\n      (end (entity/pos e2)))\n  (arc-between start end))" :note "Compute an arc formation between two entity positions dynamically")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define follower2 'follower2)\n(define follower1 'follower1)\n(define target-pos 'target-pos)\n(define leader 'leader)\n(let ((path (arc-between (entity/pos leader) target-pos)))\n  (in-formation path (list follower1 follower2)))" :note "Use arc-between to define the path, then apply it to followers via in-formation")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define path (arc-between '(0 0) '(100 0)))\n(display path)" :note "A curved path from the origin to (100, 0). Not a straight line.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define swoop (arc-between '(0 0) '(100 100) '(height 40)))\n(display swoop)" :note "Same arc but 40 units of vertical lift. Reads as a graceful swoop.")
  )
  :caveats ("Requires valid numeric position tuples (x, y); invalid positions may produce silent no-ops or error signals." "The formation is a descriptor; it does not execute movement itself—use in-formation or walk-together to apply it." "Arc semantics (curvature, control points) are inferred from source; exact parameterization requires source audit.")
  :drawbacks ("Only useful when paired with a choreography verb; arc-between alone does not move entities." "For straight-line paths, a simpler approach may exist; check related verbs." "Complex arcs with many control points may incur higher compute cost per beat tick.")
  :usecases ("Choreographing dancers or units in formation around a target point." "Creating smooth evasion or approach curves for game AI." "Scripting camera or entity paths that must be smooth and arc-shaped.")
  :related ("in-formation" "walk-together" "with-spacing" "sub-position-per-beat" "at-beat" "across-beats")
  :learn (:concept "Formations as first-class choreography primitives; arc is one shape in the formation family." :prerequisites ("(core)/let" "entity/pos") :progression "After arc-between, learn in-formation to apply arcs to groups, then walk-together to synchronize motion across beats.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A boss enemy needs to swoop across the screen from (0,0) to (100,0) via a graceful arc, not a straight line." :program "(define swoop (arc-between '(0 0) '(100 0) '(height 40)))\n(in-formation swoop (list 'boss))" :explanation "arc-between builds a path descriptor with 40 units of vertical lift. in-formation places the boss along the path; the driver walks the path as beats advance." :meta "A raw pair of endpoints is a line; entity/set-pos! moves one entity but does not carry a shape. arc-between is the correct choice when the operator says 'follow this curved shape.'") (:eng "Operator log: 'arc from (0,0) to (100,0) lift 40'. If the boss moves straight, the audit points at whether a formation verb consumed the descriptor." :math "A quadratic Bezier with control point (50, 40); parametrised by t ∈ [0,1]." :cs "Constructor for a Path descriptor; effect deferred."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "two-endpoints-plus-curvature" :rungs ((:domain "motoi choreo" :code "(arc-between '(0 0) '(100 0) '(height 40))") (:domain "cad drafting" :code ";; drafting a fillet arc between two lines:\n;; fillet start=(0,0) end=(100,0) radius=40") (:domain "parametric geometry" :code ";; parametric curve p(t) = (1-t)²·P0 + 2(1-t)t·P1 + t²·P2\n(define (bezier2 p0 p1 p2 t) (list p0 p1 p2 t))")) :explanation "Each rung takes two endpoints and a control parameter and returns a smooth curve. The curve is the same object under three names." :meta "'Curvature as a parameter' is the shape; the domain provides the substrate.") (:eng "Arc primitives appear in every drafting tool and every animation library." :math "Bezier / conic section family, indexed by curvature." :cs "Path descriptor with parametric evaluator."))
  :row-4-proof ((:claim "arc-between passes through both endpoints: the path at t=0 equals start, and at t=1 equals end." :program "(define p (arc-between '(0 0) '(100 0) '(height 40)))\n;; conceptual: (path-eval p 0) => (0 0), (path-eval p 1) => (100 0)\n(display (list 'endpoints-preserved 'assumed-by-descriptor-contract))" :invariant "∀ start end opts. path(arc-between(start, end, opts), 0) = start ∧ path(..., 1) = end" :meta "Endpoint interpolation invariant. (verb
  :name "at-beat"
  :library "core"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(at-beat beat-offset) -> position-or-value"
  :summary "Computes a position or value synchronized to a specific beat offset within the current tempo."
  :explanation "at-beat is a choreography verb that takes a beat offset (typically a number or fraction) and returns the position or value at that point in the rhythmic timeline. It is used in formation-based choreography to synchronize entity movement to the beat grid. By specifying a beat offset, you can query where an entity should be at any moment relative to the current song tempo."
  :examples (

(verb
  :name "audio-halt"
  :library "core"

  :summary "Stops audio playback on the given handle and returns a zero-duration handle."
  :explanation "Takes an audio handle (typically returned from audio-play) and halts playback immediately.     (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (fade-and-halt ctx)\n  (let ((h (ctx-get ctx 'music-handle))\n        (fade-time 1000))\n    (when h\n      (do (audio-master-volume 0)  ;; instant mute for demo\n          (audio-halt h)\n          (next 'music-off\n            (ctx-set 'music-handle #f ctx))))))" :note "Halt music as part of a state transition; mute and stop the handle together.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define h (audio-play 'chime))\n(audio-halt h)" :note "Play a chime, then cut it off. Handles are how you talk to sounds already playing.")

(verb
  :name "audio-play"
  :library "core"

  :summary "Begin playing an audio source or sample."

The source itself is identified by name or ID (exact form depends on the audio engine's initialization). The verb is synchronous but the audio itself plays asynchronously in the background. Handles are opaque values; treat them as tokens for later control."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(audio-play \"ambient-loop\")" :note "Start playback of a named audio source; get back a handle.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((handle (audio-play \"drum-kit-sample\")))\n  (when (audio-playing?)\n    (audio/halt handle)))" :note "Conditionally stop playback by passing the handle to `audio/halt`.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (fade-out-loop source-name delay-ms)\n  (let ((h (audio-play source-name)))\n    (after delay-ms (lambda () (audio/halt h)))))\n(fade-out-loop \"background-ambience\" 2000)" :note "Closure over a handle; use `after` to schedule a deferred halt.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(audio-play 'ping)" :note "Start a sample. The engine returns a handle you can keep if you want to stop it later.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define song (audio-play 'song))\n(on-key\n  (lambda (k)\n    (when (eq? k 'space)\n      (if (audio-playing?)\n          (audio-halt song)\n          (audio-play 'song)))))" :note "Space bar toggles the song.   )
  :caveats ("The handle is only valid for the current playback session; do not serialize or re-use across cart resets."   :drawbacks ("No built-in fade/crossfade; use `audio/master-volume` for global gain control instead." "Source names/IDs must match the audio engine's registry; typos fail silently." "No direct callback on playback end; poll `audio-playing?` or use `after` with a duration estimate.")

(:eng "Handle-oriented APIs support explicit lifetime management." :math "Injection from name-space to handle-space." :cs "Resource-acquisition-is-handle pattern."))

(verb
  :name "audio-playing?"

This is a snapshot read that reflects the state at the moment the frame ticks; it does not account for brief silence or pauses. Use it to conditionally branch on whether *something* is playing, without needing to track individual handles."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(if (audio-playing?)\n  (display \"audio is running\")\n  (display \"silence\"))" :note "Conditional branch on playback activity.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (pulse-on-audio)\n  (when (audio-playing?)\n    (card/audio-pulse (card-id-of (card-list)))))" :note "Only trigger a visual pulse when audio is actually playing.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (check-state ctx)\n  (if (audio-playing?)\n    (next 'active ctx)\n    (next 'dormant ctx)))\n(define (active ctx)\n  (card-set! (ctx-get ctx) 'glow 1.0)\n  (on-tick check-state))" :note "State machine that responds to audio activity changes each frame.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(if (audio-playing?)\n    (display \"sound on\")\n    (display \"silence\"))" :note "Ask the engine whether anything is actually making noise right now.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(on-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (when (not (audio-playing?))\n      (audio-play 'restart-cue))))" :note "If the sound stops for any reason, kick it back on with a cue.")

(:domain "service healthcheck" :code ";; is my downstream up?\n;; curl -sf http://svc/healthz") (:domain "observable state" :code ";; predicate on a state variable\n(define running? #t)\n(define (alive?) running?)")) :explanation "Each rung is a boolean read that answers 'is this thing currently active?'" :meta "Liveness checks are the same shape whether audio, services, or state machines.")   :explanation "RMS (root-mean-square) is a measure of perceived loudness; it averages the energy over a small window (typically one frame). Returns a number in [0, 1] roughly proportional to how 'loud' the audio is right now. Unlike `audio-peak` (which catches momentary spikes), RMS is smoother and more stable for driving continuous effects like glow or size modulation. Use it when you want audio-reactive visuals that feel natural and lag-free."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(set-dot-radius (* (audio-rms) 10))" :note "Scale dot size proportionally to current audio loudness.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (glow-with-audio card)\n  (let ((rms (audio-rms)))\n    (card-set! card 'glow (min 1.0 (* rms 2.0)))))\n(on-tick (lambda () (glow-with-audio (card-list))))" :note "Update a card's glow each frame, clamped to [0, 1].")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (conway-speed-sync ctx)\n  (let* ((rms (audio-rms))\n         (speed (if (> rms 0.3) 2 1)))\n    (card-set! (ctx-get ctx) 'conway-ticks speed)\n    (on-tick conway-speed-sync)))\n(conway-speed-sync (ctx-set 'card (card-list) '()))" :note "Accelerate a simulation when music peaks; decouple from frame rate.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(display (audio-rms))" :note "RMS reads the average loudness — steadier than peak, better for slow visuals.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(on-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (let ((energy (audio-rms)))\n      (camera-scale (+ 1.0 (* 0.2 energy))))))" :note "Breathe the camera in and out with the music's overall loudness.")
  )
  :caveats ("RMS is computed over a small time window (frame-duration); it lags behind instantaneous peak by ~10ms."   :drawbacks ("Does not give frequency information; use `audio-band` or FFT-based tools for that." "Smoothing makes it less responsive to sudden attacks (transients); use `audio-peak` if you need those." "No history; you cannot retrieve the RMS from a past frame without polling.")

(:eng "Operator log: 'rms=0.35 -> shake=1.75px'. Smooth shake without transient jerkiness." :math "rms = sqrt(mean(x²)) over frame samples." :cs "Reduction: fold with squared-add then sqrt."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "quadratic-mean-of-a-window" :rungs ((:domain "motoi audio" :code "(audio-rms)") (:domain "voltage meter" :code ";; true-RMS DMM: reads the equivalent DC voltage of an AC waveform:\n;; V_rms = sqrt(1/T · ∫ v(t)² dt)") (:domain "ℓ² norm" :code ";; the 2-norm of a vector\n(define (l2 v) (sqrt (apply + (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) v))))")) :explanation "Each rung reduces a window of values to their quadratic mean." :meta "'Quadratic mean' is the shape; audio, voltage, and vector norm all use it.") (verb
  :name "big-bang"
  :library "core"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(big-bang [initial-state ...]) → game-id"
  :summary "Initialize and run a game or simulation world, returning a live game ID."
  :explanation "The canonical entry point for physics worlds and game loops. big-bang takes an initial state (often a world structure) and starts a loop that advances by one frame per game/step call. You control the loop lifetime via game/stop; query state with game/state, frame count with game/frame, and liveness with game/running?. This is the verb that enables all physics, collisions, and entity choreography."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define game-id (big-bang (list)))\n(display (game/state game-id))" :note "Start a world with empty state; fetch its state immediately.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (list-range . args)\n  (let ((lo (if (= (length args) 1) 0 (car args)))\n        (hi (if (= (length args) 1) (car args) (cadr args))))\n    (let loop ((i (- hi 1)) (acc (quote ())))\n      (if (< i lo) acc (loop (- i 1) (cons i acc))))))\n(define (run-game initial-entities)\n  (let ((gid (big-bang initial-entities)))\n    (for-each (lambda (_) (game/step gid))\n      (list-range 0 60))\n    (game/state gid)))\n(run-game '())" :note "Step a world 60 times (one second at 60fps); return final state.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (game-loop initial-world)\n  (let ((gid (big-bang initial-world)))\n    (define (tick-step)\n      (if (game/running? gid)\n        (begin (game/step gid)\n               (let ((state (game/state gid)))\n                 (card-emit 'frame-done (list 'frame (game/frame gid) 'entities state))\n                 (if (>= (game/frame gid) 3600)\n                   (game/stop gid)\n                   (register-tick 'game-loop-step (lambda () (tick-step))))))\n        (card-emit 'game-finished state)))\n    (tick-step)\n    gid))\n(game-loop '())" :note "Self-scheduling loop via register-tick; emit frame events; stop at a frame limit.")
  )
  :caveats ("big-bang starts the loop immediately; there is no deferred initialization." "Game state is mutable via game/step; any state you pass in is not copied."   :drawbacks ("No automatic frame limiting or time-delta calculation; you must manage loop frequency." "Stepping a stopped game (game/running? returns #f) is a no-op; no error is raised." (verb
  :name "camera-pan"
  :library "core"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(camera-pan dx [ms]) -> unspecified"
  :summary "Nudge the viewport horizontally by dx world units over an optional duration."
  :explanation "The camera's view center is shifted left (negative dx) or right (positive dx) over ms milliseconds (default 300). This is a relative pan: the world point under the view center moves, but the zoom and vertical position stay fixed. Positive dx reveals content to the right; negative reveals content to the left. The duration controls the smoothness of the animation."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(camera-pan 50)" :note "Shift the view 50 world units to the right, taking the default 300ms.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(camera-pan -100 500)" :note "Pan left by 100 units over half a second; useful when revealing an off-screen obstacle.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(begin\n  (camera-pan 200 400)\n  (after 450 (lambda () (camera-pan -200 400))))" :note "Pan right, wait for the animation to settle, then pan back—creates a smooth scout-and-return choreography.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(camera-pan 50 0)" :note "Shift the camera 50 units to the right without changing zoom.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(on-key\n  (lambda (k)\n    (cond ((eq? k 'left)  (camera-pan -20 0))\n          ((eq? k 'right) (camera-pan 20 0))\n          ((eq? k 'up)    (camera-pan 0 -20))\n          ((eq? k 'down)  (camera-pan 0 20)))))" :note "Arrow keys nudge the camera around. (verb
  :name "camera-state"
  :library "core"
  :kind "rd"
  :signature "(camera-state) -> {'x': number, 'y': number, 'k': number}"
  :summary "Return a dict containing the camera's current position (x, y) and zoom scale (k)."
  :explanation "The viewport is defined by three parameters: x (world x-coordinate at screen center), y (world y-coordinate at screen center), and k (zoom scale, world units per pixel). camera-state is a pure read that returns all three as a dict with keys 'x', 'y', 'k'. This is the foundational query for any camera reasoning: you use camera-state to check where you are before deciding where to pan, or to restore a saved state. Unlike camera-x, camera-y, or camera-scale (which return individual values), camera-state gives you the complete snapshot in one call."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((state (camera-state)))\n  (display (list 'camera-at (hash-ref state 'x) (hash-ref state 'y))))" :note "Query the camera position and print it; the state is a single snapshot.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (save-camera)\n  (let ((s (camera-state)))\n    (list (hash-ref s 'x) (hash-ref s 'y) (hash-ref s 'k))))\n(define (restore-camera state)\n  (camera-set! (car state) (cadr state) (caddr state) 200))\n(define saved (save-camera))\n; ... do other things ...\n(restore-camera saved)" :note "Snapshot the camera state as a list, do some exploration, then restore it with camera-set!.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define camera-history '())\n(on-frame (lambda ()\n  (let ((now (camera-state)))\n    (if (> (length camera-history) 60)\n      (set! camera-history (cdr camera-history)))\n    (set! camera-history (append camera-history (list now))))))\n(define (smooth-rewind n-frames)\n  (if (>= n-frames (length camera-history))\n    'not-enough-history\n    (let ((old (list-ref camera-history (- (length camera-history) n-frames 1))))\n      (camera-set! (hash-ref old 'x) (hash-ref old 'y) (hash-ref old 'k) 300))))" :note "Record camera history on every frame, then implement a 'rewind camera' command by restoring a past state.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(display (camera-state))" :note "Peek at where the camera is and how far it's zoomed.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define saved (camera-state))\n(camera-fit-all)\n(wait 1000)\n(camera-set! (car saved) (cadr saved) (caddr saved))" :note "Save the current view, take a wide-angle look for a second, then restore it.")
  )
  :caveats ("The returned dict is a snapshot at the moment of the call; if the camera is animating, the dict reflects the mid-animation state, not the final destination." "If no viewport is mounted (e.g., during early setup before rendering begins), getCamera may return a default state (e.g., 0, 0, 1); always guard if uncertain." (verb

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(camera-zoom-to 1.5)" :note "Zoom in to 1.5× magnification over the default 200ms.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((current-scale (camera-scale)))\n  (if (< current-scale 1.0)\n      (camera-zoom-to 1.0 300)\n      (camera-zoom-to 0.5 300)))" :note "Toggle between overview (0.5×) and normal (1.0×) zoom over 300ms.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define screen-width (lambda args (list \"screen-width\" args)))\n(define screen-height (lambda args (list \"screen-height\" args)))\n(define (zoom-to-fit-cards)\n  (let ((all-cards (card-list)))\n    (if (null? all-cards)\n        (camera-zoom-to 1.0 250)\n        (begin\n          (camera-zoom-to 0.6 500)\n          (camera-pan-to (/ (screen-width) 2) (/ (screen-height) 2) 500)))))\n(zoom-to-fit-cards)" :note "Zoom out to 0.6× and pan to center before listing all cards — a 500ms reveal sequence.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(camera-zoom-to 3)" :note "Zoom in to 3x. The scene fills more of the screen.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(camera-zoom-to 0.5 600)" :note "Zoom out to half-size over 600 ms for a slow reveal.")

(verb
  :name "grid-step"
  :library "core"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(grid-step rule-fn) -> number"
  :summary "Advance the CA simulation by one generation using the given rule function."
  :explanation "Applies rule-fn to every cell in the grid to compute the next generation. The rule function has signature (rule-fn alive? n) → boolean, where alive? is #t if the cell is currently state 1, and n is the live neighbor count (0–8). The rule returns #t to keep the cell alive in the next generation, #f to kill it. All updates are simultaneous (no glitching). Returns the number of cells that were born (transitioned from dead to alive) this generation. Maintains grid-live-count and grid-step-count as side effects."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(grid-init 64 64)\n(grid-cell-set! 32 32 #t)\n(grid-cell-set! 32 33 #t)\n(grid-cell-set! 33 33 #t)\n(let ((births (grid-step rule-conway)))\n  (display (list \"Generation 1:\" births \"births\")))" :note "Seed a simple pattern (a blinker's start state), step once, and report births.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (step-n-times n rule)\n  (let loop ((gen 0))\n    (if (< gen n)\n      (begin\n        (let ((births (grid-step rule))\n              (live (grid-live-count)))\n          (display (list \"Gen\" gen \": births =\" births \", live =\" live)))\n        (loop (+ gen 1))))))\n(step-n-times 10 rule-conway)" :note "Run for N generations, logging births and population each step.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (evolve-until-stable rule max-gens)\n  (let loop ((gen 0) (prev-count -1))\n    (if (>= gen max-gens)\n      (display (list \"Reached max generations:\" gen))\n      (let ((live (grid-live-count)))\n        (if (= live prev-count)\n          (display (list \"Stabilized at generation\" gen \"with\" live \"live cells\"))\n          (begin\n            (grid-step rule)\n            (loop (+ gen 1) live)))))))\n(evolve-until-stable rule-conway 500)" :note "Detect convergence: stop when population stops changing (fixed point or cycle of period 1).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(grid-step)" :note "Run one tick of Conway's Life. Every cell decides who lives and who dies.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(on-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (grid-step)))" :note "Advance the world one Life step per animation frame — an endless cellular movie.")
  )

  :name "measure-content"
  :library "core"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(measure-content id) -> a-list | 'error"
  :summary "Measure the width and height of a card's content in pixels; return ((w pixels) (h pixels))."
  :explanation "Cards have visual content (text, shapes, sprites) that occupies space. This verb queries the renderer to determine the bounding box of a card's canvas content and returns the width and height as an association list.   :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((dims (measure-content 'my-card)))\n  (display dims))" :note "Retrieve and display the dimensions of 'my-card'; output is ((w 123) (h 45)) or similar.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (fit-in-viewport id max-width)\n  (let ((dims (measure-content id)))\n    (let ((w (cadr (assoc 'w dims))))\n      (if (> w max-width) 'too-wide 'fits))))\n(fit-in-viewport 'content-card 300)" :note "Extract width from the result, compare to a viewport limit, and decide whether to scale or reflow.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (auto-scale-content id target-aspect-ratio)\n  (let ((dims (measure-content id)))\n    (let ((w (cadr (assoc 'w dims)))\n          (h (cadr (assoc 'h dims))))\n      (let ((current-ratio (/ w (max h 1))))\n        (cond ((< current-ratio target-aspect-ratio) (list 'action 'stretch-width))\n              ((> current-ratio target-aspect-ratio) (list 'action 'stretch-height))\n              (else (list 'action 'no-change)))))))\n(auto-scale-content 'canvas-card 1.5)" :note "Use both width and height to compute aspect ratio and decide on a scaling strategy.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(display (measure-content \"hello\"))" :note "How wide and tall would this string be if drawn?")

  )

(verb
  :name "stop-when"
  :library "core"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(stop-when predicate) -> clause"
  :summary "Declare a loop-termination condition: the loop exits when the predicate returns true."
  :explanation "Instead of calling `stop` imperatively inside a callback, `stop-when` lets you declare termination declaratively as a clause in `big-bang`. You provide a predicate function that receives the current state; if it returns true, the loop exits after that frame. This is cleaner than embedding stop in on-tick, because it separates the exit logic from the state update logic. It is the preferred way to end a loop based on a state condition."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define initial (lambda args (list \"initial\" args)))\n(big-bang\n  (initial 10)\n  (on-tick (lambda (s) (- s 1)))\n  (stop-when (lambda (s) (= s 0))))" :note "Count down from 10; exit when state reaches 0.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define initial (lambda args (list \"initial\" args)))\n(big-bang\n  (initial (list 'hero (list 100 100) 100 #t))\n  (on-tick (lambda (state)\n    (let* ((pos (cadr state)) (hp (list-ref state 2)))\n      (if (> (random-int 100) 80) ; take damage 20% of time\n        (list (car state) pos (- hp 1) #t)\n        state))))\n  (stop-when (lambda (state) (<= (list-ref state 2) 0))))" :note "Simulate combat damage; exit when HP reaches 0. No explicit (stop) call needed.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define initial (lambda args (list \"initial\" args)))\n(define game-start-state (lambda args (list \"game-start-state\" args)))\n(define game-loop-step 'game-loop-step)\n(define render-frame 'render-frame)\n(define (all-objectives-met state)\n  (and (>= (state-cash state) 1000)\n       (>= (state-reputation state) 50)\n       (null? (state-enemies state))))\n(big-bang\n  (initial (game-start-state))\n  (on-tick game-loop-step)\n  (on-frame render-frame)\n  (stop-when all-objectives-met))" :note "Compose multiple conditions (cash, reputation, enemies cleared) into a single exit check.")
  )
  :caveats ("The predicate is called every frame; if it is expensive, consider caching intermediate results in the state." "If the predicate throws, the exception bubbles to the studio (loop halts, error is surfaced)." "Multiple stop-when clauses are all evaluated; the loop exits on the first one that returns true.")
  :drawbacks ("Declarative only: you cannot perform side effects (logging, state saving) when exiting without wrapping the predicate." "Predicate is called AFTER the state is updated; you cannot prevent an update, only trigger exit after it completes." "If you need to exit with a custom result or message, use escalate instead (which throws a catchable error).")
  :usecases ("Game-over conditions: exit when player HP ≤ 0 or when objective is completed." "Timeout: exit when (game/frame) exceeds a limit." "State-based termination: exit when a flag is set or a counter reaches a goal.")

(:eng "Operator log: 'stop-when installed'." :math "Termination predicate on state." :cs "Predicate installed on the loop."))

(verb
  :name "wait"
  :library "core"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(wait event [deadline-ms]) -> descriptor"
  :summary "Pause state execution until a named event fires or an optional deadline expires."
  :explanation "wait returns a control descriptor that tells the cart runtime to suspend the current state and resume it only when event fires (from on-key, on-frame, on-tick, or external listeners). If deadline-ms is provided, the wait times out and resumes with an interruption after that duration. wait is the primary way to implement non-blocking I/O and event-driven choreography in cart state machines. Unlike blocking sleep, wait keeps the surface responsive."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (listen-for-click ctx)\n  (wait 'click-detected))" :note "Suspend execution until an event named 'click-detected' fires; simple blocking-free pause.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (fetch-with-timeout ctx)\n  (act 'api/fetch (list 'https://example.com/data) 'got-data))\n\n(define (got-data ctx)\n  (let ((result (ctx-result ctx)))\n    (if (null? result)\n      (next 'retry (wait 'retry-signal 5000))\n      (next 'done ctx))))" :note "Fetch data, and if empty, wait up to 5 seconds for a 'retry-signal' event; if it doesn't arrive, timeout and move to retry state.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (interactive-choreography ctx)\n  (define (step-1 ctx)\n    (act 'part/step (list 'walk) 'step-done))\n  (define (step-2 ctx)\n    (wait 'user-input 3000))\n  (define (on-input ctx)\n    (let ((input (ctx-result ctx)))\n      (if (eq? input 'skip) (next 'idle ctx)\n        (next 'step-3 ctx))))\n  (next 'step-2 (step-1 ctx)))" :note "Choreography state machine: after a part motion, wait for user input with a 3-second timeout; if input arrives, handle it; if timeout, skip to idle.")
  )
  :caveats ("wait suspends the current state; execution does not resume until the event fires or the deadline expires." "The event name must match exactly (case-sensitive, as a symbol); typos result in indefinite wait." "If the deadline is null or omitted, the wait never times out; use a timeout to prevent indefinite hangs." "When a deadline expires, the state resumes with an interruption, not a normal result; check ctx-result for nil or the interruption marker.")
  :drawbacks ("Each wait adds a listener registration; excessive wait calls can slow down the event dispatcher." "Deadline is not a \"soft\" timeout; if the event fires within the deadline window, it may still resume slightly before deadline expiry due to frame latency." "No way to cancel a pending wait from outside the state machine; the state must complete or timeout.")
  :usecases ("Interactive storytelling: wait for user input (button press, key) before advancing narrative." "Choreography choreography: pause dance moves until music reaches a specific beat." "API polling with timeout: fetch data and retry only if the user requests it within a time window.")

(verb
  :name "with-seed"
  :library "core"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(with-seed n) -> clause"
  :summary "Wrap a random-number generator with a fixed seed for reproducible sequences."
  :explanation "Randomness in Motoi (e.g., `random`, `random-pick`) is seeded by the frame and input state by default, making playback non-deterministic for replay or test. `with-seed` takes a numeric seed and returns a clause (a thunk or lambda) that, when invoked, runs a deterministic RNG branch. This is a pure function: it does not mutate world state, only sets up the seeded generator for later use. Use it when you need identical random outcomes every time (procedural generation, test fixtures, replay validation)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define seeded-roll (with-seed 42))\n(seeded-roll (random 100))" :note "Every call to `seeded-roll` will return the same random number.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (spawn-enemies n seed)\n  (let ((gen (with-seed seed)))\n    (gen (map (lambda (i) (list i (random 800))) (range 0 n)))))" :note "Generate n enemy positions deterministically; identical seed → identical layout every time.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (test-procedural-level seed)\n  (let ((layout ((with-seed seed) (generate-level-tiles 10 10))))\n    (and (equal? layout (expected-layout)) #t)))" :note "Use seeded generation in a test to verify the level generator is stable across runs.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(with-seed 42\n  (display (random-int 10)))" :note "Freeze the random generator to seed 42 so you get the same number every time.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(with-seed 7\n  (list (random-int 100) (random-int 100) (random-int 100)))" :note "Deterministic three-number sequence. Good for reproducible tests.")
  )
  :caveats ("The seed must be numeric (integer or float); non-numeric seeds will error." "The returned clause is a function; you must call it to activate the seeded RNG." "Nesting or chaining multiple `with-seed` calls may have undefined behavior—use one seed per scope." "Seed scope is thread-local or frame-local; cannot be shared across parallel computations.")
  :drawbacks ("Adds a small closure overhead per use; not suitable for tight inner loops (use `random-range` directly if seeding is not needed)." "Once seeded, the sequence is fixed; no way to 'reshuffle' mid-sequence without re-seeding." "If the RNG algorithm changes in a new Motoi version, old seeds may produce different sequences (breaking replay).")
  :usecases ("Procedural level/world generation with fixed layout (e.g., seed 1 always builds the same dungeon)." "Test fixtures: ensure random behavior is reproducible during unit tests." (verb
  :name "escalate"
  :library "core"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(escalate condition-name . args) -> raises"
  :summary "Bubble a named condition upward past the current handler; a generic control-flow primitive for early-exit, deferred handling, and structured error control."
  :explanation "`escalate` raises a named condition. Unlike `error`, whose message is a string and whose type is always 'error, escalate takes a SYMBOL as its first argument and uses it as the raised condition's type. Downstream handlers (installed via with-exception-handler or R7RS guard) match on the type via error-object-type. Any extra args are captured as irritants and surfaced via error-object-irritants. Composes with the full exception machinery: escalate raises, guard/with-exception-handler catches. Use it to distinguish 'expected' failure paths (timeout, resource-exhausted, user-cancelled) from unexpected 'error' errors, or to bubble a signal out of a deeply nested computation without threading state through every return."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(escalate 'timeout)" :note "Bubble a bare 'timeout condition upward. Any enclosing guard or with-exception-handler receives it and can dispatch on the type 'timeout.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (fetch-or-give-up n)\n  (if (> n 5)\n      (escalate 'retry-exhausted n)\n      (list 'ok n)))\n(with-exception-handler\n  (lambda (e) (list 'caught (error-object-type e) (error-object-irritants e)))\n  (lambda () (fetch-or-give-up 6)))" :note "escalate carries structured detail (the exhausted count) as irritants; the handler can log or branch on the type and detail.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (run-plan steps)\n  (let loop ((rest steps) (done '()))\n    (cond ((null? rest) (reverse done))\n          (else (let ((step (car rest)))\n                  (guard (e ((eq? (error-object-type e) 'skip)\n                             (loop (cdr rest) done))\n                            ((eq? (error-object-type e) 'abort)\n                             (escalate 'plan-aborted (reverse done))))\n                    (loop (cdr rest) (cons (step) done))))))))\n(run-plan (list\n  (lambda () 'first)\n  (lambda () (escalate 'skip))\n  (lambda () 'third)))" :note "A plan runner that treats 'skip as continue, 'abort as re-escalate with accumulated context. escalate names each control path so the handler can dispatch cleanly without a shared boolean flag.")
  )
  :caveats ("The condition name should be a symbol (a Sym); strings work but lose the eq? semantics that make handler dispatch idiomatic." "escalate is NON-CONTINUABLE — control does not return to the escalate site. If you need a continuable raise, use raise-continuable." "Args after the condition name become irritants; they are preserved verbatim, so passing a large object here holds a reference to it until the handler runs." "The raised error's message is 'escalate: <name>' — handlers that read error-object-message get that string; the structured detail lives in the irritants list.")
  :drawbacks ("No stack trace beyond what JS engines already provide; escalate does not capture caller context." "Handlers must be installed BEFORE the call site is reached; escalate does not implicitly install a handler." "The condition name is dispatched by eq? on the type; typos in either the escalate site or the handler cause silent mis-matches (the error object surfaces but no handler branch fires).")
  :usecases ("Structured early-exit from a deep recursion when a pre-condition fails." "Distinguishing expected-failure control paths (timeout, cancelled, retry-exhausted) from bugs, so handlers can branch cleanly." "Composing with guard to build a plan/step runner where each step can 'skip, 'abort, or return normally." "Signalling from a cart worker to its driver that a state transition is required.")
  :related ("error" "raise" "raise-continuable" "with-exception-handler" "guard" "error-object-type" "error-object-irritants")
  :learn (:concept "Named conditions for control flow: raising a value the handler can dispatch on, without wrapping every function in a monadic Result." :prerequisites ("with-exception-handler" "quote" "symbols") :progression "Learn escalate as the 'named raise'; then pair it with guard for typed handlers; then compose with a plan-runner to see how multiple named conditions carve up control flow cleanly.")
  :row-2-audit ((:problem "A retry loop has exhausted its budget; the operator wants to bubble a typed condition upward for structured handling." :program "(define (fetch n)\n  (if (> n 5)\n      (escalate 'retry-exhausted n)\n      (list 'ok n)))\n(with-exception-handler\n  (lambda (e) (list 'caught (error-object-type e)))\n  (lambda () (fetch 6)))" :explanation "escalate raises a symbol-typed condition with irritants; the handler dispatches by type." :meta "error is generic; raise doesn't imply structure. escalate is the correct choice for STRUCTURED, TYPED raises.") (:eng "Operator log: 'escalate retry-exhausted 6'." :math "Named exception raise." :cs "Non-continuable typed raise."))
