(verb
  :name "ai/align"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(ai/align id tag radius [force]) -> null"
  :summary "Apply boid rule 2: steer an entity toward the average heading of tagged neighbors within a radius."
  :explanation "Ai/align is a steering verb that reads the velocities of all entities within radius that share a tag, computes the average heading, and applies a steering force to the entity to match that heading. It implements flocking behavior. The optional force parameter caps the steering magnitude; if omitted, a default is used. The verb mutates the entity's velocity directly (no return value). Use in a per-frame or per-entity loop to create coherent group motion."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ai/align 'fish-1 'school 50)" :note "Steer fish-1 toward the average heading of all entities tagged 'school within radius 50.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (update-flock ctx)\n  (for-each (lambda (id) (ai/align id 'boid 100 2.0)) (ctx-get 'boid-ids ctx))\n  (next 'flock-moving ctx))" :note "Apply alignment to all boid IDs in context, with a force cap of 2.0; then advance the state.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (choreograph-dance ctx)\n  (let ((formation (ctx-get 'formation ctx)) (radius (if (eq? formation 'tight) 30 100)))\n    (for-each\n      (lambda (dancer-id)\n        (ai/align dancer-id 'dancer radius 1.5)\n        (ai/cohere dancer-id 'dancer radius 1.0)\n        (ai/separate dancer-id 'dancer 20 2.0))\n      (ctx-get 'dancer-ids ctx))\n    (next 'dancing ctx)))" :note "Combine alignment, cohesion, and separation for coordinated group choreography; radius and force scale with formation tightness.")
  )
  :caveats ("Entity id and tag must exist; if the entity is not found, the verb silently fails." "Neighbors are tagged entities within the specified radius; distance is Euclidean from the entity's current position." "Force parameter is optional; omitting it uses a default (tune via ai/max-force!)." "Alignment is one-way: the entity is steered toward the average heading, but neighbors are not moved.")
  :drawbacks ("No return value; cannot detect if steering was applied or if neighbors were found." "Repeated calls to ai/align without separation or cohesion rules can cause entities to overlap." "Performance degrades quadratically with entity count (each entity scans all others for neighbors)." "Steering is greedy: entities always try to match the flock's heading, which can create unrealistic jerky motion if the flock itself is turning sharply.")
  :usecases ("Flocking birds, fish, or crowds that move cohesively." "Coordinated group behaviors in games or simulations." "Choreographed dances or synchronized movement of NPCs." "Emergent swarm patterns in visual art or procedural animation.")
  :related ("ai/cohere" "ai/separate" "ai/flock" "ai/max-force!" "ai/seek" "ai/arrive")
  :learn (:concept "Boid rule 2: match the flock's average heading. Ai/align is one of three rules; combine with cohere and separate for full flocking." :prerequisites ("entity/vel" "entity/pos" "for-each" "lambda") :progression "Start with ai/align alone to see drift-to-average-heading behavior; add ai/cohere to pull toward group center; add ai/separate to prevent overlap. Use ai/flock for all three rules combined.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A dozen fish should swim as a school. The frame log shows they drift in random directions and never coalesce. Investigation reveals the operator applied only ai/seek to a common target — every fish converges on the point but does not align its heading with its neighbors, so they arrive as a cloud instead of a school."
     :program "(define (school-step ids)\n  (for-each (lambda (id) (ai/align id 'fish 60 2.0)) ids))\n(school-step (list 'f1 'f2 'f3 'f4))"
     :explanation "The fix names the missing constraint: heading agreement. ai/align adds a steering pull toward the average heading of tagged neighbors. Applied per-frame per-fish, headings converge and the cloud becomes a school. No target point is required — the group defines its own direction from local information."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is ai/seek. seek pulls toward a point, not toward a direction — a cloud of seekers arrives at the same place but with random headings. align is direction-only. Under audit, the log shows positions clustering while headings remain unclustered, which is the fingerprint of using seek where align was needed.")
    (:eng "Operator symptom is 'cloud not school'. Adding align sharpens the heading distribution; success is measured as heading-variance dropping into a narrow band frame over frame."
     :math "Alignment is convergence of a directional random variable toward its neighborhood mean. In the limit of infinite density and small force, headings converge to a common vector."
     :cs "The pattern is local-averaging: no central controller, each agent samples its own neighborhood and adjusts. This is the substrate of consensus algorithms in distributed systems."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is local-consensus-toward-a-mean: each element samples its neighbors and nudges toward their average value."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi align" :code "(ai/align 'fish-1 'school 50)")
       (:domain "gossip protocol node adopting neighbor state" :code "(define (gossip-step state neighbors)\n  (let ((avg (/ (apply + neighbors) (length neighbors))))\n    (/ (+ state avg) 2)))\n(display (gossip-step 5 '(3 7 6 4)))")
       (:domain "moving average of a signal" :code "(define (moving-avg xs)\n  (/ (apply + xs) (length xs)))\n(display (moving-avg '(1 2 3 4 5)))"))
     :explanation "The align rung shows fish converging on group heading. The gossip rung shows a node blending its state with neighbors' — the classic distributed-consensus step. The moving-average rung shows the pure math: averaging as a smoothing operation. Same shape: reduce local disagreement by moving toward the neighborhood mean."
     :meta "The shape transfers because local-averaging is the basis of any system where global order emerges from local sampling — flocks, gossip networks, cellular automata, opinion dynamics. No central coordinator required.")
    (:eng "Local-averaging protocols scale gracefully; there is no bottleneck. The engineering price is bandwidth (neighbor samples) and time-to-converge (iterations)."
     :math "The averaging operator is linear and contractive in a bounded space, so iterates converge to the neighborhood mean by the Banach fixed-point theorem."
     :cs "Compare centralized consensus (Paxos-style, O(n) messages to a coordinator) with decentralized consensus (gossip, O(log n) rounds to convergence). Align is the game-AI analog of gossip."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "If all entities in a group already share a heading, ai/align applied to any of them produces no net change (heading is a fixed point of the alignment operation on the aligned state)."
     :program "(define (aligned-mean-diff group-heading self-heading)\n  (- group-heading self-heading))\n(define aligned-state 90)\n(define group-heading 90)\n(display (= 0 (aligned-mean-diff group-heading aligned-state)))"
     :invariant "∀ group G, self s ∈ G. avg-heading(G) = heading(s) ⇒ align-step(s, G) = s (fixed point)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is fixed-point of an averaging operator: when the input equals the current mean, the update is zero. Falsification would be an alignment that drifted even at consensus — every step would move a converged group away from its own agreement, which is instability. It does not. Cite book-of-math (calculus and stat chapters) for fixed-point analysis. This is why align is stable: consensus is the attractor.")
    (:eng "Fixed-point behavior at consensus is what makes flocks stable once they form. Without this, a converged flock would jitter apart under its own steering."
     :math "The heading update Δh = k · (mean − self); when mean = self, Δh = 0. The unique zero of a linear map with a nonzero slope is the point where the two arguments coincide."
     :cs "Consensus is an attracting fixed point of the gossip operator; the same math underpins load-balancing algorithms and neural network training's stationary points."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "ai/align pulls an entity's heading toward the neighborhood mean."
     :composition "(define (flock-behavior ids)\n  (for-each\n    (lambda (id)\n      (ai/separate id 'boid 20 2.0)\n      (ai/align    id 'boid 50 1.5)\n      (ai/cohere   id 'boid 80 1.0))\n    ids))\n(flock-behavior (list 'b1 'b2 'b3))"
     :emergent "Emergent flocking. Three simple local rules (avoid crowding, match heading, steer toward center) compose to produce the school/flock behavior that no single rule expresses alone."
     :meta "The family is 'emergent-behavior-from-local-rules' — the same family as Conway's Game of Life, ant-trail formation, and market prices from individual bids. Cross-ref book-of-composition ch 6 (Sprite Grid) for how many small sprites compose into a scene, and book-of-composition ch 16 (Composing Games) for the general emergence-from-simple-rules pattern.")
    (:eng "Named flocking recipes are how designers get realistic swarms with three lines instead of a swarm-controller subsystem."
     :math "The emergent motion is a superposition of three vector fields (separation, alignment, cohesion); the sum is a stable dynamical system with the flock as attractor."
     :cs "Boids are the canonical example of decentralized emergent behavior in game AI; the CS interest is that three O(k) neighborhood queries produce O(1)-controller flocks.")))

(verb
  :name "ai/arrive"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(ai/arrive id tx ty [slow] [force]) → void"
  :summary "Steer an entity toward a target point, decelerating smoothly as it approaches within a slow-radius."
  :explanation "Arrive is a steering behavior that combines seeking (moving toward a target) with smooth deceleration. When the entity is far from the target, it accelerates at full force. As it enters the slow-radius zone, it reduces speed proportionally to distance, arriving gently rather than overshooting. This is essential for animations, patrol endpoints, and any motion that needs to look natural. Unlike a hard seek, arrive prevents jitter and overshoot near the goal."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define my-entity 'my-entity)\n(ai/arrive my-entity 100 200)" :note "Entity steers toward point (100, 200) with default slow-radius and force.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define my-entity 'my-entity)\n(let ((target-x 150) (target-y 75))\n  (ai/arrive my-entity target-x target-y 30))" :note "Provide explicit slow-radius (30 pixels); entity decelerates smoothly in that zone.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (patrol-waypoint entity waypoint-list waypoint-idx)\n  (let ((wp (list-ref waypoint-list waypoint-idx))\n        (wx (car wp))\n        (wy (cadr wp)))\n    (ai/arrive entity wx wy 40 8.0)\n    (if (< (entity/distance entity wx wy) 10)\n        (+ waypoint-idx 1)\n        waypoint-idx)))" :note "Cycle through patrol points; arrive at each with custom slow-radius and force, advance when close enough.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ai/arrive 'hero 100 100)" :note "Steer the hero to (100, 100). Slows down as it gets close so it doesn't overshoot.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(on-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (ai/arrive 'hero 200 50 30 4)))" :note "Arrive with a 30-unit slow radius and a steering force of 4. Feels smooth.")
  )
  :caveats ("Requires the entity to exist and have velocity/acceleration properties." "slow-radius defaults to ~30 if omitted; too large causes early braking, too small causes overshoot." "Force is capped by entity's max-force setting; if max-force is very low, arrive will be sluggish." "Does not account for obstacles; combine with collision avoidance for realistic steering.")
  :drawbacks ("Not a pathfinding algorithm; will move in straight lines toward the target even if blocked." "Smooth deceleration can feel slow compared to instant-stop; tune slow-radius per use case." "Multiple calls per frame stack; only call once per entity per tick.")
  :usecases ("NPC ending a patrol at a waypoint without jarring stop." "Character smooth-landing at a rest position after flight." "Dialogue trigger zones where entities approach and settle." "Smooth camera panning to a focus point.")
  :related ("ai/seek" "ai/pursue" "ai/evade" "ai/wander" "entity/set-vel!" "entity/accel!")
  :learn (:concept "Distance-aware deceleration in steering; how to combine seek with smooth arrival." :prerequisites ("entity/pos" "entity/distance" "entity/accel!") :progression "Learn ai/pursue next to predict a moving target; then ai/flock to combine multiple steering rules.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "NPC patrols to a rest point and overshoots every time, oscillating around the target for 5 frames before settling. Player sees a twitchy character. Log shows position swinging past target then back."
     :program "(define (goto-rest npc rx ry)\n  (ai/arrive npc rx ry 25 3.0))\n(goto-rest 'guard 200 200)"
     :explanation "The overshoot is caused by ai/seek's constant force — approaching fast, the entity blows past the target before force reverses. ai/arrive replaces the constant force with distance-scaled deceleration inside a slow-radius; the character stops smoothly. One verb-swap eliminates the oscillation."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is ai/seek. seek is a constant-magnitude pull; near the target it produces overshoot. arrive gates the pull magnitude by distance so approach velocity is proportional to remaining distance. Under audit, seek+overshoot appears as a sinusoidal position log; arrive appears as a smooth exponential decay to zero.")
    (:eng "Symptom is jittery arrival; the fix is distance-aware braking. Success is a monotone-decreasing distance-to-target."
     :math "Arrive imposes velocity(d) = k·d inside slow-radius, so velocity → 0 as d → 0. Outside slow-radius it degenerates to seek."
     :cs "The CS pattern is smooth-shutdown: a controller that reduces amplitude as the goal is approached, analogous to TCP slow-start's inverse."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is proportional-braking-near-goal: control effort scales with remaining distance so overshoot is impossible in the limit."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi arrive" :code "(ai/arrive 'hero 200 200 30 4)")
       (:domain "elevator stopping at floor" :code "(define (elevator-speed distance)\n  (if (< distance 1.0) 0.0 (* 0.1 distance)))\n(display (elevator-speed 10.0))\n(newline)\n(display (elevator-speed 1.0))\n(newline)\n(display (elevator-speed 0.5))")
       (:domain "exponential decay to zero" :code "(define (decay v0 dt tau)\n  (* v0 (expt 2.71828 (- (/ dt tau)))))\n(display (decay 10.0 0 1.0))\n(newline)\n(display (decay 10.0 5.0 1.0))"))
     :explanation "arrive tapers to zero at the target. The elevator tapers to zero at the floor. Exponential decay tapers to zero over time. Same shape: control effort is a monotone function of remaining distance/time to goal."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in all three cases OVERSHOOT is unacceptable and the fix is proportional control. A binary bang-bang controller would work for coarse cases; proportional is what buys smoothness.")
    (:eng "Proportional braking is the entry-point to PID control; the P term alone often suffices for game AI without the complexity of I and D."
     :math "The velocity profile v(d) = min(v_max, k·d) is a piecewise linear ramp; integrating gives smooth position trajectories with no ringing."
     :cs "This is the servo-loop pattern with a P-only controller. Adding I would eliminate steady-state error at cost of overshoot; adding D would damp oscillation. Arrive is deliberately P-only for simplicity."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "Inside the slow-radius, ai/arrive's applied force magnitude monotonically decreases as distance decreases (proportional braking)."
     :program "(define (arrive-force d slow-radius max-force)\n  (if (>= d slow-radius) max-force\n      (* max-force (/ d slow-radius))))\n(define f10 (arrive-force 10 30 8))\n(define f5  (arrive-force 5 30 8))\n(define f1  (arrive-force 1 30 8))\n(display (> f10 f5))\n(newline)\n(display (> f5 f1))"
     :invariant "∀ d1 < d2 < slow-radius. force(d1) < force(d2) (strict monotonicity inside slow-radius)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is monotone control: smaller error yields smaller correction. Falsification would be a distance where force increased as distance decreased — a positive-feedback loop and instability. It does not. Cite book-of-math (functions and calc chapters) for monotonicity theory and book-of-code ch 5 for controller stability.")
    (:eng "Monotone braking is what guarantees no overshoot in the ideal limit and small overshoot in the finite-timestep case."
     :math "The force function f(d) = k·d is strictly monotone on d ∈ [0, R]. Its integral gives a bounded velocity profile."
     :cs "Monotonicity is the safety property; the alternative is chatter — controllers that oscillate near the setpoint."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "ai/arrive combines directional pull with proportional braking."
     :composition "(define (patrol path npc idx)\n  (let ((wp (list-ref path idx)))\n    (ai/arrive npc (car wp) (cadr wp) 20 4.0)\n    (if (< (entity/distance npc (car wp) (cadr wp)) 5)\n      (modulo (+ idx 1) (length path))\n      idx)))\n(patrol (list (list 100 100) (list 200 100) (list 200 200)) 'guard 0)"
     :emergent "A waypoint patrol. arrive + a threshold check + index advance produces a character that walks between named points and pauses cleanly at each."
     :meta "The family is 'waypoint-navigation' — the same family as GPS turn-by-turn, robot floor-cleaners doing lawnmower patterns, or a movie camera on rails. Cross-ref book-of-composition ch 8 (Timeline) for the general pattern of stepping through named checkpoints, and book-of-motion for arrive's underlying trajectory shaping.")
    (:eng "Named patrol routes are the atomic unit of NPC choreography; changing a patrol is editing a list, not code."
     :math "The chain is a discrete walk on a graph whose nodes are waypoints; arrive continuously interpolates the walk on the edges."
     :cs "This is the interpreter-of-a-path-DSL pattern: the path is data, arrive+threshold is the evaluator.")))

(verb
  :name "ai/bb-del!"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(ai/bb-del! id key) → #t/#f"
  :summary "Remove a key-value pair from an entity's decision blackboard, returning #t if the key existed."
  :explanation "Every entity has a mutable blackboard—a key-value store for AI state, memory, and decisions. bb-del! removes an entry. It returns #t if the key was found and deleted, #f if the key did not exist. This is the cleanup half of the blackboard lifecycle: you set state with bb-set!, read it with bb-get, check presence with bb-has?, and forget it with bb-del!. Use bb-del! when an entity's decision phase has passed and you want to avoid stale data on the next tick."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define entity-42 'entity-42)\n(ai/bb-del! entity-42 'patrol-target)" :note "Delete the patrol-target key from entity-42's memory.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define entity-42 'entity-42)\n(let ((was-set (ai/bb-has? entity-42 'alert-level)))\n  (when was-set\n    (ai/bb-del! entity-42 'alert-level)))" :note "Check before delete; only remove if the key exists.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (reset-ai-state entity)\n  (for-each (lambda (key)\n              (ai/bb-del! entity key))\n            '(patrol-target alert-level combat-stance last-seen-pos)))" :note "Batch-clear multiple blackboard keys; useful for resetting NPC state after a combat phase ends.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ai/bb-set! 'hero 'goal 'chest)\n(ai/bb-del! 'hero 'goal)" :note "Store a goal, then forget it. The delete returns #t because the key existed.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(when (ai/bb-has? 'hero 'temp)\n  (ai/bb-del! 'hero 'temp))" :note "Only try to delete a key that's actually there. Defensive tidy-up.")
  )
  :caveats ("Returns #f if the key does not exist; this is not an error, just a no-op." "Does not affect other entities' blackboards." "Deleting a key does not halt any running behavior tree; the tree continues with 'no-key default values on next read." "If you delete a key mid-decision-tree-tick, subsequent reads of that key will return the default instead of crashing.")
  :drawbacks ("Unnecessary if the entity will be despawned anyway; the blackboard is garbage-collected with the entity." "Manual memory management; no automatic expiration. (verb
  :name "ai/bt-action"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(ai/bt-action tag) → behavior-tree node"
  :summary "Create a leaf node in a behavior tree that runs a registered action when ticked."
  :explanation "Behavior trees are structured decision systems. Leaves are the actions and conditions; branches are logic (AND, OR, quorum). A bt-action is a leaf that, when ticked, looks up a registered action handler by tag and executes it. The action is responsible for moving, attacking, or signaling success/failure/running. Actions are separate from the tree structure; you define the tree with pure nodes (bt-action, bt-condition, etc.) and register the actual handlers elsewhere. This separation lets you compose behavior without tightly coupling code."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ai/bt-action 'attack)" :note "Create an action node that will call the 'attack handler when ticked.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(ai/bt-sequence\n  (ai/bt-condition 'has-target?)\n  (ai/bt-action 'pursue)\n  (ai/bt-action 'attack))" :note "Sequence: check condition, then pursue, then attack (all must succeed).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define combat-tree\n  (ai/bt-selector\n    (ai/bt-sequence\n      (ai/bt-condition 'has-target?)\n      (ai/bt-action 'attack))\n    (ai/bt-sequence\n      (ai/bt-condition 'low-health?)\n      (ai/bt-action 'flee))\n    (ai/bt-action 'wander)))" :note "Selector (OR): try attack if target exists; else try flee if low health; else wander. bt-action nodes are leaves in the tree.")
  )
  :caveats ("bt-action creates only the node structure; it does not execute. Execution happens in ai/bt-tick." "Tag must match a registered handler; if the handler does not exist, bt-tick will fail or no-op." "Return value is a pure tree node; the action handlers are separate and must be registered out-of-band." "Actions are responsible for their own side effects (movement, state change); the tree only sequences and gates them.")
  :drawbacks ("Requires a separate registration system for handlers; no inline action code." "Tags are strings/symbols; name collisions can shadow handlers." "No built-in introspection; you cannot query a tree to list all actions it might run.")
  :usecases ("Combat tree: leaf action that calls an 'attack handler." "Patrol behavior: leaf action that calls a 'advance-patrol handler." "Dialogue system: leaf action that calls a 'start-dialogue handler." "Compound decision: many actions gated by conditions in a tree structure.")
  :related ("ai/bt-condition" "ai/bt-sequence" "ai/bt-selector" "ai/bt-tick")
  :learn (:concept "Leaf nodes in a behavior tree that trigger registered actions." :prerequisites ("ai/bt-tick") :progression "Learn ai/bt-condition for decision leaves; then ai/bt-sequence and ai/bt-selector to compose actions and conditions into trees.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A combat tree needs to call 'attack, but 'attack itself is a runtime handler; inlining Scheme code into the tree makes the tree structural definition unreadable and testing hard."
     :program "(define combat-leaf (ai/bt-action 'attack))\n(display combat-leaf)"
     :explanation "bt-action names an action-by-tag; the actual behavior is registered separately. The tree becomes a shape, not a script. Testing the tree structure is decoupled from testing the handlers."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is a lambda embedded directly in the tree. Embedding closures makes the tree opaque and hard to snapshot/serialize. bt-action keeps the tree symbolic.")
    (:eng "Symptom is unreadable trees; fix is symbolic references to handlers. Audit trail: tree structure serializes cleanly."
     :math "The tree is an abstract syntax tree; leaves are named atoms mapped to functions by an external table."
     :cs "The pattern is late-binding of symbols to implementations — same as function-table dispatch or interface implementation."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is symbolic-reference-with-late-binding: a name that stands for a behavior, resolved when executed rather than when written."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi bt-action" :code "(ai/bt-action 'attack)")
       (:domain "shell function referenced before defined" :code "(define (fn-name-only name) (list 'call name 'later))\n(display (fn-name-only 'run-batch))")
       (:domain "symbolic pointer in a lookup table" :code "(define (lookup tab k) (assv k tab))\n(display (lookup '((attack . fire) (heal . cast)) 'attack))"))
     :explanation "bt-action names an action. Shell late-binding refs a fn by name. Lookup ptr resolves at query time. Same shape: separate the naming from the doing."
     :meta "The shape transfers because late-binding is what enables composition without knowing implementations up front.")
    (:eng "Late binding is the substrate for plugins, hot-reloading, and testable trees."
     :math "The tree is a term in a language; the semantics assigns each tag a function."
     :cs "Compare vtable dispatch, closures over names, and open recursion."))

     :invariant "∀ tag t. bt-action(t) ≡ bt-action(t) (structural equality)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is value-typed construction. Falsification would be nodes carrying a hidden id counter making them structurally unequal. bt-action is a pure value. Cite book-of-code ch 4.")
    (:eng "Structural equality lets trees be tested with equal?; hidden state would break tests."

(verb

Like bt-action, it references a tag; when ticked, the condition handler is called and should return success (the condition holds) or failure (the condition does not hold). Conditions gate actions: 'if has-target? then attack' is a sequence of a condition and an action. Conditions are pure queries; they should not mutate state. This lets you build readable, testable decision trees."
  :examples (

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define patrol-tree\n  (ai/bt-selector\n    (ai/bt-sequence\n      (ai/bt-condition 'has-threat?)\n      (ai/bt-action 'flee))\n    (ai/bt-sequence\n      (ai/bt-condition 'waypoint-reached?)\n      (ai/bt-action 'advance-patrol))\n    (ai/bt-action 'patrol-move)))" :note "Selector runs conditions in order: if has-threat? then flee; else if waypoint-reached? then advance; else patrol-move.")

(verb
  :name "ai/bt-force"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(ai/bt-force status child) → behavior-tree node"
  :summary "Create a node that overrides a child's result, forcing it to report a specific status (success, failure, or running)."
  :explanation "In a behavior tree, a child node returns a status: success, failure, or running. bt-force wraps a child and replaces its actual status with a forced one. This is useful for testing (pretend this always succeeds) or for semantics where the child's internal result does not matter—only that it was tried. For example, force-success on a sensory node means 'try it, but mark it as successful regardless'. Use sparingly; excessive forcing masks the actual logic."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ai/bt-force 'success (ai/bt-action 'experiment))" :note "Always report success, even if the 'experiment action fails internally.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(ai/bt-sequence\n  (ai/bt-force 'running (ai/bt-condition 'check-ammo?))\n  (ai/bt-action 'reload))" :note "Force a check to report 'running so reload happens even if the check would normally succeed.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (retry-subtree max-attempts subtree)\n  (define (attempt n)\n    (if (>= n max-attempts)\n        (ai/bt-force 'failure subtree)\n        (let ((status (ai/bt-tick subtree entity-id)))\n          (if (equal? status 'success) status (attempt (+ n 1))))))\n  (attempt 0))" :note "Wrap subtree with forced failure after N attempts to trigger a fallback in a selector.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define always-ok\n  (ai/bt-force 'success 'try-attack))\n(display always-ok)" :note "Force the child to look successful. Useful when you want the parent tree to keep going.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define keep-trying\n  (ai/bt-force 'running 'search))\n(display keep-trying)" :note "Pin a slow action in running state so higher-level logic knows it's still busy.")
  )
  :caveats ("Overrides the child's actual result; do not use when you need real feedback." "Child is still ticked (side effects run); only the return status is forced." "Forced status values are 'success', 'failure', or 'running' (symbols)." "Excessive forcing makes trees hard to debug; use only when semantically necessary.")
  :drawbacks ("Hides real failures; if you force-success a failing action, bugs become invisible." "Performance: child is executed but result is discarded; wasteful if child is expensive." "Readability: forced status contradicts the child's actual behavior, confusing readers.")
  :usecases ("Testing: force a behavior subtree to succeed so you can test downstream logic." "Semantics: mark a node as 'running' to keep a parent selector on the same branch next tick." "Recovery: force a failed node to success so the behavior tree continues trying alternatives." "Stubbing: force a child to failure to trigger a fallback action before the real action is implemented.")
  :related ("ai/bt-invert" "ai/bt-selector" "ai/bt-sequence" "ai/bt-tick")
  :learn (:concept "Status override in behavior trees; decoupling result from logic." :prerequisites ("ai/bt-tick" "ai/bt-action" "ai/bt-condition") :progression "Learn ai/bt-invert to negate a status; then ai/bt-selector to see how forced statuses affect branch selection.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "A tree branch should keep trying to reach a hard-to-reach spot but not block a selector's later fallbacks. If the child returns failure, the selector moves on; if it returns success, the tree ends. We want 'try but don't stop the world' semantics."
     :program "(define keep-trying\n  (ai/bt-force 'running (ai/bt-action 'reach)))\n(display keep-trying)"
     :explanation "Wrapping the action in bt-force with 'running makes the parent selector treat it as still working. The tree does not commit the branch as done, and later fallbacks remain reachable."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is bt-invert. invert swaps success/failure; force overrides regardless of the child. Under audit, using invert here would flip pass/fail but not achieve 'running' state — the semantics is different.")
    (:eng "Symptom is trees committing too early. Fix is explicit force to running."
     :math "Force is a constant map on the status codomain."
     :cs "The pattern is status-override — same as HTTP middleware that always returns 200 for health checks."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is result-decoration: wrap a computation and replace its result with a fixed value."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi bt-force" :code "(ai/bt-force 'success (ai/bt-action 'try))")
       (:domain "shell command that ignores exit code" :code "(define (ignore-fail cmd) (list 'shell cmd '|| 'true))\n(display (ignore-fail 'flaky-net-call))")
       (:domain "constant function on codomain" :code "(define (const c) (lambda (x) c))\n(display ((const 'ok) 'ignored))"))
     :explanation "bt-force overrides the return. Shell || true ignores failure. Constant function discards its input. Same shape: replace an output with a fixed value regardless of computation."
     :meta "The shape transfers because sometimes the CALLER knows what result should stand, not the callee.")
    (:eng "Result-decoration is how ops teams make flaky components look reliable to upstream."
     :math "The composition force ∘ f collapses f's codomain to a point."
     :cs "Same pattern as noexcept wrappers, defer-recover in Go, or try/catch that returns a default."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "bt-force with a chosen status s always returns s regardless of child result."
     :program "(define (force s child-result) s)\n(define (test)\n  (and (eq? (force 'success 'failure) 'success)\n       (eq? (force 'success 'success) 'success)\n       (eq? (force 'failure 'running) 'failure)))\n(display (test))"
     :invariant "∀ (s, c). force(s, c) = s"
     :meta "The CS pattern is constant-function-on-status. Falsification would be a leak of the child result. It does not leak. Cite book-of-code ch 3.")
    (:eng "The invariant lets you rely on the override; without it, override semantics is broken."
     :math "The force function is a constant map; its image is a single point in the status space."

  :row-5-emergence (

    (:base "ai/bt-force overrides the child's status."

(verb
  :name "ai/bt-invert"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(ai/bt-invert child) → node"
  :summary "Swap success/failure of a behavior-tree child: returns a node that negates the child's status."
  :explanation "A behavior tree decorator that logically inverts the outcome of its child node. When the child succeeds, the inverted node fails; when the child fails, it succeeds. The child itself is unchanged; only the result is flipped."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define guard-id 'guard-id)\n(define patrol-blocked\n  (ai/bt-invert (ai/bt-sequence\n    (ai/bt-condition 'path-clear)\n    (ai/bt-action 'move-to-waypoint))))\n(ai/bt-tick patrol-blocked guard-id)" :note "Inverts a sequence: succeeds only if the whole sequence does not complete (path is blocked or move fails).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define soldier-id 'soldier-id)\n(define defensive\n  (ai/bt-selector\n    (ai/bt-invert (ai/bt-condition 'health-critical))\n    (ai/bt-sequence\n      (ai/bt-action 'take-cover)\n      (ai/bt-action 'heal))))\n(ai/bt-tick defensive soldier-id)" :note "Selector tries inverted health check first; if health is NOT critical, succeeds and skips healing. Otherwise executes cover-and-heal sequence.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define not-hungry (ai/bt-invert 'hungry?))\n(display not-hungry)" :note "Wrap a check to flip its meaning. Now the node succeeds when the child fails.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define at-rest\n  (ai/bt-invert (ai/bt-condition 'moving?)))\n(display at-rest)" :note "Build 'not-moving' from a 'moving?' check without writing a new condition.")
  )
  :caveats ("Inverts only the final status; does not re-run the child or undo its side effects." "Useful for logic, but overuse can make tree intent hard to read—consider renaming or restructuring instead." "Running status does not invert; a child that returns running will still return running through the inverter.")
  :drawbacks ("No performance gain or loss; purely a logical wrapper." "Can obscure intent if the child action name is already negative (e.g., inverted 'no-threat' reads awkwardly).")
  :usecases ("Guard logic: 'succeed if enemy is NOT in sight' (invert a sight condition)." "Failure-driven recovery: 'if the primary action does not work, do this' (invert a success condition to trigger fallback)." "Defensive posture: 'skip healing if health is NOT critical' (invert a danger threshold).")
  :related ("ai/bt-sequence" "ai/bt-selector" "ai/bt-condition" "ai/bt-action" "ai/bt-tick")
  :learn (:concept "Logical negation in behavior trees: the NOT gate that flips success/failure." :prerequisites ("ai/bt-tick" "ai/bt-condition" "ai/bt-action") :progression "Learn ai/bt-force to unconditionally set a status, then explore ai/bt-sequence and ai/bt-selector to compose complex logic.")

     :explanation "bt-invert reuses in-cover? to derive not-in-cover? without adding a new handler. One decorator, one negation, no doubled handlers."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is authoring a new 'not-in-cover?' condition. That doubles the registry surface and the two conditions can drift out of sync. bt-invert derives the negation mechanically.")

(verb
  :name "ai/cohere"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(ai/cohere id tag radius [force]) → void"
  :summary "Boid rule 3: steer an entity toward the center of mass of nearby tagged allies, implementing flock cohesion."
  :explanation "Boid flocking has three rules: separation (avoid crowding), alignment (match heading), and cohesion (steer toward the flock center). `ai/cohere` implements the third rule. It finds all entities nearby (within radius) tagged with the given tag, computes their center of mass, and applies a steering force to move the subject entity toward that center. This creates the cohesive 'sticking together' behavior seen in bird flocks and fish schools. Use it with ai/separate and ai/align to create full flocking, or use it alone for gentler grouping. The optional force argument caps the steering; defaults to a reasonable value if omitted."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define all-birds '())\n(define (flock-step)\n  (for-each (lambda (bird)\n    (ai/cohere bird 'flock 30))  ; 30-unit cohesion radius\n    all-birds))\n\n(flock-step)" :note "Each bird steers toward the center of all other birds within 30 units and tagged 'flock'.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define all-birds '())\n(define (advanced-flock)\n  (for-each (lambda (bird)\n    (ai/separate bird 'flock 10)  ; avoid close neighbors\n    (ai/align bird 'flock 20)     ; match neighbor heading\n    (ai/cohere bird 'flock 30 5)) ; steer toward center, capped force\n    all-birds))\n\n(advanced-flock)" :note "Three boid rules in sequence: separate (collision avoidance), align (velocity matching), cohere (cohesion). Together they create realistic flocking.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define herbivores 'herbivores)\n(define (predator-prey)\n  (let ((prey-team 'herbivore)\n        (predator-team 'carnivore))\n    \n    ; Prey flock together for safety\n    (for-each (lambda (herbivore)\n      (ai/separate herbivore prey-team 5)\n      (ai/align herbivore prey-team 15)\n      (ai/cohere herbivore prey-team 25 3))\n      herbivores)\n    \n    ; Predators hunt individually but loosely group\n    (for-each (lambda (carnivore)\n      (let ((target (closest-prey carnivore)))\n        (ai/pursue carnivore target)\n        (ai/cohere carnivore predator-team 40 1)))  ; weak cohesion\n      carnivores)))\n\n(predator-prey)" :note "Two teams with different flocking strategies: prey use strong cohesion for defense, predators have weak cohesion while hunting (they stay loose to surround prey).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ai/cohere 'bird 'flock 50)" :note "Steer this bird toward the middle of nearby flockmates within 50 units.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(for-each\n  (lambda (id)\n    (ai/cohere id 'flock 40 2))\n  (entity/all))" :note "Apply the cohesion rule to every entity in the flock each step. Force of 2 keeps it gentle.")
  )
  :caveats ("ai/cohere finds neighbors dynamically each call; for large groups, this can be slow—consider caching neighbors if you cohere many times per tick." "The radius is hard cutoff; entities at radius + 1 unit are not included, so tuning radius is critical to group size." "force capping affects steering magnitude but not direction; weak force does not break cohesion, just slows response.")
  :drawbacks ("Can create deadlock or oscillation if an entity is equidistant from multiple directions—consider ai/align and ai/separate to smooth the group." "No built-in separation from other tags; if multiple teams should cohere within their groups but not across groups, tag carefully." "The flock center is computed every call; in large groups, this is O(n) per entity, O(n²) total per cycle. ai/flock combines all three rules and may be faster.")
  :usecases ("Swarms: insects or robots that maintain group cohesion (ant colonies, drone swarms)." "Herds: grazing animals that stick together for safety." "Flock predator defense: prey school together to confuse attackers." "Loose formations: military units or teams that maintain loose spatial grouping while pursuing individual objectives.")

     :meta "The wrong sibling is ai/seek toward a fixed rally point. Fixed points fail when the herd itself moves; cohere uses the DYNAMIC center of mass, which moves with the herd.")

(verb
  :name "ai/decide"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(ai/decide id choices) → status"
  :summary "Evaluate a utility-based choice set and fire the highest-scoring action, returning the action's result status."
  :explanation "Utility-based AI is an alternative to behavior trees and state machines: each decision is an evaluation of all options' scores, and the winner is executed immediately. `ai/decide` takes an entity id and a list of choice specs (each pairing a tag name with a scoring function). It evaluates the score for each choice, picks the one with the highest score (breaking ties arbitrarily), then fires the associated registered action and returns its status. This is faster than evaluating full trees for small decision sets and is more readable than nested if-else logic. Useful for tactical AI: 'what's the best action to take right now?'"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define soldier-id 'soldier-id)\n(define choices\n  (list (cons 'attack (lambda (id) (if (target-nearby? id) 10 0)))\n        (cons 'flee (lambda (id) (if (hurt? id) 8 0)))))\n\n(ai/decide soldier-id choices)" :note "Two choices scored by simple conditions. If target is nearby, attack scores 10; if hurt, flee scores 8. Highest scorer wins.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define warrior-id 'warrior-id)\n(define (threat-level id)\n  (let ((enemy-dist (distance-to-nearest-enemy id))\n        (my-health (current-health id)))\n    (* (/ 100 (max enemy-dist 1)) (/ my-health 100))))\n\n(define choices\n  (list (cons 'aggressive-attack (lambda (id) (if (> (threat-level id) 5) 12 0)))\n        (cons 'defensive-shoot (lambda (id) (if (> (threat-level id) 2) 7 1)))\n        (cons 'retreat (lambda (id) (if (< (threat-level id) 1) 5 0)))))\n\n(ai/decide warrior-id choices)" :note "Threat level combines distance and health into a single metric. Three actions scored based on threat: high threat → aggressive, medium → defensive, low → retreat.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define mercenary-id 'mercenary-id)\n(define (tactical-choice id)\n  (define (attack-score id)\n    (let ((target (nearest-enemy id))\n          (ammo (get-ammo-count id)))\n      (if (and target (> ammo 0))\n        (+ (* 2 (max 0 (- 50 (distance-to id target))))\n           (* ammo 0.5))\n        0)))\n  \n  (define (defend-score id)\n    (let ((allies (friendly-units-nearby id 30)))\n      (if (> (length allies) 0)\n        (+ 5 (length allies))\n        0)))\n  \n  (define (loot-score id)\n    (let ((items (items-nearby id 20)))\n      (if (> (length items) 0)\n        (+ 3 (* (length items) 2))\n        0)))\n  \n  (ai/decide id\n    (list (cons 'shoot attack-score)\n          (cons 'cover defend-score)\n          (cons 'loot loot-score))))\n\n(tactical-choice mercenary-id)" :note "Each choice's score is a weighted combination of game state (distance, ammo, allies, loot). Decision adapts to current situation dynamically.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(display (ai/decide 'hero '((attack 0.8) (flee 0.3))))" :note "Score each option. The higher score wins. The chosen action fires.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (choose hero-id hp-frac)\n  (ai/decide hero-id\n    (list (list 'attack (- 1 hp-frac))\n          (list 'flee   hp-frac))))\n(display (choose 'hero 0.2))" :note "As health falls, fleeing scores higher. The hero decides for themselves.")
  )
  :caveats ("All choices' scoring functions are called each decision; if scoring is expensive, cache results or use a coarser decision frequency." "Ties are broken arbitrarily (typically first in list, but no guarantee); use ai/utility to read the winning action without executing, if you need tie-breaking logic." "If all choices score 0, one is still chosen and executed; consider adding a 'do-nothing' choice if inaction is valid." "The winning action is executed immediately; there is no intermediate evaluation step—use ai/utility to preview the choice." "Status returned is the action's status; if the action returns 'running', ai/decide will return 'running', requiring another call next tick to resume.")
  :drawbacks ("O(n) in the number of choices; with many options, scoring becomes a bottleneck." "No fallback if the winning action fails unexpectedly; for resilience, wrap ai/decide in a behavior-tree selector." "No learning or history; each decision is independent. For learning, use ai/policy instead (which bakes in learned Q-values)." "Scoring function bugs are hard to debug—add logging to understand why a choice scored higher than expected.")
  :usecases ("Tactical combat: evaluate attack, defend, flee, heal and pick the best option each frame." "Pawn shop behavior: score different goods (sell high-value, buy low-cost, hoard rare items) and execute the winner." "Creature behavior: animals score feeding, resting, mating, defending nest and pick highest priority action." "Loot AI: prioritize which items to pick up based on rarity, carrying capacity, and current needs.")
  :related ("ai/utility" "ai/policy" "ai/policy-act" "ai/bt-tick" "ai/bt-selector")
  :learn (:concept "Utility-based decision-making: argmax over scored choices." :prerequisites ("ai/utility") :progression "Use ai/decide for dynamic choices; for precomputed optimal play, learn ai/policy and ai/policy-act to deploy learned greedy policies.")

"Steering is cumulative; multiple steering calls in one frame stack their effects.")

  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define bird-id 'bird-id)\n(ai/flock bird-id 'flock 80 4.0)" :note "Bird flocks with others tagged 'flock' within 80-pixel radius, force cap 4.0")

  )
  :caveats ("Flock uses a fixed internal weighting of the three rules; use separate calls to ai/separate, ai/align, ai/cohere if you need custom weights."   :drawbacks ("Less flexible than hand-tuning the three rules separately; if you need different weights, call ai/separate, ai/align, ai/cohere directly." "Does not handle obstacles; combine with ai/wall! or ai/separate-from-obstacles for collision-aware flocking.")

(verb
  :name "ai/flow-field"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(ai/flow-field grid tx ty) → field id"
  :summary "Precompute a flow field (potential field) from a goal point using breadth-first propagation."
  :explanation "Flow-field takes a grid (created by ai/grid), a goal location (tx, ty), and floods the grid with direction vectors that point toward the goal. Every passable cell stores the optimal next step toward (tx, ty), creating a potential field. The result is a field id that can be queried with ai/flow-at or used to steer entities with ai/follow-flow. This is more efficient than pathfinding on every frame if many entities need to reach the same goal."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((grid (ai/grid 50 50)))\n  (ai/flow-field grid 25 25))" :note "Create a 50×50 grid, compute flow field toward center (25, 25)")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define hero-id 'hero-id)\n(let ((grid (ai/grid 100 100)))\n  (ai/wall! grid 50 50)\n  (ai/wall! grid 50 51)\n  (let ((field (ai/flow-field grid 90 90)))\n    (ai/follow-flow hero-id field 5.0)))" :note "Create grid with wall obstacles, compute flow field toward goal, steer entity along it")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (swarm-to-target grid target-x target-y swarm-ids)\n  (let ((field (ai/flow-field grid target-x target-y)))\n    (for-each (lambda (id)\n                (let ((fx (ai/flow-at field (entity/x id) (entity/y id))))\n                  (if (> (+ (abs (car fx)) (abs (cadr fx))) 0.01)\n                    (ai/follow-flow id field 6.0)\n                    (entity/set-vel! id 0 0))))\n              swarm-ids)))" :note "Compute one field, steer entire swarm toward it; halt units that reach goal")
  )

"Propagation only reaches passable cells; unreachable cells will have zero flow." (and (< (abs (- (entity/x u) goal-x)) 5)\n                                         (< (abs (- (entity/y u) goal-y)) 5))))\n                  (if at-goal?\n                    (entity/set-vel! u 0 0)\n                    (ai/follow-flow u field 6.0))))\n              units)))" :note "Converge swarm on goal, halt units once they arrive within threshold")

  )

  :drawbacks ("Requires precomputed path; dynamic obstacle avoidance is not built-in." "Path must be recomputed if obstacles change; consider ai/flow-field for dynamic environments." (verb
  :name "ai/wander"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(ai/wander id [force] [jitter]) -> void"
  :summary "Apply a deterministic, smooth meander to an entity's motion using seeded noise."
  :explanation "Wandering is useful for NPCs that should move aimlessly but believably—not randomly twitchy, but smoothly exploratory. ai/wander applies a steering impulse each frame, parameterized by the entity's id and the current frame count, so the same entity in the same frame always wanders the same direction (deterministic). The optional force caps the strength of the impulse; jitter controls smoothness (higher = more erratic). Internally uses (frame, id) as a noise seed."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define zombie (world/spawn 'zombie 10 10))\n(on-tick (lambda ()\n           (ai/wander zombie)))" :note "Zombie meanders smoothly every frame with default force and jitter.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define npc-list (map (lambda (i) (world/spawn 'npc (random 100) (random 100))) (list 1 2 3)))\n(on-tick (lambda ()\n           (for-each (lambda (npc)\n                       (ai/wander npc 0.5))\n                     npc-list)))" :note "Three NPCs wander with reduced force (0.5), creating a calmer motion.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (patrol-or-wander ent target-list)\n  (if (null? target-list)\n      (ai/wander ent 0.3 0.2)\n      (ai/pursue ent (car target-list) 1.0)))\n(on-tick (lambda ()\n           (world/each (lambda (ent)\n                         (let ((targets (world/find ent 'threat)))\n                           (patrol-or-wander ent targets)))\n                       'agent)))" :note "Agents wander during downtime but switch to pursuit when threats appear.")
  )
  :caveats ("Determinism is keyed to (frame, entity-id): replaying the same frame with the same entity always produces the same wander direction, but changing frame or entity id changes the noise sample." "Optional force defaults to a fixed value (check runtime docs); jitter defaults to moderate smoothness." "Wander alone does not constrain entities to a bounds; they may walk off-screen unless you add barriers or use ai/arrive.")
  :drawbacks ("Smooth but aimless: not suitable for pathfinding or goal-oriented motion." "Determinism from frame count means the trajectory is predictable if an observer knows the seed formula." "Does not interact with obstacles; walls and collisions must be handled separately.")
  :usecases ("NPCs exploring an open area during idle time." "Creating the sense of life: creatures that move believably when the player isn't watching." "Procedurally generated patrol routes without explicit waypoint lists.")
  :related ("ai/pursue" "ai/evade" "ai/arrive" "ai/flock")
  :learn (:concept "Deterministic noise: steer smoothly and reproducibly by hashing (frame, entity-id)." :prerequisites ("entity/set-vel!" "on-tick") :progression "Combine ai/wander with ai/pursue or ai/flee to switch between exploration and reaction.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "Idle NPCs stand perfectly still — the world feels lifeless. But we don't want them to have a goal; we want them to LOOK alive without anything specific to do."
     :program "(define (idle-life npc)\n  (ai/wander npc 1.0 0.5))\n(idle-life 'shopkeeper)"
     :explanation "ai/wander applies deterministic seeded-noise steering: smooth pseudo-random meander. NPCs appear alive without a goal."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is random walk with actual RNG. That's non-deterministic — replay diverges, tests flake. Wander uses (frame, id) as seed, so replays are reproducible.")
    (:eng "Symptom is dead-still NPCs. Fix is deterministic wander."
     :math "Wander uses (frame, id) as a deterministic noise seed."
     :cs "The pattern is seeded-noise-instead-of-RNG."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is deterministic-noise: use a hash of (context, id) instead of a true random source."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi wander" :code "(ai/wander 'zombie)")
       (:domain "reproducible cargo build with locked hashes" :code "(define (build-lock crates) (list 'cargo 'build 'with 'cargo.lock))\n(display (build-lock 'my-app)))")
       (:domain "Perlin noise" :code "(define (perlin x y) (list 'seeded-noise x y))\n(display (perlin 10 20))"))
     :explanation "wander is deterministic pseudo-random. cargo lock is deterministic builds. Perlin is deterministic 2D noise. Same shape: reproducibility despite apparent randomness."
     :meta "The shape transfers because tests and replay need determinism, but visual output can look random.")
    (:eng "Determinism is what makes debugging noise-driven behaviors possible."
     :math "Pseudo-random noise is a deterministic function of the seed."

  :row-4-proof (

     :program "(define (wander-hash frame id) (modulo (+ frame id) 360))\n(display (= (wander-hash 100 42) (wander-hash 100 42)))"
     :invariant "∀ (frame, id). wander-force(frame, id) = wander-force(frame, id)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is deterministic-noise. Falsification would be a wander whose replay diverged from the original. Cite book-of-code ch 3.")
    (:eng "Reproducibility is what enables replay-testing of wander-heavy AI."
     :math "The noise function is total on (frame, id)."
     :cs "Same math as content-addressed builds."))
  :row-5-emergence (

(verb
  :name "ai/waypoints"
  :library "ai"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(ai/waypoints grid path) -> list-of-[wx wy]"
  :summary "Convert a grid cell path (from A*) into world-space waypoints at cell centers."
  :explanation "A* returns cell coordinates [cx, cy]; direct movement to cell corners looks jerky. ai/waypoints transforms a cell path into smooth world-space waypoints at each cell's center, ready to pass to ai/follow-path. This is the bridge between discrete pathfinding and continuous motion."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define my-entity 'my-entity)\n(define g (ai/grid 10 10))\n(define path (ai/path g 0 0 5 5))\n(define waypts (ai/waypoints g path))\n(ai/follow-path my-entity waypts)" :note "Convert the A* cell path to world waypoints, then steer the entity along them.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define goal-y 'goal-y)\n(define goal-x 'goal-x)\n(define guard 'guard)\n(define (patrol-to goal)\n  (let* ((g (ai/grid 20 20))\n         (cell-path (ai/path g (entity/x guard) (entity/y guard) goal-x goal-y))\n         (wp (ai/waypoints g cell-path)))\n    (ai/follow-path guard wp 5.0)))\n(patrol-to (list 100 100))" :note "Compute the grid-based path from guard to goal, convert to world waypoints, and follow.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (dynamic-waypoint-recompute ent grid goal-x goal-y)\n  (let* ((ex (entity/x ent)) (ey (entity/y ent))\n         (path (ai/path grid ex ey goal-x goal-y))\n         (wp (if (equal? path 'no-path)\n                 '()\n                 (ai/waypoints grid path))))\n    (if (null? wp)\n        (escalate 'unreachable (list goal-x goal-y))\n        (ai/follow-path ent wp 2.0))))\n(on-tick (lambda ()\n           (dynamic-waypoint-recompute player grid boss-x boss-y)))" :note "Recompute waypoints every frame, handling the case where no path exists.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define grid (ai/grid 16 16))\n(define wps (ai/waypoints grid '((0 0) (1 0) (2 0))))\n(display wps)" :note "Turn a three-cell path into world-space waypoints at cell centers.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define grid (ai/grid 32 32))\n(define path (ai/path grid '(0 0) '(10 10)))\n(define wps (ai/waypoints grid path))\n(display wps)" :note "Run A* on the grid, then convert the cell path into waypoints an entity can steer through.")
  )
  :caveats ("Requires a valid grid and a path list in the format returned by ai/path (list of [cx, cy] pairs)." "If path is 'no-path (the sentinel returned when A* fails), ai/waypoints will error; check path before calling." "World coordinates assume a fixed grid cell size; ensure the grid scale matches your world units.")
  :drawbacks ("One-way conversion: waypoints lose information about the underlying grid." "Does not smooth corners or optimize waypoint density; if you want smoother steering, post-process the result." "Grid scale is implicit; passing the wrong grid for a path produces wrong world coords.")
  :usecases ("Converting discrete pathfinding into smooth motion for entities." "Building a behavior that navigates cluttered environments without teleporting between obstacles." "Real-time AI: recompute path each frame and stream new waypoints to ai/follow-path.")
  :related ("ai/path" "ai/follow-path" "ai/grid")
  :learn (:concept "Coordinate transformation: convert from grid (discrete) to world (continuous) space." :prerequisites ("ai/path" "ai/grid") :progression "After ai/waypoints, use ai/follow-path to make entities move along the waypoint list.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "A* returns cell coordinates but ai/follow-path expects world coordinates. Feeding cells directly makes the entity jerk between corners."
     :program "(define waypoints (ai/waypoints grid path))\n(ai/follow-path 'unit waypoints 2.0 4.0)"
     :explanation "ai/waypoints converts cell paths to world-space waypoints at cell centers. Motion becomes smooth."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is manual coord-conversion inline. That works but hides the intent; waypoints names the conversion.")
    (:eng "Symptom is jerky motion between grid corners. Fix is cell→world conversion."
     :math "Waypoints scales cell coords by cell size."
     :cs "The pattern is coord-transform."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is unit-conversion-between-spaces: transform from one coordinate frame to another."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi waypoints" :code "(ai/waypoints grid '((0 0) (1 1)))")
       (:domain "pixel to display-percentage" :code "(define (px-to-pct px screen-w) (/ px screen-w))\n(display (px-to-pct 640 1280))")
       (:domain "unit vector scaling" :code "(define (scale v k) (map (lambda (x) (* x k)) v))\n(display (scale '(1 2 3) 10))"))
     :explanation "Waypoints scales cell to world. Pixel-to-percentage rescales for display. Vector scaling rescales for magnitude. Same shape: multiply by scale factor."
     :meta "The shape transfers because coordinate transformations are the fundamental bridge between logical and physical spaces.")
    (:eng "Named coordinate conversions are essential for keeping logical and physical spaces separate."
     :math "The transformation is a linear map from ℤ² to ℝ²."
     :cs "Same pattern as viewport transforms in rendering."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "ai/waypoints preserves order: the i-th waypoint corresponds to the i-th cell in the path."
     :program "(define path '((0 0) (1 1) (2 2)))\n(define wps '((10 10) (30 30) (50 50)))\n(display (= (length path) (length wps)))"
     :invariant "∀ (grid, path). length(waypoints(grid, path)) = length(path) ∧ order-preserved"
     :meta "The CS pattern is order-preservation. Falsification would be a rearrangement of waypoints. Cite book-of-code ch 3.")
    (:eng "Order-preservation is what makes the conversion trustable."
     :math "The map is a bijective sequence transformation."
     :cs "Same math as list-map preserving length and order."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "ai/waypoints converts a cell path to world waypoints."
     :composition "(define (route-unit unit grid tx ty)\n  (let ((path (ai/path grid (entity/x unit) (entity/y unit) tx ty)))\n    (if (equal? path 'no-path)\n      'unreachable\n      (ai/follow-path unit (ai/waypoints grid path) 2.0 4.0))))\n(route-unit 'u 'g 10 10)"
     :emergent "A pathfinding pipeline. path + waypoints + follow-path produces the compile-link-run sequence of unit navigation."
     :meta "The family is 'multi-stage-pipeline' — the same family as compile-link-execute, ETL pipelines, or Unix pipes with staged data transformation. Cross-ref book-of-composition ch 10 (FX Chain) for pipeline patterns.")

;;;   Row 3 (WHERE ELSE · Dim)  — same shape in 3 substrates (verb/metaphor/math)

;; ═══ 59 verbs in library alg ═══

(verb
  :name "alg/apply-symmetry"
  :library "alg"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(alg/apply-symmetry dihedral-element point) -> point"
  :summary "Apply a dihedral symmetry to a 2-D point, returning the transformed coordinates."
  :explanation "The dihedral group Dₙ represents the symmetries of a regular n-gon: rotations and reflections. This verb takes an element from such a group (encoded as a bitwise integer) and a 2-D point (as a list or pair), and returns the point after applying that symmetry. Use this when you need to test whether a spatial pattern respects a given symmetry, or to generate equivalent configurations by symmetry."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code ";; Rotate a point 90° using D_4 (square symmetry)\n(alg/apply-symmetry 1 (list 1 0))" :note "Apply the first non-identity rotation to the point (1,0); expect approximately (0,1).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code ";; Generate orbit of a point under all D_4 symmetries\n(define square-group (alg/dihedral 4))\n(define pt (list 1 0))\n(map (lambda (sym) (alg/apply-symmetry sym pt))\n     (alg/op square-group))" :note "Map each symmetry over the point to see all 8 positions (or fewer if the point lies on an axis of symmetry).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (filter pred xs)\n  (let loop ((xs xs) (acc '()))\n    (cond ((null? xs) (reverse acc))\n          ((pred (car xs)) (loop (cdr xs) (cons (car xs) acc)))\n          (else (loop (cdr xs) acc)))))\n;; Check if a decorator pattern is symmetric under D_6 (hexagon)\n(define hex-group (alg/dihedral 6))\n(define pattern-point (list 0.5 0.866))\n(define orbit (map (lambda (sym) (alg/apply-symmetry sym pattern-point))\n                   (alg/op hex-group)))\n(define is-fixed? (= 1 (length (filter (lambda (p) (equal? p pattern-point)) orbit))))\nis-fixed?" :note "Compute the full orbit; if the orbit has size 1, the point is fixed by all symmetries (sits at the center).")
  )
  :caveats ("Point representation must be consistent (list or pair) across calls." "Dihedral elements are bitwise-encoded; obtain them from alg/dihedral or alg/op." "Floating-point precision may cause near-equal points to not satisfy equal? tests; consider geometric tolerance for comparison.")
  :drawbacks ("Not applicable to non-2D geometries; use geom/rotate and geom/reflect-line for finer control." "Bitwise encoding limits to small n (typically n ≤ 16); larger symmetry groups are better handled via alg/orbit.")
  :usecases ("Validate that a tiling or crystal pattern respects dihedral symmetry." "Generate all rotations and reflections of a marker or icon in a game." "Check fixed points under a symmetry group action.")
  :related ("alg/dihedral" "alg/orbit" "alg/op" "geom/rotate" "geom/reflect-line")
  :learn (:concept "Symmetry groups act on geometric objects by applying transformations; encoding actions bitwise enables fast iteration." :prerequisites ("alg/dihedral" "alg/op") :progression "After mastering point application, learn alg/orbit to compute the full orbit under a group action, then alg/stabilizer to find fixed-point sets.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "A sprite artist places a decoration at (3, 1) on a hex tile and needs every rotational and reflected copy for the six-fold pattern. The audit question: is the placement stable — that is, does the emitted set of positions actually respect the D_6 group we declared, or did we drift into ad-hoc trigonometry that would fail a symmetry check?"
     :program "(define hex (alg/dihedral 6))\n(define seed (list 3 1))\n(define orbit (map (lambda (s) (alg/apply-symmetry s seed)) (alg/op hex)))\n(list (length orbit) (car orbit))"
     :explanation "Line 1 builds the dihedral group of the hexagon. Line 2 fixes the seed point. Line 3 maps every group element over the seed via alg/apply-symmetry. The count on line 4 tells the operator whether all 12 symmetries produced distinct points (generic position) or fewer (point on a symmetry axis). The verb answers the audit because the group element drives the transform — no hand-rolled sin/cos to drift."
     :meta "geom/rotate would have taken an angle in radians and quietly produced 12 different floats for what should be one canonical action. alg/apply-symmetry takes the group element itself, so equality of symmetries is equality of integers.")
    (:eng "The operator sees one function call per symmetry; the log shows the enum, not a float — easier to grep."
     :math "The verb realizes the action D_n × R^2 → R^2 as a homomorphism from the abstract group to the affine group of the plane."
     :cs "Group element is an int; dispatch is O(1); no floating-point equality on the group side."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A finite group acting on an ambient set — the shape is 'element carries object to object'."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "alg action on a point"    :code "(alg/apply-symmetry 1 (list 1 0))")
       (:domain "framebuffer scene rotate" :code "(scene/rotate stage (quarter-turn))")
       (:domain "matrix action on a vector":code "(matrix/mul-vec R v)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is our verb: a group element applied to a 2-D point. Rung 2 is the same shape at the scene level — the framebuffer rotates a whole layer under one quarter-turn action. Rung 3 is the linear-algebra crystal: a matrix R times a vector v. All three read 'act g on x', and all three respect composition: (act g (act h x)) = (act (compose g h) x)."
     :meta "The shape transfers because 'group acts on set' is one of the oldest abstractions in mathematics; any concrete rotation, permutation, or matrix multiplication is an instance.")
    (:eng "The same shape shows up in the sprite pipeline, the scene rotate call, and the linear-algebra layer, so an engineer who learns one carries the other two."
     :math "Group action: G × X → X with g·(h·x) = (gh)·x and e·x = x."
     :cs "The action is a two-argument function; encoding the group element as an int lets us memoize compositions."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "Applying the identity element leaves the point unchanged; applying a symmetry then its inverse returns the original point."
     :program "(define D4 (alg/dihedral 4))\n(define p (list 3 5))\n(define g 2)\n(define inv-g (alg/inverse D4 g))\n(define round-trip (alg/apply-symmetry inv-g (alg/apply-symmetry g p)))\n(and (equal? p (alg/apply-symmetry 0 p))\n     (equal? p round-trip))"
     :invariant "∀ x ∈ R^2. e · x = x   ∧   ∀ g ∈ D_n, x ∈ R^2. g^{-1} · (g · x) = x"
     :meta "Identity + inverses are the group-action axioms. A counter-example — any point p and any group element g for which round-trip differs from p — would prove the encoding is broken and the group is not acting. This is the algebraic-invariant frame; see book-of-math ch-advanced-04 (Groups & Symmetry).")
    (:eng "The test is one line and prints #t; SRE can add it to a smoke check for the geometry pipeline."
     :math "The two axioms above define an action; every symmetry group acting on a plane obeys them."
     :cs "The invariant is a property test; use it as a fuzzer seed by drawing random p and g."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "alg/apply-symmetry takes a group element and a point and returns the transformed point."
     :composition "(define hex (alg/dihedral 6))\n(define seed (list 4 0))\n(define orbit\n  (let loop ((gs (alg/op hex)) (acc '()))\n    (cond ((null? gs) (reverse acc))\n          (else (loop (cdr gs)\n                      (cons (alg/apply-symmetry (car gs) seed) acc))))))\norbit"
     :emergent "An orbit — the closed set of all images of one point under the whole group."
     :meta "Chaining apply-symmetry with a fold over the group elements produces the classical 'orbit' pattern; the same family shows up in Burnside counting, in graphics tile enumeration, in molecular chemistry symmetry classes. See book-of-composition ch-16 (composing games) for tile-map applications.")
    (:eng "The emergent orbit is exactly what a tile decorator ships to the sprite grid — one code path, one set of positions."
     :math "Orbit-stabilizer theorem: |orbit(x)| · |stab(x)| = |G|."
     :cs "Fold over group elements = O(|G|); cache the orbit once per seed, reuse across frames."))
)

(verb
  :name "alg/center"
  :library "alg"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(alg/center group) -> list"
  :summary "Compute the center Z(G), the set of elements that commute with every element of the group."
  :explanation "The center of a group G is the subgroup Z(G) = {g ∈ G : g·x = x·g for all x ∈ G}. It consists of all elements that commute with everything. In an abelian group, the center is the entire group; in a non-abelian group, it is a proper subgroup. The center reveals structural information: its size and structure constrain the conjugacy classes and tell you how 'commutative' the group is."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code ";; Center of the cyclic group C_5\n(define C5 (alg/cyclic 5))\n(alg/center C5)" :note "Expect the entire group (all 5 elements), since cyclic groups are abelian.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code ";; Center of the dihedral group D_3 (symmetries of equilateral triangle)\n(define D3 (alg/dihedral 3))\n(define center (alg/center D3))\n(alg/order D3)" :note "D_3 has order 6; its center contains only the identity and possibly a central rotation. Compare sizes to see how non-abelian D_3 is.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code ";; Verify that the center is trivial (only identity) for S_4\n(define S4 (alg/symmetric 4))\n(define center-S4 (alg/center S4))\n(= 1 (length center-S4))" :note "S_4 (symmetric group on 4 elements) has a trivial center; this verifies the structural property that S_n has trivial center for n ≥ 3.")
  )
  :caveats ("Computing the center requires checking commutativity of all pairs; for large groups (|G| > 100) this may be slow." "The result is always a list, even if the center is trivial (singleton {e})." "For groups with |G| > 12, some operations note 'use-backend'; the center computation itself is available but may be slow.")
  :drawbacks ("For very large groups, this is a brute-force quadratic algorithm; no clever polynomial-time algorithm for general groups." "The center alone does not determine the group structure; combine with alg/conjugacy-classes for a richer picture.")
  :usecases ("Determine how abelian a group is: large center → more commutative." "Identify central elements for representation theory (characters are class functions on the center)." "Check if a given subgroup is central or compare the structure of two groups.")
  :related ("alg/conjugacy-classes" "alg/is-abelian?" "alg/cosets" "alg/op")
  :learn (:concept "The center of a group measures how much the group deviates from being abelian; it is the kernel of the map g ↦ (conjugation by g)." :prerequisites ("alg/op" "alg/cyclic" "alg/dihedral") :progression "Learn alg/conjugacy-classes to see how the center partitions the group, then study alg/cosets and alg/is-normal? to understand quotient structures.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"

(verb
  :name "alg/conjugacy-classes"

  :summary "Partition the group into conjugacy classes: maximal sets of mutually conjugate elements."
  :explanation "Two elements g and h are conjugate if h = xgx⁻¹ for some x in the group. The conjugacy classes form a partition of G. Elements in the same conjugacy class have the same order and similar algebraic properties. The conjugacy class structure is a core invariant of a group: two isomorphic groups have the same conjugacy class structure. This is essential for group classification and representation theory."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code ";; Conjugacy classes of C_4 (cyclic)\n(define C4 (alg/cyclic 4))\n(alg/conjugacy-classes C4)" :note "Expect 4 singleton classes {e}, {1}, {2}, {3} because all elements are in their own class (abelian group).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code ";; Conjugacy classes of D_3 (triangle symmetry, order 6)\n(define D3 (alg/dihedral 3))\n(define classes (alg/conjugacy-classes D3))\n(map length classes)" :note "Expect class sizes like (1 1 3 1), revealing that rotations by 120° and 240° are conjugate (both reflections of the same structure).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code ";; Analyze class structure to test non-isomorphism\n(define D4 (alg/dihedral 4))\n(define Q8 (alg/group-from-table '((0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7)\n                                    (1 0 3 2 5 4 7 6)\n                                    (2 3 0 1 6 7 4 5)\n                                    (3 2 1 0 7 6 5 4)\n                                    (4 5 6 7 0 1 2 3)\n                                    (5 4 7 6 1 0 3 2)\n                                    (6 7 4 5 2 3 0 1)\n                                    (7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0))))\n(define d4-classes (map length (alg/conjugacy-classes D4)))\n(define q8-classes (map length (alg/conjugacy-classes Q8)))\n(equal? (sort d4-classes <) (sort q8-classes <))" :note "D_4 and Q_8 (quaternion group) both have order 8 but different class structures; comparing sorted class sizes is a quick non-isomorphism test.")
  )
  :caveats ("The result is a list of lists; outer list has one entry per conjugacy class, inner lists contain elements." "In an abelian group, each conjugacy class is a singleton; expect |classes| = |G|." "For |G| > 12, computation may be slow or flagged as over budget.")
  :drawbacks ("Computing all conjugacy classes is O(|G|²) in the worst case; no faster general algorithm." "Conjugacy class structure alone does not fully determine a group (non-isomorphic groups can share class structures).")
  :usecases ("Verify group isomorphism or non-isomorphism by comparing class structure." "Build character tables and representations of a group." "Analyze the structure of a group to understand its quotients and normal subgroups.")
  :related ("alg/center" "alg/is-isomorphic?" "alg/is-normal?" "alg/cosets")
  :learn (:concept "Conjugacy is an equivalence relation; conjugate elements are 'alike' in the group's structure.
