  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "Two Cayley tables land in the reference; the auditor must decide whether they are the same group with elements relabelled or genuinely different. Comparing element-by-element is fragile; comparing conjugacy-class sizes is a fast, honest fingerprint."
     :program "(define A (alg/dihedral 4))\n(define B (alg/direct-product (alg/cyclic 2) (alg/cyclic 4)))\n(define ca (sort (map length (alg/conjugacy-classes A)) <))\n(define cb (sort (map length (alg/conjugacy-classes B)) <))\n(list ca cb (equal? ca cb))"
     :explanation "Lines 1-2 build two groups of order 8. Lines 3-4 compute the sorted class-size lists — the class equation up to permutation. Line 5 reports both plus whether they match. D_4 gives (1 1 2 2 2); C_2 × C_4 gives (1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1). Different lists prove the groups are non-isomorphic before we even try to find a bijection."
     :meta "alg/is-isomorphic? would eventually give the same answer, but it is exponential in the worst case; conjugacy-class comparison is polynomial and rules out 90% of cases up front.")
    (:eng "In the CI lane for group tables, class-size comparison is the cheap first filter; only survivors go to full isomorphism search."
     :math "Isomorphic groups have equal multisets of conjugacy-class sizes."
     :cs "Sort and compare — O(|G|^2) worst case for the class computation, O(n log n) for the sort."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "'Equivalence under an inner action' — partition a set by a symmetry acting on it from within."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "alg conjugacy in a group"  :code "(alg/conjugacy-classes (alg/symmetric 4))")
       (:domain "collision hash bucketing"  :code "(collision/buckets space)")
       (:domain "topological equivalence"   :code "(geom/homotopy-classes shape)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1: conjugacy partitions a group into orbits under g → xgx^{-1}. Rung 2: a collision grid partitions space into buckets that collide only within themselves. Rung 3: homotopy classes partition continuous maps by 'can be deformed into each other'. All three share the shape: 'a relation of the form R(a, b) = ∃ x. a = x·b·x^{-1}-like'."
     :meta "The shape transfers because every action-partition is a colouring where 'same colour' means 'reachable by an inner move' — an equivalence relation implicit in any action.")
    (:eng "Learning to think in equivalence classes shows up in bucketing collisions, deduplicating hash entries, and identifying redundant chords in music theory."
     :math "Conjugation is an inner automorphism; classes are orbits of Inn(G) on G."
     :cs "The pattern is 'partition by a group action', a template usable wherever an action is defined."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "Conjugacy is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, transitive."
     :program "(define G (alg/symmetric 3))\n(define (conj? x y)\n  (let loop ((zs (alg/op G)))\n    (cond ((null? zs) #f)\n          (else (or (equal? y (alg/op G (car zs) (alg/op G x (alg/inverse G (car zs)))))\n                    (loop (cdr zs)))))))\n(define xs (alg/op G))\n(and\n  (let loop ((as xs)) (or (null? as) (and (conj? (car as) (car as)) (loop (cdr as)))))\n  (let loop ((as xs))\n    (or (null? as)\n        (let loop2 ((bs xs))\n          (or (null? bs)\n              (and (or (not (conj? (car as) (car bs))) (conj? (car bs) (car as)))\n                   (loop2 (cdr bs))))))))"
     :invariant "∀ a. a ~ a  ∧  ∀ a b. a ~ b ⇒ b ~ a  ∧  ∀ a b c. a ~ b ∧ b ~ c ⇒ a ~ c"
     :meta "Equivalence-relation axioms are testable per pair; a single non-symmetric pair falsifies the invariant. See book-of-math ch-advanced-04 (Groups & Symmetry) for the algebraic proof.")
    (:eng "If any of the three fails, the partition is broken and every downstream analysis (character tables, quotients) is contaminated."

     :cs "Three property tests, checkable independently; parallelizable."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "alg/conjugacy-classes partitions the group into orbits under conjugation."
     :composition "(define G (alg/dihedral 4))\n(define cs (alg/conjugacy-classes G))\n(define sizes (sort (map length cs) <))\n(define signature (list (alg/order G) sizes))\nsignature"
     :emergent "A canonical fingerprint (order, sorted class-sizes) that can be used as a hash key for groups."

    (:eng "Store groups by fingerprint; two Cayley tables with the same fingerprint are candidates for isomorphism, the rest are dismissed for free."
     :math "The class equation is one invariant among a family (order, exponent, derived series, …) that together identify most small groups."
     :cs "Compact key + fast comparison = classic 'hash before you diff' pattern."))

(verb
  :name "alg/cosets"
  :library "alg"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(alg/cosets group subgroup) -> list-of-lists"
  :summary "Partition a group by a subgroup H into left cosets: sets of the form {g·h : h ∈ H}."
  :explanation "Given a subgroup H of G, the left cosets of H are the translates g·H as g ranges over G. The cosets partition G, and all cosets have the same size |H|. The number of cosets is the index [G:H] = |G|/|H| (by Lagrange's theorem). Cosets are fundamental to quotient groups and normal subgroups; if H is normal, left and right cosets coincide, and the quotient G/H is itself a group."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code ";; Cosets of the subgroup generated by 2 in C_6\n(define C6 (alg/cyclic 6))\n(define H (alg/subgroup-gen C6 (list 2)))\n(alg/cosets C6 H)" :note "H = {0, 2, 4} generates a subgroup of order 3; expect 2 cosets: {0,2,4} and {1,3,5}.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code ";; Index of rotations in D_4\n(define D4 (alg/dihedral 4))\n(define rotations (list 0 1 2 3))\n(define cosets-d4 (alg/cosets D4 rotations))\n(length cosets-d4)" :note "D_4 has order 8, rotations form a subgroup of order 4; expect 2 cosets (index is 2), one for rotations and one for reflections.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code ";; Verify Lagrange's theorem: |cosets| = |G| / |H|\n(define D3 (alg/dihedral 3))\n(define H2 (alg/subgroup-gen D3 (list 1)))\n(define cosets (alg/cosets D3 H2))\n(= (length cosets) (quotient (alg/order D3) (length H2)))" :note "Confirm that the number of cosets times subgroup size equals the group size, validating Lagrange's theorem.")
  )
  :caveats ("Cosets partition the group; the total number of elements across all cosets is |G|." "All cosets have size |H|; if they don't, either the input is not a valid subgroup or the implementation has failed." "Left cosets may differ from right cosets if H is not normal in G.")
  :drawbacks ("Computing cosets requires iterating over all elements; O(|G|·|H|) time." "Cosets depend on the specific subgroup; to quotient properly, you need H to be normal (check with alg/is-normal?).")
  :usecases ("Compute the index [G:H] of a subgroup (number of cosets)." "Verify Lagrange's theorem (|G| = [G:H]·|H|) for a given group and subgroup." "Determine if a subgroup is normal by checking if left and right cosets coincide.")
  :related ("alg/subgroup-gen" "alg/index" "alg/is-normal?" "alg/center")
  :learn (:concept "Cosets are the 'translates' of a subgroup; they partition the group and give rise to quotient structures." :prerequisites ("alg/subgroup-gen" "alg/op") :progression "Use alg/index to count cosets, then explore alg/is-normal? to determine when cosets form a group under multiplication.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "An operator wants to check whether a subgroup H of G is a candidate for building the quotient G/H. Before any quotient work, the audit requires that left and right cosets coincide (normality)."
     :program "(define G (alg/dihedral 4))\n(define H (alg/subgroup-gen G (list 1)))\n(define L (alg/cosets G H))\n(define R (map (lambda (c) (map (lambda (h) (alg/op G h (car c))) H)) L))\n(equal? (map (lambda (c) (list->set c)) L)\n        (map (lambda (c) (list->set c)) R))"
     :explanation "Line 1 builds D_4. Line 2 picks the rotation-subgroup. Line 3 computes left cosets. Line 4 rebuilds them from the right side. Line 5 compares as sets. Any mismatch means the subgroup is not normal, and the quotient G/H is not well-defined."
     :meta "alg/is-normal? gives a boolean; alg/cosets gives the actual partition, so the operator can log which coset differs — a diagnosis, not just a verdict.")
    (:eng "In an audit, showing the offending coset is far more useful than a bare #f."
     :math "H ⊴ G ⇔ gH = Hg for all g."
     :cs "Coset equality is set equality; use sorted lists or hash-sets."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "'Partition of a whole into equal-sized tiles' — a decomposition where each tile is a translate of one anchor."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "alg cosets in a group"     :code "(alg/cosets G H)")
       (:domain "grid tile decomposition"   :code "(grid/tile-plane tile-shape)")
       (:domain "coset-space of a lattice"  :code "(lattice/fundamental-domain L)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1: cosets tile the group with copies of H. Rung 2: a grid decomposition tiles the plane with translated copies of one tile. Rung 3: the fundamental domain of a lattice is one coset representative for R^n / L. The shape 'anchor + translates' is the same in all three."
     :meta "The shape transfers because 'quotient by a subgroup' is the algebraic name for 'tile the space by an equivalence'.")
    (:eng "Anyone who has drawn a grid understands cosets: pick a tile, translate it everywhere, cover the plane."
     :math "Cosets partition G into |G|/|H| equal-sized sets."
     :cs "Storing coset representatives is the standard trick for compact quotient representation."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "Distinct cosets are disjoint, and every element belongs to exactly one coset."
     :program "(define G (alg/dihedral 3))\n(define H (alg/subgroup-gen G (list 1)))\n(define cs (alg/cosets G H))\n(define all-elts (alg/op G))\n(define union-size (apply + (map length cs)))\n(define pairwise-disjoint?\n  (let loop ((cs cs))\n    (cond ((null? cs) #t)\n          ((null? (cdr cs)) #t)\n          (else (and (null? (filter (lambda (x) (member x (cadr cs))) (car cs)))\n                     (loop (cdr cs)))))))\n(and (= union-size (alg/order G)) pairwise-disjoint?)"
     :invariant "∀ g ∈ G. ∃! coset C. g ∈ C  (partition property)"
     :meta "The partition axiom: covers and disjointness. A counter-example would be any element appearing in two cosets, which would falsify the coset relation itself. See book-of-math ch-advanced-04 (Groups & Symmetry).")
    (:eng "Partition tests are cheap and catch bugs where the coset algorithm silently double-counts."
     :math "This is Lagrange's theorem's setup: |G| = [G:H] · |H|."
     :cs "Union-find style datastructures embody the same partition invariant."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "alg/cosets partitions G into left cosets of H."
     :composition "(define G (alg/cyclic 12))\n(define H (alg/subgroup-gen G (list 4)))\n(define cs (alg/cosets G H))\n(define quotient-rep (map car cs))\nquotient-rep"
     :emergent "A quotient-representative list — one canonical name per coset, which is the element set of G/H."
     :meta "The pattern is 'quotient by choosing representatives', which is the same shape as picking canonical strings in a normalization step (Unicode NFC, path canonicalization). See book-of-composition ch-13 (save-load).")
    (:eng "Representatives are how you store an element of a quotient without storing the entire coset."
     :math "G/H is a group iff H is normal; the operation on representatives is well-defined."
     :cs "Representative selection is idempotent (canonicalization); compose with hashing for fast equality."))
)

(verb
  :name "alg/cycles->perm"
  :library "alg"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(alg/cycles->perm degree cycles-list) -> permutation"
  :summary "Build a permutation of degree n from a list of disjoint cycles."
  :explanation "Every permutation can be written uniquely as a product of disjoint cycles. This verb inverts that: given a degree (the set size) and a list of cycles (each cycle is a list of moved elements), it constructs the permutation. This representation is central to permutation group theory."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code ";; Build the 3-cycle (1 2 3) in S_4\n(alg/cycles->perm 4 (list (list 1 2 3)))" :note "Creates a permutation where 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, and 4→4 (fixed).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code ";; Build a product of two disjoint transpositions\n(define perm (alg/cycles->perm 5 (list (list 0 1) (list 3 4))))\n(alg/perm-sign perm)" :note "Two transpositions give even parity (sign +1). The cycles are disjoint, so they commute.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code ";; Convert a cycle representation to permutation, compute order\n(define cycles (list (list 0 1 2) (list 3 4)))\n(define perm (alg/cycles->perm 5 cycles))\n(alg/perm-order perm)" :note "Order is the LCM of cycle lengths: lcm(3, 2) = 6. This permutation returns to identity after 6 applications.")
  )
  :caveats ("Cycles must be disjoint (no element appears in more than one cycle)." "All elements from 0 to degree-1 are implicitly present; unmapped elements are fixed points (1-cycles are omitted)." "Empty cycle list represents the identity permutation.")

       (:domain "sprite frame keyframes"    :code "(animation/from-keys frames)")

(verb
  :name "alg/cyclic"
  :library "alg"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(alg/cyclic n) -> group"
  :summary "Construct the cyclic group ℤ/nℤ of order n under addition modulo n."
  :explanation "The cyclic group of order n is the simplest group structure: all elements are powers of a single generator g, so the group is {e, g, g², …, g^(n-1)}. It is abelian and every element generates a subgroup. In the additive form ℤ/nℤ, the group operation is (a + b) mod n. Cyclic groups classify: every finite cyclic group of order n is isomorphic to ℤ/nℤ. They are also fundamental building blocks for more complex groups via direct products."

;; ═══ 3 verbs in library animation ═══

(verb
  :name "animation/budget"
  :library "animation"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(animation/budget) -> (tier remaining)"
  :summary "Returns a snapshot of the current animation budget: tier level and remaining capacity."
  :explanation "Animation budgets govern how many concurrent animations can run on the surface before reflow kicks in or performance throttles. This verb probes the runtime's current budget state (tier name and how much capacity remains in that tier). The result is non-deterministic because it depends on what animations are currently playing and the system's load. Use this to decide whether to spawn a new animation or defer it."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((budget (animation/budget)))\n  (display (list 'tier (car budget) 'remaining (cadr budget))))" :note "Probe the budget and print its tier and remaining capacity.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (spawn-if-budget-allows card-id)\n  (let ((budget (animation/budget)))\n    (if (> (cadr budget) 0)\n      (card-ease-aside card-id)\n      (display 'budget-exhausted))))\n(spawn-if-budget-allows 'mycard)" :note "Check remaining capacity before triggering an easing animation; skip if exhausted.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define initial-ctx '())\n(define (adaptive-animation-loop state)\n  (let* ((budget (animation/budget))\n         (tier (car budget))\n         (remaining (cadr budget)))\n    (cond\n      ((> remaining 5) (next 'spawn-many (ctx-set 'tier tier state)))\n      ((> remaining 0) (next 'spawn-one (ctx-set 'tier tier state)))\n      (else (next 'wait-for-budget state)))))\n(adaptive-animation-loop initial-ctx)" :note "Steer branching logic based on budget tier and capacity in a state-machine loop.")
  )
  :caveats ("Result is a snapshot; capacity changes immediately as animations play or complete." "Tier names and numeric ranges are runtime-defined and opaque to user code." "Does not block or wait; it is a pure read of the current state.")
  :drawbacks ("Cannot predict future budget pressure—only reflects now." "If budget is exhausted, subsequent animation requests may be queued or dropped silently." "High-frequency polling of animation/budget is redundant; check once per frame or major decision.")
  :usecases ("Deciding whether to spawn a new animation before calling card-ease-aside or camera-pan." "Adaptive rendering: degrading animation fidelity when budget is constrained." "Profiling: tracking when the animation tier downgrades under load.")
  :related ("animation/reflow-policy" "animation/set-reflow-policy" "camera-pan" "scene/spawn-many")
  :learn (:concept "non-deterministic runtime probes—reading mutable state snapshots to steer control flow" :prerequisites ("(core)/let" "(core)/if" "(core)/define") :progression "Next learn animation/reflow-policy (what policy governs reflow during animation) and animation/set-reflow-policy (how to change it).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator is running an on-frame loop that spawns a fresh sprite tween each tick. Under normal load the timeline is smooth. During a busy scene (many concurrent animations already in flight) the newest spawns start dropping frames and the timeline judders. The operator needs a decision gate: before spawning, ask the runtime whether there is room, and if not, defer or skip. The choice is between three verbs that all sound like they might answer this — animation/budget, animation/reflow-policy, and system/health. Only one of them reports the animation-tier capacity directly, and only that reading is a safe basis for a per-frame gate."
     :program "(define (maybe-spawn sprite-id target)\n  (let ((room (animation/budget)))\n    (if (> room 4)\n      (begin (motion/move-to sprite-id target) 'spawned)\n      'deferred)))\n(display (maybe-spawn 'star-1 (list 100 100)))\n(newline)\n(display (maybe-spawn 'star-2 (list 200 200)))\n(newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines the audit gate as a function taking a sprite identifier and a target point. Line 2 reads the current animation budget into `room` — a single integer reflecting how many more animations the runtime is willing to schedule right now. Line 3 branches on that reading: if the budget is comfortably above a small threshold, the sprite gets tweened via motion/move-to and the caller learns 'spawned; otherwise the caller learns 'deferred and the spawn is silently skipped. The two display calls show the gate firing twice in the same tick — both succeed at rest because the initial budget is 16, well above the threshold. The audit tape shows: budget-read, decision, outcome, in that order."
     :meta "Why animation/budget and not a sibling: animation/reflow-policy reports the reflow strategy (a symbol like 'auto), not capacity — you cannot compare a symbol to a number to make a gate. system/health returns a wider process-level report and would over-answer this question. animation/budget is the honest read for the animation-tier gate; the auditor can point at the number, at the threshold, and at the branch, and every step of the reasoning is visible. If a sibling had been used the audit trail would either not exist (reflow-policy has no number) or be so wide it would fail to justify the specific animation-spawn decision.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is the frame-budget probe. Every time the runtime is asked to add work, it may or may not have room; a probe verb lets the operator gate the request. The engineering rule is: probe once per decision, not per candidate — polling in a tight loop dilutes the reading and burns cycles for no signal (see book-of-animation ch05 on timing discipline). The verb never blocks and never throws, so it is safe to call anywhere including from a render callback."
     :math "The reading is a nonnegative integer sampled from a monotonically bounded resource. The audit-safe use is a decision function d(read) → {spawn, defer}, where d is a step function whose threshold is fixed at authoring time. The correctness of the gate depends only on d being pure with respect to its argument — the reading itself may drift between calls, which is a property of the world, not the verb."
     :cs "This is a state-probe: a pure read of a piece of runtime state that is mutated by parties other than the caller. The CS pattern is a producer/consumer capacity check; the classic anti-pattern is check-then-act with a wide gap between the check and the action, which invites TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) drift. Row-2 keeps check and act on adjacent lines to shrink that gap."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A capacity probe: read the current headroom of a bounded resource so the caller can decide whether to enqueue more work. The verb reports 'how much room is left,' and the caller acts on the answer."
     :rungs ((:domain "animation" :code "(if (> (animation/budget) 4) 'spawn 'defer)")
             (:domain "kitchen ticket rail" :code "(if (> (tickets-remaining) 2) 'take-order 'stop-seating)")
             (:domain "semaphore counter" :code "(if (> (sem-permits) 0) 'acquire 'wait)"))
     :explanation "In the animation domain the resource is scheduler capacity and the caller is a spawner; the reading gates whether the next tween is placed on the timeline. In the kitchen the resource is open tickets on the expediter rail and the caller is the host; the reading gates whether a new party is seated or asked to wait. In the semaphore case the resource is permits in a counting semaphore and the caller is a worker; the reading gates whether the worker enters the critical section. The three substrates differ in what the resource IS, but the SHAPE — probe a counter, branch on threshold, either commit or defer — is the same."
     :meta "The shape transfers because all three cases share the same relation between a resource, a probe, and a gated commit. The probe is idempotent within a single tick, the resource has a hard ceiling, and the branch chooses between commit and defer. Any substrate that satisfies those three properties can borrow the shape wholesale — the pattern is not about animation, it is about probes-that-gate-commits.")
    (:eng "Engineering-wise this is capacity-based back-pressure: the caller declines to add work rather than letting the queue overflow. Log the reading and the branch outcome so a later reader can see WHY the system stopped taking work. See book-of-animation ch05 for how timing loops adopt this shape."
     :math "The shape is a threshold predicate on a nonnegative integer state: g(s) = (s > k). The gate g is a monotone Boolean of a monotone reading, so the composite gate is well-defined regardless of concurrent decrement pressure on s."
     :cs "In CS terms this is a nonblocking capacity check — the read-side of a bounded producer/consumer channel. Contrast with a blocking take-when-available (which is a coroutine yield) or an exception-based fail-fast (which raises on empty). All three are legitimate; the probe-and-branch form is the loosest and cheapest."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "animation/budget is a pure read within a single evaluation step: two consecutive calls with no intervening work return the same value, and the value is a nonnegative integer."
     :program "(define a (animation/budget))\n(define b (animation/budget))\n(define c (animation/budget))\n(display (list 'a= a 'b= b 'c= c))\n(newline)\n(display (and (eq? a b) (eq? b c)))\n(newline)\n(display (and (integer? a) (>= a 0)))\n(newline)"
     :invariant "∀ t. let a = read(t), b = read(t) (no scheduler activity between reads) → a = b ∧ a ∈ ℤ≥0"
     :meta "The pattern is state-observation-purity: within an atomic slice of scheduler time the probe is a function, not a stream. The invariant is falsified by any interleaving where an animation completes between the two reads (in which case the equality relaxes to a ≥ b), so the honest statement is 'pure within a slice, monotone-non-increasing across slices in the absence of new spawns.' See book-of-code ch10 for the state-machine framing of tick-scoped purity, and book-of-math ch01 for the natural-number domain of the reading. What would falsify the claim: any single evaluation where two adjacent reads returned different values with no scheduler tick between them. The runtime holds the invariant.")
    (:eng "The engineering payoff is that gate expressions can be written naively: `(if (> (animation/budget) k) ...)` does not need a lock, does not need a snapshot, does not need a retry. The purity is what makes the code readable."
     :math "The claim lives in ℤ≥0 (natural numbers). Two-read equality is reflexivity of `=` on a value produced by a pure function; the ≥ 0 half is a range constraint on the codomain. Nothing higher-order is required."
     :cs "This is the read-purity condition for lock-free readers of a monotone counter. Related patterns: seqlocks (a fancier form that still exposes a stable read), RCU (read-copy-update). The probe here is the simplest instance."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "animation/budget is a per-tick probe of scheduler headroom."
     :composition "(define (spawn-with-cap n)\n  (if (or (= n 0) (<= (animation/budget) 4))\n    'stopped\n    (begin\n      (motion/move-to (list 'star n) (list (* n 10) (* n 10)))\n      (spawn-with-cap (- n 1)))))\n(display (spawn-with-cap 3))\n(newline)"
     :emergent "throttle — a bounded producer that stops emitting the moment the downstream signals it is full"
     :meta "The composition chains animation/budget (probe) with motion/move-to (commit) inside a recursion. What emerges is the throttle family: a producer that halts on a downstream signal rather than letting the queue overflow. The same family appears as token-bucket rate limiters in network stacks, as high-water-mark back-pressure in streaming pipelines, and as the classic bounded work-queue in an executor. In book-of-composition ch16 this pattern is called out as one of the core back-pressure shapes for composing games (spawn budget on enemies, particles, sound voices). What makes it a throttle and not a plain loop is that the terminating condition is EXOGENOUS — the loop stops because the world signals it should, not because the caller finished a fixed list."
     )
    (:eng "The operational win of a throttle is that the system's degradation mode is 'do less' rather than 'crash.' If the runtime is under load the throttle produces fewer things; the user sees a slower scene, not a broken one. Log the stop reason so the operator can distinguish 'reached end of list' from 'throttled by budget.'"
     :math "The throttle is a fold with an early-exit condition: fold f z xs, exiting when g(state) is false. The exit function g is `(> budget k)`, evaluated at each step against a resource that other threads may be draining."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is bounded producer (or, equivalently, watermark-triggered back-pressure). Familiar siblings: Erlang's flow-controlled mailboxes, TCP's receive-window-driven pacing, node.js's writable-stream `.write()` returning false to signal back-pressure. Motoi's animation/budget occupies the same slot in the animation subsystem.")))

(verb
  :name "animation/reflow-policy"
  :library "animation"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(animation/reflow-policy) -> policy-symbol"
  :summary "Returns the current default policy governing DOM reflow behavior during animations."
  :explanation "While animations run, the system can either reflow the DOM eagerly (allowing real-time measurement at a cost) or defer reflow until the animation completes (faster, but stale measurements). This verb returns the current global policy. It is deterministic—the policy does not change unless animation/set-reflow-policy is called. Use it to understand what reflow behavior is in effect, or to restore a prior policy after a temporary override."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((policy (animation/reflow-policy)))\n  (display (list 'current-policy policy)))" :note "Inspect the current reflow policy.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (with-eager-reflow body)\n  (let ((prior (animation/reflow-policy)))\n    (animation/set-reflow-policy 'eager)\n    (begin body)\n    (animation/set-reflow-policy prior)))\n(with-eager-reflow (lambda () (card-ease-aside 'mycard)))" :note "Save the current policy, switch to eager, run animation, restore the prior policy.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (measure-with-animation measurement-fn)\n  (let ((policy (animation/reflow-policy)))\n    (cond\n      ((eq? policy 'eager)\n       (measurement-fn))\n      (else\n       (animation/set-reflow-policy 'eager)\n       (let ((result (measurement-fn)))\n         (animation/set-reflow-policy policy)\n         result)))))\n(let ((h (measure-with-animation (lambda () (card-rect 'mycard)))))\n  (display h))" :note "Conditionally enable eager reflow only if needed for accurate measurement, then restore.")
  )
  :caveats ("The set of policy symbols and their semantics are opaque; treat the return value as an enumeration." "Changing the policy mid-animation may have no effect on that animation; it applies to future animations." "Policy is global; changing it affects all concurrent animations.")
  :drawbacks ("Eager reflow is slower (forces layout recalculation). Deferred reflow is faster but may cause measurements to be stale." "No per-animation override; the policy is all-or-nothing for the whole system.")
  :usecases ("Querying the current reflow mode to decide whether measurements are safe." "Implementing transactional animation control (save/restore policy around a critical section)." "Profiling: checking which policy is active before tuning animation performance.")
  :related ("animation/budget" "animation/set-reflow-policy" "system/health" "scene/clear")
  :learn (:concept "reading configuration state deterministically; understanding that deterministic reads enable safe save/restore patterns" :prerequisites ("(core)/let" "(core)/eq?" "(core)/begin") :progression "Next learn animation/set-reflow-policy (how to change the policy) and animation/budget (how to monitor runtime capacity).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator is about to run a sequence of measurements against animated sprites — reading positions, sizes, or derived geometry mid-animation for a report. Some readings are only trustworthy if the layout is up-to-date on every animation frame; others tolerate a small lag. The runtime exposes a global policy that controls this trade-off, but the operator does not know what the policy currently IS. The sibling verbs animation/budget and animation/set-reflow-policy do not answer this — one reports capacity, the other mutates. Only animation/reflow-policy returns the current setting."

Line 4 reads it again after some hypothetical idle work has happened; if nothing has called animation/set-reflow-policy in the meantime, the two readings agree.      :math "The verb is a nullary function into a small finite set of symbols. Two calls with no intervening write to the same underlying cell return the same symbol — a purity property in the discrete setting."
     :cs "This is a getter for a global configuration cell. The CS pattern is a stateless read of stateful data; the read carries no locks and never blocks.   :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A configuration-reader: probe a piece of state whose value influences downstream behavior, and use the answer to tag or steer subsequent work. The reader itself changes nothing; it only reports."
     :rungs ((:domain "animation" :code "(let ((p (animation/reflow-policy))) (list 'tagged-with p))")
             (:domain "kitchen order pad" :code "(let ((mode (kitchen-mode))) (list 'ticket-under mode))")

  :row-4-proof (

     :meta "The pattern is read-idempotence plus write-through-round-trip: reading is a fixed point (repeated reads collapse to one), and any write followed by a restoring write returns the observable state to where it began. What would falsify this: if a background scheduler could rewrite the policy cell between two consecutive reads and no writer had been called, the equality would break.     (:eng "Deterministic getters let the operator write straight-line code around configuration reads: no locks, no retry, no snapshot ceremony. Half the value of the invariant is that it makes the calling code simpler."

  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "animation/reflow-policy is a nullary read of the current reflow policy."
     :composition "(define (with-policy p body-fn)\n  (let ((prior (animation/reflow-policy)))\n    (animation/set-reflow-policy p)\n    (let ((result (body-fn)))\n      (animation/set-reflow-policy prior)\n      result)))\n(display (with-policy 'eager (lambda () (list 'measured (animation/reflow-policy)))))\n(newline)\n(display (animation/reflow-policy))\n(newline)"

     :cs "The CS pattern name is scoped resource / dynamic-extent parameter (also 'context manager,' 'RAII,' or 'unwind-protect'). (verb
  :name "animation/set-reflow-policy"
  :library "animation"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(animation/set-reflow-policy policy) -> null"
  :summary "Sets the global default reflow policy governing DOM behavior during animations."
  :explanation "Use this to switch between eager and deferred (or other) reflow modes.   :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(animation/set-reflow-policy 'deferred)\n(display 'reflow-set-to-deferred)" :note "Switch to deferred reflow for faster animation playback.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (high-performance-sequence)\n  (animation/set-reflow-policy 'deferred)\n  (card-ease-aside 'card1)\n  (card-ease-aside 'card2)\n  (animation/set-reflow-policy 'eager))\n(high-performance-sequence)" :note "Batch multiple animations in deferred mode, then switch back to eager.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (with-policy policy body-fn)\n  (let ((prior (animation/reflow-policy)))\n    (animation/set-reflow-policy policy)\n    (let ((result (body-fn)))\n      (animation/set-reflow-policy prior)\n      result)))\n(with-policy 'eager (lambda () (card-toss 'mycard (list 100 100))))" :note "Higher-order function that temporarily overrides policy, ensuring restoration even if body-fn has side effects.")

  :caveats ("Policy change is immediate and global; all running and future animations are affected." "Changing the policy mid-animation does not interrupt or alter that animation." "Policy names and available options are opaque; passing an unknown symbol may be silently ignored or error." "This is a state change; use with discipline in pure contexts (e.g., do not call from a measurement function).")
  :drawbacks ("Global policy is coarse: cannot set different policies for different animations." "Forgetting to restore the prior policy can leak policy state across unrelated animations." "Eager reflow every frame incurs a layout cost on every animation frame; use sparingly.")
  :usecases ("Optimizing a batch of animations by switching to deferred mode, then back to eager." "Temporarily enabling eager reflow for a measurement-heavy animation sequence." "Implementing a scoped policy override (via a helper like with-policy above).")
  :related ("animation/reflow-policy" "animation/budget" "scene/spawn-many" "camera-pan" "motion/move-to")
  :learn (:concept "state-changing operations and save/restore patterns—using reads to enable safe mutations" :prerequisites ("(core)/let" "(core)/define" "animation/reflow-policy") :progression "Practice writing save/restore wrappers (with-policy style) before using animation/set-reflow-policy in production code.     (:problem "The operator is about to run a burst of ten motion tweens back to back. Under the default reflow policy each tween triggers a layout pass, which is fine for one tween but redundant for a burst — the intermediate layouts are never observed. The operator wants to switch the runtime into a mode that defers layout until the burst ends, run the burst, and then switch back. The choice is which verb performs the switch: animation/reflow-policy only reads, animation/budget only reports capacity, and animation/set-reflow-policy is the only verb whose signature (`(policy) -> null`) permits a write. The auditor's question at the end of the burst will be: 'was the policy restored?' — so the audit trail needs the write to be paired with a restore."
     :program "(define prior (animation/reflow-policy))\n(animation/set-reflow-policy 'deferred)\n(motion/move-to 'star-1 (list 10 10))\n(motion/move-to 'star-2 (list 20 20))\n(motion/move-to 'star-3 (list 30 30))\n(animation/set-reflow-policy prior)\n(display (list 'policy-after (animation/reflow-policy)))\n(newline)\n(display (list 'restored? (eq? (animation/reflow-policy) prior)))\n(newline)"

Line 6 restores the policy to `prior` — the audit-mandated restore step.      :meta "Why animation/set-reflow-policy and not a sibling: animation/reflow-policy would return the current policy but never change it — the burst optimization requires the change. animation/budget would report scheduler headroom but has no bearing on layout cost.     (:eng "Operationally, every setter in a system needs a restore discipline. The runtime does not restore for you — it will happily leave the policy at 'deferred forever if the operator forgets.      :math "The verb is a state transformer: policy × state → state. The composition set(p); set(q) has the effect of set(q) alone (the second write wins), which is the write-latest property of a single-cell register."
     :cs "This is a setter for a global configuration cell. The CS pattern is a writer of a single-writer, many-reader location; the classical failure mode is a lost-restore where the caller forgets to pair the set with a symmetric set-back. Row 2 shows the paired form; Row 5 packages it into a reusable wrapper."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A configuration-writer: assign a new value to a global cell, changing how downstream code behaves until the next assignment. The value is chosen from a small enum, and the assignment takes effect immediately for all future reads."
     :rungs ((:domain "animation" :code "(animation/set-reflow-policy 'deferred)")

             (:domain "sign bit of a two's-complement register" :code "(register-set-msb! r #t)"))

In the traffic-light substrate the write flips a phase-controller cell that governs which lane sees green; every physical light on the north-south corridor changes on the next controller tick. In the register substrate the write sets a specific bit in a hardware cell; every downstream instruction that reads the register now sees the new sign. The three cases differ enormously in latency, in blast radius, and in the type of value being written, but the SHAPE — a nullary-return write into a small-enum global — is identical."
     :meta "The shape transfers because all three cases share the same relation between a writer, a cell, and a downstream reader. There is no ceremony (no ack, no promise, no confirmation); the writer trusts the callee to record the value and every subsequent reader to observe it.     (:eng "Engineering-wise the caution about setters is universal: log the write, log the restore, and if the code can panic between the two, wrap it. Silent leaks of setter state are one of the most durable classes of production bug because there is no per-request trail of who set what to what."
     :math "A state transformer indexed by a discrete parameter. The set of transformers forms a monoid under composition where the identity is set(current) and the group law is set(p); set(q) = set(q)."

     :invariant "∀ p ∈ Policy. set(p); read() = p; ∀ p₁ … pₙ ∈ Policy. set(p₁); …; set(pₙ); read() = pₙ"
     :meta "The pattern is the register-write contract: a single-cell store obeys write-then-read (the read after the write returns the written value) and last-write-wins (only the most recent write is observable). What would falsify the claim: any intervening scheduler activity that mutates the policy between the last set and the read, or a runtime where the setter is asynchronous and does not take effect before the next read.     (:eng "The write-then-read contract lets the operator reason locally: if I write p, the next read returns p. That local reasoning is what makes it possible to write short paired blocks (set; do work; set-back) rather than long ceremonies with locks and confirmations."

  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "animation/set-reflow-policy is a nullary-return write of a global reflow policy."
     :composition "(define (bracket-policy p thunk)\n  (let ((prior (animation/reflow-policy)))\n    (animation/set-reflow-policy p)\n    (let ((result (thunk)))\n      (animation/set-reflow-policy prior)\n      result)))\n(define (burst)\n  (motion/move-to 'a (list 1 1))\n  (motion/move-to 'b (list 2 2))\n  (motion/move-to 'c (list 3 3))\n  'burst-done)\n(display (bracket-policy 'deferred burst))\n(newline)\n(display (list 'policy-after (animation/reflow-policy)))\n(newline)"

;;; 05-artifact.slat — Motoi Scheme Reference · Chapter 05 · library artifact
;;;
;;; 4 verbs in this library. Read chapter 00-intro.slat first.

;;;
;;; ─── THE ROW RULES (summary — full doctrine in 00-intro.slat) ───
;;;
;;; Every verb in this chapter has 5 rows. Each row does ONE job. Row
;;; contamination unbalances training data. If you author or edit a verb,
;;; STAY IN LANE.
;;;
;;;   Row 1 (HOW · Composition) — the verb written well; 1/3/5 module ladder
;;;   Row 2 (WHEN · Audit)      — operator's problem + this-verb-not-a-sibling
;;;   Row 3 (WHERE ELSE · Dim)  — same shape in 3 substrates (verb/metaphor/math)
;;;   Row 4 (WHY · Proof)       — claim + runnable test + ∀-invariant
;;;   Row 5 (WITH WHAT ELSE)    — chained verbs → named emergent pattern
;;;
;;; Every row carries the three-discipline lens: :eng · :math · :cs.
;;; No philosopher names in entries (they live in 00-intro.slat).
;;; Real Motoi domains only (no card/*, shop/*, cine/*, flower/*).
;;; Every code block RUNS through ./bin/motoi (or is marked :runs "spec-only").
;;;
;;; Introspection is a first-class chapter — see 00b-introspection.slat.
;;; Before authoring, run: python3 scripts/audit-reference-rows.py
;;; Before folding, run: python3 scripts/compliance-check-runnable.py
;;;

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Library artifact — 4 verbs.")

(chapter :number "05" :library "artifact" :verb-count 4 :training-eligible #t)

;; ═══ 4 verbs in library artifact ═══

(verb
  :name "artifact/cite"
  :library "artifact"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(artifact/cite id) -> ['pending' msg]"
  :summary "Asynchronously retrieves an artifact by ID and dispatches a curator:artifact-cite event with the result."
  :explanation "artifact/cite takes an artifact ID (symbol or string) and issues a GET request to the artifact API endpoint. The result is dispatched as a CustomEvent (curator:artifact-cite) with detail containing ok, artifact data, and any error. This is a fire-and-forget pattern: it returns immediately with a pending status and does not block on the HTTP response. Listen for the CustomEvent to receive the actual artifact."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(artifact/cite 'my-sketch-42)" :note "Retrieve artifact with ID 'my-sketch-42'; result arrives asynchronously as an event")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define ctx '())\n(let ((id (ctx-result ctx)))\n  (artifact/cite id))" :note "Derive the ID from context (e.g., prior action result) and cite it")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define artifact-id 'artifact-id)\n(define ctx '())\n(begin\n  (artifact/cite artifact-id)\n  (next 'await-cite-event ctx))" :note "Cite an artifact and transition to a state that listens for the curator:artifact-cite event")
  )
  :caveats ("No ID argument returns an error tuple; empty/null IDs are rejected." "The call is asynchronous and non-blocking; the artifact data is not returned immediately." "Requires a window.dispatchEvent listener (e.g., via JavaScript event binding) to observe the result." "Network failure or API error is reflected in the event detail, not in the return value.")
  :drawbacks ("Fire-and-forget pattern makes it hard to chain in pure Scheme; you must use state transitions or event listeners." "Does not return the artifact directly; requires coupling to JavaScript event handling." "If the event listener is not set up, the result is silently lost.")
  :usecases ("Fetching a saved artifact (image, code, design, document) for display or further processing." "Referencing an artifact by ID in a workflow where the artifact was previously saved." "Integrating artifact retrieval into a multi-step state machine where the result triggers a later transition.")
  :related ("artifact/save" "artifact/delete" "artifact/list")
  :learn (:concept "Artifact I/O as an asynchronous event-driven pattern; separating request from response." :prerequisites ("ctx-result" "next") :progression "After artifact/cite, learn artifact/save to create artifacts, then artifact/list to query multiple artifacts.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "A saved sketch was rendered five minutes ago and the operator now wants to display its payload again in a new card. The id is on record; the payload is not in memory. The audit question: which verb is the honest answer to 'fetch by id, one row, from the artifact store'?"
     :program "(define ctx '())\n(define target-id (card-get ctx 'saved-sketch-id))\n(artifact/cite target-id)\n(next 'await-cite-event ctx)"
     :explanation "Line 1 sets up an empty ctx placeholder (real ctx arrives from the caller). Line 2 pulls the id the operator wants to fetch from card state — nothing else on the card is being touched. Line 3 issues the fetch: artifact/cite takes exactly one argument (the id), issues the GET, and returns the ['pending' msg] tuple immediately. Line 4 hands control to the state named 'await-cite-event, which is where the CustomEvent listener has been registered. When the server replies, the listener receives detail.artifact and the state machine advances."
     :meta "Not artifact/list — list would need a filter alist and return an array of zero-or-more artifacts, forcing the caller to loop and pick. Not artifact/save — save WRITES, and the operator is READING. Not artifact/delete — delete is destructive and needs the destructive-permission grant, which is heavier than a read. artifact/cite is the one-id-one-record read verb; using anything else would fail the audit for either over-fetch (list) or wrong-effect-class (save/delete).")
    (:eng "The operator sees an immediate ['pending' msg] tuple in the log and knows the request left the process; the actual arrival is a curator:artifact-cite event on window. If the listener is missing, the event fires into nothing — the SRE lesson is 'wire the listener before you fire the verb, or the trace goes dark.' Grounded in book-of-computing ch15 (operating systems and networks) — the fire-and-forget pattern lives inside the same event-loop discipline as UNIX signals."

    (:eng "The pattern lets the operator build a change-detection UI without needing server-push infrastructure. The cost is proportional to the polling interval times the batch size."
     :math "The change signal Δ(t) = |R(t)| − |R(t−δ)| is the discrete derivative of the result-size series. Alert-on-positive is the sign detector. Book-of-math ch-advanced-03 (recurrence) covers the sequence."
     :cs "Poll-based observers are the fallback when push isn't available; the pattern converts a pull API into a push signal by adding a scheduler and a last-known-state slot. Book-of-code ch09 (registers, counters) covers the counter role; book-of-composition ch08 (timeline) covers the tick.")))

(verb
  :name "artifact/save"
  :library "artifact"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(artifact/save options) -> ('pending msg) ; options is an alist with (kind . k) (payload . d) required, (title . t) (bot . b) (tags . ts) (source-url . u) optional"
  :summary "Asynchronously saves an artifact with metadata (kind, payload, title, tags) to the artifact store and dispatches a curator:artifact-save event."
  :explanation "artifact/save accepts keyword arguments defining an artifact: :kind (required), :payload (required), and optional :title, :bot, :tags, :source-url. It issues a POST/PUT request to persist the artifact and returns immediately with a pending status, dispatching a CustomEvent (curator:artifact-save) when the server responds. This allows you to save results (sketches, code, images, documents) to a persistent store without blocking execution."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define my-svg-string 'my-svg-string)\n(artifact/save `((kind . sketch) (payload . ,my-svg-string)))" :note "Save a sketch artifact with auto-generated ID and title")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define ctx '())\n(artifact/save `((kind . code)\n                 (payload . ,(ctx-result ctx))\n                 (title . \"Generated Function\")\n                 (tags . (auto-generated draft))))" :note "Save generated code with a title and multiple tags")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define ctx '())\n(let ((result (ctx-result ctx)))\n  (artifact/save `((kind . design)\n                   (payload . ,result)\n                   (title . ,(card-get ctx 'artifact-name))\n                   (bot . my-agent)\n                   (tags . ,(list 'production (card-get ctx 'version))))))" :note "Save an artifact with metadata from context and card state, then transition to await the save event")
  )
  :caveats ("Both :kind and :payload are required; missing either returns an error tuple without making a request." "The call is asynchronous; the server-generated artifact ID is not returned immediately." "Requires a window.dispatchEvent listener to observe the result (which includes the new artifact ID)." ":bot defaults to 'cart' if not specified." ":tags must be an array; non-array tag values are ignored.")
  :drawbacks ("Fire-and-forget pattern; no synchronous ID or confirmation." "Large payloads may incur network latency." "Duplicate saves with identical kind/payload may create multiple artifacts if called rapidly." "No built-in deduplication or conflict resolution.")
  :usecases ("Saving generated code, designs, or images for later retrieval or export." "Creating a checkpoint or snapshot of work at a key milestone." "Archiving results from a computation or workflow for auditing." "Implementing 'Save' and 'Save As' buttons in a card or form.")
  :related ("artifact/cite" "artifact/delete" "artifact/list")
  :learn (:concept "Persistent I/O and artifact lifecycle; saving typed, tagged data with metadata." :prerequisites ("let" "ctx-result" "next") :progression "After artifact/save, learn artifact/list to query saved artifacts, then artifact/cite to retrieve by ID.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "An in-memory computation produced a payload (say, a generated SVG sketch) that the operator wants to keep for later retrieval — after the session ends, after a reload, after handoff to another workflow. The audit question: which verb turns a live in-memory value into a durable, id-addressable, kind-tagged record?"
     :program "(define ctx '())\n(define payload (ctx-result ctx))\n(artifact/save `((kind    . sketch)\n                 (payload . ,payload)\n                 (title   . \"Session output — sketch v1\")\n                 (tags    . (draft session-42))))\n(next 'await-save-confirm ctx)"
     :explanation "Line 1 is the ctx placeholder. Line 2 pulls the in-memory value from ctx-result — this is the runtime handoff between the compute stage and the persist stage. Lines 3–6 fire artifact/save with the required (kind, payload) plus optional title and tags. The verb returns ['pending' msg] immediately; the server allocates the id and returns it via curator:artifact-save. Line 7 hands control to a state that reads detail.artifact.id, stashes it, and moves on."
     :meta "Not artifact/cite — cite is a read; there is nothing to read yet, the record does not exist. Not artifact/list — list enumerates existing records, and again the record does not exist. Not artifact/delete — nothing is being removed. Not a plain in-memory set! — a plain assignment does not survive a reload. artifact/save is the only verb whose job is 'create a durable, addressable record from a value.' Any sibling fails the audit for the same reason: none of them CREATE.")
    (:eng "The operator sees one ['pending' msg] on the log and one curator:artifact-save event carrying the server-generated id. That id is the receipt — without it the artifact is orphaned. SRE reflex: always attach a listener that captures detail.artifact.id BEFORE firing the verb, or the id can be lost. Grounded in book-of-computing ch04 (where to write user data) — durable state has a home; save is the door to that home."
     :math "The operation is a function payload × metadata → id where id ∈ freshly-allocated ids. It is not idempotent — two identical saves produce two distinct ids. The domain is arbitrary payload values; the codomain is the id space."
     :cs "Effect class = io + async + create. The keyword-argument alist carries both required fields (kind, payload) and optional metadata. Book-of-code ch08 (memory latches, flip-flops) covers the durable-storage tier; book-of-composition ch13 (save-load) covers the round-trip discipline for save-then-cite."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is create-durable-record-with-server-issued-key. The caller provides content and hints; the server provides identity."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "artifact"  :code "(artifact/save `((kind . sketch) (payload . ,svg)))")
       (:domain "postal"    :code ";; you deposit a package at the courier's counter with a customs\n;; declaration slip (kind: fragile, contents: glass, sender: you).\n;; The clerk assigns a tracking number, tags the package, files\n;; the record, and later mails you back the tracking number. The\n;; slip is your alist; the number is your id.")
       (:domain "logic"     :code ";; INSERT INTO store (kind, payload, title, tags)\n;;   VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)\n;;   RETURNING id;\n;; server-generated primary key; caller supplies content, receives\n;; identity. The record is only reachable AFTER the RETURNING\n;; clause hands back the id."))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is the verb. Rung 2 is the courier analog: you supply the content, the counter supplies the tracking number, and the record is filed in the archive under that number — you cannot retrieve the package later without the number, which is why the confirmation event matters. Rung 3 is SQL INSERT with RETURNING id: the same request/response shape at the database boundary. Both non-verb rungs share the essential asymmetry — content flows in from the caller, identity flows back from the store."
     :meta "The shape transfers because durable creation everywhere splits responsibility across the boundary: the caller knows what to store, the store knows where and under which key. Any system with a primary-key allocator on the server side has this shape — databases, object stores, mail systems, ticketing systems, tax filings.")
    (:eng "In every rung, the receipt is load-bearing. Losing the id means losing the artifact; the SRE discipline is to persist the id to a durable slot (ctx, card state, local storage) before advancing the state machine."

     :cs "Server-issued key allocation is the standard alternative to client-generated UUIDs; the choice affects race conditions and offline behavior. Book-of-code ch09 (registers, counters) covers the counter that issues the id; book-of-composition ch13 (save-load) covers the round-trip."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "artifact/save preserves the payload under round-trip: for any save that returns id and any subsequent cite of id, the artifact payload delivered by cite equals the payload that was saved, provided no delete or update intervenes."
     :program ";; Round-trip payload-preservation check. DOM-hosted; symbolic in\n;; the headless motoi runtime.\n(define saved-payload '(vertices (0 0) (1 0) (1 1) (0 1)))\n(define saved-id #f)\n(define fetched-payload #f)\n(add-event-listener 'curator:artifact-save\n  (lambda (ev) (set! saved-id (get-detail ev 'id))))\n(add-event-listener 'curator:artifact-cite\n  (lambda (ev) (set! fetched-payload\n                     (get-detail ev 'payload))))\n(artifact/save `((kind    . polygon)\n                 (payload . ,saved-payload)))\n;; after the save event fills saved-id:\n(artifact/cite saved-id)\n;; after the cite event fills fetched-payload:\n(define check\n  (lambda () (equal? saved-payload fetched-payload)))\n;; (check) => #t\n"
     :invariant "∀ payload, kind. let id = save(kind, payload) in cite(id).payload = payload  (before any delete or update of id)."
     :meta "The engineering consequence is that save + cite together form a durable identity for the payload — the same value can be re-materialized after a reload. Falsifier: any lossy encoding on the store side (payload trimming, encoding conversion) would break the invariant. CS pattern name: round-trip preservation (a functor's naturality condition applied to the store's serialization). Book-of-code ch08 (memory latches) covers the durable-slot side. :runs \"spec-only\" — DOM-hosted; the runtime binding is a stub in headless motoi.")
    (:eng "The proof matters when a user reports 'my saved sketch came back different.' If the invariant holds by construction, the report indicates a store-tier bug — a broken invariant, not user error. The audit direction is: check the store's serialization, not the client's code."
     :math "Round-trip: cite ∘ save = id (on the payload projection). This is a retract in the categorical sense — save has a left inverse. Book-of-math ch-advanced-04 (groups, symmetry) covers retracts."
     :cs "The pattern is round-trip preservation, the same property that makes JSON serialize/parse safe for JSON-shaped values, that makes gzip round-trip pure bytes, and that makes a save-then-load work in any editor. Book-of-code ch08 covers the durable-slot side; book-of-composition ch13 (save-load) covers the round-trip discipline directly."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "artifact/save creates a durable, id-addressable, kind-tagged record from an in-memory payload."
     :composition "(define history '())\n(define (checkpoint! payload label)\n  (artifact/save `((kind    . checkpoint)\n                   (payload . ,payload)\n                   (title   . ,label)\n                   (tags    . (checkpoint auto)))))\n(add-event-listener 'curator:artifact-save\n  (lambda (ev)\n    (let ((id    (get-detail ev 'id))\n          (title (get-detail ev 'title)))\n      (when (member 'checkpoint (get-detail ev 'tags))\n        (set! history (cons (cons id title) history))))))\n\n;; usage — take a snapshot at every major milestone:\n(checkpoint! current-state \"start\")\n;; ... work ...\n(checkpoint! current-state \"after-phase-1\")\n;; ... more work ...\n(checkpoint! current-state \"after-phase-2\")"
     :emergent "a snapshot — specifically an append-only checkpoint history: every save adds one more (id, title) entry to a growing list, and the list itself is a timeline of durable rewind points."
     :meta "This is the same family as git commits (each commit is an addressable snapshot), as VM snapshots (each entry rewindable), as a database WAL (each record replayable). Book-of-composition ch13 (save-load) covers the snapshot/restore side directly. Log signature: 'N checkpoints across the session, average payload size M, average interval Δt.'")
    (:eng "The pattern gives the operator undo across sessions, incident-response rewind points, and audit trails — all as a byproduct of routine save calls. Storage grows monotonically, so eviction policy (delete oldest checkpoints past N) is a real concern."
     :math "The history is an ordered sequence (chronological, append-only) that models a natural-number-indexed family of store states. Book-of-math ch-advanced-03 (sequences, recurrence) covers indexed families."
     :cs "The snapshot pattern is the append-only side of event-sourcing and log-structured storage. Book-of-code ch08 (latches, flip-flops) covers per-checkpoint durability; book-of-composition ch13 (save-load) covers the pattern's shape; book-of-computing ch07 (write log) covers the log discipline that makes checkpoints usable.")))

;;; 06-assert.slat — Motoi Scheme Reference · Chapter 06 · library assert
;;;
;;; 3 verbs in this library. Read chapter 00-intro.slat first.

;;;
;;; ─── THE ROW RULES (summary — full doctrine in 00-intro.slat) ───
;;;
;;; Every verb in this chapter has 5 rows. Each row does ONE job. Row
;;; contamination unbalances training data. If you author or edit a verb,
;;; STAY IN LANE.
;;;
;;;   Row 1 (HOW · Composition) — the verb written well; 1/3/5 module ladder
;;;   Row 2 (WHEN · Audit)      — operator's problem + this-verb-not-a-sibling
;;;   Row 3 (WHERE ELSE · Dim)  — same shape in 3 substrates (verb/metaphor/math)
;;;   Row 4 (WHY · Proof)       — claim + runnable test + ∀-invariant
;;;   Row 5 (WITH WHAT ELSE)    — chained verbs → named emergent pattern
;;;
;;; Every row carries the three-discipline lens: :eng · :math · :cs.
;;; No philosopher names in entries (they live in 00-intro.slat).
;;; Real Motoi domains only (no card/*, shop/*, cine/*, flower/*).
;;; Every code block RUNS through ./bin/motoi (or is marked :runs "spec-only").
;;;
;;; Introspection is a first-class chapter — see 00b-introspection.slat.

;;; Before folding, run: python3 scripts/compliance-check-runnable.py
;;;

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Library assert — 3 verbs.")

(chapter :number "06" :library "assert" :verb-count 3 :training-eligible #t)

;; ═══ 3 verbs in library assert ═══

(verb
  :name "assert/check-with"
  :library "assert"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(assert/check-with pred value message) -> value | raises"
  :summary "Predicate assertion: run `pred` on `value`; if it returns falsy, raise an 'assertion-failed condition with the value + message. On pass, return the value so it chains inside expressions."
  :explanation "The lightest assertion Motoi ships. Pass a predicate procedure, a value, and a short human-readable message. If the predicate returns truthy, the value flows through unchanged (so you can drop the check inline: `(let ((n (assert/check-with positive? x \"n>0\"))) …)`). If the predicate returns #f, #!null, or #!undefined, the check raises an ErrorObject whose type is 'assertion-failed and whose irritants are the offending value. If the predicate itself throws, the failure is re-wrapped as an assertion-failed condition so the caller sees a uniform surface. Handlers catch via with-exception-handler or R7RS guard and can dispatch on error-object-type."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(assert/check-with positive? 3 \"must be positive\")" :note "Returns 3 unchanged — the predicate passes.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (safe-sqrt x)\n  (let ((n (assert/check-with (lambda (v) (>= v 0)) x \"n must be nonneg\")))\n    (sqrt n)))\n(safe-sqrt 16)" :note "Chain the check inside a let-binding so bad inputs raise before the sqrt call. Passes with 4; if called with -1, raises assertion-failed.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (deposit account amount)\n  (assert/check-with number? amount \"amount must be numeric\")\n  (assert/check-with positive? amount \"amount must be positive\")\n  (assert/check-with (lambda (a) (< a 10000)) amount \"amount capped at 10000\")\n  (+ (cdr (assq 'balance account)) amount))\n(deposit (list (cons 'balance 100)) 42)" :note "Stack multiple checks at the top of a function as a lightweight contract. Each failure raises with a distinct message; the caller's guard sees all three types the same way.")
  )
  :caveats ("The predicate MUST be a procedure; passing a value there raises 'assertion-arg-error, not a normal assertion failure." "If the predicate throws, the throw is re-wrapped as assertion-failed and the inner message is preserved in the raised message. The original stack is lost." "Message may be a string OR a symbol; both are stringified. Longer messages are better for humans; short symbols are faster to author." "Truthy return values other than #t (numbers, strings, procedures) all count as pass — this matches Scheme's usual truthiness.")
  :drawbacks ("Runtime cost is one procedure call + one truthy test per assertion. Cheap, but not free; strip assertions from hot loops if they're not paying their way." "No structured detail beyond the value and message; use assert/audit-verify for shape checks that return a failure path." "Cannot suppress the assertion; the only ways to skip it are to remove the call or catch the failure and continue.")
  :usecases ("Pre-condition checks at function entry (numeric args, non-empty lists, positive amounts)." "Post-condition checks before returning a computed value." "Sanity checks inside a let-binding: the value flows through on pass, raises on fail." "Building lightweight contracts without importing a full contract system.")
  :related ("assert/invariants" "assert/audit-verify" "error" "raise" "escalate" "with-exception-handler" "guard")
  :learn (:concept "Predicate assertions as an inline sanity gate: run a check, pass the value through, or raise a structured condition." :prerequisites ("lambda" "predicates like positive? or number?" "with-exception-handler") :progression "Start with a single assert/check-with at a function's entry; then stack a few to build a mini-contract; then upgrade to assert/audit-verify when you need to check the SHAPE of an object rather than a single scalar.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The physics tick keeps producing NaN positions three ticks after the score jumps to a suspicious value. The operator watching the log knows the drop happened somewhere inside the step but the crash surfaces later, deep in the render pass, where the stack trace is useless. The engineer needs a check that raises AT THE MOMENT the bad value is born, not five frames downstream where it is unrecoverable."
     :program "(define (advance-entity e dt)\n  (let ((vx (cadr (assq 'vx e))))\n    (assert/check-with number? vx \"vx must be numeric at tick entry\")\n    (assert/check-with pair? e \"entity must be a pair-list\")\n    (+ vx (* dt 9.8))))\n(display (advance-entity (list (list 'vx 3.0)) 0.016)) (newline)"
     :explanation "The function pulls vx from the entity alist and runs a numeric check before it enters any arithmetic. If vx is #f, a symbol, or #!null (the three most common ways an entity forgets to initialize a field) the assertion fires immediately with the offending value in irritants and a stack that points at THIS line, not at the sqrt call five frames later that finally NaN-poisoned the framebuffer. The passing value flows through unchanged so the surrounding math sees no wrapper. The check costs one call plus one truthy test per tick — measured cheap enough to leave enabled in production loops as long as they are not inner render loops."
     :meta "Chosen over raw error/raise because assert/check-with raises with a STRUCTURED error-type ('assertion-failed) that the audit lane's handler can pattern-match on. A bare (raise ...) buries the failure kind in a string and the operator has to grep the log to know whether they are looking at an assertion or an unrelated crash. Chosen over assert/audit-verify because vx is a single scalar — the spec-tree walk that audit-verify does is overkill for one field. Chosen over assert/invariants because a batch check does not short-circuit — for a per-tick guard we WANT short-circuit; the first bad value should stop the tick, not run three more checks that all fail the same way.")
    (:eng "Operator log will show `assertion-failed: vx must be numeric at tick entry` at the exact tick number, with the entity's id in the surrounding context. Alerting: page on 'assertion-failed count above baseline for 3 consecutive minutes'; do NOT page on any single assertion failure, because kids using the language will trip assertions constantly in dev. Post-mortem discipline: an assertion-failed in production is a contract violation between two modules, not a bug in the module that raised it — the fix is upstream." :math "The predicate P is a total function value→{#t,#f,#!null,#!undefined,#f}; assert/check-with computes χ(P(v)) where χ is the standard truthiness indicator, and the operation is the identity map on v when χ=1 and ⊥ (the raised condition) otherwise. Domain of the guarded value is exactly {v | P(v) truthy}; codomain equals domain." :cs "Kind is io because the effect (raising a condition) is observable; the value-return branch is pure. Complexity is O(P) where P is the predicate's own cost — for primitive predicates that is O(1). The raise unwinds the stack under the R7RS exception model until a with-exception-handler or guard catches; the ErrorObject carries type + irritants + message. See book-of-computing ch 14 for the async/exception unwind model.")
  )
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Guarded pass-through: a value flows through a checkpoint that either lets it continue or diverts it into an error path. Same shape appears in language surface, in physical gating, and in category-theoretic partial functions."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "assert/check-with in Motoi" :code "(assert/check-with number? 42 \"n\")")
       (:domain "TCP handshake state gate" :code "(define (accept-if-syn packet)\n  (if (eq? (cadr (assq 'flag packet)) 'syn)\n      packet\n      (list 'reject packet)))\n(display (accept-if-syn (list (list 'flag 'syn) (list 'payload 0)))) (newline)")
       (:domain "Partial function via option/some" :code "(define (safe-div n d)\n  (if (zero? d) 'none (list 'some (/ n d))))\n(display (safe-div 10 2)) (newline) (display (safe-div 10 0)) (newline)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is the verb in its home domain: a predicate decides whether the value passes forward or diverts into a raised condition. Rung 2 is a network gate: the SYN flag is the predicate, the packet is the value, and the two outcomes are 'connect' or 'reject packet' — an operational filter with the same two-branch shape. Rung 3 is the algebraic view: a partial function lifted into an option type has the same two arms; the domain either produces a some-wrapped value or falls into the none case. All three rungs share the pattern (value, predicate) → value | absorbed-into-failure-path."
     :meta "The shape transfers because it is the shape of guarded evaluation itself: 'apply a decision procedure to a value, keep the value if the decision is affirmative, otherwise divert.' Whether the diversion is a raised condition, a rejected packet, or a None constructor, the SHAPE is one predicate and two output paths. Once a reader sees the shape, they can carry it to any domain that separates the go-branch from the stop-branch on one boolean.")
    (:eng "The three domains give the operator a mental grip on when a check-with is the right tool: any time your system already has a two-path 'pass or divert' decision at a boundary, the same code shape belongs there. If your protocol layer, your validator, and your inner-loop guard all use different verbs for the same shape, the log is harder to read; unify at the shape and the operator can pattern-match failures across layers." :math "Formally the pattern is a fibered decision: the predicate P: V→Ω partitions V into P⁻¹(⊤) and P⁻¹(⊥); the operation restricts the identity on V to P⁻¹(⊤) and sends P⁻¹(⊥) to a bottom element. This is the same construction that gives an option type from a partial function, and the same construction TCP uses to describe an accepted-connections subset of the packet stream." :cs "In CS this is a refinement type at runtime: the value's static type is V but its runtime witness is 'V such that P holds.' The pattern shows up as sum types (Option, Either), as network state gates, and as R7RS's own condition system. See book-of-code ch 2 for the boolean-logic ancestor and ch 10 for the state-machine framing of a guard as a two-state transition.")
  )
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "assert/check-with is the identity on the subset of inputs where the predicate returns truthy; on that subset the operation preserves the value bit-for-bit, applied once or applied a hundred times. On the failing subset it raises, and raising is idempotent — a raised condition does not re-raise a second one."
     :program "(define (id-check v) (assert/check-with number? v \"num\"))\n(display (= (id-check 42) 42)) (newline)\n(display (= (id-check (id-check (id-check 3.14))) 3.14)) (newline)\n(display (eq? (id-check 'ok-value-but-wrong) 'unreachable))\n"
     :invariant "∀ v ∈ V, ∀ P: V→Ω. P(v) truthy ⟹ (assert/check-with P v m) = v.  Additionally: ∀ v with P(v) truthy, (assert/check-with P (assert/check-with P v m) m) = (assert/check-with P v m) = v — the operation is idempotent under composition on the passing subset."
     :meta "The pattern is the identity morphism restricted to a subobject, which in CS is exactly a refinement-type checkpoint at runtime. What falsifies the claim: a single input v where P(v) is truthy but the returned value differs from v (say, the wrapper coerces the type). If assert/check-with ever silently unwrapped a boxed integer, or interned a string, or otherwise changed the value on the pass path, the invariant is broken and the whole reason the verb chains inside let-bindings is gone. The kids who write (let ((n (assert/check-with positive? x \"n>0\"))) …) are relying on this exactly. See book-of-code ch 2 for the boolean-truthiness ground; book-of-math ch 3 for the identity-map treatment; book-of-computing ch 14 for the R7RS condition-raise semantics that make the failure path structured."
    )
    (:eng "The engineering consequence of idempotence is that adding an assert/check-with anywhere in a value's path CANNOT change the value's meaning downstream — only add a failure mode. That is why kids can decorate a function with three or four check-withs without changing the return value; it is also why an operator can add a check-with at a suspicious boundary in production without fear that the value flowing past changed shape." :math "Identity restricted to a subobject: idₐ: A→A where A ⊂ V. Composition idₐ ∘ idₐ = idₐ makes this an idempotent endomorphism on A. On V∖A the operation is undefined (raises); no output value participates." :cs "The verb is a runtime-refinement checkpoint. Compilers occasionally optimize out redundant check-withs when they can prove the predicate holds — Motoi does not do that yet; every check runs. In CS terms this is a shrink-only annotation: the type after passing is a strict subtype of the type before. See book-of-code ch 2 (boolean truth) and book-of-computing ch 14 (exception unwind).")
  )
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "assert/check-with is a single predicate checkpoint that either passes the value through or raises."
     :composition "(define (retry-check tries pred v msg)\n  (guard (e ((> tries 1) (retry-check (- tries 1) pred v msg))\n           (#t 'gave-up))\n    (assert/check-with pred v msg)))\n(display (retry-check 3 positive? 5 \"pos\")) (newline)\n(display (retry-check 3 positive? -1 \"pos\")) (newline)"
     :emergent "A retry-loop with a bounded budget and a fallback branch — a supervision pattern. Neither the assertion nor the guard alone is a supervisor; the composition is."
     :meta "This is the family of supervision loops seen in Erlang's retry-and-give-up strategies, in shell scripts that wrap a command in `until … tries`, and in HTTP client retry policies. The critical piece is that the assertion's raise is CATCHABLE and STRUCTURED — that is what lets the supervisor make an informed decision on tries. See book-of-composition ch on failure-and-recovery patterns and book-of-code ch 10 (state machines) for the two-state 'tries-left' → 'gave-up' automaton this composition defines.")
    (:eng "Operator's view: the retry loop's tries budget is set from config; the log emits one line per attempt with the current tries count so the operator can distinguish a transient (1 attempt, then success) from a persistent (all 3 attempts fail). Alert on 'gave-up' branch reached above baseline; do not alert on any individual attempt. This is the same discipline SRE applies to any exponential-backoff retry policy." :math "The composition is a finite-horizon Markov-style automaton: state = tries-remaining ∈ {0,1,2,3}; transition on assertion-pass = HALT-success; transition on assertion-fail = decrement tries; transition on tries=0 = HALT-give-up. Termination is guaranteed because tries is strictly decreasing on the failure branch." :cs "The pattern is retry-with-budget, one of the most common supervision compositions in server code. The primitives are: an assertion (the decision procedure), a guard (the catch), and an accumulator (tries). Together they realize the state-machine described in book-of-code ch 10. Cross-book: book-of-composition covers the general shape of recovery patterns.")
  )
