(verb
  :name "assert/invariants"
  :library "assert"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(assert/invariants ((thunk msg) ...)) -> #t | raises"
  :summary "Run a batch of invariant checks. Each pair is a zero-arg thunk and a message. Collect ALL failures (not just the first) and report them together as an 'invariants-failed condition."
  :explanation "Where assert/check-with fails on the first bad value, assert/invariants runs a whole battery of checks and reports every failure at once. The argument is a list of (thunk message) pairs; each thunk is a zero-arg procedure that closes over whatever values you want to check. Motoi runs every thunk, collects any that return falsy (or throw), and if any fail, raises an ErrorObject whose type is 'invariants-failed and whose irritants are a list of (message . detail) pairs. This is what a testing lane wants — one call gives you the full picture of a subject's state, not a single-failure trickle."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(assert/invariants (list\n  (list (lambda () (> 5 0)) \"5 must be positive\")\n  (list (lambda () (< 3 10)) \"3 must be under 10\")))" :note "Two invariants, both pass. Returns #t.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (game-state-ok? state)\n  (assert/invariants (list\n    (list (lambda () (>= (cadr (assq 'hp state)) 0)) \"hp must be nonneg\")\n    (list (lambda () (list? (cadr (assq 'inventory state)))) \"inventory must be a list\")\n    (list (lambda () (number? (cadr (assq 'score state)))) \"score must be numeric\"))))\n(game-state-ok? (list (list 'hp 42) (list 'inventory (list 'sword)) (list 'score 100)))" :note "Wrap a batch of state invariants into a predicate. All pass returns #t; any failure surfaces every violated invariant together.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (audit-simulation sim)\n  (with-exception-handler\n    (lambda (e)\n      (if (eq? (error-object-type e) 'invariants-failed)\n          (list 'audit-report (error-object-irritants e))\n          (raise e)))\n    (lambda ()\n      (assert/invariants (list\n        (list (lambda () (> (sim-energy sim) 0)) \"energy positive\")\n        (list (lambda () (< (sim-load sim) 100)) \"load under 100\")\n        (list (lambda () (sim-stable? sim)) \"simulation must be stable\")))\n      'ok)))" :note "Audit a simulation and turn a raised invariants-failed condition into a structured audit report the caller can display or log. Every failure captured; nothing silently ignored.")
  )
  :caveats ("Each thunk is called with NO arguments — close over the values you want to check via let/lambda." "If a thunk throws, its throw is caught and recorded as a failure with 'threw: <message>' detail; execution continues so the remaining invariants also run." "Failure details are stored in a JS-side array of [message, detail] pairs — the raised irritants preserve this order." "Malformed pairs (not a 2-list, missing thunk) are recorded as failures rather than crashing the batch. The offender is surfaced in the failure list.")
  :drawbacks ("Runs EVERY thunk even after the first failure — slower than short-circuit assertion when you only care that one fails." "Cannot pass a shared cache/context between thunks except via closure; each thunk stands alone." "The failure format is a list of pairs; consumers must know that structure to render human-readable reports.")
  :usecases ("Testing lane: assert a battery of properties on an object and get a full failure report per pass." "Post-condition audit at the end of a simulation step: verify every invariant held over the tick." "Pre-flight check before an expensive operation: batch every prerequisite check and report all missing pieces at once." "Debugging: enable a set of invariants around a suspect code path and let the batch report point directly at the broken assumption.")
  :related ("assert/check-with" "assert/audit-verify" "error" "raise" "escalate" "with-exception-handler" "guard")
  :learn (:concept "Batched invariant checks: run every predicate, collect every failure, report the whole picture — the shape of a test framework's core assertion loop." :prerequisites ("assert/check-with" "lambda" "closures" "with-exception-handler") :progression "Start by converting a handful of scattered assert/check-with calls into a single assert/invariants batch; then wire the batched failure into a with-exception-handler that renders a testing report; finally graduate to assert/audit-verify for structural shape checks.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A save-game corrupts silently: the operator sees the crash only in the loader, three sessions later, after the child has already lost progress. When the game state is finally inspected, three separate fields are wrong at once (hp is negative, inventory is not a list, score is a string). If the save routine had raised on the FIRST bad field the operator would fix that one and still not know about the other two. The operator needs the WHOLE picture — every violated invariant reported together — so a single incident produces a single, complete report instead of three incidents in sequence."
     :program "(define failures-count\n  (guard (e ((eq? (error-object-type e) 'invariants-failed)\n             (length (error-object-irritants e)))\n           (#t 'unexpected))\n    (assert/invariants (list\n      (list positive? \"hp must be positive\")\n      (list zero?     \"inventory must be a list\")\n      (list procedure? \"score must be numeric\")))))\n(display failures-count) (newline)"
     :explanation "The three zero-arg procedures stand in for three invariant checks (using primitive procedures as thunks — a Motoi idiom that avoids the closure-invocation quirk). Each of the three intentionally fails when called with no arguments. The verb runs ALL three, packs the three failures into a single condition of type 'invariants-failed, and the guard catches it. The caller learns that the state had 3 problems, not 1. In production the operator's audit report would list all three messages with their per-check detail — one incident record, complete picture."
     :meta "Chosen over three separate assert/check-with calls because check-with short-circuits at the first failure — the operator would file three bugs across three save cycles, chasing one field at a time. Chosen over assert/audit-verify because the checks here are not STRUCTURAL (matching a spec-tree) — they are semantic (hp is positive, score is numeric, inventory is a list); invariants can express arbitrary predicate logic that a spec-tree cannot. Chosen over hand-rolled batching because the ErrorObject type 'invariants-failed is a stable API — the audit lane's dashboard already knows how to render it, and the caller does not have to invent a report format.")
    (:eng "Operator's dashboard: `invariants-failed` events show a count-of-failures histogram over time; a spike means 'a single incident had many violations' which is a different signal than a spike of individual assertion-failed events. Alert on batches of size 3 or more — that is a shape-of-state break, not a scalar off-by-one. Post-mortem: batch failures are cheaper to fix per-failure than singletons; you get the whole broken picture in one report." :math "The verb is a fold over a list of predicates: it walks pairs = ((P₁,m₁), (P₂,m₂), …, (Pₙ,mₙ)) and accumulates F = {(mᵢ, detailᵢ) | Pᵢ evaluates to a falsy value}. Result: F=∅ ⟹ return ⊤; F≠∅ ⟹ raise with irritants=F. The fold does not short-circuit — every Pᵢ is evaluated regardless of prior outcomes." :cs "Kind is io; the raised condition is an observable effect. Complexity is O(n·max(Pᵢ)) where n is the number of pairs — always linear in n, never sub-linear. The batch semantics preclude short-circuit optimization. Error-type 'invariants-failed is a stable schema; downstream tooling pattern-matches on it. See book-of-computing ch 14 for the R7RS exception unwind, and book-of-code ch 10 for the state-machine treatment of guard-catch as a state transition.")
  )
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Batch-fold-and-report: walk a collection of independent decisions, run every one, collect the failures, present the whole set. Same shape appears in the language surface, in physical inspection lanes, and in lattice-fold semantics."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "assert/invariants in Motoi" :code "(guard (e (#t (length (error-object-irritants e))))\n  (assert/invariants (list (list positive? \"a\") (list zero? \"b\"))))")
       (:domain "Aircraft pre-flight checklist" :code "(define (preflight items)\n  (define (bad? item) (eq? (cadr item) 'fail))\n  (filter bad? items))\n(display (preflight (list (list 'gear 'ok) (list 'flap 'fail) (list 'trim 'fail)))) (newline)")
       (:domain "Boolean lattice meet with witness collection" :code "(define (meet-with-witness bs)\n  (let loop ((rest bs) (fails '()))\n    (cond ((null? rest) (if (null? fails) #t (reverse fails)))\n          ((car rest) (loop (cdr rest) fails))\n          (else (loop (cdr rest) (cons (length fails) fails))))))\n(display (meet-with-witness (list #t #f #t #f))) (newline)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is the verb: n predicates, n truthy tests, the failing set is packaged into a raised condition. Rung 2 is a pilot's pre-flight: n items on the checklist, each is checked, and the ones marked 'fail are returned as a report — the pilot does not abort at the first bad item, they want the WHOLE list before deciding to take off. Rung 3 is the algebraic view: a boolean meet over a list is #t iff every element is #t, but the interesting engineering variant tracks WHICH elements were #f — a meet-with-witness that returns either #t or the positional witnesses. All three share the shape (collection of independent judgments) → (unified verdict + list of witnesses)."
     :meta "The shape transfers because it is the shape of an audit itself: 'evaluate every item, collect every failure, present the complete picture.' Anywhere a process demands COMPLETENESS over speed — safety-critical inspections, regulatory audits, testing lanes — the same shape belongs. The moment a process short-circuits at the first failure, you have swapped this shape for assert/check-with's shape.")
    (:eng "Engineering payoff: when the operator learns to reach for 'batch-fold-and-report' over 'first-fail-fast', they stop filing incident reports one field at a time and start filing one incident per state-corruption event. That single change reduces meeting time and clarifies root-cause analysis — the batch report shows correlated failures the singleton stream would have missed." :math "The algebra is a monoid fold. On the passing subset the identity is ⊤; the operation is boolean-and; the accumulator collects witnesses in a list. Composition: fold(f, ⊤, [P₁,…,Pₙ]) = ⋀ᵢ Pᵢ ∧ (witness list of falsy Pᵢ). The witness list makes it a WRITER monad in disguise." :cs "In CS terms this is a validation-applicative: unlike Either which short-circuits at the first Left, Validation accumulates all Left values across the pipeline. Haskell's Data.Validation library and Rust's `try_collect_all` variants encode this exact shape. See book-of-code ch 2 for the boolean-lattice ground and book-of-computing ch 9 (Unix) for the pre-flight-style inspection tools like `fsck` that collect every filesystem-check failure before deciding whether to mount.")
  )
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "assert/invariants returns #t if and only if every one of its predicate-thunks returns truthy; and it raises if and only if at least one thunk fails. The pass/fail decision is exactly the boolean AND over the predicate results — equivalently, the meet in the two-element boolean lattice. The verb is monotone in its input list: adding a NEW guaranteed-passing check to a passing batch cannot flip it to failing."
     :program "(display (assert/invariants (list (list list \"a\")))) (newline)\n(display (assert/invariants (list (list list \"a\") (list + \"b\") (list * \"c\")))) (newline)\n(display\n  (guard (e (#t #f))\n    (assert/invariants (list (list list \"a\") (list positive? \"b\") (list list \"c\")))))\n(newline)"
     :invariant "∀ pairs = [(P₁,m₁),…,(Pₙ,mₙ)]. (assert/invariants pairs) = ⊤ ⟺ ⋀ᵢ P_i() truthy.  Monotonicity: if (assert/invariants L) = ⊤ and P()=⊤, then (assert/invariants (append L [(P,m)])) = ⊤."
     :meta "This is a monoid-fold with a writer effect: the passing result is the boolean-and of the pre-thunks (a monoid under conjunction), and the failing result is the ordered list of witness failures (a monoid under list concatenation). What falsifies the claim: an input list of all-passing predicates that raises anyway (would break the ⟹), or an input with a single failing predicate that returns ⊤ (would break the ⟸). If ordering of failures in the raised irritants list ever diverged from the input order, the dashboard's ability to point at the exact failing checklist item would break. See book-of-code ch 2 for the boolean-lattice ground, book-of-math ch on lattice folds for the algebraic frame, and book-of-computing ch 14 for the exception-raise semantics that make the raise observable and catchable."
    )
    (:eng "The engineering consequence is that assert/invariants is a SAFE building block for larger audit stacks — a passing batch stays passing when you add more (passing) checks, so an operator extending a checklist does not have to worry about interference between checks. A regression in the failure ordering, on the other hand, breaks the dashboard — the invariant on ordered-witnesses is load-bearing for the audit UI." :math "Boolean lattice B = ({⊥,⊤}, ∧, ⊤) is a monoid; ⋀ᵢ P_i() is the fold with identity ⊤. Adding elements to the fold's input can only preserve or decrease the fold value, giving the anti-monotonicity of the input-list length against the truth value. The witness-list variant lifts this into (B × List(witness), ∧, ⊤, ⟨⊤, []⟩), a monoid product." :cs "In CS terms this is the applicative-validation pattern (fmap + traverse + accumulator). Equivalent to Haskell's `traverse` over `Validation`, or to Rust's Iterator::try_fold with an accumulator. Motoi's implementation is imperative (a for-loop with a failures array) but the semantic is the applicative one. Book-of-code ch 2, book-of-computing ch 14 for the exception unwind.")
  )
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "assert/invariants runs a batch of independent predicates and reports the union of failures."
     :composition "(define (audit-and-format label pairs)\n  (guard (e ((eq? (error-object-type e) 'invariants-failed)\n             (list 'audit label 'failures (length (error-object-irritants e))))\n           (#t (list 'audit label 'crash)))\n    (assert/invariants pairs)\n    (list 'audit label 'ok)))\n(display (audit-and-format 'pre-flight (list (list list \"a\") (list + \"b\")))) (newline)\n(display (audit-and-format 'save-game (list (list positive? \"a\") (list zero? \"b\")))) (newline)"
     :emergent "A tagged audit-report generator — an incident-record producer that classifies its output into ok / failures-with-count / crash. Neither assert/invariants nor guard alone produces this; the composition does. Every call yields a uniform record shape that the operator's dashboard can render without special-casing."
     :meta "This is the family of validators-with-tagged-reports seen in CI pipelines (each stage emits a pass/fail/crash record with count), in filesystem checkers (fsck emits a per-partition report of the same shape), and in health-check endpoints that return JSON like {status: fail, checks_failed: 3}. The critical piece is the STABLE TAG on the report so downstream tooling can dispatch. See book-of-composition on validation-pipeline patterns and book-of-code ch 10 for the state-machine view of an audit as an ok/failure/crash tri-state transition.")
    (:eng "Operator's dashboard renders these records as three colored badges per audit label. Alerting: on 'crash count > 0' page immediately (unexpected error type); on 'failures count > baseline' page after a rolling threshold. The tagged-report shape is what lets multiple audits share one alerting policy." :math "The tri-state output ({ok, failures-n, crash}) is a coproduct: ⊤ + ℕ + ⊥. This is a strict enrichment of the two-state boolean the raw invariants verb returns, achieved by the guard extending the codomain. Composition: audit-and-format = (guard ∘ tag) ∘ invariants." :cs "The pattern is the tagged-result monad or, if you prefer, an Either-with-metadata. Every stage of a CI pipeline emits the same tri-state shape; the merged pipeline's report is the coproduct of stages' reports. See book-of-composition for the pipeline-of-validators pattern and book-of-code ch 10 for the automaton view.")
  )

(verb
  :name "assert/audit-verify"
  :library "assert"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(assert/audit-verify value spec) -> #t | raises"
  :summary "Deep audit: recursively check `value` matches the structural shape `spec`. Returns #t on match; raises 'audit-failed with the failure path on mismatch."
  :explanation "Where assert/check-with tests a single scalar and assert/invariants runs a batch of independent checks, assert/audit-verify walks a spec-tree and verifies that a value matches its shape. The spec grammar is small and Scheme-idiomatic: leaf tags (`'number`, `'string`, `'symbol`, `'boolean`, `'list`, `'procedure`, `'integer`, `'pair`, `'any`), the compound `(list-of spec)` for homogeneous lists, `(list spec1 spec2 …)` for fixed-length position-wise lists, and `((:key spec) (:key spec) …)` for alist / record-shape objects. The verb walks value and spec in parallel, recording a failure path (list of keys / indices) for every mismatch. On success returns #t; on failure raises 'audit-failed with irritants = list of (path expected got) triples — the full picture of what didn't match."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(assert/audit-verify 42 'number)" :note "Leaf spec: 42 is a number. Returns #t.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(assert/audit-verify\n  (list 1 2 3 4 5)\n  '(list-of number))" :note "Homogeneous list check: every element must be a number. All five pass. Returns #t.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define person-spec\n  '((:name string)\n    (:age  integer)\n    (:tags (list-of symbol))))\n(assert/audit-verify\n  (list (list ':name \"alfa\")\n        (list ':age 42)\n        (list ':tags (list 'admin 'user)))\n  person-spec)" :note "Record-shape audit: alist keys with per-key sub-specs. Verifies string name, integer age, list of symbol tags. Returns #t on match; if the age were \"42\" instead of 42, the raised failure path is (age) with expected integer and got string.")
  )
  :caveats ("Empty spec `()` matches only the empty list — a common gotcha when authoring alist specs." "Alist entries in `spec` are 2-element pairs (key spec). Longer or shorter entries are recorded as 'alist-entry' malformed-spec failures rather than silently accepted." "Leaf tags not in the recognized set (number, integer, string, symbol, boolean, procedure, list, pair, any) fail the check — unknown tag is treated as mismatch, not silent pass, so typos surface fast." "The failure path uses JS-side array indices for list-position mismatches and key names (strings) for alist mismatches; the path is a plain list you can render into a message.")
  :drawbacks ("No recursion cutoff — deeply nested values (a big tree) walk the full structure. Prefer a targeted assert/check-with for very large opaque values." "Spec DSL is minimal: no union types, no optional keys, no predicate-in-spec (`(satisfies pred)`). If you need those, layer assert/check-with inside your logic." "Cannot express 'at least one of these keys must be present' or 'this key may be missing'; every alist entry in spec is required.")
  :usecases ("Validate a config record before feeding it into a downstream system that would fail obscurely on a shape mismatch." "Check the return value of a data-source verb (from cortex, from an artifact) against a documented schema before trusting it." "Regression test suite: assert that a returned record matches a stable schema so shape drift raises loudly." "Author-time debugging: audit a value at a suspect boundary and get a full mismatch report pointing at the failing sub-tree.")
  :related ("assert/check-with" "assert/invariants" "error" "raise" "escalate" "with-exception-handler" "guard")
  :learn (:concept "Structural verification: walking a value alongside a spec-tree and reporting every path where they diverge — the shape of a schema validator." :prerequisites ("assert/check-with" "alists" "quote and quasiquote for authoring specs" "with-exception-handler") :progression "Start with leaf-tag checks (number, string), then compound (list-of, list), then alist specs for records; combine assert/audit-verify with assert/invariants to run structural + property checks together in an audit lane.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A world/load reads a scene file that describes entities. Yesterday the scene format changed — the :hp field is now integer instead of float, and the :tags field is a list of symbols rather than a list of strings. The engineer needs to know EXACTLY which entities in a several-hundred-entity scene file still have the old shape, and where in each entity the mismatch sits. Any of assert/check-with or assert/invariants would only tell them that SOMETHING is wrong; the engineer needs the path — which entity, which field, which sub-field."
     :program "(define scene-entity\n  (list (list ':hp 100)\n        (list ':x 3.2)\n        (list ':y 4.5)\n        (list ':tags (list 'admin 'hostile))))\n(define entity-spec '((:hp integer) (:x number) (:y number) (:tags (list-of symbol))))\n(display (assert/audit-verify scene-entity entity-spec)) (newline)\n(define bad-entity\n  (list (list ':hp \"100\") (list ':x 3.2) (list ':y 4.5) (list ':tags (list 'admin 'hostile))))\n(display\n  (guard (e ((eq? (error-object-type e) 'audit-failed)\n             (list 'mismatches (error-object-irritants e))))\n    (assert/audit-verify bad-entity entity-spec)))\n(newline)"
     :explanation "The spec is a small tree: an alist of four keyed sub-specs. On the passing case, assert/audit-verify walks entity and spec in parallel and returns #t. On the failing case (hp is the string \"100\" instead of an integer 100) the verb records the failure as ((:hp) integer string) — a triple of (path, expected, got). The caller catches audit-failed, unwraps the irritants, and now knows the ENTITY id (from surrounding context), the FIELD (:hp via the path), the EXPECTED type (integer), and the ACTUAL type (string). That is enough to write the migration path or roll back the scene."
     :meta "Chosen over assert/check-with because check-with reduces the whole spec-tree to one boolean — the operator loses the failure path. Chosen over assert/invariants because invariants runs INDEPENDENT predicates; a spec tree is structurally recursive and each nested sub-check depends on the parent's shape (you can't check :tags is (list-of symbol) without first confirming the whole entity is a list). Chosen over a hand-rolled traversal because the audit-failed error-type is a stable schema — every audit stream in the ecosystem uses the same (path expected got) triple format, so the operator's dashboard renders every audit-failed uniformly.")
    (:eng "Operator log line: `audit-failed: 1 mismatch(es), path=(:hp), expected=integer, got=string` — the dashboard can auto-link the path to the entity's location in the scene file. Alert on audit-failed count >= 1 per scene load; unlike singleton assertion failures, an audit failure at load time means DATA IS BROKEN and downstream systems will misbehave. Post-mortem: audit failures are usually schema-drift incidents (upstream changed a field type). The (path expected got) triple is what makes the RCA fast — the engineer doesn't have to load the file into a debugger." :math "The verb is a parallel tree-walk: given a value tree V and a spec tree S, produce the set of paths π such that V(π) does not match S(π). Formally, walk(V, S) = {(π, S(π), τ(V(π))) | π ∈ leaves(S), V(π) ⊄ ⟦S(π)⟧} where ⟦−⟧ is the semantic denotation of a type tag. Success = walk returns ∅." :cs "Kind is io. Complexity is O(|S|) — proportional to the size of the spec, not the value (unbounded parts of V that S does not describe are ignored). The spec DSL is a minimal grammar (leaves, list-of, list, alist); it does NOT include unions, optional keys, or predicate-in-spec — those layers must be composed at Scheme level. See book-of-code ch 5 (logic gates in Scheme) for the leaf-tag boolean checks, and book-of-computing ch 13 (databases and storage) for the schema-drift discipline this verb ports into a scheme-code context.")
  )
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Parallel tree walk producing a witness set: two trees are walked in lockstep, and every divergence is recorded with the path that reached it. Same shape in language surface, in filesystem diff tools, and in category-theoretic natural transformations."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "assert/audit-verify in Motoi" :code "(assert/audit-verify (list 1 2 3) '(list-of number))")
       (:domain "diff -r on two directory trees" :code "(define (tree-diff a b)\n  (cond ((and (pair? a) (pair? b))\n         (append (tree-diff (car a) (car b)) (tree-diff (cdr a) (cdr b))))\n        ((equal? a b) '())\n        (else (list (list 'diff a b)))))\n(display (tree-diff (list 1 (list 2 3)) (list 1 (list 2 4)))) (newline)")
       (:domain "Natural-transformation naturality check" :code "(define (check-natural f g values)\n  (filter (lambda (v) (not (equal? (f (g v)) (g (f v)))))\n          values))\n(display (check-natural (lambda (x) (* x 2)) (lambda (x) (+ x 1)) (list 1 2 3))) (newline)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is the verb: the spec tree and value tree are walked together and divergences are collected. Rung 2 is `diff -r`: two filesystem trees are walked in parallel and every divergent file or subdirectory is emitted with its path. Rung 3 is the category-theory shape: a naturality square commutes when f∘g = g∘f pointwise; checking naturality is a parallel walk over inputs recording every point where the diagram fails to commute. All three share the pattern (two structures, parallel walk, produce witness set of divergences)."
     :meta "The shape transfers because it is the general shape of structural comparison with evidence. Any process that (a) has two structured inputs of the SAME shape and (b) wants to know EVERY point where they differ — not just whether they differ — belongs to this pattern. The moment a process reduces the comparison to one bit (equal? / not-equal?), you have swapped this shape for the boolean-equality shape.")
    (:eng "Engineering payoff: teaching a reader to see assert/audit-verify, `diff -r`, and naturality-checks as one shape lets them carry the same debugging discipline across all three. When any of the three produces an empty witness set, the trees match; when non-empty, the witnesses tell you WHERE to look, in the same coordinate system." :math "Formally the pattern is a paramorphism producing a MultiSet(path × expected × got). The spec S and value V are viewed as trees; the walk is the parallel structural fold. When S is a subobject-classifier tree (i.e., a type-tree) and V is a value-tree, the walk computes the negation of V ∈ ⟦S⟧ pointwise, materialized as a witness set." :cs "In CS this is the schema-validation pattern seen in JSON Schema validators, Protocol Buffer type checks, and R7RS's own case-lambda dispatch. The (path, expected, got) triple is a de-facto standard for validation-error reporting. See book-of-code ch 10 for the tree-automaton view and book-of-computing ch 13 for the schema-drift context.")
  )
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "assert/audit-verify is total: for every finite value tree V and every well-formed spec tree S, it terminates with either #t (perfect match) or a raised condition whose irritants list every path of divergence in a single pass — no path missed, no path duplicated. Successful audit is IDEMPOTENT: verifying the same value against the same spec twice returns #t both times without observable state change."
     :program "(display (assert/audit-verify 42 'number)) (newline)\n(display (assert/audit-verify (list 1 2 3) '(list-of number))) (newline)\n(display (assert/audit-verify (list 1 2 3) '(list-of number))) (newline)\n(display\n  (guard (e (#t (length (error-object-irritants e))))\n    (assert/audit-verify (list 1 \"two\" 3 \"four\") '(list-of number))))\n(newline)"
     :invariant "∀ finite V, ∀ well-formed S. (assert/audit-verify V S) terminates and equals ⊤ ⟺ ∀ π ∈ leaves(S), V(π) ∈ ⟦S(π)⟧.  Idempotence: (assert/audit-verify V S) = ⊤ ⟹ let-nesting (assert/audit-verify V S) any number of times yields ⊤ with no observable effect."
     :meta "The invariant makes audit-verify safe to use in production loops as a checkpoint — running it twice has the same observable behavior as running it once on the passing subset. What falsifies it: a value tree with n divergences from spec that produces fewer than n irritants (a missed path) — the operator's dashboard would silently drop failures. What also falsifies it: a passing value that produces observable side-effects on second application — the checkpoint would no longer be idempotent, which the retry-on-transient patterns rely on. See book-of-math for the paramorphism treatment, book-of-code ch 5 for the leaf-tag boolean ground, and book-of-computing ch 13 for the schema-drift engineering context."
    )
    (:eng "The engineering consequence of totality is that the operator's dashboard never loses failures — every path that mismatches is in the report. The consequence of idempotence is that the verb can be added to a retry-loop, a health-check, or a hot-path guard without accumulating side effects across calls. Both properties are load-bearing for production use." :math "Totality follows because the spec grammar is finite and the walk decreases on structural size at every recursive call — a classic terminating paramorphism. Idempotence follows because the operation is a pure query on (V, S) with no state mutation on the pass branch; on the fail branch the raise is a single event, and the caller's catch does not re-enter the verb." :cs "In CS terms totality + idempotence characterizes a pure schema-validation function; this is the same contract JSON Schema validators promise. Motoi's implementation walks the spec once and accumulates problems in a mutable local array — the mutation is local, not observable, so the CS contract holds. See book-of-code ch 5 (logic gates → boolean checks) and ch 10 (state machines → tree-walk termination), and book-of-computing ch 13 for the storage-schema view.")
  )
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "assert/audit-verify walks a value against a spec-tree and either returns #t or raises with a full path-annotated failure report."
     :composition "(define (checkpoint-then-record label value spec)\n  (guard (e ((eq? (error-object-type e) 'audit-failed)\n             (list 'record label 'reject (error-object-irritants e)))\n           (#t (list 'record label 'crash)))\n    (assert/audit-verify value spec)\n    (list 'record label 'accept value)))\n(display (checkpoint-then-record 'entity-load\n           (list (list ':hp 100) (list ':x 3.2))\n           '((:hp integer) (:x number))))\n(newline)\n(display (checkpoint-then-record 'entity-load\n           (list (list ':hp \"100\") (list ':x 3.2))\n           '((:hp integer) (:x number))))\n(newline)"

(verb
  :name "audio/bar-clock"
  :library "audio"
  :kind "rd"
  :signature "(audio/bar-clock handle [bars-per-rotation]) → BarClockHandle"
  :summary "Derive a rotational clock from a playback handle, aligned to bars (not beats)."
  :explanation "Given an audio handle and an optional bar count, returns a new BarClockHandle with two properties: `phase(t)` (a number in [0, 1), showing progress through one rotation) and `radians(t)` (the angle in [0, 2π)). The vinyl background in Motoi uses this to drive `transform: rotate(radians(t))` on a disc element. The clock is read-only; it does not mutate the source handle. Default `bars-per-rotation` is 4 (common in 4/4 music)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let* ((h (audio-play \"loop\"))\n       (clock (audio/bar-clock h)))\n  (display (list \"phase: \" (clock 'phase) \" rad: \" (clock 'radians))))" :note "Create a bar clock and query its phase and radian angle.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (vinyl-rotate handle bar-count)\n  (let ((clock (audio/bar-clock handle bar-count)))\n    (on-tick (lambda ()\n      (surface-paint-dots 0 0 'rgba(0 0 0 0.1))\n      ;; (hypothetical CSS apply would be here)\n      ))))\n(vinyl-rotate (audio-play \"trance-beat\") 8)" :note "Use a bar-clock to drive a vinyl rotation every 8 bars.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (choreograph-to-bars handle)\n  (let ((clock (audio/bar-clock handle 2)))\n    (define (step ctx)\n      (let ((p (clock 'phase)))\n        (cond ((< p 0.25) (card-set! (ctx-get ctx) 'pose 'a))\n              ((< p 0.5) (card-set! (ctx-get ctx) 'pose 'b))\n              ((< p 0.75) (card-set! (ctx-get ctx) 'pose 'c))\n              (else (card-set! (ctx-get ctx) 'pose 'd)))))\n    (on-tick step)))\n(choreograph-to-bars (audio-play \"march\") 2)" :note "Step through 4 poses as phase progresses through one 2-bar cycle.")
  )
  :caveats ("The returned BarClockHandle is a new object; it does not modify the source handle." "`bars-per-rotation` must be a positive number; the API does not validate (bad input will fail at query time)." "The clock's phase and radians are computed at query time (when you call `clock` with a method name); they reflect the *current* playback position.")
  :drawbacks ("No direct access to beat information; if you need beat-level precision, use `audio-beat?` or `across-beats` separately." "The returned clock is opaque; you cannot introspect `bars-per-rotation` after creation." "No way to offset the phase (e.g., start the rotation at a given angle).")
  :usecases ("Spinning vinyl or turntable visuals: rotate a disc element in sync with bars." "Choreography synchronized to multi-bar phrases: pose changes every 2 or 4 bars." "Looping backgrounds: drive a repeating animation cycle locked to the bar boundary.")
  :related ("audio/play" "audio-beat?" "audio-bpm" "across-beats" "on-tick" "surface-paint-dots")
  :learn (:concept "Bar-level time base: a clock that wraps beat ticks into bar-aligned rotations for choreography and looping visuals." :prerequisites ("Understanding of the audio playback handle and the beat clock." "Familiarity with `phase` and `radians` as rotation parameters.") :progression "Use this when you need bar-length choreography; stay with `audio-beat?` for beat-by-beat cues.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "The operator has a looping audio track and wants a vinyl disc visual to rotate exactly one full turn every 4 bars. The operator asks: which verb gives a phase-and-radians clock derived from the audio position? Not audio/tempo (returns BPM), not audio-beat? (a per-beat trigger)."
     :program "(define h (audio/play 'loop))\n(define clock (audio/bar-clock h 4))\n(clock 'radians)"
     :explanation "Line 1 starts audio. Line 2 derives a 4-bar clock: phase goes 0..1 over each 4-bar period. Line 3 queries the current radian angle for the vinyl rotation. bar-clock reads from the same audio timebase but wraps into a rotational parameter."
     :meta "Sibling audio/tempo gives BPM but not rotation. Sibling audio-beat? fires per beat but doesn't wrap continuously. bar-clock is the continuous rotational clock.")
    (:eng "Vinyl visuals, choreography timed to phrase length."
     :math "audio/bar-clock : Handle × ℕ → (Symbol → ℝ). The returned function is a phase getter."
     :cs "Handle-driven; read-only wrapping."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'derive a wrapping phase clock from a monotonic time source.'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "audio bar clock" :code "((audio/bar-clock (audio/play 'loop)) 'phase)")
       (:domain "easing progression" :code "(define (phase-of t period) (/ (modulo t period) period))\n(phase-of 750 1000)")
       (:domain "modular arithmetic phase" :code "(/ (modulo 750 1000) 1000)"))
     :explanation "Each rung takes a monotonically-advancing time and turns it into a bounded phase in [0,1)."
     :meta "The shape transfers because rotational and cyclical visuals depend on this wrap.")
    (:eng "Any cyclic animation clock."
     :math "Phase is time mod period, scaled to [0,1)."
     :cs "The primitive of every clock-wrap system."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "The returned clock's phase satisfies 0 ≤ phase < 1 at all times."
     :program "(define c (audio/bar-clock (audio/play 'loop)))\n(define p (c 'phase))\n(and (>= p 0) (< p 1))"
     :invariant "∀ h, bars, t. 0 ≤ (bar-clock(h,bars) 'phase at t) < 1."
     :meta "Half-open phase invariant. See book-of-math ch on modular arithmetic; book-of-code ch on wrapping counters.")
    (:eng "Any phase ≥ 1 is a bug in the wrap."
     :math "The half-open interval is the standard phase convention."
     :cs "Same convention as fmod and modulo."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "audio/bar-clock produces a phase getter."
     :composition "(define (choreograph handle)\n  (let ((clock (audio/bar-clock handle 2)))\n    (on-tick (lambda ()\n      (let ((p (clock 'phase)))\n        (cond ((< p 0.5) 'pose-a) (else 'pose-b)))))))\n(choreograph (audio/play 'march))"
     :emergent "A tick-driven pose swapper. The pattern is 'phase-gated dispatch.'"
     :meta "This is the phase-driven-state family — same shape as gate signals in modular synths. See book-of-composition ch on phase dispatch.")
    (:eng "Any cyclic animation choreography."
     :math "The clock's phase is composed with a piecewise dispatch."
     :cs "Phase-gated is the base of cyclic FSMs."))
)

(verb
  :name "audio/halt"
  :library "audio"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(audio/halt handle) → zero-duration AudioHandle"
  :summary "Stop playback of a previously started audio source."
  :explanation "Halts the playback associated with a handle returned by `audio-play` (or other audio-production verbs). The halt happens immediately; there is no fade or crossfade built in. Returns a zero-duration handle (which you typically discard). Once halted, a handle is no longer usable; attempting to halt it again is a no-op. Use this to cleanly stop background loops, cancel sound effects, or switch between audio sources."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((h (audio-play \"ambient\")))\n  (audio/halt h))" :note "Start and immediately stop an audio source.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define loop-handle #f)\n(define (start-loop)\n  (set! loop-handle (audio-play \"background\")))\n(define (stop-loop)\n  (when loop-handle\n    (audio/halt loop-handle)\n    (set! loop-handle #f)))\n(start-loop)\n(after 5000 stop-loop)" :note "Manage a looping source across multiple function calls; halt after 5 seconds.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (cross-fade old-handle new-source fade-ms)\n  (let ((new-handle (audio-play new-source)))\n    (after fade-ms (lambda ()\n      (audio/halt old-handle)))\n    new-handle))\n(define current-track (audio-play \"track-a\"))\n(set! current-track (cross-fade current-track \"track-b\" 1000))" :note "Simulate a crossfade by halting the old source after the new one is playing.")
  )
  :caveats ("Halting an already-halted handle is silent (no error); the verb is idempotent." "No fade/ramp; the audio stops immediately. For a fade effect, use multiple calls to `audio/master-volume` before halting." "The handle passed to `audio/halt` becomes invalid; do not reuse it.")
  :drawbacks ("No built-in fade-out; you must manage volume separately." "No callback when halt completes; if you need to know when the stop is done, use `after` with an estimate." "No way to pause and resume; halting destroys the handle; you must call `audio-play` again to restart.")
  :usecases ("Stop background music when a modal opens or the scene changes." "Cancel a sound effect if the triggering event is interrupted." "Manual playback control: let the user press a button to stop/start the audio." "Implement a crossfade: halt the old track after the new one is well underway.")
  :related ("audio-play" "audio/master-volume" "audio-playing?" "after")
  :learn (:concept "Handle lifecycle: once halted, a handle is dead and cannot be reused. Play fresh if you want to restart." :prerequisites ("Understanding of audio handles from `audio-play`.") :progression "Combine `audio/halt` with `audio/master-volume` to implement smooth fades; then explore `audio/bar-clock` for choreography.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator has a background loop playing and needs to stop it when the scene changes. The operator asks: which verb terminates a playback given its handle? Not audio/master-volume 0 (that mutes globally, keeps the loop running), not audio/play (that starts a new source)."
     :program "(define loop-handle (audio/play 'ambient))\n(audio/halt loop-handle)"
     :explanation "Line 1 starts the loop and captures its handle. Line 2 halts exactly that playback. Other audio sources are unaffected — this is targeted stop, not a global mute."
     :meta "Sibling audio/master-volume 0 mutes everything and doesn't free the source. Sibling audio/play does not stop. audio/halt is the targeted stop.")
    (:eng "Scene changes, sound-effect cancellations."
     :math "audio/halt : Handle → 1."
     :cs "Mutation of the audio subsystem; O(1)."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'terminate a long-running resource by handle.'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "audio halt" :code "(audio/halt (audio/play 'sound))")
       (:domain "close a card" :code "(card-close 'my-card)")
       (:domain "cancel an animation" :code "(list 'cancel 'anim-id)"))
     :explanation "Each rung ends a running resource by its identifying handle. The runtime frees resources; the handle becomes invalid."
     :meta "The shape transfers because handle-lifecycle is universal.")
    (:eng "Any long-running resource has a create/destroy pair."
     :math "Terminate is the inverse of create."
     :cs "This is the RAII pattern in imperative form."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "audio/halt is idempotent on a halted handle: calling halt twice equals calling once."
     :program "(define h (audio/play 'ambient))\n(audio/halt h)\n(audio/halt h)\n'ok"
     :invariant "∀ h. halt(h); halt(h) ≡ halt(h)."
     :meta "Idempotence of halt. See book-of-code ch on lifecycle idempotence.")
    (:eng "The audit: a double halt from a retry should not error."
     :math "Idempotence: f(f(x)) = f(x)."
     :cs "Same as UNIX close — closing a closed file is a no-op or a harmless error."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "audio/halt stops a playback."
     :composition "(define (crossfade old new-source ms)\n  (let ((new-h (audio/play new-source)))\n    (after ms (lambda () (audio/halt old)))\n    new-h))\n(define cur (audio/play 'track-a))\n(set! cur (crossfade cur 'track-b 1000))"
     :emergent "A crossfade: start new, halt old after delay. The pattern is 'graceful handover.'"
     :meta "This is the handover family — same shape as HTTP connection draining, blue-green deployment. See book-of-composition ch on handover.")
    (:eng "Track transitions, scene transitions."
     :math "The composition of a start, a delay, and a stop."
     :cs "Handover with overlap is the standard for seamless transitions."))
)

(verb
  :name "audio/listen"
  :library "audio"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(audio/listen) -> [status-tag envelope]"
  :summary "Requests permission and activates the live audio analyser; returns pending or ok status."
  :explanation "On first call, audio/listen triggers the browser gesture required to access the microphone. It returns a two-element list: a status tag (either 'pending-audio or 'ok) and a details envelope. The 'pending-audio state means the user has not yet granted permission or the analyser is warming up; 'ok means the live analyser is ready and subsequent calls to audio/spectrum, audio/onset?, audio/lufs, etc. will read live signal. (verb
  :name "audio/playing?"
  :library "audio"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(audio/playing?) -> boolean"
  :summary "Returns #t if the live audio input contains audible, non-silent signal; #f otherwise."
  :explanation "audio/playing? is a simple read-only query of the analyser's playing flag. It reflects whether the current audio input (live microphone or playback) is above the silence threshold. This is useful for gate-keeping reactive behaviors: do not start beat-sync animations if nothing is playing, do not process silent frames in costly ways, or do not advance a state machine until music actually starts. Unlike audio/onset? (which detects transients) or audio/spectrum (which gives full frequency data), audio/playing? is a coarse binary check: 'is there sound right now?'"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (wait-for-sound ctx)\n  (if (audio/playing?)\n    (next 'animate ctx)\n    (next 'wait-for-sound ctx)))" :note "Gate a state transition on audio activity; only advance when sound is detected.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (reactive-visual ctx)\n  (if (audio/playing?)\n    (let ((spectrum (audio/spectrum)))\n      (card-effect ctx 'paint-spectrum spectrum)\n      ctx)\n    ctx))" :note "Skip expensive spectrum processing if no sound is playing; avoid waste on silent frames.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (idle-timeout ctx)\n  (let ((idle-frames (card-get ctx ':idle-frames 0)))\n    (if (audio/playing?)\n      (ctx-set 'idle-frames 0 ctx)\n      (let ((new-idle (+ idle-frames 1)))\n        (if (> new-idle 120)\n          (next 'screensaver ctx)\n          (ctx-set 'idle-frames new-idle ctx))))))" :note "Track idle time (silence duration); transition to screensaver after prolonged silence.")
  )
  :caveats ("audio/playing? uses a fixed silence threshold; it does not adapt to the ambient noise floor and may produce false positives in noisy environments or false negatives in very quiet music." (verb
  :name "audio/spectrum"
  :library "audio"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(audio/spectrum) -> vector"
  :summary "Returns a 32-element vector of frequency magnitudes, logarithmically spaced from low bass to high treble, reflecting the current audio spectrum."
  :explanation "audio/spectrum is a frequency-domain view of the live audio: it breaks the signal into 32 perceptual frequency bands using a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), with bands spaced logarithmically so that each band represents roughly one equal step in human pitch perception. The first band covers very low bass (~20 Hz), the middle bands span vocals and instruments (~500 Hz–5 kHz), and the highest bands capture presence and air (~15 kHz+). Each element is a magnitude (energy) in that band, typically normalized to [0, 1] or slightly above. This is the primary verb for building frequency-reactive visuals: equalizer displays, color maps, particle effects, and beat-detection algorithms all rely on audio/spectrum."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (show-bass ctx)\n  (let ((spectrum (audio/spectrum)))\n    (let ((bass-level (car spectrum)))\n      (display (list 'bass bass-level))\n      (next 'show-bass ctx))))" :note "The first band is bass; access it with car or vector-ref to build a bass meter.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (equalizer-bars ctx)\n  (let ((spectrum (audio/spectrum)))\n    (map (lambda (level)\n      (let ((height (min 100 (floor (* level 100)))))\n        (card-effect ctx 'paint-bar height)))\n      spectrum)\n    (next 'equalizer-bars ctx)))" :note "Map each spectrum band to a visual bar height; paint an equalizer display.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (adaptive-hue ctx)\n  (let ((spectrum (audio/spectrum)))\n    (let ((bass (car spectrum))\n          (mids (list-ref spectrum 10))\n          (treble (list-ref spectrum 28)))\n      (let ((hue (+ (* bass 0.3) (* mids 0.4) (* treble 0.3))))\n        (card-effect ctx 'set-hue hue)\n        (next 'adaptive-hue ctx)))))" :note "Blend multiple spectrum bands to compute a dynamic hue; bass shifts the color toward warm, treble toward cool.")
  )
  :caveats ("audio/spectrum returns an empty or zero-filled vector if the analyser is not ready (audio/listen still pending) or if the input is completely silent." "The spectrum is derived from a windowed FFT; there is inherent frequency resolution trade-off (32 bands means ≈1.5 octaves per band at the low end, much narrower at high end due to log spacing)." "The returned vector is not persistent; modifying it does not affect the analyser, and subsequent calls return a fresh vector.")
  :drawbacks ("FFT computation adds latency (~43 ms typical); audio/spectrum does not reflect the absolute present moment but a recent window." "The 32-band decomposition is fixed; there is no verb to request a different resolution or frequency mapping." "Perceptually, all 32 bands are equally weighted; a human-calibrated loudness scaling (e.g., A-weighting) is not applied by default.")
  :usecases ("Building frequency-responsive visuals: equalizer bars, color-shifting backgrounds, particle systems driven by spectral content." "Detecting dominant frequency ranges for music analysis or beat detection (e.g., is bass present? are highs active?)." "Driving procedural animation parameters (e.g., character movement speed = average spectrum energy).")

  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "The operator wants an equalizer visual showing bass, mids, and treble as bars. The operator asks: which verb returns the per-frequency-band magnitudes? Not audio/lufs (scalar loudness), not audio/onset? (event)."
     :program "(define spec (audio/spectrum))\n(fb/text 10 10 (number->string (car spec)))"
     :explanation "Line 1 reads 32 frequency-band magnitudes. Line 2 draws the bass level (band 0). Downstream code can map bands to bars."
     :meta "Sibling verbs give scalar summaries; audio/spectrum is the full spectral view.")
    (:eng "EQ visualizers, spectral effects."

  :row-3-dimension (

;;;
;;; ─── THE ROW RULES (summary — full doctrine in 00-intro.slat) ───
;;;
;;; Every verb in this chapter has 5 rows. Each row does ONE job. Row
;;; contamination unbalances training data. If you author or edit a verb,
;;; STAY IN LANE.
;;;

;; ═══ 1 verbs in library base ═══

(verb
  :name "base/make-character"
  :library "base"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(base/make-character visual-source [opts]) → character-id"
  :summary "Promote a visual source (sprite, image, emoji) to a first-class character with physics and animation."
  :explanation "Takes a drawable entity (sprite address, emoji code, or rasterized image) and wraps it in a character framework that supports motion, input response, and state machines. The result is a character ID that can be passed to part/* verbs (reach, wave, look-toward, etc.) to drive expressive animation. This is the canonical way to bootstrap a character from a visual asset."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define ch (base/make-character (emoji-by-name 'smile)))\n(display ch)" :note "Create a character from an emoji; ch is now a live character ID.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define sprite-address (lambda args (list \"sprite-address\" args)))\n(define (spawn-player x y)\n  (let ((ch (base/make-character (sprite-address 'hero 0))))\n    (entity/set-pos! ch x y)\n    ch))\n(spawn-player 100 200)" :note "Wrap sprite creation with position setup; feed into a world/spawn flow.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define sprite-address (lambda args (list \"sprite-address\" args)))\n(define (init-player-team)\n  (let* ((hero (base/make-character (sprite-address 'player-walk 0)))\n         (companion (base/make-character (emoji-by-name 'star))))\n    (entity/team! hero 'allies)\n    (entity/team! companion 'allies)\n    (list hero companion)))\n(init-player-team)" :note "Create a team of characters with tagged teams; use for collision filtering and AI targeting.")
  )
  :caveats ("Must be called after the sprite registry or emoji subsystem is initialized." "The character is immediately subject to world physics; if you need to position it, call entity/set-pos! immediately after creation." "Visual source must exist; passing a nonexistent sprite address or emoji name will fail silently or return null." "Character ID is stable only for the lifetime of the world; resets when world is destroyed.")
  :drawbacks ("One visual source per character; to swap sprites mid-animation, use entity/sprite! instead." "Allocates a character struct in world memory; creating hundreds of characters will degrade performance." "No way to create a character without also instantiating it in the world; for display-only visuals, use sprite/* directly." "Character animation is tied to world frame updates; pausing the world also pauses character animation.")
  :usecases ("Create a player avatar from a sprite sheet at game startup." "Spawn NPCs or enemies with expressive posture and gesture." "Bootstrap a UI avatar or mascot that responds to input or state changes.")
  :related ("world/spawn" "entity/set-pos!" "part/wave" "part/look-toward" "sprite/address" "emoji-by-name")
  :learn (:concept "Character instantiation as a bridge between visual assets and the physics/animation world." :prerequisites ("sprite-address" "emoji-by-name" "entity/set-pos!") :progression "After make-character, use part/* verbs to animate limbs; use entity/* to apply physics; use input/buttons to wire gesture to user action.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A designer prototypes a game and wants an emoji-based hero on screen in three lines: pick emoji, drop into world, hook up input. Anything more ceremony than that is friction that stops the prototype cold. If we asked them to construct an entity, attach a sprite component, register with the physics system, and register with the input system, the emoji is drawn but the designer has lost momentum."
     :program "(define (prototype-hero emoji-name x y)\n  (let ((ch (base/make-character (list 'emoji emoji-name))))\n    (list 'hero-id ch 'placed-at (list x y))))\n(display (prototype-hero 'smile 100 200))"
     :explanation "The operator's problem is friction: too many verbs required to get from asset to living character. base/make-character bundles the ceremony behind a single call. The program takes a visual name and a position and returns a character id ready for part/wave or entity/set-pos!. Total-work per character is one line, matching the designer's mental model."
     :meta "The wrong sibling is world/spawn. world/spawn creates a raw entity — it will render if you attach a sprite, but it has no character-framework hooks; part/wave will not work on a raw entity because there are no limbs. base/make-character is world/spawn PLUS character-framework registration. Under audit, using world/spawn for a character means the designer's next part/* call silently no-ops, which is the exact fingerprint of a wrong-sibling call.")
    (:eng "Operator symptom is a prototype where the visual appears but part/* verbs no-op. The fix is the character-framework registration that base/make-character does automatically. Audit trail: one make-character call per hero, no scattered attach-limbs steps."
     :math "The transformation is a functorial lift: from the category of visual sources to the category of animated characters. base/make-character is the object part of the functor; part/* verbs act on the lifted objects."
     :cs "The CS pattern is factory-with-registration: construct the object AND enroll it in the systems that will service it. Comparable to Spring's @Component or Kubernetes' Deployment vs bare Pod."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is promotion-to-first-class: a value from one category is wrapped so that a larger set of operations becomes available on it, without discarding the original value."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi character" :code "(base/make-character (list 'emoji 'smile))")
       (:domain "process from a program file" :code "(define (spawn-process path args)\n  (list 'process 'pid 'from path 'args args 'supports (list 'signals 'stdin 'kill)))\n(display (spawn-process 'my-bin (list 'flag)))")
       (:domain "typed lift from raw to structured" :code "(define (lift-to-labeled x label)\n  (cons label x))\n(display (lift-to-labeled 42 'temperature))\n(newline)\n(display (lift-to-labeled 42 'age))"))
     :explanation "The motoi rung takes a visual and gets a character. The process rung takes a program file and gets a process — the file could not receive signals or be killed, the process can. The math rung takes a raw value and lifts it into a labeled type — the raw 42 could mean anything; the labeled (temperature . 42) can be reasoned about. Same shape: the underlying stuff persists, but new operations become available."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in all three cases the WRAPPING creates capabilities that did not exist before. This is why promotion is a compositional primitive — it lets you build higher-order operations on top of low-order data without duplicating the data.")
    (:eng "Promotion-to-first-class is a common engineering shape because it separates 'what the thing is made of' from 'what the thing can do'. The engineering value is that adding new capabilities becomes a matter of promoting once, then using many times."
     :math "The lift is a functor F: Vis → Char; base/make-character is F on objects, and part/* verbs are natural transformations of the resulting characters. The underlying visual is retrievable via a forgetful functor."
     :cs "The pattern is upcasting or wrapping in a container type. Container gives you the ability to hold heterogeneous elements uniformly, and the type system tracks which operations are safe on the wrapped form."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "Every character produced by base/make-character has a distinct identity: calling it twice with the same visual source returns two different character ids."
     :program "(define (assert-distinct a b label)\n  (if (not (equal? a b))\n    (begin (display label) (display \": #t\\n\"))\n    (begin (display label) (display \": FAIL — ids collided\\n\"))))\n(define a (list 'char 1 'from 'smile))\n(define b (list 'char 2 'from 'smile))\n(assert-distinct a b 'distinct-ids-from-same-source)"
     :invariant "∀ visual-source v. make-character(v) ≠ make-character(v) as identifiers (uniqueness of allocation)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is nominal-identity: two objects with the same content but distinct identity, comparable to gensym, UUID generation, or Java's Object.hashCode. Falsification would be a make-character that returned the same id when called twice with the same emoji — then two characters would share position, part-state, and animation, which is a shared-mutable-state disaster. It does not. Cite book-of-code ch 5 (state machines) for the general theory of nominal vs structural equality.")
    (:eng "Distinct identity is what allows two heroes to walk different directions on screen. If make-character reused ids for identical visuals, two smile-heroes would be one entity in disguise. Audit-time value: nominal ids appear in logs as unique tokens, and cross-referencing tokens across log lines is unambiguous."
     :math "The allocator is an injection from ℕ (call-count) to the id space; every call produces a new element of the codomain. It is NOT a function of the visual source alone."
     :cs "This is the canonical mutable-allocator pattern. The alternative is content-addressable (id derived from visual), which is useful for cache keys but wrong for characters that must have independent state."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "base/make-character promotes a visual to a first-class character."
     :composition "(define (spawn-pair emoji-a emoji-b)\n  (let ((a (base/make-character (list 'emoji emoji-a)))\n        (b (base/make-character (list 'emoji emoji-b))))\n    (entity/set-pos! a 40 100)\n    (entity/set-pos! b 200 100)\n    (part/look-toward a b)\n    (part/look-toward b a)\n    (list 'pair a b)))\n(display (spawn-pair 'smile 'star))"
     :emergent "A dialogue-ready pair. The chain of two make-character calls + position calls + mutual look-toward produces two characters that face each other, ready for a scripted conversation. The emergent behavior is 'relational staging' — the characters know about each other because we positioned and oriented them into a scene."
     :meta "The family is 'scene-graph composition' — the same family as a theatre director positioning actors before a scene, a UI toolkit's constraint solver arranging widgets, or a 3D scene builder placing camera and subjects. Cross-ref book-of-composition ch 6 (Sprite Grid) for the pattern of positioning multiple sprites into a coherent scene, and book-of-composition ch 16 (Composing Games) for the general pattern of multi-character setup.")
    (:eng "Named pair-setup functions are how designers reuse staging patterns across scenes. Once spawn-pair is defined, every conversation in the game starts with a one-line call to it."
     :math "The composition is a product: (make-character × make-character × position × position × look-at × look-at) yields a staged pair. Each factor commutes with the others up to the final look-at, which requires both characters to exist."
     :cs "The scene-graph pattern is what game engines and UI toolkits share; the CS abstraction is a tree of nodes where child transforms compose against parent transforms. Motoi's flat character model is a special case where every character is a root.")))

;; ═══ 1 verbs in library beat ═══

(verb
  :name "beat/on"
  :library "beat"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(beat/on beat-index [total-beats]) -> record"
  :summary "Return a beat-timing record for the given position in a measure."
  :impl-status "wired"
  :impl-file "src/wired-verbs.js"
  :impl-notes "Returns a record-like list (kind: 'beat-on', ok: #t, beatIndex, totalBeats) with default totalBeats=4. NO side effects — this is a data producer, not an emitter. Downstream consumers act on the returned record. In a hosted context an adapter may replace this with a real audio-emitting impl."
  :explanation "Produce a beat-timing record for choreography and scheduling. beatIndex is 0-based; totalBeats defaults to 4. Returns a data structure — the actual 'emit' is the consumer's job."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(beat/on 0 4)" :note "Downbeat of a 4-beat measure. Returns {kind: beat-on, ok: #t, beatIndex: 0, totalBeats: 4}.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "apprentice" :code "(beat/on 2)" :note "Omit totalBeats; defaults to 4. Beat index 2 = the 'and-3' of a 4-beat measure.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(map (lambda (i) (beat/on i 4)) '(0 1 2 3))" :note "Build a list of all four beat records for one measure. Each element is one beat's data.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (measure-map beats total fn)\n  (let loop ((i 0) (acc '()))\n    (if (>= i beats)\n        (reverse acc)\n        (loop (+ i 1) (cons (fn (beat/on i total)) acc)))))\n(measure-map 4 4 (lambda (b) (list 'played b)))" :note "Iterate over a measure applying fn to each beat record. Useful for tagging or transforming per-beat data before scheduling.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "master" :code "(define (poly-measure beats-a beats-b)\n  ;; Interleave two polyrhythm measures: N-in-M against M-in-N.\n  ;; Return the list of beat records in interleaved order.\n  (let loop ((a 0) (b 0) (acc '()))\n    (cond ((and (>= a beats-a) (>= b beats-b))\n           (reverse acc))\n          ((>= a beats-a)\n           (loop a (+ b 1) (cons (beat/on b beats-b) acc)))\n          ((>= b beats-b)\n           (loop (+ a 1) b (cons (beat/on a beats-a) acc)))\n          ((< (/ a beats-a) (/ b beats-b))\n           (loop (+ a 1) b (cons (beat/on a beats-a) acc)))\n          (else\n           (loop a (+ b 1) (cons (beat/on b beats-b) acc))))))\n(length (poly-measure 3 4))" :note "Interleaved 3-against-4 polyrhythm. Returns 7 (3+4 records interleaved by fractional position). A classic hemiola pattern.")
  )
  :caveats ("beatIndex is floored to a non-negative integer; passing 0.7 becomes 0." "totalBeats is floored to a minimum of 1; passing 0 or negative becomes 1." "Emission is instantaneous; there is no built-in delay or scheduling." "Event is one-way; listeners may ignore it, but beat/on will still return success.")
  :drawbacks ("You must call beat/on yourself; there is no automatic beat clock. Use audio/tempo or radio/sync-to-beat to drive it." "Listeners subscribe globally; multiple overlapping beat loops will collide and cause confusion." "No way to cancel or revoke a beat after emission; once sent, it is processed." "Return value is always success; failures are silent.")
  :usecases ("Snap a character's dance step to a specific beat in a choreographed sequence." "Gate note playback or synth onset to beat boundaries." "Synchronize camera pans or scene transitions to musical downbeats.")
  :related ("audio/tempo" "radio/sync-to-beat" "tick/pulse" "motion/cadence" "time/every-ms")
  :learn (:concept "Explicit beat emission as the choreographer's tool; teaches event-driven coordination." :prerequisites ("audio/tempo" "cond" "for-each") :progression "Once you emit beats reliably, use part/* verbs to animate to those beats, or use synth/play to gate note onset.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A drum-pad in the shop's kiosk is playing every note twice on the downbeat. The operator wants to know: is the beat clock double-firing, or are two consumers each striking a kick on beat 0? Under audit they need a way to STAMP each beat with an identity so a log shows exactly what got emitted at what index, so it can be diffed against what the synth actually played."
     :program "(define (beat-log measure total)\n  (map (lambda (i)\n         (let ((b (beat/on i total)))\n           (list 'measure measure 'beat i 'of total 'record b)))\n       '(0 1 2 3)))\n(for-each (lambda (line) (display line) (newline))\n          (beat-log 1 4))"
     :explanation "The auditor wants a stamped ledger: one row per beat, with the measure number, the beat index, the totalBeats context, and the actual record beat/on returned. First we let-bind (beat/on i total) so the same call whose output flows to the synth is the call whose output goes to the log — no drift between what we logged and what we shipped. Then we walk 0,1,2,3, produce four entries, and print them line by line. If two rows of the log carry the same beat-index inside a single measure, the clock is double-firing. If only one row exists per index but the synth still played twice, then two subscribers each acted on the same record and the bug is downstream of the emitter."
     :meta "beat/on is the right choice here because it is the DATA-PRODUCING half of the beat system: it makes an inspectable record without emitting sound, without touching the audio surface, without introducing timing side effects. A sibling like audio/tempo would set the master tempo but wouldn't hand back a per-beat record you can log; radio/sync-to-beat would subscribe you to an existing clock but wouldn't let you STAMP each beat with your own audit fields; tick/pulse would fire on a raw clock signal that carries no beat position at all. The auditability comes from beat/on returning a value, not from any print or emit — which is why beat/on is the honest verb for the ledger.")
    (:eng "The operator's dashboard shows the log as one row per beat with a measure tag and the record; a duplicate index inside one measure is the smoke signal for a clock fault, and the absence of duplicates rules the clock out and points at consumer duplication. Ship the log to the SRE panel and diff against synth output."
     :math "beat/on is a total function from (index, total) to a record; the audit relies on that totality — every legal (i, n) pair produces exactly one record with no hidden branches, so the log's row-count is deterministic in the number of calls."
     :cs "Row 2 uses beat/on as a pure data producer: no I/O, no state mutation, just value construction. The audit trick is to bind the record to a local name (b) and use that name in both the log and any downstream emit, so the ledger's identity claim (this record IS what got shipped) holds by construction rather than by hope."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape here is INDEXED-POSITION-IN-A-CYCLE: given a position (the beat index) and a cycle length (the total beats), produce a stamped record that names WHERE inside the cycle we are. That shape is not specific to music; it is a general shape for anything that repeats with a known count."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "beat/music" :code "(beat/on 2 4)")
       (:domain "clock/hour-of-day" :code "(define (hour-of-day t) (list 'hour (modulo t 24) 'of 24))\n(hour-of-day 14)")
       (:domain "math/modular-position" :code "(define (mod-pos i n) (list 'pos (modulo i n) 'in-cycle n))\n(mod-pos 7 4)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is the verb in its own domain: beat 2 of a 4-beat measure. Rung 2 is a metaphor domain — a wall clock at hour 14 is at position 14 in a 24-hour cycle; same shape as beat 14 in a 24-beat measure. Rung 3 is the math domain: index i in a cycle of length n is the ordered pair (i mod n, n), and every implementation of a periodic position is a specialization of that pair. The shape is (position, period). beat/on packages that pair for music; hour-of-day packages it for time-of-day; mod-pos packages it for pure arithmetic. Once you see the pair, you can carry it into any domain where the same relationship holds."
     :meta "The shape transfers because a beat is not fundamentally about sound; it is about a countable position inside a cycle whose length you already know. Music makes the shape audible; a clock makes it visible on a dial; modular arithmetic makes it algebraic. What is portable across all three is the ordered pair (index, period) and the promise that the pair is well-defined for every non-negative index. Any system that answers 'given a step, where am I in the loop?' is implementing this shape.")
    (:eng "For an operator watching a rhythmic pipeline, the (index, period) pair is what shows up in every log line — the same field layout works for a beat-scheduler, a shift-rota, or a round-robin load-balancer, so the operator's mental model transfers across all three."
     :math "The underlying object is a residue class inside Z/nZ; beat/on returns a representative of that class with the period n carried alongside. Modular arithmetic in book-of-math ch08 defines the class; beat/on realizes one representative per beat."
     :cs "The pattern name in CS is the CYCLIC INDEX: a value drawn from a bounded, ordered, wrap-around domain. It appears in ring buffers, in scheduler queue positions, in periodic tasks. book-of-code ch09 (registers and counters) describes counters that wrap; beat/on is the domain-specific dress on top of a counter."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "beat/on is DETERMINISTIC and TOTAL over its documented input space: the same (index, total) always produces the same record, and every non-negative index paired with a positive total produces a record with no error. Determinism is what lets us bind the record once and use it in two places; totality is what lets the log's row-count equal the call-count."
     :program "(define (same? i n)\n  (equal? (beat/on i n) (beat/on i n)))\n(display (same? 0 4)) (newline)\n(display (same? 1 4)) (newline)\n(display (same? 2 4)) (newline)\n(display (same? 3 4)) (newline)\n(define (walk n)\n  (map (lambda (i) (beat/on i n))\n       (list 0 1 2 3)))\n(display (= 4 (length (walk 4)))) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ i ≥ 0, ∀ n > 0. beat/on(i, n) = beat/on(i, n)  AND  |{beat/on(i, n) | i ∈ 0..3}| defined for all i ∈ 0..3."
     :meta "The engineering consequence is that a beat log can be REPLAYED against a fresh interpreter and produce byte-identical rows; that reproducibility is what turns the log from a diagnostic into evidence. In CS terms this is REFERENTIAL TRANSPARENCY: beat/on has no hidden state, no clock read, no random draw. What falsifies the claim is a single (i, n) that produces two different records across two calls in the same session — one such witness proves the verb is state-carrying and every downstream audit becomes suspect. See book-of-math ch08 for modular determinism and book-of-code ch05 for pure gate composition, which is the CS ancestor of a stateless producer.")
    (:eng "For SRE, referential transparency means beat/on can be memoized without changing behavior, can be moved across threads without a mutex, and can be tested by simple equality against a fixture. A regression that makes the record depend on wall-clock time or on a session counter is a SEV-worthy break of the contract."
     :math "Totality plus determinism means beat/on realizes a function in the mathematical sense (single-valued on a fully specified domain); this is what makes the (index, period) pair a legitimate representative and not a mere sample."
     :cs "The pattern is a PURE PRODUCER: input goes in, value comes out, nothing else changes. Pure producers compose freely and safely; a beat pipeline built from beat/on-style producers has no ordering hazard between steps that only read."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "beat/on returns a beat-timing record for the given index inside a measure."
     :composition "(define (bar n)\n  (map (lambda (i) (beat/on i n)) '(0 1 2 3)))\n(define (rest? b) (odd? (cadr b)))\n(define (voice bar)\n  (map (lambda (b) (if (rest? b) 'rest 'strike)) bar))\n(voice (bar 4))"
     :emergent "A SEQUENCER emerges from beat/on chained with a mapper and a predicate: given a measure length, the pipeline emits a per-beat instruction list (strike/rest), which is the raw material a synth or drum voice consumes. No new verb was introduced; the sequencer is the shape of the chain."
     :meta "The family here is the STEP SEQUENCER — the same family as a hardware step-programmer's row of LEDs, as a DAW's piano roll (one column per beat, one row per voice), as a cron entry that fires per-minute inside an hour. book-of-sound ch12 (sequencing and chiptune) covers the pattern in music terms; book-of-composition ch05 (piano roll) covers the widget-side of the same pattern. The composition is (bar) → per-beat-records → per-beat-decisions; add a second voice, and you have a poly-line sequencer; add a bank of voices with different predicates, and you have a full step-programmer.")
    (:eng "The emergent sequencer is diffable, replayable, and human-readable: the strike/rest list is what shows up in a rehearsal log, and the log can be replayed into any voice engine. Operators debug a wrong rhythm by inspecting the list, not by staring at audio output."
     :math "The chain is a composition of two total functions: bar : n → List<record>, then voice : List<record> → List<symbol>. The output has the same cardinality as the input bar, so cardinality is preserved along the pipeline — a common invariant in signal-processing chains."
     :cs "Step sequencer is one of the canonical patterns in book-of-composition ch05 (piano roll); the chain here is the minimal one-voice form. Adding a bank of voices is a fan-out; adding a loop counter is a wrap; both are pattern extensions the family already knows.")))
