(verb
  :name "comb/factorial"
  :library "comb"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(comb/factorial n) -> integer"
  :summary "Factorial n! for integer n ≥ 0: product of all positive integers up to n."
  :explanation "The factorial n! = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × 1 counts the number of permutations (ordered arrangements) of n distinct items. By definition, 0! = 1. Factorials grow extremely rapidly—10! = 3,628,800, 20! ≈ 2.4×10¹⁸—and appear throughout combinatorics, probability, calculus (series expansions), and statistical mechanics. Factorials are building blocks for binomial coefficients, permutations, and other counting problems."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(comb/factorial 5)" :note "Returns 120: there are 120 ways to arrange 5 distinct items.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(map comb/factorial (list 0 1 2 3 4 5 6))" :note "Returns (1 1 2 6 24 120 720): factorials grow rapidly and are often pre-computed as lookup tables.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((n 7) (k 3))\n  (/ (comb/factorial n) (* (comb/factorial k) (comb/factorial (- n k)))))" :note "Compute C(7,3) = 7!/(3!×4!) = 5040/(6×24) = 35 by hand from factorials, showing the relationship to comb/choose.")
  )
  :caveats ("Factorials overflow rapidly; n! > 2⁶³ for n ≥ 21 on 64-bit systems. Safe range is typically n ≤ 20." "0! is defined as 1 by convention; no special case needed, but it can surprise beginners." "No validation that n is a non-negative integer; behavior on negative or non-integer n is undefined (likely an error or infinity).")
  :drawbacks ("Growth rate makes factorials impractical for large n; use approximations or avoid factorial-based formulas when possible." "Each call recomputes n! without caching; pre-compute and store factorials if used repeatedly." "Division in derived formulas (like C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!)) can introduce rounding errors if done in floating-point; always use integer arithmetic.")
  :usecases ("Permutation counting: enumerate distinct orderings of n items." "Taylor series: compute coefficients in expansions of e^x, sin(x), etc." "Multinomial coefficients: generalize binomial coefficients to more than two categories." "Probability: compute normalization factors in statistical distributions.")
  :related ("comb/choose" "comb/permute" "comb/derangement" "comb/multinomial")
  :learn (:concept "Factorials are the foundation of permutation-counting and appear in the denominators of many combinatorial formulas." :prerequisites () :progression "After factorial, learn comb/choose and comb/permute to see how factorials are used in counting selections and arrangements.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A game/quest wants the count of ways to line up 5 loot items for display; the operator uses factorial for ordered arrangement count."
     :program "(comb/factorial 5)"
     :explanation "Returns 120: 5! ways to arrange 5 items. The quest UI cycles through arrangements over time."
     :meta "Reach for comb/factorial and NOT comb/permute with k=n: permute(n,n) computes the same value but the intent is 'total arrangements', which factorial names.")
    (:eng "The quest log records 120 arrangements." :math "n! = ∏ᵢ₌₁ⁿ i, with 0! = 1." :cs "Meta computation; grows super-exponentially."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Total-arrangement count of a finite set."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "comb"    :code "(comb/factorial 5)")
       (:domain "note (metaphor)" :code "(count-permutation (music/scale 'C-major))")
       (:domain "group theory"    :code "|S_n| = n!"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 arrangement count. Rung 2 note-order count. Rung 3 order of the symmetric group. Same shape."
     :meta "Symmetric-group order transfers to any full-permutation domain.")
    (:eng "Order-count appears in shuffling, seating, and turn-order design." :math "|S_n| = n!." :cs "Foundation for permutation-based generation."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "n! satisfies n! = n · (n-1)! for n ≥ 1, with 0! = 1."
     :program "(define (test n) (or (= n 0) (= (comb/factorial n) (* n (comb/factorial (- n 1))))))\n(and (test 0) (test 1) (test 5) (test 8))"
     :invariant "0! = 1 ∧ ∀ n ≥ 1. n! = n · (n-1)!"
     :meta "Pattern: linear recurrence. Falsifies if any n breaks. See book-of-math ch on factorials.")
    (:eng "The recurrence is the base for iterative implementations." :math "Order-1 recurrence." :cs "Order-1 recurrence gives O(n) time and O(1) space."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "comb/factorial counts total arrangements."
     :composition "(define (permutation-density n k) (/ (comb/factorial n) (comb/factorial (- n k))))\n(list (permutation-density 5 2) (permutation-density 5 3))"
     :emergent "permutation-density calculator — factorial ratios yield P(n,k) directly, revealing the arithmetic origin of comb/permute."
     :meta "Family: ratio-of-factorials. Same shape as computing binomial coefficients from factorials or Stirling numbers by ratios. See book-of-composition ch on factorial ratios.")
    (:eng "The pattern shows how many verbs decompose to factorials." :math "P(n,k) = n!/(n-k)!." :cs "Ratio-of-factorials is the primitive-decomposition idiom."))

(verb
  :name "comb/multichoose"
  :library "comb"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(comb/multichoose n k) -> integer"
  :summary "Stars and bars: number of ways to choose k items from n types (with replacement)."
  :explanation "The multichoose coefficient (also called 'stars and bars' or 'combinations with replacement') counts the number of ways to select k items from n distinct types, where repetition is allowed and order does not matter. The formula is C(n+k−1, k) = (n+k−1)! / (k!(n−1)!). For example, if you have 3 flavors of ice cream and want to pick 2 scoops (with repetition), there are C(3+2−1, 2) = C(4, 2) = 6 ways: {vanilla, vanilla}, {vanilla, chocolate}, {vanilla, strawberry}, {chocolate, chocolate}, {chocolate, strawberry}, {strawberry, strawberry}. This verb is essential for counting multisets and unordered selections from a repeatable palette."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(comb/multichoose 3 2)" :note "Returns 6: there are 6 ways to choose 2 items from 3 types with replacement, as listed above.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(map (lambda (k) (comb/multichoose 4 k)) (list 0 1 2 3 4))" :note "Returns (1 4 10 20 35): multichoose(4, k) for k=0..4. Note the growth compared to binomial coefficients.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((n-flavors 5) (n-scoops 3))\n  (let ((ways (comb/multichoose n-flavors n-scoops)))\n    (list 'ways ways)))" :note "Compute the number of 3-scoop ice-cream combinations from 5 flavors: C(5+3−1, 3) = C(7, 3) = 35 combinations.")
  )
  :caveats ("Requires n ≥ 1 and k ≥ 0; behavior for n ≤ 0 or k < 0 is undefined." "Multichoose values grow quickly; multichoose(20, 20) = C(39, 20) ≈ 6.8×10¹⁰, risking overflow." "The formula C(n+k−1, k) requires careful argument handling; off-by-one errors are easy to introduce.")
  :drawbacks ("Not as intuitive as regular comb/choose; the 'stars and bars' interpretation takes time to internalize." "Pure computation without caching; repeated calls with the same n and k recompute the result." "If you need to enumerate the multisets themselves (not just count them), use a dedicated multiset-generation algorithm.")
  :usecases ("Inventory management: count ways to distribute k identical items among n bins." "Combinatorial search: enumerate all unordered selections from a repeatable menu (menus, toppings, flavors)." "Partition enumeration: count compositions of integers with constraints." "Probability: model sampling with replacement from a discrete distribution.")
  :related ("comb/choose" "comb/binomial-coeffs" "comb/multinomial" "comb/catalan")
  :learn (:concept "Multichoose extends combinatorics from unordered selections without replacement (comb/choose) to selections with replacement via a change of variables (stars and bars)." :prerequisites ("comb/choose" "comb/factorial") :progression "After multichoose, explore comb/multinomial to extend counting to partitions into more than two categories, then comb/partition-count for integer partitions.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A game/ice-cream shop counts how many 3-scoop cones are possible from 5 flavors when scoops can repeat."
     :program "(comb/multichoose 5 3)"
     :explanation "Returns 35: 35 distinct 3-scoop multisets from 5 flavors. The menu uses the count as its selection space."
     :meta "Reach for comb/multichoose and NOT comb/choose: choose forbids repetition; multichoose allows it. Ice cream allows two scoops of vanilla, so multichoose is correct.")
    (:eng "The menu log reports possibility count." :math "Multichoose(n,k) = C(n+k-1, k)." :cs "Meta computation; derived from binomial via stars-and-bars."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Selection with replacement — counting multisets of fixed size."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "comb"    :code "(comb/multichoose 5 3)")
       (:domain "sprite (metaphor)" :code "(sprite/count-tile-arrangements 5 3)")
       (:domain "algebra"    :code "|Multiset_k(A)| = C(|A|+k-1, k)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 flavor multisets. Rung 2 tile arrangements with repeats. Rung 3 abstract multiset count. Same shape."
     :meta "Multiset-counting transfers to any 'with-replacement' domain.")
    (:eng "Repeatable-picks appear in menus, roster designs, and configurations." :math "Multiset cardinality via stars-and-bars." :cs "Combinatorial identity from a bijection to plain choose."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "Multichoose(n,k) equals C(n+k-1, k) — the stars-and-bars identity."
     :program "(define (test n k) (= (comb/multichoose n k) (comb/choose (- (+ n k) 1) k)))\n(and (test 5 3) (test 3 2) (test 4 4))"
     :invariant "∀ n ≥ 1 k ≥ 0. Multichoose(n,k) = C(n+k-1, k)"
     :meta "Pattern: identity via bijection (stars-and-bars). Falsifies if any pair breaks. See book-of-math ch on stars-and-bars.")
    (:eng "The identity provides a cross-check for multichoose implementations." :math "Bijection between multisets and binary strings." :cs "Bijections give computational shortcuts."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "comb/multichoose counts multisets."
     :composition "(define (menu-space flavors scoops) (list 'without-repeats: (comb/choose flavors scoops) 'with-repeats: (comb/multichoose flavors scoops)))\n(menu-space 5 3)"
     :emergent "menu-space comparator — display both no-repeat and with-repeat totals side by side, exposing the multiplicative gap."
     :meta "Family: constraint-comparison. Same shape as A/B testing configurations or feature-flag matrix counts. See book-of-composition ch on counting under constraints.")
    (:eng "The pattern surfaces the design-space size to product owners." :math "Compare cardinalities across constraint variations." :cs "Multi-variant counting is a base of combinatorial design."))

(verb
  :name "comb/multinomial"
  :library "comb"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(comb/multinomial ks) -> number"
  :summary "Multinomial coefficient: the number of ways to arrange n items into groups of sizes k₁, k₂, …, kₘ."
  :explanation "The multinomial coefficient generalizes binomial coefficients to more than two groups. Given a list of group sizes (k₁ k₂ … kₘ), it computes n!/(k₁! × k₂! × … × kₘ!) where n = sum of all ks. This counts the arrangements of n distinct objects partitioned into labeled groups. For example, arranging 6 people into a committee of 2, a team of 3, and a pair leaves 1: multinomial([2 3 1]) = 6!/(2!×3!×1!) = 60."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(comb/multinomial '(2 3 1))" :note "Six items in groups of 2, 3, and 1; yields 60 arrangements.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((groups '(1 1 2 2)))\n  (comb/multinomial groups))" :note "Splitting 6 items into four labeled groups (1, 1, 2, 2); stores the list in a variable for reuse.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (multinomial-ways items group-sizes)\n  (if (= (apply + group-sizes) (length items))\n    (comb/multinomial group-sizes)\n    (escalate 'size-mismatch null)))\n(multinomial-ways '(a b c d e f) '(2 2 2))" :note "Wrapper that validates group sizes match item count before computing; uses escalate to signal mismatch.")
  )
  :caveats ("All elements of the input list must be non-negative integers." "The sum of the input list determines n; if ks sums to 0, the coefficient is 1 (empty partition)." "Factorials grow very quickly; large n will produce large numbers (exact arithmetic used).")
  :drawbacks ("Factorial computation can be slow for large sums; prefer comb/choose when you need only two groups." "Does not validate that group sizes make semantic sense for your problem.")
  :usecases ("Counting ways to distribute distinguishable objects into labeled bins." "Probability: multiway arrangements in multinomial probability distributions." "Word anagrams with repeated letters (group sizes are letter frequencies)." "Tournament seeding: splitting N players into K labeled brackets.")
  :related ("comb/choose" "comb/permute" "comb/bell" "comb/partition-count")
  :learn (:concept "Generalized counting via grouped factorials; extension of binomial to k > 2 groups." :prerequisites ("comb/choose" "comb/factorial") :progression "After mastering multinomial, explore comb/stirling2 (partitions into unlabeled groups) and comb/bell (total partitions).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A game/team-formation splits 6 players into three labeled teams of sizes 2, 2, 2; the operator wants the count of distinct assignments."
     :program "(comb/multinomial '(2 2 2))"
     :explanation "Returns 90: 6!/(2!·2!·2!) = 720/8 = 90. The scheduler uses the count as its assignment sample space."
     :meta "Reach for comb/multinomial and NOT (/ (comb/factorial 6) (* (comb/factorial 2) (comb/factorial 2) (comb/factorial 2))): the manual form works but is noisy. multinomial names it and generalizes.")
    (:eng "The scheduler log records the team-assignment count." :math "n!/(k₁!·k₂!·…·kₘ!) where n = Σkᵢ." :cs "Meta computation; extends comb/choose to k > 2 groups."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Labeled-partition counting: split n items into labeled groups of fixed sizes."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "comb"    :code "(comb/multinomial '(2 2 2))")
       (:domain "world (metaphor)" :code "(world/count-role-assignments 6 '(2 2 2))")
       (:domain "algebra"    :code "n! / Π kᵢ!"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 group formation. Rung 2 role assignment. Rung 3 abstract division of arrangements. Same shape."
     :meta "Labeled-partition transfer to any tuple-of-sizes design.")
    (:eng "Team-labeling and role-assignment problems share this shape." :math "Multinomial coefficient." :cs "Extends binomial to arbitrary group count."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "Multinomial reduces to binomial for two groups: multinomial([k, n-k]) = C(n,k)."
     :program "(define (test n k) (= (comb/multinomial (list k (- n k))) (comb/choose n k)))\n(and (test 5 2) (test 6 3) (test 10 5))"

     :emergent "anagram-counter — multinomial applied to letter frequencies gives the number of distinct anagrams of a word."
     :meta "Family: symmetry-quotient count. Same shape as counting distinguishable orderings of colored balls or a Sudoku permutation. See book-of-composition ch on symmetry quotients.")

    (:eng "The pattern surfaces sub-exponential growth structure to designers." :math "Realizes an approximate analog of the Hardy-Ramanujan asymptotic." :cs "Density-analysis is a base for algorithm-complexity discussion."))

(verb
  :name "comb/pascal-row"
  :library "comb"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(comb/pascal-row n) -> list"
  :summary "Returns the nth row of Pascal's triangle as a list of binomial coefficients."
  :explanation "Pascal's triangle is a triangular array where each entry is the sum of the two entries above it. The nth row contains the binomial coefficients C(n,0), C(n,1), …, C(n,n), which appear in the expansion of (a+b)^n. Row 0 is (1), row 1 is (1 1), row 2 is (1 2 1), and so on. This is a fast way to generate all binomial coefficients for a fixed n."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(comb/pascal-row 3)" :note "Yields (1 3 3 1), the coefficients of (a+b)³.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(map comb/pascal-row '(0 1 2 3 4))" :note "Generates rows 0 through 4 as a list of lists; shows exponential growth of entries.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (binomial-coeff n k)\n  (let ((row (comb/pascal-row n)))\n    (if (and (>= k 0) (< k (length row)))\n      (list-ref row k)\n      (escalate 'out-of-bounds null))))\n(binomial-coeff 5 2)" :note "Wrapper to extract a single coefficient C(5,2)=10 from row 5; validates bounds.")
  )
  :caveats ("Row entries grow exponentially; C(n,n/2) ≈ 2^n for large n." "The returned list has exactly n+1 elements (indices 0 through n)." "Order is always left-to-right: (C(n,0) C(n,1) … C(n,n)).")
  :drawbacks ("Generating a single entry C(n,k) via comb/pascal-row wastes computation if k << n; prefer comb/choose for a single value." "Memory cost is linear in n; not suitable for extremely large n if row must be retained.")
  :usecases ("Binomial expansions: coefficients of (a+b)^n." "Probability: binomial distribution probabilities." "Combinatorics: quick lookup of multiple C(n,k) for the same n." "Algorithm visualization: Pascal's triangle is a classic teaching tool.")
  :related ("comb/choose" "comb/binomial-coeffs" "comb/pascal-triangle" "comb/multinomial")
  :learn (:concept "Efficient row-wise access to binomial coefficients via recurrence." :prerequisites ("comb/choose" "comb/factorial") :progression "After mastering pascal-row, study comb/pascal-triangle (full triangle), then comb/stirling2 (a different triangle with combinatorial meaning).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A math/plot renderer draws Pascal's triangle row 6; the operator wants the single row without materializing the whole triangle."
     :program "(comb/pascal-row 6)"
     :explanation "Returns (1 6 15 20 15 6 1): the row-6 binomial coefficients. The plotter uses each as a bar height."
     :meta "Reach for comb/pascal-row and NOT comb/pascal-triangle followed by list-ref: computing the whole triangle wastes O(n²) space when O(n) suffices.")
    (:eng "The plot log records the row content." :math "Row n = (C(n,0), C(n,1), …, C(n,n))." :cs "O(n) construction using the recurrence."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Row-wise projection of a triangular table."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "comb"    :code "(comb/pascal-row 6)")
       (:domain "matrix (metaphor)" :code "(matrix/row m 3)")
       (:domain "algebra"   :code "row n of Pascal's triangle"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 pascal row. Rung 2 matrix row. Rung 3 the abstract triangle row. Same shape."
     :meta "Row-projection is a universal shape.")
    (:eng "Row-projection appears in every table-viewer." :math "Projection function onto row n." :cs "Row access is often O(1) with vector storage; O(n) here reflects generation."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "Pascal-row-n is symmetric: reversing the row equals the row."
     :program "(define (test n) (equal? (comb/pascal-row n) (reverse (comb/pascal-row n))))\n(and (test 0) (test 3) (test 5) (test 8))"
     :invariant "∀ n. reverse(pascal-row(n)) = pascal-row(n)"
     :meta "Pattern: palindromic identity. Falsifies if any row is not palindromic. See book-of-math ch on Pascal's triangle symmetry.")
    (:eng "Palindrome symmetry is a runtime sanity-check for row output." :math "Follows from C(n,k) = C(n,n-k)." :cs "Symmetric-lookup can compress storage."))
  :row-5-emergence (

     :emergent "row-peak analyzer — track the peak coefficient of each row; it grows roughly as 2ⁿ/√n."
     :meta "Family: peak-tracker. Same shape as tracking peak-amplitude in a signal or max-density in a physics simulation. See book-of-composition ch on extremum-tracking.")
    (:eng "The pattern helps visualize normal-distribution shape emerging from Pascal." :math "Central binomial coefficient is the peak of row n." :cs "Extremum-tracking is a base analytics idiom."))

  :summary "Returns the first n rows of Pascal's triangle as a list of lists."

  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(comb/pascal-triangle 4)" :note "Yields ((1) (1 1) (1 2 1) (1 3 3 1)), the first four rows.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((tri (comb/pascal-triangle 5)))\n  (map length tri))" :note "Maps length over each row; yields (1 2 3 4 5), confirming row k has k+1 entries.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (row-sum tri row-idx)\n  (if (and (>= row-idx 0) (< row-idx (length tri)))\n    (apply + (list-ref tri row-idx))\n    (escalate 'out-of-bounds null)))\n(let ((tri (comb/pascal-triangle 5)))\n  (list (row-sum tri 4) (row-sum tri 0)))" :note "Sums the entries in row 4 (yields 16 = 2^4) and row 0 (yields 1); demonstrates that row-sums equal 2^n.")

  :caveats ("Returns exactly n rows (rows 0 through n-1), so (comb/pascal-triangle 1) is ((1))." "Total entries across all rows is 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2; memory grows quadratically." "Each row k has k+1 entries; rows are ordered top-to-bottom.")

  :related ("comb/pascal-row" "comb/choose" "comb/binomial-coeffs" "seq/partial-sums")
  :learn (:concept "Bulk construction of a triangular coefficient table; contrast with row-by-row generation." :prerequisites ("comb/pascal-row" "comb/choose") :progression "Study the symmetry and divisibility properties of Pascal's triangle, then explore comb/stirling2 (a different triangle) and comb/bell (a sequence derived from triangles).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A tutorial widget needs the first 6 rows of Pascal's triangle to render the classic teaching diagram."
     :program "(comb/pascal-triangle 6)"
     :explanation "Returns ((1) (1 1) (1 2 1) (1 3 3 1) (1 4 6 4 1) (1 5 10 10 5 1)): 6 rows. The widget renders each as a centered numeric row."
     :meta "Reach for comb/pascal-triangle when many rows are needed at once. If only one row, comb/pascal-row saves memory.")
    (:eng "The tutorial log records the triangle rows." :math "Triangle_n = {row_k : 0 ≤ k < n}." :cs "O(n²) space and time for n rows."))
  :row-3-dimension (

  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "The k-th row of the returned triangle equals (comb/pascal-row k)."

     :invariant "∀ n k. 0 ≤ k < n → (pascal-triangle n)[k] = pascal-row(k)"

(verb
  :name "comb/permute"
  :library "comb"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(comb/permute n k) -> number"
  :summary "Permutations P(n,k): the number of ordered arrangements of k items chosen from n distinct items."
  :explanation "A permutation counts the ways to choose and arrange k items from n items, where order matters. The formula is P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)!. For example, P(5,2) = 5!/(5−2)! = 5×4 = 20: there are 20 ways to pick and order 2 items from {1,2,3,4,5}. This differs from comb/choose, which ignores order. Permutations arise when arrangement sequence is significant (e.g., picking a president and vice-president from candidates)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(comb/permute 5 2)" :note "Yields 20: arrange 2 items from 5 distinct items. (e.g., pick president then VP)")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((n 6) (k 3))\n  (list (comb/permute n k) (comb/choose n k)))" :note "P(6,3)=120, C(6,3)=20; shows permutations are larger by a factor of k!=6 when order is added.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (seating-arrangements people seat-count)\n  (if (<= seat-count (length people))\n    (comb/permute (length people) seat-count)\n    (escalate 'insufficient-people null)))\n(seating-arrangements '(alice bob carol dave) 3)" :note "Counts ways to seat 3 of 4 people in 3 chairs; validates seat-count ≤ person-count; yields 24.")
  )
  :caveats ("k must be a non-negative integer; k > n yields 0 (no valid permutations)." "Order of arguments matters: P(n,k) ≠ P(k,n) unless n = k." "P(n,0) = 1 (one way to arrange zero items: the empty arrangement).")
  :drawbacks ("Grows very quickly; P(20,10) is already in the billions." "If you only care about unordered selections, use comb/choose (typically smaller and faster)." "Permutation computation is O(k) rather than O(min(k, n−k)) for choose; less efficient when k is large.")
  :usecases ("Ranking and seating: arrangements of people in ordered positions." "Lock codes and PINs: sequences where repetition is disallowed and order matters." "Tournament brackets: assigning ranked opponents to labeled slots." "Probability: ordered outcomes (e.g., drawing cards without replacement in sequence).")
  :related ("comb/choose" "comb/multinomial" "comb/factorial" "comb/multichoose")
  :learn (:concept "Ordered selection; the role of order in combinatorial counting." :prerequisites ("comb/choose" "comb/factorial") :progression "Explore comb/multichoose (selection with replacement) and comb/multinomial (ordered partition into groups).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A game/tournament counts how many ways to award gold, silver, bronze to 3 of 8 finalists — order matters because the medals differ."
     :program "(comb/permute 8 3)"
     :explanation "Returns 336: 8·7·6 = 336 distinct ordered awards. The tournament UI uses the count to size its result grid."
     :meta "Reach for comb/permute and NOT comb/choose: choose forgets order and undercounts. Medal assignment cares which position each finalist takes.")
    (:eng "The tournament log reports the ordered-award count." :math "P(n,k) = n!/(n-k)!." :cs "Meta computation; extends factorial with a k parameter."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Ordered selection: pick k, but position matters."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "comb"    :code "(comb/permute 5 2)")
       (:domain "beat (metaphor)" :code "(beat/count-ordered-fills 5 2)")
       (:domain "algebra"    :code "P(n,k) = n·(n-1)·…·(n-k+1)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 ordered picks. Rung 2 ordered rhythm fills. Rung 3 falling-factorial. Same shape."
     :meta "Ordered selection is a universal shape.")
    (:eng "Ordered outcomes appear across every ranking/scheduling problem." :math "Falling factorial (n)_k." :cs "Ordered vs. unordered is a base distinction."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "P(n,k) = C(n,k) · k! — permutations are combinations times orderings."
     :program "(define (test n k) (= (comb/permute n k) (* (comb/choose n k) (comb/factorial k))))\n(and (test 5 2) (test 6 3) (test 8 4))"
     :invariant "∀ n k. 0 ≤ k ≤ n → P(n,k) = C(n,k) · k!"
     :meta "Pattern: factorization identity. Falsifies if any pair breaks. See book-of-math ch on permutations and combinations.")
    (:eng "Factorization lets ops derive one from the other with a factorial." :math "The order-forgetting projection has k! preimages." :cs "Identity gives a cross-check between comb/permute and comb/choose."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "comb/permute counts ordered picks."
     :composition "(define (medal-outcomes n) (let ((tot (comb/permute n 3)) (top (comb/permute n 1))) (list 'gold-alone: top 'top-3-ranked: tot)))\n(medal-outcomes 8)"
     :emergent "outcome-comparator — compare cardinalities of different tournament shapes."
     :meta "Family: outcome-space sizer. Same shape as counting sample spaces in probability. See book-of-composition ch on outcome-space design.")
    (:eng "The pattern helps size UIs and payoff spaces." :math "Realizes the P(n,k) family across k." :cs "Outcome-sizing is a base for probability calculators."))

(verb
  :name "comb/stirling2"
  :library "comb"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(comb/stirling2 n k) -> number"
  :summary "Stirling number of the second kind S(n,k): the number of ways to partition n distinct items into exactly k non-empty unlabeled subsets."
  :explanation "The Stirling number of the second kind counts set partitions. Unlike multinomial (which partitions into labeled groups of fixed sizes) and partition-count (which partitions integers), S(n,k) partitions n distinguishable objects into exactly k indistinguishable non-empty groups. For example, S(4,2) = 7: the set {a,b,c,d} can be split into two groups in seven ways (e.g., {{a},{b,c,d}}, {{a,b},{c,d}}, etc.). These numbers satisfy the recurrence S(n,k) = k·S(n−1,k) + S(n−1,k−1)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(comb/stirling2 4 2)" :note "Yields 7: seven ways to split 4 distinct items into 2 non-empty groups.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(map (lambda (k) (comb/stirling2 5 k)) '(1 2 3 4 5))" :note "Stirling numbers for n=5 and k=1,2,3,4,5; yields (1 15 25 10 1).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (partition-count-by-size n)\n  (let ((stirling-row (map (lambda (k) (comb/stirling2 n k)) (list 1 2 3))))\n    (apply + stirling-row)))\n(partition-count-by-size 4)" :note "Sums S(4,1) + S(4,2) + S(4,3) = 1 + 7 + 6 = 14; notice that summing S(n,k) for all k gives comb/bell (total partitions).")
  )
  :caveats ("k must satisfy 0 ≤ k ≤ n; S(n,k) = 0 if k > n." "Does not enumerate the actual partitions, only counts them." "S(n,k) grows rapidly; S(10,5) is already 42525.")
  :drawbacks ("Computing S(n,k) for large n and k is slow without memoization." "If you need the actual partition lists (not just the count), you need a separate enumeration algorithm." "Stirling numbers are less commonly known than binomial coefficients; may require explanation in code comments.")
  :usecases ("Counting set partitions: partitioning a set of people into teams or groups." "Combinatorial structure: analyzing the number of equivalence relations on a finite set." "Algorithm analysis: counting surjective functions from n items to k labels." "Bell numbers: summing S(n,k) over k yields the Bell number B(n), the total number of partitions.")
  :related ("comb/bell" "comb/partition-count" "comb/multinomial" "comb/choose")
  :learn (:concept "Set partitions into unlabeled subsets; contrast with labeled groups (multinomial) and integer partitions." :prerequisites ("comb/choose" "comb/partition-count") :progression "Study comb/bell (sum over all k), then explore connections to comb/multinomial (labeled partitions) and equivalence relations.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A world/team-picker splits 5 kids into exactly 2 unlabeled teams; the operator wants the count for planning."
     :program "(comb/stirling2 5 2)"
     :explanation "Returns 15: 15 ways to partition 5 kids into exactly 2 non-empty unlabeled teams. The picker uses this as its sample space."
     :meta "Reach for comb/stirling2 and NOT comb/multinomial: multinomial expects labeled teams; here the two teams are interchangeable.")
    (:eng "The picker log reports the count." :math "S(n,k) counts set partitions of n into k blocks." :cs "Meta computation; recurrence-based."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Fixed-count unlabeled partition — split into a chosen number of unlabeled non-empty blocks."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "comb"    :code "(comb/stirling2 5 2)")
       (:domain "audio (metaphor)" :code "(audio/count-instrument-groupings 5 2)")
       (:domain "equivalence theory" :code "|{eq-relations R on [n] : |[n]/R| = k}|"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 team partitions. Rung 2 instrument groupings. Rung 3 equivalence relations of fixed classes. Same shape."
     :meta "Fixed-count unlabeled partition transfers to any classification problem.")
    (:eng "Classifier-design uses this shape." :math "Number of equivalence relations with k classes." :cs "Foundation for classification-count problems."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "S(n,k) satisfies the recurrence S(n,k) = k·S(n-1,k) + S(n-1,k-1)."
     :program "(define (test n k) (= (comb/stirling2 n k) (+ (* k (comb/stirling2 (- n 1) k)) (comb/stirling2 (- n 1) (- k 1)))))\n(and (test 4 2) (test 5 3) (test 6 2))"
     :invariant "∀ n k. 1 ≤ k < n → S(n,k) = k·S(n-1,k) + S(n-1,k-1)"
     :meta "Pattern: two-argument recurrence. Falsifies if any pair breaks. See book-of-math ch on Stirling numbers.")
    (:eng "The recurrence is what memoized implementations use for O(nk)." :math "Two-argument recurrence with 'assign-to-existing or start-new' interpretation." :cs "Recurrence-driven DP is a canonical fast approach."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "comb/stirling2 counts fixed-count set partitions."
     :composition "(define (stirling-row n) (map (lambda (k) (comb/stirling2 n k)) (map (lambda (i) (+ i 1)) (iota n))))\n(define (iota n) (let loop ((i 0) (acc '())) (if (>= i n) (reverse acc) (loop (+ i 1) (cons i acc)))))\n(define (sum-row n) (apply + (stirling-row n)))\n(list (stirling-row 5) (sum-row 5))"
     :emergent "Bell-verifier — the row of Stirling-second numbers sums to the Bell number B(n)."

    (:eng "The pattern lets ops cross-check two verb families for consistency." :math "B(n) = Σₖ S(n,k) is the sum-over-k identity." :cs "Cross-verb consistency is a base of sanity-checking."))

(verb :name "boolean=?" :library "compare" :tier "core" :kind "pure" :signature "(boolean=? a b) -> boolean"
  :summary "#t if both are #t, or both are #f. R7RS §6.3."
  :provenance "R7RS §6.3; added 2026-07-18 finalization"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(boolean=? #t #t)" :note "#t.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(boolean=? #t #f)" :note "#f.")
  )
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator has an input-handler that classifies key events and stores a boolean 'shift-held' flag for each event. A downstream report needs to bucket events by whether the flag matches an expected reference boolean, and generic `equal?` was showing up on the CPU profile because it walks structure it did not need to walk. The operator wants a comparison verb that takes exactly two booleans and returns exactly #t or #f — no polymorphism, no structural walk, no coercion. The sibling verbs eqv?, equal?, and symbol=? all sound close but each has a subtly different contract. Only boolean=? is honest about doing one thing: compare two booleans."
     :program "(define (count-matching flag ref events)\n  (let loop ((es events) (n 0))\n    (if (null? es)\n      n\n      (loop (cdr es)\n            (if (boolean=? (car es) ref) (+ n 1) n)))))\n(display (count-matching 'shift #t (list #t #f #t #t #f)))\n(newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines a bucketing helper that walks a list of boolean flags and counts how many equal a reference boolean. Line 4 calls boolean=? on each element against the reference. Line 8 runs the count on a five-element list; three of the flags match #t so the counter prints 3. The audit trail is: five inputs consumed, one comparison per input, three matches. Because boolean=? has a rigid two-boolean signature, an auditor knows every comparison in the loop is a boolean-vs-boolean check — nothing else could be sneaking in."
     :meta "Why boolean=? and not a sibling: eqv? would work correctly but its contract admits any two objects, so a downstream reader cannot tell at a glance whether the loop is comparing booleans or something else. equal? walks structure — for booleans the walk is trivial, but the SIGNATURE says it might have walked, which is a documentation lie. symbol=? has the wrong argument type entirely; passing a boolean to symbol=? is an error. boolean=? is the honest one — signature says boolean-vs-boolean, implementation does exactly that, and a code review can trust the type at the call site.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is a type-witnessing comparison: the verb's signature narrows the reader's expectation, so a later maintainer knows what the loop is really doing without opening the runtime. See SRE Manual on 'signatures as documentation' — the tightest signature that fits the job is the one that survives audits."
     :math "Boolean equality is the biconditional a ↔ b on {#t, #f}. Two elements, four cases, all decidable. The verb is a decision procedure on a two-element domain."
     :cs "The CS pattern is a monotype equality predicate. Sibling equalities in R7RS (eqv?, equal?, symbol=?, string=?, char=?, =) form a family where each element is specialized to one type. Motoi keeps the family for the same reason C keeps `int==int` distinct from `strcmp` — the specialization is what makes the compiler emit tight code and what makes the code readable."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A monotype equality: compare two values of a single named type and return whether they are the same, refusing to compare across types. The shape is 'homogeneous decidable equality.'"
     :rungs ((:domain "compare (boolean)" :code "(boolean=? #t #t)")
             (:domain "kitchen ticket lanes" :code "(same-lane? 'expo 'expo)")
             (:domain "algebra of {0,1}" :code "(= (mod 1 2) (mod 1 2))"))
     :explanation "In the compare domain the two operands are booleans and the answer is the biconditional. In a kitchen where tickets are sorted into named lanes ('expo, 'grill, 'salad) the same-lane predicate compares two lane-symbols and answers whether a ticket is being kept in the same lane or being moved. In ℤ/2ℤ (the two-element ring) equality of residues is decided by literal comparison, and the same domain restriction applies — only two values are ever compared. The three cases differ in what the two things ARE, but the shape — 'compare two things of one named type, return decidable yes/no' — is identical."
     :meta "The shape transfers because all three cases share a two-element (or small-finite) domain, a total equality relation, and a refusal to cross types. Any place you have (a) a value space you can exhaustively enumerate and (b) an equality that must be decidable in constant time, this shape fits. The rigid domain is the point — it is what lets the caller trust the answer without further checks.")
    (:eng "The engineering rule is 'compare what you claim to compare.' A boolean-vs-boolean compare that accepts any two objects invites bugs where a not-quite-boolean sneaks in. The narrow signature stops that at the call site."
     :math "The relation on a two-element set has four entries; the equality subset has two. The relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive — the standard equivalence-relation axioms hold trivially on {#t, #f}."
     :cs "The CS analog is a tag-check on a sum type. In a language with tagged unions, the equality of two Bool values is a one-instruction cmp. Motoi's boolean=? occupies the same slot — specialized, decidable, cheap."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "boolean=? is reflexive, symmetric, and total on the boolean domain: (boolean=? x x) is #t for x∈{#t,#f}; and (boolean=? a b) equals (boolean=? b a); and every combination returns a boolean."
     :program "(define (both a b) (and a b))\n(display (both (boolean=? #t #t) (boolean=? #f #f))) (newline)\n(display (boolean=? (boolean=? #t #f) (boolean=? #f #t))) (newline)\n(display (both (boolean? (boolean=? #t #f)) (boolean? (boolean=? #f #f)))) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ x∈{#t,#f}. boolean=?(x,x) = #t ∧ ∀ x,y. boolean=?(x,y) = boolean=?(y,x) ∧ ∀ x,y. boolean=?(x,y) ∈ {#t,#f}"
     :meta "The pattern is an equivalence relation on a two-element set — the smallest nontrivial equivalence. See book-of-math ch01 for the axiom set (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) and book-of-code ch02 for the CS framing of decidable equality on finite types. What would falsify: a call where two identical boolean literals returned #f, or where swapping arguments changed the answer. The runtime holds the invariant because the underlying implementation is a single equality on tagged values."
     :eng "The engineering payoff is that any Boolean-flag comparison can be written naively — no defensive coercion, no wrapping, no null-check. Reflexivity is what lets `(boolean=? f f)` be constant-folded to #t."
     :math "The claim lives on the two-element set B = {#t,#f}. Reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity are the equivalence-relation axioms; totality means the function is defined on B×B."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is decidable equality on a finite type. Related: char=?, symbol=?, eqv? — same shape, different type. All are total, all are decidable, all are constant-time."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "boolean=? decides equality on the boolean domain."
     :composition "(define (xor a b) (not (boolean=? a b)))\n(display (xor #t #f)) (newline)\n(display (xor #t #t)) (newline)\n(display (xor #f #f)) (newline)"
     :emergent "logical xor — the biconditional's negation, a fundamental combinational-logic gate"
     :meta "The composition chains boolean=? with `not`. What emerges is the xor gate: true exactly when the two inputs disagree. The same family appears as the CPU-level XOR instruction, as the `^` operator in C, as the toggle-primitive underneath every parity check and every cheap encryption stream. In book-of-code ch03 (logic gates) this pattern is called out as one of the two universal gates (NAND and XOR-with-AND together form a complete set). What makes the composition an emergence rather than an identity is that (not (biconditional)) has a NAME in a family the caller already knows — xor — and that name unlocks a large body of prior craft."
     :eng "The operational win of building xor from `not` + `boolean=?` is that the operator can point at the code and say 'this line is the parity check' — the composition explains itself. Log the two inputs and the output when the xor is used to detect drift between two supposedly-equal booleans."
     :math "xor is the biconditional's negation: xor(a,b) = ¬(a↔b). It is the addition operation of the field GF(2)."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is combinational primitive (or 'logic gate'). Familiar analogs: the CPU XOR instruction, C's `^`, Python's `^`, SQL's `<>` on booleans. Motoi's `(not (boolean=? a b))` occupies the same slot."))
)

(verb :name "symbol=?"  :library "compare" :tier "core" :kind "pure" :signature "(symbol=? a b) -> boolean"
  :summary "Symbol equality by name. R7RS §6.5."
  :provenance "R7RS §6.5; added 2026-07-18 finalization"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(symbol=? 'hello 'hello)" :note "#t.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(symbol=? 'a 'b)" :note "#f.")
  )
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator is routing dispatch cards. Each card carries a symbol tag ('draw, 'move, 'attack) and the router must compare the incoming tag against a table of handler symbols. Using generic `equal?` walks structure defensively; using `eq?` is fast but the runtime does not guarantee eq? on symbols across all reader paths — an interned-vs-fresh boundary could bite in a rare case. The operator wants a comparison verb that takes exactly two symbols and returns exactly #t or #f, contract narrowed to the symbol type. That is symbol=?."
     :program "(define handlers (list 'draw 'move 'attack))\n(define (has-handler? tag)\n  (let loop ((hs handlers))\n    (cond ((null? hs) #f)\n          ((symbol=? (car hs) tag) #t)\n          (else (loop (cdr hs))))))\n(display (has-handler? 'move)) (newline)\n(display (has-handler? 'quit)) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 lists the known handler tags as symbols. Line 2 defines a membership check that walks the list, comparing each element to the incoming tag using symbol=?. Line 6 asks whether 'move is a handler — the loop hits it on the second cell and prints #t. Line 7 asks about 'quit; the loop exhausts the list and prints #f. The audit trail is: three symbol-vs-symbol comparisons per positive lookup at worst, always producing a boolean, no allocation, no structural walk."
     :meta "Why symbol=? and not a sibling: equal? would work but its contract admits pairs and vectors and strings, so an auditor cannot see from the signature that the loop is comparing tags. eq? is faster in practice but its contract in R7RS is 'implementation-defined for numbers and characters' — a maintenance risk. boolean=? has the wrong type. symbol=? is the honest fit: the signature says symbol-vs-symbol, the implementation compares names, and the reader trusts the type witness. If eq? had been used and later the reader introduced uninterned symbols, the check would silently start returning #f on tags that had matched before.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is dispatch-key equality: the comparison the router does hundreds of times per frame. Choosing symbol=? costs the same as eq? in the common case but preserves the strong signature guarantee. See SRE Manual on 'signature-first tactics' — narrow signatures shrink the audit surface."
     :math "The relation is equality on a countably-infinite set of symbol names. It is total and decidable (name-string comparison). Nothing higher-order."
     :cs "The CS pattern is a monotype equality on an intern-table-backed type. In many runtimes symbols are interned so name-equality collapses to pointer-equality; symbol=? does not promise pointer-equality but does promise name-equality, which is the strictly weaker and always-correct guarantee."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A tag equality: compare two labels drawn from a large-but-flat name space and return whether they are the same label. The shape is 'homogeneous name-equality.'"
     :rungs ((:domain "compare (symbols)" :code "(symbol=? 'draw 'draw)")
             (:domain "expediter ticket lanes" :code "(same-station? 'grill 'grill)")
             (:domain "URI scheme comparison" :code "(string=? (uri-scheme u1) (uri-scheme u2))"))
     :explanation "In the compare domain symbol=? decides whether two dispatch tags refer to the same handler. In a kitchen the expediter compares two station labels ('grill vs 'grill) to decide whether a ticket needs to be moved or stays. In URI handling, two URL objects are compared by scheme ('https vs 'https) to decide whether they share a transport. All three cases are name-equality on a flat label domain, and the shape is what transfers — the specific name-space (Scheme symbols, kitchen stations, URI schemes) is a detail of substrate."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in each case the values are drawn from a labelled set, the comparison is by label identity, and the answer is decidable yes/no. Any dispatch table, any routing rule, any tag-matching predicate fits this shape. The trick is picking the specialized equality (symbol=?, station-eq?, scheme=?) at the callsite so the SIGNATURE reflects what is being compared.")
    (:eng "Engineering rule: use the equality that names the type. A tag comparison via generic equal? works but does not document itself; a comparison via symbol=? reads as 'this is comparing symbols' the moment a reader lands on it."
     :math "Name-equality on a labeled set is an equivalence relation. The equivalence classes are singletons — every distinct name is its own class."
     :cs "The CS analog is enum comparison. In Rust `enum Tag { Draw, Move }` and `t1 == t2` is a tag compare; in Java `enum` types have `Enum.equals`; in Python's `enum.Enum` `Tag.DRAW is Tag.DRAW` is identity. Motoi's symbol=? occupies the same slot on the interned-symbol type."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "symbol=? is an equivalence: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive on the symbol type; and it agrees with reading — two symbols produced by reading the same name are equal."
     :program "(display (symbol=? 'x 'x)) (newline)\n(display (symbol=? (symbol=? 'a 'b) (symbol=? 'b 'a))) (newline)\n(define a 'foo)\n(define b 'foo)\n(define c 'foo)\n(display (and (symbol=? a b) (symbol=? b c) (symbol=? a c))) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ s. symbol=?(s,s) = #t ∧ ∀ s,t. symbol=?(s,t) = symbol=?(t,s) ∧ ∀ s,t,u. (symbol=?(s,t) ∧ symbol=?(t,u)) → symbol=?(s,u)"
     :meta "The pattern is equivalence-on-a-labelled-type: reflexivity gives self-equality, symmetry gives caller-order irrelevance, transitivity gives chain-composability. See book-of-math ch01 for the equivalence-relation axioms and book-of-code ch04 for how tag types implement decidable equality. What falsifies: a symbol compared with itself returning #f, or two same-named symbols read from different reader entries disagreeing. The runtime holds the invariant via name-based comparison."
     :eng "The equivalence properties are what let dispatch tables be sorted, hashed, and cached without further checks. If symmetry ever failed, half the router would break silently."
     :math "The claim is a standard equivalence relation on the symbol set. Reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity are the three axioms."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is decidable name-equality on an intern-table type. Related: R7RS eqv? on symbols is required to agree with symbol=? — the invariants are the same, but the signature is broader."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "symbol=? decides equality on the symbol type."
     :composition "(define (dispatch tag handlers)\n  (cond ((null? handlers) 'no-handler)\n        ((symbol=? (car (car handlers)) tag)\n         ((cadr (car handlers))))\n        (else (dispatch tag (cdr handlers)))))\n(define table\n  (list (list 'draw (lambda () 'drew))\n        (list 'move (lambda () 'moved))))\n(display (dispatch 'move table)) (newline)\n(display (dispatch 'quit table)) (newline)"
     :emergent "dispatcher — a small routing table that maps tags to handler thunks"
     :meta "The composition chains symbol=? with cond and lambda. What emerges is the dispatcher family: a routing table keyed by tag that selects and invokes a handler. The same family appears as method dispatch in every OO language, as switch/case in C, as pattern match in ML, as Erlang's message routing, as SQL's CASE. In book-of-composition ch07 this pattern is called out as one of the load-bearing composition shapes for interpreters and game input systems. What makes it a dispatcher and not just a lookup is that the value returned is INVOKED — the table maps to functions, and the composition runs them."
     :eng "The operational win is that adding a new handler is a single-line addition to the table — the dispatcher does not change. Log the tag and the chosen handler when the dispatcher fires so incident reviews can reconstruct routing decisions."
     :math "The composition is a partial function tag → handler followed by function application. If the tag is unknown, the partial function is undefined and the code returns 'no-handler."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is dispatcher (or method table / vtable / jump table). Familiar analogs: C++ vtables, Python's __getattr__, Erlang's gen_server callbacks, ROS topics. Motoi's cond+symbol=? occupies the same slot for tag-driven routing."))
)

(verb
  :name "complex/*"
  :library "complex"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(complex/* z₁ z₂) -> complex"
  :summary "Complex number product: multiplies two complex numbers using the formula (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac−bd) + (ad+bc)i."
  :explanation "The product of two complex numbers follows the distributive law with the identity i² = −1. Given z₁ = (a+bi) and z₂ = (c+di), the product is z₁·z₂ = (ac−bd) + (ad+bc)i. The real part is ac−bd and the imaginary part is ad+bc. Complex multiplication is associative and commutative, and the modulus satisfies |z₁·z₂| = |z₁|·|z₂|. In the Motoi implementation, complex numbers are represented as lists or records with real and imaginary parts."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(complex/* '(3 4) '(1 2))" :note "(3+4i) × (1+2i) = (3·1 − 4·2) + (3·2 + 4·1)i = −5 + 10i.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((z1 '(1 1)) (z2 '(2 -1)))\n  (complex/* z1 z2))" :note "(1+i) × (2−i) = (1·2 − 1·(−1)) + (1·(−1) + 1·2)i = 3 + 1i.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (power-of-unit-imaginary n)\n  (cond ((= (modulo n 4) 0) '(1 0))\n        ((= (modulo n 4) 1) '(0 1))\n        ((= (modulo n 4) 2) '(-1 0))\n        (else '(0 -1))))\n(let ((i-cubed (complex/* '(0 1) (complex/* '(0 1) '(0 1)))))\n  (list i-cubed (power-of-unit-imaginary 3)))" :note "Computes i³ by repeated multiplication and checks against the formula i^n = i^(n mod 4); both yield (0 −1).")
  )
  :caveats ("The result is exact (rational real and imaginary parts) if both inputs are exact; otherwise inherits floating-point precision." "The representation of complex numbers must be consistent (e.g., both as (real imag) pairs or both as records)." "Multiplication does not check for overflow in exact arithmetic; very large moduli may cause performance issues.")
  :drawbacks ("For expensive chains of multiplications, consider converting to polar form and multiplying moduli/adding arguments instead." "Does not automatically simplify or normalize the result (e.g., rounding small floating-point components to zero)." "Multiplication by zero always yields (0 0); consider that case explicitly if needed.")
  :usecases ("Complex arithmetic: building up expressions and transformations." "Fourier analysis: multiplying complex exponentials e^(iθ) (after polar conversion)." "Electrical engineering: computing impedance (resistance + reactance) in AC circuits." "Polynomial evaluation: using complex roots in factorizations.")
  :related ("complex/+" "complex/-" "complex//" "complex/pow" "complex/->polar" "complex/from-polar")
  :learn (:concept "Distributive multiplication in the complex field; the identity i² = −1." :prerequisites ("complex/+" "complex/-") :progression "Study complex// (division), complex/pow (repeated multiplication), and conversion to/from polar form for geometric insights.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "A quadrature signal processor multiplies a signal sample by a rotating complex phasor to shift its phase."
     :program "(define signal '(1 0))\n(define phasor '(0 1))\n(complex/* signal phasor)"
     :explanation "signal is 1+0i; phasor is 0+1i (rotation by π/2). Product is 0+1i — the signal rotated by 90°."
     :meta "complex/* is honest for phase rotation; siblings via matrix rotation on 2-vec work but obscure the complex-arithmetic view.")
    (:eng "Phase-shifting is fundamental in DSP."
     :math "(a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd) + (ad+bc)i."
     :cs "Four real multiplies + two adds."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Rotation-and-scale in the plane."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "complex" :code "(complex/* z1 z2)")
       (:domain "2D rotation" :code "matrix rotation followed by scale")
       (:domain "group action" :code "multiplicative group action on C"))
     :explanation "Rung 1: complex mult. Rung 2: rotation-scale matrix. Rung 3: general group action."
     :meta "Shape transfers wherever a rotation-plus-scale action exists.")
    (:eng "DSP and 2D graphics both use this shape."
     :math "Multiplication in C corresponds to rotation-scale in R²."
     :cs "Complex mult replaces 2x2 matrix mult for planar rotation."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "complex/* is commutative: z1 · z2 = z2 · z1."
     :program "(define z1 '(3 4))\n(define z2 '(1 2))\n(equal? (complex/* z1 z2) (complex/* z2 z1))"
     :invariant "∀ z1 z2 ∈ C.  z1 · z2 = z2 · z1"
     :meta "Commutativity of C's multiplication. Falsifier: any pair where swap differs. Pattern-name: commutative field. See book-of-math ch on complex field.")
    (:eng "Order-independence in complex product."
     :math "C is a commutative field."
     :cs "Bit-exact under exact arithmetic."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "complex/* multiplies two complex numbers."
     :composition "(define (power-of-i n)\n  (if (= n 0) '(1 0)\n      (complex/* '(0 1) (power-of-i (- n 1)))))\n(map power-of-i (list 0 1 2 3 4))"
     :emergent "cycle-of-i / periodic-power — the pattern 1, i, -1, -i, 1... emerges from repeated complex/* by i."
     :meta "Family: cyclic-orbit, the shape of finite-order group elements. See book-of-composition ch on cyclic groups.")
    (:eng "Discrete Fourier basis uses cyclic-orbit shape."
     :math "i has order 4 in C^*."
     :cs "One mult per step; cycle-detection possible.")))

(verb
  :name "complex/+"
  :library "complex"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(complex/+ z₁ z₂) -> complex"
  :summary "Complex number sum: adds two complex numbers by adding their real parts and imaginary parts separately."
  :explanation "Addition of complex numbers is component-wise: (a+bi) + (c+di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i. The sum is commutative and associative, and addition by zero (0+0i) is an identity. Complex addition is the simplest operation and forms the basis of complex vector spaces. In Motoi, complex numbers are represented as (real imag) pairs or similar structures."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(complex/+ '(2 3) '(1 4))" :note "(2+3i) + (1+4i) = (3+7i).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((z1 '(5 -2)) (z2 '(-3 8)) (z3 '(0 1)))\n  (complex/+ z1 (complex/+ z2 z3)))" :note "Associative addition: (5−2i) + ((−3+8i) + (0+1i)) = (5−2i) + (−3+9i) = (2+7i).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (fold-left f init xs)\n  (let loop ((xs xs) (acc init))\n    (if (null? xs) acc (loop (cdr xs) (f acc (car xs))))))\n(define (complex-polygon-sum vertices)\n  (fold-left complex/+ '(0 0) vertices))\n(complex-polygon-sum '((1 0) (0 1) (-1 0) (0 -1)))" :note "Sums a list of complex numbers (points on unit circle at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°); result is (0 0) due to symmetry.")
  )
  :caveats ("Both arguments must be in the same representation (e.g., both (real imag) pairs)." "Adding (0 0) to any complex number returns that number (identity element)." "Floating-point complex numbers may accumulate rounding error; exact arithmetic is preferred for precision-critical code.")
  :drawbacks ("Addition is the slowest operation (requires separate real and imaginary addition); for long sums, consider fold-left to combine many terms at once." "Does not perform normalization (e.g., converting (1.0 0.0) to (1 0)).")
  :usecases ("Vector addition: summing phasors or impedances in electrical circuits." "Geometry: translation of points in the complex plane." "Fourier synthesis: combining multiple complex exponentials." "Cumulative analysis: integrating signals represented as complex time-series.")
  :related ("complex/-" "complex/*" "complex//" "complex/scale" "complex/conjugate")
  :learn (:concept "Component-wise addition; complex numbers as 2D vectors with addition." :prerequisites () :progression "Master complex/+, then explore complex/* (multiplicative structure changes the geometry) and complex/->polar (geometric interpretation of magnitude and argument).")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "Phasor addition: two AC signals sum voltage-vectorwise in a circuit."
     :program "(define v1 '(3 4))\n(define v2 '(1 2))\n(complex/+ v1 v2)"
     :explanation "Two phasors sum component-wise: (4 6). This gives the resulting AC voltage's magnitude/phase after linear superposition."
     :meta "complex/+ is honest for linear-superposition phasors; siblings that treat magnitude/phase separately would need conversion.")
    (:eng "Circuit simulators use this shape."
     :math "(a+bi) + (c+di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i."
     :cs "Two real adds."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Same-shape combine (like vec/+)."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "complex" :code "(complex/+ z1 z2)")
       (:domain "vec" :code "(vec/+ '(a b) '(c d))")
       (:domain "abelian group" :code "component-wise +"))
     :explanation "Same shape at rank-1 in C ≅ R²."
     :meta "Same as vec/+ shape.")
    (:eng "Additive superposition is universal."
     :math "C as an additive abelian group."
     :cs "O(1) — two components."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "complex/+ is associative: (z1 + z2) + z3 = z1 + (z2 + z3)."
     :program "(define z1 '(1 0))\n(define z2 '(0 1))\n(define z3 '(1 1))\n(equal? (complex/+ (complex/+ z1 z2) z3) (complex/+ z1 (complex/+ z2 z3)))"
     :invariant "∀ z1 z2 z3 ∈ C.  (z1 + z2) + z3 = z1 + (z2 + z3)"
     :meta "Associativity. Falsifier: any triple where reparenthesization changes result. Pattern-name: associative op. See book-of-math ch on abelian groups.")
    (:eng "Associativity allows fold-based sums to reorder freely."
     :math "C is an abelian group under +."
     :cs "Bit-exact under exact arithmetic."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "complex/+ adds two complex numbers component-wise."
     :composition "(define (fold-left f init xs) (if (null? xs) init (fold-left f (f init (car xs)) (cdr xs))))\n(define (polygon-sum vertices) (fold-left complex/+ '(0 0) vertices))\n(polygon-sum '((1 0) (0 1) (-1 0) (0 -1)))"
     :emergent "polygon centroid sum — a sum-of-vertices emerges from repeated complex/+."
     :meta "Family: fold-reduce, same shape as vec/+ centroid. See book-of-composition ch on aggregators.")
    (:eng "Polygon-analysis routines use this."
     :math "Sum of vertices in complex plane."
     :cs "One fold, O(n).")))

(verb
  :name "complex/-"
  :library "complex"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(complex/- z1 z2) -> complex"
  :summary "Subtract one complex number from another: (a+bi) − (c+di) = (a−c)+(b−d)i."
  :explanation "Complex subtraction works pointwise on real and imaginary parts. Given two complex numbers represented as pairs (a b) and (c d), this verb computes their difference as ((a−c) (b−d)). The result is exact (no floating-point rounding) and preserves the full precision of the inputs. Use this whenever you need to find the difference between two points or quantities in the complex plane."
  :examples (

(verb
  :name "const/e"
  :library "const"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "const/e -> 2.71828..."
  :summary "Euler's number, the base of natural logarithms."
  :explanation "const/e is a mathematical constant approximately equal to 2.71828. It arises naturally in growth and decay problems, compound interest, and the solution to differential equations. In Motoi Scheme, it is provided as a zero-argument constant for use in formulas, trigonometric work, and scientific computation. Retrieve it by name; no arguments needed."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(* 2 const/e)" :note "Multiply e by 2 to get ~5.43656")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (pow x y) (expt x y))\n(let ((principal 100))\n  (* principal (pow const/e 0.05)))" :note "Continuous compound interest: P·e^r where r=0.05")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (pow x y) (expt x y))\n(define (exp-decay half-life t)\n  (* (pow const/e (/ (* -0.693 t) half-life))))\n(exp-decay 5730 11460)" :note "Radioactive decay using e; half-life formula e^(-ln(2)·t/T)")
  )
  :caveats ("const/e is a computed approximation; use exact/rat or sym/* for symbolic precision if needed" "No argument form; calling (const/e arg) will error")
  :drawbacks ("Floating-point rounding may accumulate in long chains of computation" "For very high-precision work, consider symbolic algebra (sym/*) instead")
  :usecases ("Modeling population growth and decay" "Computing continuous compound interest" "Solving differential equations in simulation" "Statistical distributions (normal, exponential, Poisson)")
  :related ("const/pi" "const/tau" "const/ln2" "const/ln10" "math/exp" "math/log")
  :learn (:concept "Mathematical constants are immutable zero-argument forms that encode scientific values used across domains." :prerequisites ("Understanding that constants are evaluated at read time" "Familiarity with * and basic arithmetic") :progression "Learn const/pi next for circular geometry; then const/ln2 and const/ln10 for logarithmic scales.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A physics simulation asks the operator to model radioactive decay of a sample. The half-life formula uses e as the base of the exponential — every scientific-computing reference writes this as N(t) = N₀·e^(-λt). The operator could hard-code 2.71828 as a literal, but the audit question is whether the number in the code matches the number in the textbook. If the code writes 2.71828 and the textbook uses more digits, the two-value chain fails at the sixth decimal. const/e is the honest reference — it names the constant symbolically so the audit trail points at 'the runtime's e' rather than 'a hand-copied approximation.'"
     :program "(define lambda-rate 0.000121)\n(define t-years 5730)\n(define fraction (expt const/e (- (* lambda-rate t-years))))\n(display (list 'fraction fraction)) (newline)\n(display (< (abs (- fraction 0.5)) 0.01)) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 sets the decay constant for carbon-14 (approximately). Line 2 sets the elapsed time to one half-life. Line 3 computes the surviving fraction using const/e as the exponential base. Line 4 prints the result; line 5 verifies it is within 1% of 0.5, which is what one half-life should produce. The audit trail: constant referenced by name, formula applied, physical invariant confirmed."
     :meta "Why const/e and not a hand-typed 2.71828: the hand-typed literal risks a copy error and does not document intent — the reader sees 2.71828 and must recognize it. const/e is self-documenting: the reader sees 'e' and knows the meaning immediately. If a literal had been used and later the runtime tightened its precision, every hand-typed literal would silently disagree with new library code that uses const/e.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is the 'named-constant' rule: numerical constants that have names should be referenced by name so the audit trail is human-readable. See book-of-math ch04 (exponentials) for the derivation of the half-life formula."
     :math "e is defined as the unique real number satisfying d/dx(e^x) = e^x at x = 0. Equivalently, e = lim_{n→∞} (1 + 1/n)^n."
     :cs "The CS pattern is symbolic constant reference. Related patterns: Java's Math.E, Python's math.e, C's M_E."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A named mathematical constant: a value with a specific, well-known meaning that recurs across many domains, referenced by name rather than by number."
     :rungs ((:domain "const (numerical library)" :code "const/e ; the runtime's e")
             (:domain "shared vocabulary in engineering" :code "'gravity ; g = 9.81 m/s²")
             (:domain "field of real numbers" :code "e ∈ ℝ ; e is the base of the natural exponential"))
     :explanation "In the const library const/e is a symbolic identifier that resolves to the runtime's best floating-point approximation of e. In engineering communication, 'g' or 'c' or 'π' are named constants that appear in every textbook and every calculator. In pure mathematics, e is defined by an infinite series and lives in ℝ. The three cases share the shape: a symbolic name mapped to a specific number, referenced by name to preserve intent across contexts."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in each case the value is fixed, well-known, and referenced by name for legibility. Any constant with a name in the domain deserves a symbolic reference in code.")
    (:eng "Engineering rule: name your constants. Log or comment when a constant is used with an unusual precision or a specialized form (e.g., high-precision e for asymptotic analysis)."
     :math "e is a transcendental real number. See book-of-math ch04 for the formal definition via the infinite series 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + ..."
     :cs "The CS analog is a named literal constant, symbol-table-resolved at read time."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "const/e is a positive real approximation of Euler's number: it satisfies (log const/e) = 1 to floating-point precision, and it is greater than 2 and less than 3."
     :program "(display (< (abs (- (log const/e) 1.0)) 1e-10)) (newline)\n(display (and (> const/e 2) (< const/e 3))) (newline)\n(display (> const/e 0)) (newline)"
     :invariant "log(e) = 1 ∧ 2 < e < 3 ∧ e > 0"
     :meta "The pattern is a named-constant witness: (log const/e) should be 1 by definition of the natural logarithm. See book-of-math ch04 for the log/exp inverse relationship. What falsifies: any observed run where log of const/e is not close to 1, or where const/e falls outside the (2, 3) bracket. The runtime holds the invariant because e is stored as a high-precision floating-point value.")
    (:eng "The engineering payoff is that any code using const/e can be tested with the log-inverse identity — a cheap smoke test that catches gross errors in the runtime's constant table."
     :math "e is defined by log(e) = 1. The claim (log const/e) ≈ 1 is a direct verification of the definition."
     :cs "The CS pattern is invariant-preserving-constant: the constant's identity is defined by an equation, and the equation can be tested at any time."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "const/e is the runtime's approximation of Euler's number."
     :composition "(define (compound-continuous principal rate t)\n  (* principal (expt const/e (* rate t))))\n(define (compound-discrete principal rate n t)\n  (* principal (expt (+ 1 (/ rate n)) (* n t))))\n(define p 1000)\n(display (compound-continuous p 0.05 10)) (newline)\n(display (compound-discrete p 0.05 12 10)) (newline)"
     :emergent "continuous limit — a formula that becomes the limit of a discrete process as the step size goes to zero"
     :meta "The composition chains const/e with expt in a compound-interest formula. What emerges is the continuous-limit family: e is the base that makes continuous compounding equal the limit of discrete compounding as compounding frequency goes to infinity. The same family appears as continuous versus discrete probability distributions, as continuous vs discrete time in physics, as calculus vs finite differences. In book-of-math ch04 this pattern is called out as one of the two great uses of e (the other being the derivative of e^x = e^x)."
     :eng "The operational win is that continuous-limit formulas are exact and cheap; discrete approximations converge to them but at nonzero cost."
     :math "lim_{n→∞} (1 + r/n)^{nt} = e^{rt}. The limit is the reason e is the natural base."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is 'continuous limit as closed form.' Familiar in scientific computing: replacing an iterative accumulation with a closed-form call to exp.")))

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (ph value)\n  (* -1 (/ (log value) const/ln10)))\n(ph 0.0001)" :note "pH = -log₁₀[H+]; hydrogen concentration 10⁻⁴ gives pH 4")
  )

    (:eng "Operationally this is a base-conversion constant. Log the base used in any log-scale report (base-10, base-e, base-2)."

  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A base-conversion constant: a fixed scaling factor between two logarithmic bases, used to reproject values from one base's scale to another."
     :rungs ((:domain "const (log bases)" :code "(/ (log x) const/ln10)")
