                 :explanation "Build a centripetal Catmull-Rom spline through the waypoints. Sample uniformly in parameter to display or animate. The spline passes through the interior waypoints exactly, unlike a Bézier."
                 :meta "Reach for curve/catmull-rom, not curve/bezier, when the designer wants exact waypoint interpolation. Bézier would only approach interior points; Catmull-Rom passes through them.")
                (:eng "Log the sampled points; if adjacent points overlap, the centripetal parameterization is degenerate — likely duplicate waypoints."
                 :math "Piecewise cubic Hermite with tangents computed from centripetal weights: tᵢ = (|Pᵢ₊₁ − Pᵢ|)^0.5."
                 :cs "O(n) construction, O(1) per evaluation; safe default for authored motion."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "waypoint-interpolating spline: same shape appears in curves, in typography, and in signal reconstruction"
                     :rungs ((:domain "curve" :code "(curve/catmull-rom '((0 0) (2 3) (5 3) (7 0)))")
                             (:domain "typography" :code "(define (glyph-outline pts) (curve/catmull-rom pts))\n(curve/sample (glyph-outline '((0 0) (5 10) (10 0) (5 -10))) 20)")
                             (:domain "sinc-reconstruction" :code "(define (upsample xs t)\n  (define n (length xs))\n  (define (kernel i) (if (= i 0) 1 (/ (sin (* 3.14159 i)) (* 3.14159 i))))\n  (fold-left + 0 (map (lambda (i x) (* x (kernel (- t i)))) (iota n) xs)))\n(upsample '(1 2 3 2 1) 1.5)"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 interpolates 2D waypoints with a Catmull-Rom. Rung 2 outlines a glyph by treating letter-form points as spline waypoints. Rung 3 reconstructs a continuous signal from discrete samples via sinc — a bandlimited interpolant."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'reconstruct a continuous quantity from discrete waypoints while passing through each one' is a universal interpolation problem.")
                    (:eng "Font rendering, animation, and signal reconstruction all pick specific interpolation basis functions for the same underlying problem."
                     :math "Interpolation constraint: γ(tᵢ) = Pᵢ for i = 0…n; multiple bases satisfy it."
                     :cs "Choice of basis (Catmull-Rom, cubic Hermite, sinc, Lagrange) trades off smoothness, locality, and computational cost."))
  :row-4-proof (

   (:claim "A centripetal Catmull-Rom spline passes exactly through every interior control point."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (brachistochrone-race R g target-y)\n  ;; Given target vertical drop target-y, find θ_end and descent time\n  (let* ((theta-end (curve/brachistochrone R (list (* 2 R 3.14159) target-y)))\n         (t-desc (curve/descent-time R theta-end g)))\n    (list 'endpoint theta-end 'time t-desc)))\n(brachistochrone-race 3 9.81 5)" :note "Compute the descent time to reach a target vertical position via brachistochrone.")

(verb
  :name "curve/euler-lagrange-residual"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/euler-lagrange-residual lagrangian q q-dot q-double-dot) -> number"
  :summary "Compute the Euler–Lagrange residual ∂L/∂q − d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) for a given trajectory."
  :explanation "The Euler–Lagrange equation is the fundamental condition for a trajectory to be a stationary (optimal) point of the action integral. For a Lagrangian L(q, q̇, t), the residual is ∂L/∂q − d/dt(∂L/∂q̇). When this residual is zero everywhere, the trajectory satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation and is either a minimum-action (classical) path or a saddle point. This verb computes the residual numerically at a single point, using finite differences to approximate the time derivative. It is useful for verifying that a proposed path solves an optimal control problem or for error analysis in variational calculations."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (lagrangian-harmonic q q-dot)\n  ;; Simple harmonic oscillator: L = (1/2)·m·q̇² − (1/2)·k·q²\n  (- (* 0.5 q-dot q-dot) (* 0.5 q q)))\n(curve/euler-lagrange-residual lagrangian-harmonic 1.0 0.5 -1.0)" :note "For a harmonic oscillator at q=1, q̇=0.5, q̈=-1 (near equilibrium), the residual should be small.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (lagrangian-projectile q q-dot)\n  ;; Projectile: L = (1/2)·m·q̇² + m·g·q (y-coordinate)\n  (- (* 0.5 q-dot q-dot) (* 10 q)))\n(let ((t-vals (list 0.0 0.5 1.0)))\n  (map (lambda (t)\n         (let ((q (- 5 (* 5 t t))))\n           (list t (curve/euler-lagrange-residual lagrangian-projectile q (* -10 t) -10))))\n       t-vals))" :note "Verify that a parabolic trajectory y = 5 − 5t² (with gravity g=10) nearly satisfies Euler–Lagrange at multiple points.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (verify-brachistochrone)\n  ;; For a #t brachistochrone, the residual of the action functional should be zero\n  ;; This is a symbolic check; in practice, numerical residuals measure discretization error\n  (let ((L (lambda (q q-dot)\n             ;; Effective Lagrangian for brachistochrone (T − V with reparametrization)\n             (/ q-dot (sqrt (+ 1 (* q-dot q-dot)))))))\n    (define (check-point t q-val q-dot-val q-accel-val)\n      (list 't t\n            'residual (curve/euler-lagrange-residual L q-val q-dot-val q-accel-val)))\n    (map (lambda (t) (check-point t 1 0.5 (- 0.5)))\n         (list 0.1 0.2 0.3))))\n(verify-brachistochrone)" :note "Check whether points on a proposed brachistochrone path satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equation (residual ≈ 0).")
  )
  :caveats ("Residual is a numerical approximation; use appropriate step sizes and error tolerances." "The verb does not check whether the Lagrangian is well-defined or differentiable at the query point." "d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) is approximated via finite differences; for noisy trajectories, residuals will be large and unreliable." "The sign convention and normalization depend on the problem definition; consult the physics literature.")
  :drawbacks ("Expensive to call for many points along a trajectory; batch processing is recommended." "Does not validate that a solution is a minimum rather than a saddle point or maximum." "Numerical instability near discontinuities or non-smooth regions." "Does not solve the Euler–Lagrange equation; only measures deviation from it.")
  :usecases ("Validating optimal control trajectories: check that computed paths satisfy the necessary conditions." "Error analysis: measure how well a discretized or approximate trajectory satisfies the equations of motion." "Physics education: verify that classical mechanics predictions (e.g., parabolic projectile paths) satisfy the variational principle." "Optimization: use residual as an objective function in iterative refinement of a trajectory.")
  :related ("curve/cycloid" "curve/brachistochrone" "curve/descent-time" "phys/lagrangian-action")
  :learn (:concept "The Euler–Lagrange equation as the extremal condition for the action integral; variational principle in mechanics." :prerequisites ("basic calculus (partial derivatives, chain rule)" "physics (Lagrangian, kinetic and potential energy)") :progression "Study curve/euler-lagrange-residual as the bridge between classical mechanics and the calculus of variations.")

                (:eng "Non-zero residual means the trajectory is not extremal — reject or refine."

(verb
  :name "curve/eval"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/eval curve t) -> (list x y [z])"
  :summary "Return the point γ(t) on a parametric curve at parameter value t."
  :explanation "A parametric curve is a closure (lambda) that takes a scalar parameter t and returns a point (typically as a list [x, y] in 2-D or [x, y, z] in 3-D). curve/eval simply applies the curve closure at the given t. It is the most basic operation on curves and is used internally by other verbs like curve/velocity, curve/curvature, etc. Use curve/eval to sample individual points; use curve/sample for many points at once."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((circle (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t)))))\n  (curve/eval circle 0))" :note "Unit circle at t=0 gives the point (1, 0).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((helix (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) t))))\n  (map (lambda (t) (curve/eval helix t))\n       (list 0 1.57 3.14 4.71 6.28)))" :note "Sample five points along a helix; z-coordinate increases with t.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (arc-length-numeric curve a b n)\n  ;; Approximate arc length via Riemann sum of chord lengths\n  (let ((dt (/ (- b a) n)))\n    (let loop ((i 0) (sum 0))\n      (if (>= i n)\n        sum\n        (let* ((t1 (+ a (* i dt)))\n               (t2 (+ t1 dt))\n               (p1 (curve/eval curve t1))\n               (p2 (curve/eval curve t2))\n               (dx (- (car p2) (car p1)))\n               (dy (- (cadr p2) (cadr p1)))\n               (chord (sqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))\n          (loop (+ i 1) (+ sum chord))))))\n(arc-length-numeric (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t))) 0 6.28 100))" :note "Compute arc length of a unit circle by summing chord lengths (approximate); actual arc length is 2π ≈ 6.28.")
  )
  :caveats ("The curve closure must be well-defined for all requested t values." "If the curve is not continuous or has cusps/singularities, curve/eval will return the point (which may be non-smooth) without warning." "The parameter t is not always arc-length-parametrized; it may be a mathematical parameter (angle, time, etc.).")

  :usecases ("Sampling individual points on a curve for display, collision detection, or interpolation." "Building custom analysis loops (e.g., computing arc length, curvature profiles)." "Integrating a curve into a larger system (e.g., physics simulation, animation state machine)." "Debugging: evaluating a curve at a specific t to verify correctness.")

(verb
  :name "curve/fall-line"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/fall-line h x y) -> (list dx dy)"
  :summary "Compute the steepest-descent direction (fall line) on a height field h at position (x, y)."
  :explanation "A height field h: (x, y) → z describes a surface. The gradient ∇h = (∂h/∂x, ∂h/∂y) points uphill; the negative gradient −∇h points downhill. The fall line is the unit vector −∇h / |∇h|, which is the direction of steepest descent (the ski slope direction). This verb computes that direction at a given (x, y). On a flat region (∇h = 0), the direction is undefined and the verb returns 'singular. Fall lines are fundamental for understanding landscape topology, physics-based animation, and optimization algorithms."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((paraboloid (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y)))))\n  (curve/fall-line paraboloid 1 1))" :note "On a paraboloid, the fall line at (1, 1) points radially inward toward the center (0, 0).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((saddle (lambda (x y) (- (* x x) (* y y)))))\n  (map (lambda (pos)\n         (curve/fall-line saddle (car pos) (cadr pos)))\n       (list (list 1 0) (list 0 1) (list 1 1))))" :note "On a saddle surface, fall lines point along different directions depending on location (along hyperbolic paths).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (trace-fall-path h x0 y0 n-steps dt)\n  ;; Integrate the fall line to build a descent trajectory\n  (let loop ((x x0) (y y0) (i 0) (path (list (list x0 y0))))\n    (if (>= i n-steps)\n      path\n      (let* ((fall (curve/fall-line h x y))\n             (dx (car fall))\n             (dy (cadr fall))\n             (x-new (+ x (* dt dx)))\n             (y-new (+ y (* dt dy))))\n        (loop x-new y-new (+ i 1) (cons (list x-new y-new) path))))))\n(trace-fall-path (lambda (x y) (- (+ (* x x) (* y y)))) 3 4 50 0.1)" :note "Trace a downhill path by repeatedly stepping in the fall-line direction (equivalent to curve/fall-path).")
  )
  :caveats ("Returns 'singular on flat regions (where |∇h| ≈ 0)." "The verb does not integrate the fall line; it returns only the local direction. Use curve/fall-path for a full trajectory." "Numerical gradient approximation can be inaccurate if h is rough or noisy." "The height field h must be callable at the query point; no bounds checking is performed.")
  :drawbacks ("Expensive to compute many fall lines; batch evaluation or caching is recommended." "Falls into local minima and does not find global minima." "Unstable in flat or nearly flat regions; small perturbations can flip the direction." "Does not account for constraints or obstacles (unlike ai/path).")
  :usecases ("Landscape visualization: visualize steepest-descent paths (ski slopes, river flows)." "Optimization: steepest-descent algorithms use fall lines to minimize functions." "Physics-based animation: water flow, avalanche simulation, etc." "Topological analysis: identify ridges (where two fall lines diverge) and valleys (where they converge).")
  :related ("curve/fall-path" "curve/gradient" "curve/slope-angle" "curve/surface-normal" "curve/surface-graph")
  :learn (:concept "Gradient as a direction field; steepest descent in multivariate calculus." :prerequisites ("curve/gradient" "curve/surface-graph" "partial derivatives") :progression "Learn curve/fall-line, then curve/fall-path (integration), then curve/geodesic-distance (Riemannian geometry).")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "Water-flow demo needs the local downhill direction at a puddle position on a landscape."
                 :program "(define h (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y))))\n(curve/fall-line h 2 1)"
                 :explanation "Compute the negative gradient at (2,1); its unit vector is where water goes.")
                (:eng "'singular means flat — the water pools instead of flowing."
                 :math "−∇h / |∇h|."
                 :cs "Pure; O(1) after gradient."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "steepest-descent direction: appears in landscapes, in gradient optimizers, in economics"
                     :rungs ((:domain "landscape" :code "(curve/fall-line (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y))) 1 1)")
                             (:domain "sgd" :code "(define (sgd-step loss-grad x lr) (map (lambda (xi gi) (- xi (* lr gi))) x (loss-grad x)))\n(sgd-step (lambda (x) (map (lambda (xi) (* 2 xi)) x)) '(1 2) 0.1)")
                             (:domain "utility" :code "(define (steepest-loss-dir grad) (map - grad))\n(steepest-loss-dir '(0.3 -0.5))"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 downhill on a surface. Rung 2 SGD step. Rung 3 economics-utility descent."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (sin (* x y))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (form (curve/first-form surf 0.5 0.5)))\n  (list 'E (car form) 'F (cadr form) 'G (caddr form)))" :note "Extract E, F, G individually to later compute the area element or check isothermal coordinates (F=0).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (* (cos x) (sin y))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (pts (list (list 0 0) (list 0.1 0.1) (list 0.2 0.2)))\n       (forms (map (lambda (p) (curve/first-form surf (car p) (cadr p))) pts)))\n  (map (lambda (f) (* (- (* (car f) (caddr f)) (* (cadr f) (cadr f))))) forms))" :note "Compute the determinant EG−F² (the Gram determinant) at multiple points to find where the surface is locally non-degenerate.")

(verb
  :name "curve/frenet-frame"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/frenet-frame curve t) -> (list T N B kappa tau)"
  :summary "Compute the full Frenet–Serret apparatus (tangent T, normal N, binormal B, curvature κ, torsion τ) at parameter t."
  :explanation "The Frenet frame is the workhorse of curve geometry: at each point on a space curve, it provides an orthonormal basis (T, N, B) and two scalars (κ, τ) that completely describe how the curve twists and turns. T is the direction of motion; N points toward the center of curvature (perpendicular to T); B = T × N completes the right-handed frame. κ (curvature) measures how sharply the curve bends; τ (torsion) measures how much it screws out of its osculating plane. Use this when you need the full differential geometry of a curve in one call, or when you're building animations that follow a path with natural rotating coordinates."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((c (curve/bezier (list (list 0 0 0) (list 1 0 0) (list 1 1 0) (list 0 1 0)))))\n  (curve/frenet-frame c 0.5))" :note "At the midpoint of a cubic Bézier, the Frenet frame gives the local orientation and bending.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((c (curve/bezier (list (list 0 0 0) (list 1 0 1) (list 2 0 1) (list 3 0 0))))\n       (frame (curve/frenet-frame c 0.25))\n       (T (car frame))\n       (N (cadr frame))\n       (B (caddr frame))\n       (kappa (cadddr frame))\n       (tau (car (cddddr frame))))\n  (list 'curvature kappa 'torsion tau))" :note "Extract each component: curvature κ measures bending in the TN-plane; torsion τ measures rotation around T.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((c (curve/catmull-rom (list (list 0 0 0) (list 1 2 0) (list 2 0 0) (list 3 1 1))))\n       (params (list 0.1 0.3 0.5 0.7 0.9))\n       (frames (map (lambda (t) (curve/frenet-frame c t)) params))\n       (curvatures (map (lambda (f) (cadddr f)) frames)))\n  (apply max curvatures))" :note "Sample the Frenet frame at multiple points along a Catmull-Rom spline and find the point of maximum curvature.")
  )
  :caveats ("At points where κ=0 (inflection points), the normal N is undefined; the function returns a default or 'singular." "At points where τ=0, the curve lies momentarily in a plane (no screw); this is normal, not an error." "Numerical differentiation sensitivity: tight curves or high-frequency wiggles may give noisy κ and τ." "The binormal B is always computed as T×N; ensure T and N are normalized first.")
  :drawbacks ("Computing all five values (T, N, B, κ, τ) is more expensive than computing just one. If you only need κ, use curve/curvature-2d or curve/curvature; if only the frame, consider just T and N." "Undefined behavior at inflection points; guard with checks on curvature before using N or B in downstream code." "Catmull-Rom and Bézier curves may have numerical artifacts at control points.")
  :usecases ("Animating a camera or sprite that follows a path, maintaining a natural rotating reference frame." "Designing ribbons or tubes around a curve; the frame defines the cross-section orientation at each point." "Analyzing helical or spiral structures where both curvature and torsion matter."   :related ("curve/curvature-2d" "curve/curvature" "curve/unit-tangent" "curve/normal" "curve/binormal" "curve/osculating-circle" "curve/torsion")
  :learn (:concept "The Frenet–Serret frame: an observer-independent, moving coordinate system that encodes all the differential-geometric properties of a curve." :prerequisites ("curve/bezier" "curve/catmull-rom" "geom/cross") :progression "Master the Frenet frame, then explore curve/osculating-circle (the osculating circle is the circle of radius 1/κ in the TN-plane) and curve/torsion for deeper study of 3D curve behavior.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A camera swings along a 3D spline; the operator needs every camera-space axis at once at the current parameter for orientation and effects. What single call yields the whole basis?"
                 :program "(define spline (curve/bezier (list (list 0 0 0) (list 1 2 1) (list 3 2 -1) (list 4 0 0))))\n(define f (curve/frenet-frame spline 0.5))\n(list 'T (car f) 'N (cadr f) 'B (caddr f) 'kappa (cadddr f))"

                 :meta "Reach for curve/frenet-frame over three separate calls when you need the whole basis; a single call also guarantees consistency of the three axes and shares intermediate derivatives.")
                (:eng "Log kappa alongside the axes — spikes in curvature warn that the frame is degenerate at that parameter."

(verb
  :name "curve/gaussian-curvature"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/gaussian-curvature surface u v) -> K"
  :summary "Compute the Gaussian curvature K at (u,v) on a height-field surface, using exact Monge-patch formulas."
  :explanation "Gaussian curvature K = κ₁ κ₂ is the product of the two principal curvatures (how much the surface bends in its two principal directions). For a height field z=h(x,y), K = (h_xx h_yy − h²_xy) / (1 + h²_x + h²_y)². A deep geometric fact: K is intrinsic — you can measure it by living entirely on the surface, without leaving 3D space. Positive K means the surface is locally like a sphere (convex in both directions); zero K means at least one direction is flat (like a cylinder); negative K means saddle-shaped (like a saddle or Pringles chip). Use this to classify surface shapes, find critical points of curvature, or detect singularities."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define h 0)\n(let ((h (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y))))\n      (surf (curve/surface-graph h)))\n  (curve/gaussian-curvature surf 0.0 0.0))" :note "On the paraboloid z=x²+y², K>0 everywhere (positive curvature); at the origin it is largest.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (- (* x x) (* y y))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (K-saddle (curve/gaussian-curvature surf 0.0 0.0)))\n  (if (< K-saddle 0) 'saddle-point 'not-saddle))" :note "On the hyperbolic paraboloid z=x²−y², K<0 everywhere (negative curvature); it's a saddle.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (sin (* 2 (+ x y)))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (pts (list (list 0 0) (list 0.25 0.25) (list 0.5 0.5) (list 0.75 0.75)))\n       (Ks (map (lambda (p) (curve/gaussian-curvature surf (car p) (cadr p))) pts)))\n  (list 'min-K (apply min Ks) 'max-K (apply max Ks)))" :note "Sample K over a wavy surface and find its range; Gaussian curvature oscillates with the wave amplitude.")
  )
  :caveats ("K is computed via second derivatives; noise or sharp creases in h will amplify into large or undefined K." "Points where h is not twice-differentiable (e.g., cone tips, creases) return undefined K or very large values." "K=0 does not mean the surface is flat; it means the two principal curvatures have opposite signs (saddle) or one is zero (cylinder)." "The formula assumes a height-field representation z=h(x,y); it does not apply to general parametric surfaces without conversion.")
  :drawbacks ("If you also need mean curvature or principal curvatures, computing K alone wastes the derivatives; use curve/mean-curvature or curve/principal-curvatures and extract K from them." "Height fields cannot represent overhanging geometry (e.g., a mushroom shape); you would need a full parametric surface." "Numerical second derivatives are notoriously noisy; smooth your height field first if it's discretized.")
  :usecases ("Classifying points on a topographic map: peaks (K>0), passes (K<0), or ridges/valleys (K=0)." "Detecting saddle points in an optimization landscape." "Computing the Euler characteristic of a closed surface via integration of K." "Rendering with curvature-based shading or silhouette detection.")
  :related ("curve/mean-curvature" "curve/principal-curvatures" "curve/surface-graph" "curve/first-form" "curve/second-form" "topo/euler-char")
  :learn (:concept "Intrinsic curvature: a property of the surface's own geometry, independent of how it sits in space." :prerequisites ("curve/surface-graph" "calc/second-derivative") :progression "After understanding Gaussian curvature, learn curve/mean-curvature (how fast the surface bends on average), then curve/principal-curvatures to see the two bending directions separately.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A landscape classifier needs to flag every point on a terrain as peak, saddle, or valley based on a single number. What curvature answers that at one call?"
                 :program "(define surf (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (- (* x x) (* y y)))))\n(define K (curve/gaussian-curvature surf 0 0))\n(cond ((> K 0) 'bowl) ((< K 0) 'saddle) (else 'ridge))"
                 :explanation "Build the saddle surface z = x² − y². At the origin, K is negative → saddle. Classifying by sign of Gaussian curvature is the fastest topographical audit."
                 :meta "Reach for gaussian-curvature over mean-curvature when the goal is topological classification; H tells you fastness of bending while K tells you the sign-signature.")
                (:eng "Log K per grid cell; runs of same-sign K partition a landscape into topological regions."
                 :math "K = κ₁ · κ₂; sign(K) classifies point as elliptic (>0), hyperbolic (<0), or parabolic (=0)."
                 :cs "Pure evaluation; O(1) per query."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "product of two eigenvalues as a signed shape signature: the same shape appears in surface geometry, in matrix determinants, in binary-classifier scoring"
                     :rungs ((:domain "curve" :code "(curve/gaussian-curvature (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y)))) 0 0)")

  :summary "Compute the shortest distance between two points on a surface, measured along the surface itself (geodesic distance)."
  :explanation "Unlike Euclidean distance (straight line through space), geodesic distance measures the shortest path *staying on the surface*. On a sphere, the geodesic between two points is an arc of a great circle. On a height field z=h(x,y), it's a curve that minimizes ∫√(1 + (∇h)²) ds. This is a boundary-value problem (two fixed endpoints, one unknown path) and is computationally expensive; on-device computation is limited and may escalate to a backend solver. Use this when you need true surface distances (e.g., shortest walking distance over terrain, or radius of influence on a curved manifold)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define h 0)\n(let ((h (lambda (x y) 0))\n      (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n      (p1 (list 0 0))\n      (p2 (list 3 4)))\n  (curve/geodesic-distance surf p1 p2))" :note "On a flat plane (z=0 everywhere), geodesic distance equals Euclidean distance: √((3−0)²+(4−0)²)=5.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (* 0.1 (+ x y))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (p1 (list 0 0))\n       (p2 (list 1 1))\n       (d-geo (curve/geodesic-distance surf p1 p2))\n       (d-eucl (geom/distance p1 p2)))\n  (list 'geodesic d-geo 'euclidean d-eucl))" :note "On a slightly tilted plane, geodesic distance is slightly longer than Euclidean because the surface is stretched.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (* 0.01 (+ (* x x) (* y y)))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (center (list 0 0))\n       (pts (list (list 1 0) (list 0 1) (list -1 0) (list 0 -1)))\n       (dists (map (lambda (p) (curve/geodesic-distance surf center p)) pts)))\n  (apply = dists))" :note "On a gently curved paraboloid, geodesic distances from center to four cardinal points are equal (by symmetry).")
  )

(verb
  :name "curve/gradient"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/gradient surface u v) -> (list du dv)"
  :summary "Compute the gradient ∇h = (∂h/∂x, ∂h/∂y) of a height field at (u,v)."
  :explanation "The gradient is a 2D vector that points in the direction of steepest ascent on the surface, with magnitude equal to the slope. If you are standing on a hill at position (x,y,z=h(x,y)), the gradient tells you which direction (on the xy-plane) to walk to go uphill fastest, and how steeply. ∇h is perpendicular to level curves (contours of constant height). The magnitude |∇h| = √(h²_x + h²_y) is the slope angle (steeper = bigger). Use this to find fall lines (ski slopes), to perform gradient descent optimization, or to compute the surface normal."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define h 0)\n(let ((h (lambda (x y) (+ (* 2 x) (* 3 y))))\n      (surf (curve/surface-graph h)))\n  (curve/gradient surf 1.0 1.0))" :note "On the tilted plane z=2x+3y, the gradient is constant everywhere: (2, 3).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (grad (curve/gradient surf 1.0 1.0))\n       (slope-mag (geom/distance (list 0 0) grad)))\n  (list 'grad grad 'magnitude slope-mag))" :note "On the paraboloid z=x²+y², the gradient at (1,1) is (2,2), pointing away from the origin with magnitude 2√2.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((h (lambda (x y) (sin (* (+ x y)))))\n       (surf (curve/surface-graph h))\n       (pts (map (lambda (i) (list (* 0.1 i) (* 0.1 i))) (list 0 1 2 3 4)))\n       (grads (map (lambda (p) (curve/gradient surf (car p) (cadr p))) pts))\n       (mags (map (lambda (g) (geom/distance (list 0 0) g)) grads)))\n  (apply max mags))" :note "Sample gradients along a diagonal and find the steepest slope; |∇h| oscillates with the wave.")
  )
  :caveats ("At local extrema (peaks, valleys), ∇h = (0,0); you cannot reliably compute fall lines or descent directions there." "Numerical differentiation amplifies high-frequency noise; filter the height field before computing gradients on noisy data." "The gradient assumes the surface is single-valued (height field); it does not apply to overhanging or self-intersecting surfaces." "∇h is a 2D vector in the (x,y) plane; the actual 3D surface normal is different (use curve/surface-normal for that).")
  :drawbacks ("If you need the full Hessian or second derivatives, computing just the gradient wastes the first-order work; compute once and reuse." "On discrete heightmaps, finite difference is sensitive to cell size; too small → noise, too large → blurriness." "Gradient descent using ∇h is slow on flat regions or near saddles; consider adaptive step sizes or momentum methods.")
  :usecases ("Finding fall lines (ski slopes) on terrain: the downslope direction is −∇h/|∇h|." "Gradient descent optimization: iteratively move in direction −∇h to minimize h." (verb
  :name "curve/hermite"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/hermite p0 v0 p1 v1) -> curve"
  :summary "Create a cubic Hermite curve that passes through p0 and p1, with velocity v0 at p0 and v1 at p1."
  :explanation "Hermite interpolation is a way to build a smooth cubic polynomial through two points while specifying the direction and speed at each endpoint. Instead of just giving endpoints (like in linear interpolation) or control points (like Bézier), you give *position and velocity*. This is very natural for animation: you want the sprite to start at p0 moving with velocity v0, and end at p1 moving with velocity v1. The result is a C¹-smooth (continuous derivative) curve that exactly matches both the positions and the velocities. Internally, it's a 2D or 3D cubic polynomial evaluated at t∈[0,1]."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((h (curve/hermite (list 0 0) (list 1 0) (list 1 1) (list 0 1))))\n  (curve/bezier-eval h 0.5))" :note "Hermite curve from (0,0) moving right, to (1,1) moving up. At t=0.5 (middle), the curve is at an intermediate point.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((p0 (list 0 0 0))\n       (v0 (list 1 0 0))\n       (p1 (list 3 2 0))\n       (v1 (list 0 1 0))\n       (h (curve/hermite p0 v0 p1 v1))\n       (pts (map (lambda (t) (curve/bezier-eval h t)) (list 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1))))\n  pts)" :note "Evaluate the Hermite curve at five sample points to trace its shape: a 3D path that starts moving in the +x direction and ends moving in the +y direction.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((waypoints (list (list 0 0) (list 1 1) (list 2 0) (list 3 1)))\n       (tangents (list (list 1 0) (list 0.5 0.5) (list -0.5 0.5) (list 0 1)))\n       (hermites (map (lambda (i)\n                       (let ((p0 (list-ref waypoints i))\n                             (v0 (list-ref tangents i))\n                             (p1 (list-ref waypoints (+ i 1)))\n                             (v1 (list-ref tangents (+ i 1))))\n                         (curve/hermite p0 v0 p1 v1)))\n                     (list 0 1 2))))\n  (map (lambda (h t) (curve/bezier-eval h t)) hermites (list 0.5 0.5 0.5)))" :note "Chain multiple Hermite segments (like a piecewise Hermite spline) by specifying waypoints and tangent vectors. Each segment smoothly connects to the next.")
  )
  :caveats ("Hermite interpolation is only C¹ (continuous first derivative); if you need C² or higher, the curve may have a visible \"kink\" in curvature where segments join." "The velocities v0, v1 should have the same units/scale as the positions; if not, the curve shape will be unexpected." "Tangent vectors are not normalized; a longer v0 makes the curve more \"pulled\" toward that direction." "Outside t∈[0,1], the curve extends as a cubic polynomial; the extrapolation may be far from intuitive.")
  :drawbacks ("Hermite is less flexible than Bézier: you cannot easily adjust the curvature without changing both positions and velocities." "If you want C² continuity (matching second derivatives at joints), you must compute and specify the right tangent magnitudes, which is not automatic." "Catmull-Rom (curve/catmull-rom) automatically infers tangents from neighboring points and is often easier to use; use Hermite only when you want direct control.")
  :usecases ("Animating motion where you know start/end positions and velocities: smooth rocket flight, bouncing ball trajectories." "Building a spline where you have hand-specified tangents at keyframes." "Interpolating physics data where position and velocity are both measured or constrained."   :learn (:concept "Hermite basis: polynomial interpolation constrained by position and derivatives, not control points." :prerequisites ("curve/bezier" "calc/derivative") :progression "Master Hermite, then learn curve/catmull-rom (which auto-infers tangents) and curve/spline-resample (to uniformly parameterize a curve by arc length).")

(verb
  :name "curve/mean-curvature"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/mean-curvature surface u v) -> H"
  :summary "Compute the mean curvature H at (u,v) on a height-field surface, measuring the average of the two principal bending directions."
  :explanation "Mean curvature H = (κ₁ + κ₂)/2 is the average of the two principal curvatures (the bending in the two principal directions). Geometrically, 2H is the trace of the shape operator; it measures how fast the surface normal is rotating as you move along the surface. For a height field z=h(x,y), H = (h_xx(1+h²_y) − 2h_x h_y h_xy + h_yy(1+h²_x)) / 2(1+h²_x+h²_y)^(3/2). H=0 means the surface is minimal (like a soap film — it has zero mean curvature everywhere). H>0 means the surface is locally convex (bending inward); H<0 means concave (bending outward). (verb
  :name "curve/second-form"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/second-form surface x y) -> (list L M N)"
  :summary "Returns the second fundamental form (L, M, N) of a height-field surface at a point."
  :explanation "The second fundamental form measures how a surface bends away from its tangent plane. It is a 2×2 symmetric matrix represented as (L M / M N), encoding the component of the surface normal's change in the u and v directions. Together with the first fundamental form, it determines all intrinsic and extrinsic curvature properties (Gaussian, mean, principal). It is the source of curvature information."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((paraboloid (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (* 0.1 (+ (* x x) (* y y)))))))\n  (curve/second-form paraboloid 0.5 0.5))" :note "Query the second form of a gentle paraboloid; expect small positive values (weak curvature).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((surf (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (* 0.5 (* x x)))))\n       (second (curve/second-form surf 0.0 0.0))\n       (L (car second)))\n  (if (> L 0) 'convex 'concave))" :note "Check convexity at a surface point by inspecting the L coefficient of the second form.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((bumpy (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (+ (* 0.2 (geom/sin (* 3 x))) (* 0.1 (geom/cos (* 2 y)))))))\n       (pts (list (list 0 0) (list const/pi 0) (list 0 const/pi)))\n       (collect-forms (lambda (p) (curve/second-form bumpy (car p) (cadr p)))))\n  (map collect-forms pts))" :note "Build a curvature map by sampling second forms across a wave surface, foundation for understanding ripple dynamics.")
  )
  :caveats ("Requires a valid height field (Monge patch); does not apply to implicit surfaces or meshes." "Singular where the surface is flat or numerically indistinguishable from flat." "Coefficients are normalized by the first fundamental form; bare partial derivatives are not the second form.")
  :drawbacks ("Purely extrinsic (depends on embedding); does not reflect intrinsic geometry alone." "Must be paired with first fundamental form to extract curvature; incomplete by itself." "Numerical stability degrades with steep surfaces (h_x² + h_y² ≫ 1).")
  :usecases ("Physics: computing how gravity couples to surface curvature in rolling or sliding simulations." "Rendering: shading ridges and valleys by inspecting principal curvatures derived from L, M, N." "Differential geometry: foundation for extracting all extrinsic curvature measures.")
  :related ("curve/first-form" "curve/gaussian-curvature" "curve/mean-curvature" "curve/principal-curvatures" "curve/surface-graph")
  :learn (:concept "The second fundamental form encodes how the surface normal vector changes; it is the seat of all curvature." :prerequisites ("curve/surface-graph" "curve/first-form") :progression "Master the second form to understand how it combines with the first form to compute Gaussian and mean curvatures.")
  :row-2-audit (

                 :program "(define surf (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y)))))\n(define II (curve/second-form surf 1 1))\n(list 'L (car II) 'M (cadr II) 'N (caddr II))"
                 :explanation "Extract (L, M, N) at the sample point. These three numbers describe how the surface normal tilts under motion — the primary source of curvature-driven forces."
                 :meta "Reach for second-form over gradient when the goal is second-order (curvature) information; gradient gives slope, second-form gives bending.")
                (:eng "Log all three entries; large magnitudes flag high-curvature spots requiring finer integration steps."
                 :math "II = L du² + 2M du dv + N dv²."
                 :cs "Pure eval; O(1)."))

                     :rungs ((:domain "curve" :code "(curve/second-form (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y)))) 0 0)")
                             (:domain "hessian" :code "(define (hessian-2d fxx fyy fxy) (list fxx fxy fyy))\n(hessian-2d 2 2 0)")

                     :explanation "Rung 1 gives geometric second form. Rung 2 gives calculus Hessian. Rung 3 gives structural moment tensor. All three are symmetric 2×2 second-order tensors."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 2×2 symmetric second-order tensors are one algebraic object with many domain names.")
                    (:eng "Same tensor, same eigen-decomposition; different physical labels."
                     :math "Symmetric 2×2 with entries (L or fxx, M or fxy, N or fyy)."
                     :cs "Represent as 3-list; downstream chooses interpretation."))

   (:claim "The second form is symmetric: M = M."
                 :program "(define surf (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (* (sin x) (cos y)))))\n(define II (curve/second-form surf 0.3 0.4))\n(equal? (cadr II) (cadr II))"
                 :invariant "∀ (u,v). II is symmetric (off-diagonal M is unambiguous)"
                 :meta "Symmetry follows from equality of mixed second partials (Clairaut). Falsified only by a broken derivative. See book-of-math on Clairaut's theorem.")
                (:eng "Regression: verify symmetry by comparing M computed two ways."

(verb

  :explanation "The slope angle is the angle between the surface and the horizontal plane, derived from the magnitude of the gradient vector ∇h = (h_x, h_y). A slope angle of 0 means flat; π/4 (45°) means the surface rises or falls at a 45-degree angle.     (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((ramp (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (* 0.5 x)))))\n  (curve/slope-angle ramp 1.0 0.0))" :note "A ramp with h_x = 0.5 has slope angle atan(0.5) ≈ 0.464 radians (≈ 26.6°).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((terrain (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (+ (* 0.1 x) (* 0.05 (* x x))))))\n       (angle (curve/slope-angle terrain 2.0 1.0)))\n  (if (> angle (/ const/pi 6)) 'steep 'gentle))" :note "Classify terrain as steep or gentle by comparing slope angle to a threshold (π/6 ≈ 30°).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let* ((bumpy (curve/surface-graph (lambda (x y) (+ (* 0.2 (geom/sin (* 2 x))) (* 0.15 (geom/cos (* 3 y)))))))\n       (grid-pts (list (list 0 0) (list 1 0) (list 0 1) (list 1 1)))\n       (angles (map (lambda (p) (curve/slope-angle bumpy (car p) (cadr p))) grid-pts))\n       (steepest (apply max angles)))\n  steepest)" :note "Survey a terrain grid to find the steepest local slope angle, useful for path planning around obstacles.")
  )

  :name "curve/torsion"
  :library "curve"

  :signature "(curve/torsion curve t) -> tau"
  :summary "Compute the torsion τ, which measures how much a 3-D curve twists out of its osculating plane."
  :explanation "Torsion quantifies the 'twist' of a space curve: how much the curve spirals or wrings as you move along it. For a planar curve, τ=0 always. For a helix, τ is constant and nonzero. Mathematically, τ = (γ′ × γ″) · γ‴ / |γ′ × γ″|². Together with curvature κ, torsion fully describes the shape and motion of the curve via the Frenet-Serret frame (T, N, B)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) (* t 0.3))))\n(curve/torsion curve 0)" :note "A helix has constant torsion; at t=0, measure how tightly it spirals in the z direction.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (* t (cos t)) (* t (sin t)) (* t t))))\n(define tau-vals (map (lambda (t) (curve/torsion curve t)) (list 0.5 1 1.5 2)))\n(list 'torsion-samples tau-vals)" :note "For a spiral with increasing pitch, compute torsion at multiple parameter values to see how twist intensity changes.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) (sin (* t 2)))))\n(define (analyze-at t) (let ((tau (curve/torsion curve t)) (kappa (curve/curvature curve t)) (frame (curve/frenet-frame curve t))) (list 'tau tau 'kappa kappa 'frame frame)))\n(analyze-at 0.7)" :note "Compute torsion alongside curvature and the full Frenet frame to build a complete picture of the curve's local geometry.")
  )
  :caveats ("If κ=0 (curvature vanishes), torsion is undefined and returns 'singular; the osculating plane does not exist." "Torsion is signed: positive and negative torsion distinguish right-handed from left-handed twist." "Numerical differentiation errors compound; smooth curves give more stable results.")
  :drawbacks ("Requires third derivative, making it more sensitive to noise than curvature (which uses only first and second)." "Only defined for 3-D curves; use curve/curvature-2d for planar curves.")
  :usecases ("Characterizing 3-D spiral and helix trajectories in animation and motion capture." "Analyzing ribbon and tube geometry in molecular biology and structural engineering." "Understanding the Frenet frame motion and twist in robotics and camera path planning." "Differentiating between curves with identical curvature but different twist.")
  :related ("curve/curvature" "curve/unit-tangent" "curve/normal" "curve/binormal" "curve/frenet-frame" "curve/osculating-circle" "curve/sample" "curve/velocity" "curve/accel")
  :learn (:concept "Torsion as the twist rate of a 3-D curve, the third fundamental invariant after curvature." :prerequisites ("curve/velocity" "curve/accel" "curve/curvature" "curve/unit-tangent" "vec/cross" "vec/dot") :progression "Master curve/curvature first; then learn curve/unit-tangent and curve/normal; finally study torsion and curve/frenet-frame as the complete geometric signature of a space curve.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A 3D animator asks: does this curve stay in a plane, or does it twist out?"
                 :program "(define c (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define tau (curve/torsion c 0.5))\n(if (< (abs tau) 0.001) 'planar 'twisting)"
                 :explanation "Extract torsion. Near zero means the curve lies in a plane; nonzero means it screws out of the osculating plane."
                 :meta "Reach for torsion over curvature to distinguish planar-bending from 3D-twisting; curvature alone can't tell a circle from a helix.")
                (:eng "Log |τ|; a persistent nonzero τ over parameter range is diagnostic for helical structures."
                 :math "τ = ((γ' × γ'') · γ''') / |γ' × γ''|²."
                 :cs "Requires third derivative; numerically sensitive."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "third-order twist measurement: same shape appears in curves, in rigid-body angular velocity, in electromagnetism"
                     :rungs ((:domain "curve" :code "(curve/torsion (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) (* 0.3 t))) 0.5)")
                             (:domain "angular-velocity" :code "(define (screw-rate axis roll-rate) (list axis roll-rate))\n(screw-rate '(0 0 1) 0.5)")
                             (:domain "twist-form" :code "(define (twist-density theta-list ds) (map / theta-list ds))\n(twist-density '(0.1 0.2 0.15) '(1 1 1))"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 measures curve torsion. Rung 2 gives rigid-body angular rate about an axis. Rung 3 divides accumulated angle by arc length. All three quantify rotation per unit motion."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'rotation per unit motion' is one primitive."
                    )
                    (:eng "Robotics, curve rendering, and rotation dynamics share this scalar."
                     :math "τ = dφ/ds along the curve."
                     :cs "Same third-derivative primitive; different physical labels."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:claim "Torsion of a planar curve is zero."
                 :program "(define c (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define tau (curve/torsion c 0.5))\n(< (abs tau) 0.01)"
                 :invariant "∀ planar γ. τ(t) = 0"
                 :meta "τ = 0 iff γ lies in a plane. Falsified by any nonzero τ on a truly-planar curve. See book-of-math on Frenet-Serret formulas.")
                (:eng "Regression: planar curves report zero torsion."
                 :math "τ = 0 ⟺ planarity."
                 :cs "One assertion."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:base "curve/torsion returns τ at a curve parameter."
                     :composition "(define helix (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) (* 0.3 t))))\n(define ts '(0 0.5 1 1.5 2))\n(define signature (map (lambda (t) (list (curve/curvature helix t) (curve/torsion helix t))) ts))\nsignature"
                     :emergent "A (κ,τ) curve signature: chaining curvature and torsion over samples yields the complete geometric signature identifying the curve up to rigid motion."
                     :meta "This is the same family as extracting an invariant fingerprint from a signal. Cross-ref book-of-motion on curve fingerprints.")
                    (:eng "Motion planners use (κ,τ) to match observed curves to authored templates."
                     :math "The pair (κ,τ) determines the curve up to rigid motion (fundamental theorem of curves)."
                     :cs "Two verbs + map over samples.")))

(verb
  :name "curve/unit-tangent"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/unit-tangent curve t) -> (t_x t_y t_z)"
  :summary "Compute the unit tangent vector T = γ′/|γ′| at parameter t, pointing in the direction of motion."
  :explanation "The unit tangent is the normalized first derivative of the curve: it points along the curve in the direction of increasing parameter, with magnitude 1. It is the foundation of the Frenet frame and encodes the instantaneous direction of travel. At stationary points (where γ′=0), T is undefined and returns 'singular."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (* t 2) (* t 3) 0)))\n(curve/unit-tangent curve 1)" :note "For a straight line, the unit tangent is constant and proportional to the direction vector (2, 3, 0) normalized.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define tangents (map (lambda (t) (curve/unit-tangent curve t)) (list 0 (/ 3.14159 2) 3.14159)))\n(list 'unit-tangents tangents)" :note "For a unit circle, the unit tangent at t=0 points in direction (0, 1, 0), at t=π/2 in (−1, 0, 0), etc., always perpendicular to the radius.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) (* t 0.2))))\n(define t-val 1.5)\n(define T (curve/unit-tangent curve t-val))\n(define N (curve/normal curve t-val))\n(define B (curve/binormal curve t-val))\n(list 'T T 'N N 'B B 'orthonormal? (and (< (abs (- (vec/dot T N) 0)) 0.001) (< (abs (- (vec/dot T B) 0)) 0.001)))" :note "Build the Frenet frame by combining unit-tangent with normal and binormal; verify orthonormality.")
  )
  :caveats ("At stationary points (γ′=0), the tangent is undefined and returns 'singular." "Sign: T points in the direction of increasing parameter, not along some global convention." "Numerical derivative errors compound at points of low speed; high-speed regions are more stable.")
  :drawbacks ("Requires only first derivative (unlike torsion), but finite-difference accuracy still depends on smooth input." "If the curve is parameterized non-uniformly (e.g., with varying speed), the unit tangent magnitude hides the speed; use curve/velocity if you need the raw derivative.")
  :usecases ("Building Frenet frames for camera orientation and path-following control." "Analyzing the direction of motion in animation and trajectory planning." "Computing surface normals via cross product of tangent vectors on a patch." "Testing curve smoothness by examining tangent continuity.")
  :related ("curve/velocity" "curve/accel" "curve/curvature" "curve/normal" "curve/binormal" "curve/frenet-frame" "curve/arc-length" "curve/speed" "curve/osculating-circle")
  :learn (:concept "Unit tangent as the direction of motion along a curve, normalized to unit magnitude." :prerequisites ("curve/velocity" "vec/normalize" "vec/norm") :progression "After understanding unit-tangent, learn curve/normal and curve/binormal to build the full Frenet frame; then study curvature and torsion to quantify how the frame twists and turns.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A sprite needs to face the direction of motion along a path. What unit vector answers?"
                 :program "(define c (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define T (curve/unit-tangent c 0.5))\nT"
                 :explanation "Extract T at the current parameter. Assign as the sprite's facing direction. As the sprite moves, T rotates to keep facing forward."
                 :meta "Reach for unit-tangent over velocity when direction alone matters; velocity's magnitude is orthogonal to that concern.")
                (:eng "T='singular means stationary point; sprite orientation must fall back to last-known-good."
                 :math "T = γ' / |γ'|."
                 :cs "One derivative + one normalize; O(1)."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "unit-length direction from a raw derivative: same shape appears in curves, in physics, in stochastic optimization"
                     :rungs ((:domain "curve" :code "(curve/unit-tangent (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)) 0.5)")
                             (:domain "physics-heading" :code "(define (heading v)\n  (let ((m (sqrt (fold-left + 0 (map * v v)))))\n    (map (lambda (x) (/ x m)) v)))\n(heading '(3 4 0))")
                             (:domain "sgd-direction" :code "(define (unit-gradient g) (let ((m (sqrt (fold-left + 0 (map * g g))))) (map (lambda (x) (/ x m)) g)))\n(unit-gradient '(2 1 3))"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 gives curve heading. Rung 2 gives physical heading. Rung 3 gives normalized SGD direction. Each normalizes a rate vector to unit length."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'direction of change' is a substrate-neutral primitive."
                    )
                    (:eng "Motion planning, physics, and optimization share this primitive."
                     :math "T = v/|v|."
                     :cs "One sqrt + one divide-map."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:claim "Unit tangent has magnitude 1."
                 :program "(define c (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define T (curve/unit-tangent c 0.5))\n(define mag (sqrt (fold-left + 0 (map * T T))))\n(< (abs (- mag 1)) 0.001)"
                 :invariant "∀ t (γ'(t)≠0). |T(t)| = 1"
                 :meta "Unit magnitude follows from normalization. Falsified by drift beyond tolerance. See book-of-math on unit vectors.")
                (:eng "Regression: |T|≈1."
                 :math "|·/|·|| = 1."
                 :cs "One assertion."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:base "curve/unit-tangent returns the direction of motion at a curve parameter."
                     :composition "(define c (curve/bezier '((0 0) (3 4) (7 4) (10 0))))\n(define (sprite-frame t)\n  (list 'pos (curve/eval c t) 'heading (curve/unit-tangent c t)))\n(map sprite-frame '(0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1))"
                     :emergent "A pose-along-path pipeline: chaining eval + unit-tangent yields (position, heading) per sample — a full sprite pose."
                     :meta "This is the same family as any authored motion + orientation timeline. Cross-ref book-of-motion on poses.")
                    (:eng "Sprite animation and camera tracking use this pose per frame."
                     :math "pose(t) = (γ(t), T(t))."
                     :cs "Composition is short; two verbs, one map.")))

(verb
  :name "curve/velocity"
  :library "curve"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(curve/velocity curve t) -> (v_x v_y v_z)"
  :summary "Compute the velocity vector γ′(t), the first derivative of the curve with respect to its parameter."
  :explanation "Velocity is the raw first derivative γ′, which points in the direction of motion and whose magnitude is the speed. Unlike the unit tangent (which normalizes to length 1), velocity retains information about how fast the curve moves through space at each parameter value. For a curve parameterized by arc length, |γ′|=1; for arbitrary parameterizations, |γ′| varies and encodes the 'speed' with respect to the parameter."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list t (* t t) (* t t t))))\n(curve/velocity curve 1)" :note "For γ(t) = (t, t², t³), the velocity at t=1 is γ′(1) = (1, 2, 3), showing how fast the curve moves in each direction.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define v (curve/velocity curve 0))\n(define speed (curve/speed curve 0))\n(list 'velocity v 'speed speed)" :note "For a unit circle parameterized by angle, velocity at t=0 is (0, 1, 0) with speed 1; at higher t, velocity direction rotates but magnitude stays constant.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define curve (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) (* 0.1 t))))\n(define t-vals (list 0 1.57 3.14 4.71))\n(define vels (map (lambda (t) (curve/velocity curve t)) t-vals))\n(define speeds (map (lambda (t) (curve/speed curve t)) t-vals))\n(define accels (map (lambda (t) (curve/accel curve t)) t-vals))\n(list 'velocities vels 'speeds speeds 'accelerations accels)" :note "Track velocity, speed, and acceleration along a helix to see how motion varies; the speed stays roughly constant, but the acceleration perpendicular component drives the curve.")
  )
  :caveats ("Velocity depends on parameterization; reparameterizing the curve changes the velocity vector (though not the geometric curve shape)." "Finite-difference errors scale with the step size ε; too small risks numerical cancellation, too large misses features." "At cusps or corners (where the curve is non-smooth), velocity may jump or be undefined.")
  :drawbacks ("Raw velocity, not normalized; to get direction independent of speed, use curve/unit-tangent." "Numerical differentiation amplifies noise in the input curve." "Requires at least 3 sample points (to use central difference); very sparse curves give poor estimates.")
  :usecases ("Computing speed and acceleration for physics simulation and motion planning." "Analyzing parametric animations to control timing and motion profile." "Feeding downstream verbs like curve/curvature and curve/torsion, which depend on derivatives." "Detecting sharp changes or cusps in a curve by examining velocity jumps.")
  :related ("curve/speed" "curve/accel" "curve/unit-tangent" "curve/curvature" "curve/arc-length" "curve/frenet-frame")
  :learn (:concept "Velocity as the first derivative, preserving information about both direction and parameterization speed." :prerequisites ("curve/eval" "curve/sample") :progression "Learn curve/velocity first; then curve/speed (magnitude); then curve/accel (second derivative); then use these to build curve/unit-tangent, curve/curvature, and the full Frenet frame.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A physics engine needs the raw velocity vector to compute momentum for a particle on a parametric path. What returns it?"
                 :program "(define path (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) (* 0.3 t))))\n(define v (curve/velocity path 0.5))\nv"
                 :explanation "Extract γ'(0.5). This is the true velocity vector at the sample; multiplied by mass gives momentum."
                 :meta "Reach for velocity over unit-tangent when magnitude matters (momentum, energy); unit-tangent has been normalized and lost the speed.")
                (:eng "Log |v|; a zero-velocity sample flags a stationary point."
                 :math "v = γ'(t)."
                 :cs "Pure eval; O(1) after derivative."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "raw first derivative preserving both direction and rate: same shape appears in curves, in physics, in signal processing"
                     :rungs ((:domain "curve" :code "(curve/velocity (lambda (t) (list t (* t t))) 1)")
                             (:domain "physics" :code "(define (finite-diff f x h) (/ (- (f (+ x h)) (f x)) h))\n(finite-diff (lambda (t) (* t t)) 1 0.01)")
                             (:domain "signal-derivative" :code "(define (diff sig)\n  (map - (cdr sig) sig))\n(diff '(0 1 4 9 16))"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 gives γ'(t). Rung 2 gives a numerical derivative. Rung 3 gives discrete differences of a signal. Each is a first-derivative operator applied to a source."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'first derivative' is one operator regardless of domain.")
                    (:eng "Physical simulations, numerical differentiation, and signal DSP share this operator."
                     :math "d/dt is a linear operator."
                     :cs "Same finite-difference stencil across domains."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:claim "Velocity magnitude equals speed."
                 :program "(define c (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define v (curve/velocity c 0.5))\n(define s (curve/speed c 0.5))\n(< (abs (- (sqrt (fold-left + 0 (map * v v))) s)) 0.001)"
                 :invariant "∀ t. |velocity(t)| = speed(t)"
                 :meta "|v| = speed is the definitional link between the two. Falsified by any drift beyond tolerance. See book-of-math on norms.")
                (:eng "Regression: |v| ≈ speed for the same parameter."
                 :math "|v| = |γ'|."
                 :cs "One assertion."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:base "curve/velocity returns γ'(t)."
                     :composition "(define path (lambda (t) (list (cos t) (sin t) 0)))\n(define (kinetic mass t)\n  (let* ((v (curve/velocity path t))\n         (v2 (fold-left + 0 (map * v v))))\n    (* 0.5 mass v2)))\n(map (lambda (t) (kinetic 1.0 t)) '(0 0.5 1 1.5))"
                     :emergent "A kinetic-energy profile: chaining velocity with mass and squared norm yields the KE at each parameter."
                     :meta "This is the same family as any energy computation from a state-and-derivative. Cross-ref book-of-motion on energy.")
                    (:eng "Physics engines log KE profiles to check for energy drift under integration."
                     :math "KE = ½ m |v|²."
                     :cs "Three operations after velocity; O(1).")))

;;; 21-domain.slat — Motoi Scheme Reference · Chapter 21 · library domain
;;;
;;; 1 verbs in this library. Read chapter 00-intro.slat first.

;;;
;;; ─── THE ROW RULES (summary — full doctrine in 00-intro.slat) ───
;;;
;;; Every verb in this chapter has 5 rows. Each row does ONE job. Row
;;; contamination unbalances training data. If you author or edit a verb,
;;; STAY IN LANE.
;;;
;;;   Row 1 (HOW · Composition) — the verb written well; 1/3/5 module ladder
;;;   Row 2 (WHEN · Audit)      — operator's problem + this-verb-not-a-sibling
;;;   Row 3 (WHERE ELSE · Dim)  — same shape in 3 substrates (verb/metaphor/math)
;;;   Row 4 (WHY · Proof)       — claim + runnable test + ∀-invariant
;;;   Row 5 (WITH WHAT ELSE)    — chained verbs → named emergent pattern
;;;
;;; Every row carries the three-discipline lens: :eng · :math · :cs.
;;; No philosopher names in entries (they live in 00-intro.slat).
;;; Real Motoi domains only (no card/*, shop/*, cine/*, flower/*).
;;; Every code block RUNS through ./bin/motoi (or is marked :runs "spec-only").
;;;
;;; Introspection is a first-class chapter — see 00b-introspection.slat.
;;; Before authoring, run: python3 scripts/audit-reference-rows.py
;;; Before folding, run: python3 scripts/compliance-check-runnable.py
;;;

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Library domain — 1 verbs.")

(chapter :number "21" :library "domain" :verb-count 1 :training-eligible #t)

;; ═══ 1 verbs in library domain ═══

(verb
  :name "domain/of"
  :library "domain"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(domain/of task-kind) -> {domain string reads list via string reason string}"
  :summary "Classify a task or escalation kind into its operational domain (e.g., 'web-research', 'self', 'payment', 'account')."
  :explanation "Every escalation, problem, or task belongs to a domain that determines how it should be routed and handled. domain/of takes a task kind (a symbol or string) and returns a classification record that includes the domain name, the knowledge sources it requires, the mechanism via which it will be resolved, and the reasoning chain. This is the data source for routing decisions: use it to decide whether a task should be handled locally, escalated to a human, or delegated to a specialized subsystem."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((result (domain/of 'account-lockout)))\n  (display 'domain-check (lambda (ctx) (surface-paint-text 'main 'debug 0 result))))" :note "Query the domain of an account-lockout task; get back a classification record.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define ctx '())\n(define (escalate-or-resolve task-kind ctx)\n  (let ((classification (domain/of task-kind)))\n    (if (equal? (cdr (assoc 'domain classification)) 'self)\n      (next 'handle-locally ctx)\n      (escalate task-kind (cdr (assoc 'reason classification))))))\n(escalate-or-resolve 'payment-dispute (ctx-set 'task 'payment-dispute ctx))" :note "Use domain/of to decide whether to handle locally or escalate; extract the reason for audit.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define ctx '())\n(define (classify-and-route task-kind ctx)\n  (let* ((classification (domain/of task-kind))\n         (domain-name (cdr (assoc 'domain classification)))\n         (reads-needed (cdr (assoc 'reads classification))))\n    (cond ((null? reads-needed)\n           (next 'handle-locally (ctx-set 'classification classification ctx)))\n          ((equal? domain-name 'web-research)\n           (act 'ask/reasoner reads-needed 'fetch-knowledge))\n          (else\n           (escalate 'unroutable (list 'domain domain-name 'reads reads-needed))))))\n(classify-and-route 'data-loss (ctx-set 'task 'data-loss ctx))" :note "Multi-path routing: check domain, examine knowledge requirements, dispatch to appropriate handler (local, research, or escalation).")
  )
  :caveats ("If task-kind is not registered in the domain registry, the return value may be a default or error record; check for the presence of expected keys." "The reads list is the minimal set; actual resolution may require additional context from the task itself." "Domain classification is static; it does not consider the current system state or user permissions.")
  :drawbacks ("Requires the task kind to be known and registered beforehand; ad-hoc task kinds will not classify cleanly." "The returned record is opaque; extracting fields requires assoc or similar list operations, which is verbose." "Classification does not guarantee successful resolution; the via mechanism may still fail if dependencies are unavailable.")
  :usecases ("Route incoming tasks to the correct handler (local, research, escalation, or human contact)." "Audit and log why a task was escalated; include the reason field in the escalation record." "Pre-filter tasks: reject those that exceed system capability before attempting resolution.")
  :related ("route/off-domain" "floor/problem?" "escalate" "ask/reasoner")
  :learn (:concept "Task classification and domain-based routing as a prerequisite for intelligent task dispatch." :prerequisites ("(core)/let" "(core)/assoc" "(core)/equal?" "escalate") :progression "Next: route/off-domain for normal-path routing, or floor/problem? to check if a task crosses safety thresholds.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "The support queue is auto-routing tickets, and last night a payment-dispute ended up in the local-handle bucket where nobody sees it for 24 hours. The operator needs to know: for a given kind-symbol, what does the router think the DOMAIN is, and by what REASON did it decide? The audit lane needs a stamped classification record per ticket so the misrouted class can be identified and the router's decision made accountable."
     :program "(define (classify-with-audit task-kind)\n  (let* ((classification (domain/of task-kind))\n         (domain-name (cdr (assoc 'domain classification)))\n         (reason (cdr (assoc 'reason classification))))\n    (list 'ticket task-kind 'routed-to domain-name 'because reason)))\n(display (classify-with-audit 'payment-dispute))\n(newline)\n(display (classify-with-audit 'account-lockout))\n(newline)"
     :explanation "The auditor wraps domain/of inside a classify-with-audit function whose return value is a stamped record: which task-kind was classified, what domain it was routed to, and the reason the classification gave. Each ticket is passed through this same function, and each ticket produces one row of ledger. When the misrouted payment-dispute is investigated, the auditor pulls its row and sees the exact (domain, reason) pair the router used. If the reason names an expected keyword — 'requires-billing-context' — the router was correct and the queue is under-staffed. If the reason is empty or points at a fallback path, the classifier's registry is missing an entry for payment-dispute and the fix is to add it there rather than blame the router."
     :meta "domain/of is the honest verb here because it is the ONLY verb whose contract carries both the domain AND the reason in one call. A sibling like floor/problem? would tell you whether a kind is currently an ACTIVE problem, but it would not say what kind of problem it is or where it should go. escalate would send the kind somewhere, but it would not record a decision — it would only record an action. route/off-domain assumes classification has already happened. What the audit needs is the reason chain, and only domain/of returns it, which is why domain/of is the accountable verb.")
    (:eng "For the operator, the (task-kind, domain, reason) triple is the audit's smallest complete unit. Ship it to the ticketing system's log; sort tickets by domain to spot classes that are getting no attention; sort by reason to find fallback strings that indicate a missing registry entry."
     :math "domain/of is a function from a task-kind symbol to a record; the record's :reason field is the WITNESS of the classification, in the sense of a mathematical witness — a piece of evidence that lets a third party verify the decision without re-running the classifier."
     :cs "The audit strategy uses domain/of as a pure lookup: the classifier does not fire an effect, it produces a data value the caller inspects. Wrapping it in a returning function (not a printing side effect) is what lets the row be stored, replayed, and re-verified. This is the auditability-through-return-value pattern."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape here is TAG-WITH-REASON: given an item, return not just a label but a label PLUS the evidence for the label. The evidence is what makes the label auditable. That shape is not specific to task classification."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "domain/classification" :code "(domain/of 'payment-dispute)")
       (:domain "medical/triage" :code "(define (triage complaint)\n  (list (cons 'level (if (equal? complaint 'chest-pain) 'red 'yellow))\n        (cons 'reason (if (equal? complaint 'chest-pain) 'cardiac-suspicion 'observe))))\n(triage 'chest-pain)")
       (:domain "logic/labeled-inference" :code "(define (label p)\n  (list (cons 'verdict (if p 'true 'false))\n        (cons 'reason (if p 'premise-holds 'premise-fails))))\n(label #t)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is the verb in its own domain: a task-kind gets classified with its reason. Rung 2 is a metaphor from a hospital emergency room: a triage nurse assigns each patient a level (red, yellow, green) AND records the reason (chest pain → cardiac suspicion). The record is what the incoming attending physician reads; the reason is what allows the physician to trust or override the level. Rung 3 is logic: a labeled proof step tags a proposition with a verdict and the reason (which premise justified it). Across all three, the label alone is insufficient; the label WITH the reason is what allows a downstream reader to trust the label or challenge it."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in every case the classification is subject to review by another actor — an auditor, a physician, a proof-checker — and that reviewer's job requires evidence, not just verdict. A verdict without a witness is opaque; a witness makes the verdict falsifiable. domain/of exports the same discipline that emergency triage and proof theory export: return the reason next to the label.")
    (:eng "In operations, the reason is what enables the runbook: an on-call engineer reading the ticket sees not only that it was routed but why, and can immediately act on the domain-specific playbook. Without the reason, every audit becomes an interview."
     :math "Formally the shape is a return value in a product type: (label, evidence). The evidence side is what makes the type honest under an external verifier. book-of-code ch10 (state machines) treats labels-with-transitions; the transition label is a related shape."
     :cs "The pattern name in CS is DECISION-WITH-JUSTIFICATION, the same shape that motivates explanation modules in expert systems and 'why' interfaces in rule engines. Any classifier that returns only the class is opaque; adding the reason turns opacity into audit."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "domain/of is DETERMINISTIC in its input alone: two calls with the same task-kind (and no intervening registry change) return classification records with the SAME :domain field and the SAME :reason field. This is what makes the reason a witness rather than a story: it is stable across calls, which lets it be diffed, re-run, and challenged."
     :program "(define c1 (domain/of 'account-lockout))\n(define c2 (domain/of 'account-lockout))\n(define (get k rec) (cdr (assoc k rec)))\n(display (equal? (get 'domain c1) (get 'domain c2)))\n(newline)\n(display (equal? (get 'reason c1) (get 'reason c2)))\n(newline)"
     :invariant "∀ k. (registry-fixed) → domain/of(k).domain = domain/of(k).domain  AND  domain/of(k).reason = domain/of(k).reason."
     :meta "The engineering consequence is that a classification report is REPRODUCIBLE — an audit rerun against the same registry against the same task-kind produces byte-identical rows, which is what turns the report into evidence. In CS terms the property is REFERENTIAL TRANSPARENCY under a fixed registry. What falsifies the claim is a single task-kind for which two consecutive calls return different (domain, reason) pairs without an intervening registry-mutation event; one such witness proves domain/of is state-carrying beyond its argument and every downstream routing decision loses its audit trail. See book-of-code ch10 (state machines) for the theory of pure lookup versus stateful lookup; a pure lookup is what audit requires here.")
    (:eng "For SRE, referential-transparency-under-fixed-registry means the classifier can be memoized (with a cache invalidated only on registry change), can be replayed against archived tickets, and can be tested with a small fixture. A regression where the reason changes across two calls in the same session is a SEV signal."
     :math "The property is a functional dependency: task-kind determines (domain, reason) — a many-to-one mapping realized in the registry. book-of-math ch-advanced-02 (combinatorics-counting) discusses such lookup tables as functions."
     :cs "The pattern is PURE LOOKUP with a mutable table underneath: the lookup itself has no observable state, and the table's state is versioned/locked separately. This is the same pattern used in DNS resolvers and in interned symbol tables."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "domain/of classifies a task-kind, returning a record with :domain, :reads, :via, and :reason."
     :composition "(define (get k rec) (cdr (assoc k rec)))\n(define (route task-kind)\n  (let* ((c (domain/of task-kind))\n         (d (get 'domain c)))\n    (cond ((equal? d 'self)         (list 'handle-locally task-kind))\n          ((equal? d 'web-research) (list 'fetch-then-handle task-kind))\n          (else                     (list 'escalate task-kind 'reason (get 'reason c))))))\n(display (route 'account-lockout))\n(newline)\n(display (route 'payment-dispute))\n(newline)"
     :emergent "A DISPATCHER emerges from domain/of chained with a cond on the domain field: one classifier and one switch produce a router that sends each incoming task-kind down its correct arm. The dispatcher is the shape of the chain; no dispatcher verb was introduced."
     :meta "The family here is the DISPATCH TABLE, the same family as URL routing in a web framework, as syscall dispatch in a kernel, as message dispatch in a queue consumer. book-of-composition ch15 (http-server) treats the same pattern applied to HTTP paths; book-of-code ch12 (cpu-fetch-decode-execute) treats it applied to instruction opcodes. A familiar analog is the switch-case at the top of a controller function that routes a request to its handler. Adding more (domain, arm) branches to the cond adds capacity to the dispatcher; adding a default arm makes the dispatcher total.")
    (:eng "The emergent dispatcher is diffable and testable: each arm is a small function, and the classifier's :reason field can be surfaced to the operator when a task lands on the escalate arm. Operators debug wrong routing by inspecting the (domain, reason) pair, not by digging through the router."
     :math "The chain is a composition of two total functions: classify : kind → record, then select : record → arm-label. Both have small finite codomains; the composition is again total."
     :cs "Dispatch table is a canonical CS pattern; book-of-code ch12 (cpu-fetch-decode-execute) explains it at the machine-instruction level. The classifier corresponds to the DECODE stage, and the cond corresponds to the EXECUTE stage's opcode branch.")))
