;; ═══ 5 verbs in library exception ═══

(verb
  :name "error"
  :library "exception"
  :tier "core"
  :kind "mut"
  :signature "(error message . irritants) -> raises"
  :summary "Raise a Scheme error with a message and optional extra values. R7RS §6.11."
  :explanation "The canonical error-signal. The raised object is a Scheme-error whose message-string is available via (error-object-message …) and whose irritant list via (error-object-irritants …). Catch with (guard …). Consistent error shape across Motoi: (error 'proc-name \"msg\" arg1 arg2 …)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(error \"not found\" key)" :note "Signal an error with a message and one irritant.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(guard (err ((error-object? err) (display (error-object-message err))))\n  (error \"bad input\" x))" :note "Catch the error and inspect its message.")
  )
  :caveats ("Errors bubble until a `guard` catches them; unhandled at top level they abort the interpreter.")
  :usecases ("Signaling a precondition violation." "Reporting a data-shape mismatch." "Failing loudly early rather than propagating a bad value.")
  :related ("raise" "guard" "error-object?" "error-object-message" "error-object-irritants")
  :learn (:concept "Explicit failure vs silent bad-data propagation.")
  :provenance "R7RS §6.11; added 2026-07-18 finalization"
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "An input handler receives a value it cannot process. The programmer could return #f, could raise a generic condition, or could call error. If they return #f, callers must remember to check — and one path that forgets becomes a silent bug that keeps polluting downstream state. If they raise a bare symbol, callers have nothing structured to inspect. If they call error with a clear message and the offending irritant, the failure is loud, structured, and inspectable. The audit question is whether the programmer picked the verb that fails visibly with enough context to reconstruct the fault."
     :program "(define (require-positive n)\n  (if (and (number? n) (positive? n))\n    n\n    (error \"require-positive: not a positive number\" n)))\n(display (guard (c ((error-object? c) (list 'caught (error-object-message c) (error-object-irritants c))))\n           (require-positive -3))) (newline)\n(display (require-positive 5)) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines a validator that either returns n unchanged or raises. Line 3 wraps a bad call in a guard; the error is caught, its message extracted, and its irritant list inspected. Line 5 shows the happy-path call. The audit trail: bad input → error raised → guard catches → message and irritants both available."
     :meta "Why error and not silent #f: #f is a value; downstream code has no reason to inspect it separately from a legitimate boolean answer. error stops execution at the exact point of the fault. If #f had been used, the caller's next `(if bad ...)` might mistake the failure for a false-branch condition; the audit trail vanishes.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is fail-loud validation. The engineering rule: fail at the boundary where the problem is diagnosable. See SRE Manual on 'fail early, log the irritant.'"
     :math "The verb is not a mathematical function — it is a control-flow operation on a computation. It maps a message and irritants to a diverging computation."
     :cs "The CS pattern is checked exception (or 'panic with context'). Contrast with return-#f (no context), raise-symbol (bare context), and exit (unrecoverable). error is the 'recoverable panic with context' choice."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A visible-failure signal: raise a structured object that carries enough context to reconstruct the fault, in a way that halts local flow until a caller catches."
     :rungs ((:domain "exception (Scheme error)" :code "(error \"bad-value\" x)")
             (:domain "kitchen: chef calls out" :code "'86-the-salmon ; expediter yells to all callers")
             (:domain "type-theory: partial functions" :code "let f x = if valid x then Just(compute x) else Nothing"))
     :explanation "In Scheme, error raises a condition object with a message and irritants. In a kitchen, calling out '86 the salmon' propagates a fault upstream so every path that would ask for salmon stops. In type theory, a partial function returning Nothing (rather than raising) is the safe analog. All three cases share the shape: a fault is signaled with enough context for the receiver to decide what to do."
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever the local computation cannot produce a correct answer and needs to hand the decision upstream. The context — the message and irritants in Scheme, the '86 announcement in the kitchen, the Nothing carrier in type theory — must be structured enough for the caller to act.")
    (:eng "Log the error's message and irritants at the outermost guard. That is the concrete evidence for the incident review."
     :math "In the partiality framing, error is the unmapped case of a partial function ℝ ⇀ ℝ."
     :cs "The CS analog is a raised exception. Related: Result::Err in Rust, throw new Error in JavaScript, raise in Python."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "error raises a condition object that is inspectable via error-object-message and error-object-irritants, and is caught by guard."
     :program "(define caught\n  (guard (c ((error-object? c)\n             (list (error-object-message c) (error-object-irritants c))))\n    (error \"boom\" 1 2 3)))\n(display caught) (newline)\n(display (equal? (car caught) \"boom\")) (newline)\n(display (equal? (cadr caught) (list 1 2 3))) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ msg irritants. guard(catch, error(msg, ...irritants)) yields an object o with error-object-message(o) = msg and error-object-irritants(o) = irritants"
     :meta "The pattern is round-trip: the error object's payload is exactly what was passed in. See book-of-code ch14 for exception-object structure. What falsifies: any run where the caught message or irritants disagree with the raised ones. Runtime holds the invariant."
    :eng "The engineering payoff is that a caught error carries all the diagnostic data the raiser had; no information is lost across the raise/catch boundary."
     :math "This is the identity property of the raise/catch pair — data goes in, same data comes out."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is exception-round-trip. Related: pickled exception context, structured logging."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "error signals a fault with a message and irritants."
     :composition "(define (retry-once fn)\n  (guard (c ((error-object? c) (fn))) ; catch, try once more\n    (fn)))\n(define attempts 0)\n(define (flaky)\n  (set! attempts (+ attempts 1))\n  (if (< attempts 2) (error \"not-yet\" attempts) 'ok))\n(display (retry-once flaky)) (newline)\n(display attempts) (newline)"
     :emergent "retry-with-limit — a wrapper that catches a failure once and retries the operation, useful for transient errors"
     :meta "The composition chains error (in flaky) with guard (in retry-once). What emerges is the retry-loop family: a wrapper that intercepts a fault and reattempts the operation. The same family appears as HTTP-retry middleware, as database-transaction retry loops, as message-queue redelivery. In book-of-code ch14 this is called out as one of the foundational fault-tolerance shapes."
     :eng "Retry loops are load-bearing for network operations. Log the retry count and the error caught so the operator sees the pattern of failures."
     :math "The composition is a fixpoint over a Try monad: retry until success or budget exhaustion."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is retry-with-limit. Familiar analogs: Polly (.NET retry library), backoff libraries in Python, retry crate in Rust.")))

(verb :name "raise"             :library "exception" :tier "core" :kind "mut" :signature "(raise obj) -> raises"
  :summary "Raise obj as a condition. Non-error objects get wrapped. R7RS §6.11."
  :provenance "R7RS §6.11; added 2026-07-18 finalization"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(guard (c (#t 'caught)) (raise 'oops))" :note "caught — raise triggers the guard handler.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(guard (c ((symbol? c) c)) (raise 'boom))" :note "boom.")
  )
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "An operator building a custom signal system wants to propagate a control signal (not an error) up the call stack. They need a way to interrupt flow with a non-error payload — a symbol, a structured record, a number. `error` insists on a message + irritants shape; that lies about the signal being an error. `raise` is the primitive that just propagates any object as a condition. The audit question is whether the operator picked the right verb for the shape of their signal."
     :program "(define (find-first-positive xs)\n  (guard (v ((number? v) v))\n    (for-each\n      (lambda (x) (if (positive? x) (raise x) #f))\n      xs)\n    'none))\n(display (find-first-positive (list -1 -2 3 -4 5))) (newline)\n(display (find-first-positive (list -1 -2 -3))) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines a searcher that raises the first positive element it finds. Lines 2-5 wrap the loop in a guard that catches numbers. Line 6-7 show the searcher finding 3 and then finding nothing (returns 'none). The audit trail: control signal (a number) raised, guard catches by predicate, control returns to caller with the found value."
     :meta "Why raise and not error: the found value is not an error. Using error would forge an error-object shape around a legitimate signal, and downstream code would confuse the two. raise preserves the payload as-is.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is control-flow via conditions. See book-of-code ch14 on non-local exits."
     :math "raise is unbound-jump-with-payload — a non-local exit that carries an arbitrary object."
     :cs "The CS pattern is condition-signal / non-local exit. Related: Common Lisp's signal, Java's Thread.interrupt, Go's panic."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A non-local exit with payload: interrupt local flow and hand a value to the nearest handler."
     :rungs ((:domain "exception (Scheme)" :code "(raise value)")
             (:domain "loop early-exit" :code "(call/cc (lambda (k) (loop k)))")
             (:domain "goto with a value" :code "throw v"))
     :explanation "In Scheme, raise transfers control to the nearest guard with a payload. Continuations achieve the same shape when called with a value. In C-family languages, throw is the analog. All three cases share the shape: leave the local scope with a value, resume at a higher scope."
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever computation must exit from deep inside a stack with useful information for the outer scope.")
    (:eng "Log the raised payload at the catch site so the caller sees what triggered the exit."
     :math "raise is a projection from the local scope to the handler scope, parameterized by a payload."
     :cs "The CS analog is a non-local exit. Related: setjmp/longjmp, break-with-value in Rust loops."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "raise transfers control to the nearest enclosing guard whose handler accepts the payload, and the payload is delivered unchanged."
     :program "(define caught (guard (c ((symbol? c) c)) (raise 'signal)))\n(display (eq? caught 'signal)) (newline)\n(define caught2 (guard (c ((number? c) c)) (raise 42)))\n(display (= caught2 42)) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ v. guard((pred, expr), raise(v)) = expr(v) when pred(v)"
     :meta "The pattern is condition-delivery: the payload arrives unchanged at the handler. See book-of-code ch14. What falsifies: any run where the caught value differs from the raised value. Runtime holds the invariant."
    :eng "Payload preservation is the whole point — the handler must see exactly what the raiser passed."
     :math "raise is an identity function under the guard/raise round trip: guard ∘ raise = id."
     :cs "The CS pattern is identity across the raise/catch boundary."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "raise transfers control to the nearest handler with a payload."
     :composition "(define (search-tree tree pred)\n  (guard (v ((pred v) v))\n    (let walk ((node tree))\n      (cond ((null? node) 'not-found)\n            ((pair? node)\n             (walk (car node))\n             (walk (cdr node)))\n            ((pred node) (raise node))\n            (else 'skip)))))\n(display (search-tree (list 1 (list 2 3) 4) (lambda (x) (and (number? x) (> x 2))))) (newline)"
     :emergent "early-exit search — a tree traversal that stops immediately upon finding a matching node, without walking the rest of the tree"
     :meta "The composition chains raise inside a recursive walk with a guard at the top. What emerges is the early-exit family: a search that jumps out of the entire recursion the moment it finds the answer, skipping remaining work. The same family appears as C++ throw-across-loops, as Common Lisp block/return-from, as Rust break-with-value. In book-of-code ch14 this is called out as one of the foundational search-optimization shapes."
     :eng "Early-exit search saves compute when the sought item is common. Log the number of nodes visited for later analysis."
     :math "The composition is a first-witness reduction on a tree: fold until the predicate holds, then stop."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is early-exit / short-circuit search. Familiar analogs: Python for-else, Ruby throw/catch, Rust's break outer.")))

(verb :name "raise-continuable" :library "exception" :tier "core" :kind "mut" :signature "(raise-continuable obj) -> raises"
  :summary "Same as raise (Motoi does not implement continuations)."
  :provenance "R7RS §6.11; added 2026-07-18 finalization"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(guard (c (#t 'caught)) (raise-continuable 'oops))" :note "caught.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(guard (c ((eq? c 'signal) 'handled)) (raise-continuable 'signal))" :note "handled.")
  )
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A programmer following R7RS wants to distinguish 'this is a recoverable, resumable warning' from 'this is an error the local code cannot continue past.' In systems with real continuations (Racket, MIT-Scheme), raise-continuable lets the handler return a value to the raiser. In Motoi, raise-continuable exists for R7RS compatibility but behaves identically to raise — the compat surface is honored so R7RS code loads, but the resume-value feature is absent. The audit question is whether the operator picked the R7RS-compat verb intentionally or by accident."
     :program "(define caught\n  (guard (c ((symbol? c) c))\n    (raise-continuable 'warning)))\n(display caught) (newline)\n(display (eq? caught 'warning)) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1-3 raise a warning as a continuable condition and catch it. Line 4 shows the caught value. Line 5 verifies the round trip. Motoi treats this identically to raise; the R7RS resume semantics is not present."
     :meta "Why raise-continuable and not raise: R7RS-compat only. If a programmer expects to write `(k v)` in the handler to resume, they need to know Motoi does not implement that.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is R7RS-compat scaffolding. See engineering docs on non-support of continuations."
     :math "raise-continuable is intended as a non-erroring signal in R7RS; in Motoi it collapses to raise."
     :cs "The CS pattern is a compat-mode alias. Related: R7RS conformance."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A conformance alias: preserve a name from a specification even when the underlying capability is absent, so code written to the spec loads and runs."
     :rungs ((:domain "exception (R7RS-compat)" :code "(raise-continuable v)")
             (:domain "abandoned kitchen station" :code "(request-eggs-benedict) ; server accepts, then serves omelet")
             (:domain "polyfilled DOM API" :code "if (!Array.prototype.at) { ... }"))
     :explanation "In Motoi, raise-continuable is an alias for raise — the spec name is preserved. In a restaurant, a menu item may be honored with a substitute. In web browsers, missing APIs are polyfilled to preserve the name. All three cases share the shape of 'preserve the interface even when the behavior differs.'"
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever backward-compatibility or spec-conformance requires the name to exist even without full behavior. Document the difference loudly.")
    (:eng "Log when a raise-continuable is caught — it should always behave like raise in Motoi, and that expectation should be visible."
     :math "The verb is treated as raise; no continuation-passing semantics."
     :cs "The CS analog is a compat shim or polyfill."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "raise-continuable behaves identically to raise in Motoi: (guard ((eq? c v) 'handled) (raise-continuable v)) equals (guard ((eq? c v) 'handled) (raise v))."
     :program "(define r1 (guard (c ((eq? c 'x) 'handled)) (raise 'x)))\n(define r2 (guard (c ((eq? c 'x) 'handled)) (raise-continuable 'x)))\n(display (eq? r1 r2)) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ v. raise-continuable(v) ≡ raise(v) in Motoi"
     :meta "The pattern is behavioral equivalence: two verbs with the same runtime effect. The R7RS distinction is honored in name only. Runtime holds this equivalence by dispatching both verbs to the same handler."
    :eng "Smoke test: the two catches return equal values."
     :math "Behavioral equivalence on the runtime state."
     :cs "The CS pattern is alias / compat shim."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "raise-continuable behaves like raise in Motoi."
     :composition "(define (assert-and-continue cond msg)\n  (if cond\n    'ok\n    (guard (c (#t 'noted-but-continued))\n      (raise-continuable msg))))\n(display (assert-and-continue #t 'skipped)) (newline)\n(display (assert-and-continue #f 'noted)) (newline)"
     :emergent "soft-assert — a warning that logs but does not halt, useful for non-critical invariant checks"
     :meta "The composition chains raise-continuable with a permissive guard that catches everything and continues. What emerges is the soft-assert family: check a condition, note if it fails, but proceed. The same family appears as warnings, deprecation notices, telemetry-only assertions. In book-of-code ch14 this is a warning-shape sibling of hard error."
     :eng "Soft asserts let you observe invariant drift in production without failing loudly."
     :math "The composition is a monadic tell (in the Writer monad sense): observe without changing the value."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is soft-assert or warning. Familiar analogs: Python's warnings module, JavaScript console.warn.")))

(verb :name "error-object-message" :library "exception" :tier "core" :kind "pure" :signature "(error-object-message e) -> string"
  :summary "Extract the message string."
  :provenance "R7RS §6.11; added 2026-07-18 finalization"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(guard (c ((error-object? c) (error-object-message c))) (error \"boom\"))" :note "\"boom\".")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(guard (c ((error-object? c) (error-object-message c))) (error \"bad-arg\" 42))" :note "\"bad-arg\".")
  )
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "An incident-review system needs to extract a human-readable message from every caught error for the log line. The error object has structured payload but the log line needs a single string. The verb error-object-message pulls just the message; error-object-irritants pulls the extra values. The audit question: did the operator log the right piece?"
     :program "(define (log-error e)\n  (list 'error (error-object-message e)))\n(define caught\n  (guard (c ((error-object? c) (log-error c)))\n    (error \"invalid input\" 42)))\n(display caught) (newline)\n(display (equal? (cadr caught) \"invalid input\")) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines a log helper that extracts message only. Line 3-4 catch an error and log it. Lines 5-6 verify the message was recovered. The audit trail: raise → catch → extract message → log."
     :meta "Why error-object-message and not error-object-irritants: the log line wants human-readable text, not values. Different audit needs use different extractors.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is the message extractor. Log the string separately from the irritants — mixing them corrupts machine-parseable logs."
     :math "The verb is a projection from an error-object to its message string. Nullary domain restriction: undefined on non-error objects."
     :cs "The CS pattern is a structured accessor. Related: Exception.getMessage in Java, error.message in JavaScript."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A structured-payload accessor: pull a specific named field out of a heterogeneous record."
     :rungs ((:domain "exception (message)" :code "(error-object-message e)")
             (:domain "kitchen order slip" :code "(order-item-name slip)")
             (:domain "record projection" :code "π_message(record)"))
     :explanation "In Scheme, the verb accesses the message field of an error object. On a kitchen ticket, an accessor pulls the item name. In relational algebra, a projection pulls one column. All three cases share the shape of 'extract one named field from a compound record.'"
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever compound records need field-by-field access.")
    (:eng "Log fields separately, not concatenated. Machine-parseable logs are easier to grep."
     :math "The verb is a projection function π_message: ErrorObj → String."
     :cs "The CS analog is a field accessor / record projection."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "error-object-message returns the string that was passed to error, unchanged."
     :program "(define caught (guard (c ((error-object? c) (error-object-message c))) (error \"exact message\" 1 2)))\n(display (equal? caught \"exact message\")) (newline)\n(define caught2 (guard (c ((error-object? c) (error-object-message c))) (error \"another\" 42)))\n(display (equal? caught2 \"another\")) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ msg. error-object-message(error(msg, ...)) = msg"
     :meta "The pattern is field-round-trip: the message you passed to error is the message you get back. See book-of-code ch14. What falsifies: any run where the returned message differs from the raised one. Runtime holds the invariant."
    :eng "Smoke test: raise a known message, catch, and compare."
     :math "The verb is a left-inverse to the message-injection of error."
     :cs "The CS pattern is structured-accessor round trip."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "error-object-message extracts the message from an error object."
     :composition "(define (format-error-report e)\n  (list 'msg (error-object-message e)\n        'irritants (error-object-irritants e)\n        'timestamp 'now))\n(define report\n  (guard (c ((error-object? c) (format-error-report c)))\n    (error \"bad-key\" 'k1 'k2)))\n(display report) (newline)"
     :emergent "structured error report — a record combining message, irritants, and metadata for downstream consumption by dashboards or alerting"
     :meta "The composition chains error-object-message with error-object-irritants and additional metadata. What emerges is the structured-error-report family: a machine-parseable object that carries all diagnostic context. The same family appears as Sentry error records, as OpenTelemetry span-events, as structured logging JSON. In book-of-code ch14 this is one of the foundational SRE-facing shapes."
     :eng "Structured error reports let dashboards group and alert intelligently. Log the report as JSON in production."
     :math "The composition is a record constructor: combine several accessors into a labeled tuple."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is structured error record. Familiar analogs: Sentry Event, OpenTelemetry ExceptionEvent, syslog CEE.")))

(verb :name "error-object-irritants" :library "exception" :tier "core" :kind "pure" :signature "(error-object-irritants e) -> list"
  :summary "Extract the irritant list."
  :provenance "R7RS §6.11; added 2026-07-18 finalization"
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(guard (c ((error-object? c) (error-object-irritants c))) (error \"boom\" 1 2 3))" :note "(1 2 3) — the irritants.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(guard (c ((error-object? c) (length (error-object-irritants c)))) (error \"x\" 'a 'b))" :note "2.")
  )
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "An incident-review system needs the machine-parseable values that accompanied an error — the offending arguments, the key that wasn't found, the numbers that were out of range. error-object-message gives the human-facing string; error-object-irritants gives the machine payload. Choosing the right verb is what turns an error into actionable diagnostics."
     :program "(define (extract-irritants e)\n  (error-object-irritants e))\n(define bad-keys\n  (guard (c ((error-object? c) (extract-irritants c)))\n    (error \"missing-keys\" 'user-id 'session-id)))\n(display bad-keys) (newline)\n(display (equal? bad-keys (list 'user-id 'session-id))) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines the irritant extractor. Lines 2-4 catch an error and pull the irritants. Lines 5-6 verify. The audit trail: raise with irritants → catch → extract → downstream inspection."
     :meta "Why error-object-irritants and not error-object-message: the diagnostic report needs values, not strings. Different extractors serve different audit lanes.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is the irritant extractor. Log the irritant list separately from the message for structured diagnostics."
     :math "The verb is a projection from an error-object to its list of extra values."
     :cs "The CS pattern is a structured accessor for extra payload."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A structured-payload accessor for the variadic-tail data: pull the list of extra values that accompanied a message."
     :rungs ((:domain "exception (irritants)" :code "(error-object-irritants e)")
             (:domain "log line with variadic values" :code "(logger.error 'bad-req 'ip ip 'reason reason)")
             (:domain "record with a list-of-values field" :code "π_values(record)"))
     :explanation "In Scheme, irritants are the tail of arguments to error. In structured logging, the variadic key/value pairs are the same shape. In relational record theory, one column can be a list-of-values. All three cases share the shape of 'variable-length extra data.'"
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever a message needs to carry a variable-length list of associated values.")
    (:eng "Log irritants separately with a name so downstream parsing knows which value is which."
     :math "The verb is a projection function π_irritants: ErrorObj → List."
     :cs "The CS analog is a variadic accessor. Related: Python's args tuple in Exception."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "error-object-irritants returns the list of values that were passed as trailing arguments to error, in order."
     :program "(define caught (guard (c ((error-object? c) (error-object-irritants c))) (error \"m\" 'a 'b 'c)))\n(display (equal? caught (list 'a 'b 'c))) (newline)\n(define caught2 (guard (c ((error-object? c) (error-object-irritants c))) (error \"m\")))\n(display (null? caught2)) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ msg args. error-object-irritants(error(msg, ...args)) = args (empty when no extras)"
     :meta "The pattern is variadic-round-trip: the irritant list matches the tail arguments. See book-of-code ch14. What falsifies: any run where the irritant list disagrees with the passed extras."
    :eng "Smoke test: raise with known extras, catch, compare."
     :math "The verb is a left-inverse of the irritant-injection: irritants(error(m, ...v)) = v."
     :cs "The CS pattern is variadic-accessor round trip."))

    (:base "error-object-irritants extracts the list of extras from an error."

     :emergent "error grouping — a bucketed count of errors keyed by the first irritant, useful for dashboards showing 'top errors by category'"
     :meta "The composition chains error-object-irritants with a grouping fold. What emerges is the error-grouping family: rather than logging each error line-by-line, group by a key and count. The same family appears as Sentry's issue grouping, as syslog rate-limiting, as Prometheus error counters. In book-of-code ch14 this is one of the foundational SRE-analytics shapes."

;;; 1 verbs in this library. Read chapter 00-intro.slat first.

;;;
;;; ─── THE ROW RULES (summary — full doctrine in 00-intro.slat) ───
;;;
;;; Every verb in this chapter has 5 rows. Each row does ONE job. Row
;;; contamination unbalances training data. If you author or edit a verb,
;;; STAY IN LANE.
;;;
;;;   Row 1 (HOW · Composition) — the verb written well; 1/3/5 module ladder
;;;   Row 2 (WHEN · Audit)      — operator's problem + this-verb-not-a-sibling
;;;   Row 3 (WHERE ELSE · Dim)  — same shape in 3 substrates (verb/metaphor/math)
;;;   Row 4 (WHY · Proof)       — claim + runnable test + ∀-invariant
;;;   Row 5 (WITH WHAT ELSE)    — chained verbs → named emergent pattern
;;;
;;; Every row carries the three-discipline lens: :eng · :math · :cs.
;;; No philosopher names in entries (they live in 00-intro.slat).
;;; Real Motoi domains only (no card/*, shop/*, cine/*, flower/*).
;;; Every code block RUNS through ./bin/motoi (or is marked :runs "spec-only").
;;;
;;; Introspection is a first-class chapter — see 00b-introspection.slat.

;;; Before folding, run: python3 scripts/compliance-check-runnable.py
;;;

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Library floor — 1 verbs.")

(chapter :number "27" :library "floor" :verb-count 1 :training-eligible #t)

;; ═══ 1 verbs in library floor ═══

(verb
  :name "floor/problem?"
  :library "floor"
  :kind "rd"
  :signature "(floor/problem? kind [ctx]) -> boolean"
  :summary "Check whether a given escalation kind represents an active problem in the floor system."
  :explanation "floor/problem? is a predicate that queries the escalation registry to determine if a particular kind (e.g., 'inventory-critical', 'shipping-delay') is currently flagged as a problem. It takes an optional context object; if omitted, it defaults to an empty context. Use this in conditional logic to branch on active floor problems: pause orders, trigger alerts, disable features, or redirect traffic."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(if (floor/problem? 'inventory-critical) (escalate 'halt-orders null))" :note "Check if inventory is critical; if so, halt order processing.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (check-fleet-health ctx) (let ((has-delay (floor/problem? 'shipping-delay ctx)) (has-fraud (floor/problem? 'fraud-alert ctx))) (cond ((and has-delay has-fraud) (escalate 'fleet-lockdown null)) ((or has-delay has-fraud) (next 'monitor ctx)))))" :note "Check multiple problem conditions and escalate differently based on which are active.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (filter pred xs)\n  (let loop ((xs xs) (acc '()))\n    (cond ((null? xs) (reverse acc))\n          ((pred (car xs)) (loop (cdr xs) (cons (car xs) acc)))\n          (else (loop (cdr xs) acc)))))\n(define (tick-health-check ctx) (let* ((probs (list 'inventory-critical 'shipping-delay 'fraud-alert)) (active (filter (lambda (kind) (floor/problem? kind ctx)) probs))) (if (> (length active) 1) (next 'multi-problem (ctx-set 'problems active ctx)) (next 'idle ctx))))" :note "Collect all active problems, escalate if more than one is true.")
  )
  :caveats ("The predicate reflects the state at the instant of the call; conditions may change immediately after." "If the kind is not registered in the escalation system, the verb returns false (not an error)." "Context is optional and typically empty unless your escalation system is state-aware; verify with your floor setup.")
  :drawbacks ("No information about severity, duration, or root cause; you only get a boolean." "Requires that the floor escalation system has been initialized; if not, all checks return false.")
  :usecases ("Order workflow: check for critical inventory before accepting new orders" "Health monitor: periodically poll for floor problems and trigger dashboards or alerts" "Feature gate: disable risky operations (e.g., bulk price changes) during fraud alerts" "Graceful degradation: route customer traffic away from a region with active shipping delays")
  :related ("escalate" "floor/problem?" "app-list" "ctx-get")
  :learn (:concept "Querying system state to make decisions in control flow." :prerequisites ("if" "cond") :progression "Master floor/problem? to understand escalation conditions, then learn escalate to trigger floor state changes, and finally design multi-problem monitoring strategies.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "The kiosk's order pipeline is REFUSING new orders and the operator does not know why. Somewhere in the guard chain a floor/problem? check returned true. The operator needs a defensive PROBE that walks all known problem kinds and reports each kind's current state, so the audit lane can point at exactly which condition is standing between an order and the till."
     :program "(define (probe-floor kinds)\n  (map (lambda (k) (list 'kind k 'active? (floor/problem? k))) kinds))\n(define (report kinds)\n  (for-each (lambda (row) (display row) (newline))\n            (probe-floor kinds)))\n(report '(inventory-critical shipping-delay fraud-alert payment-outage))"
     :explanation "The probe takes a list of the problem kinds the operator cares about and maps each one to a stamped row: the kind name, the field label 'active?', and the boolean floor/problem? returned. The report function prints one row per kind, in order. The auditor scans the printed output; any row whose active? is #t is a candidate cause of the block. The operator sees, at a glance, exactly which floor condition is asserted and can go address that specific condition or override its check. If ALL rows are #f, the block is not coming from the floor system and the operator looks upstream. Because floor/problem? is a pure read (no mutation), running the probe is safe to do during the incident and can be re-run at any time."
     :meta "floor/problem? is the honest verb here because it is the DEFENSIVE READ for the floor system: a boolean predicate, no side effect, no state mutation, returns immediately. A sibling like escalate would MUTATE the floor state — the opposite of what a probe wants — and would risk changing the very condition you were trying to observe. app-list would enumerate installed floor conditions but wouldn't say which are active. ctx-get reads the ctx object, not the floor registry. The audit needs the boolean predicate that names the CURRENT state without disturbing it, and that verb is floor/problem?.")
    (:eng "The operator's dashboard shows one line per probed kind; a single #t line explains a refused order. Escalate this probe to a tick-based watchdog and the operator has a live view of the floor condition without touching production state."
     :math "floor/problem? is a total predicate on the domain of problem kinds; the probe pattern is (map predicate kinds), which is the pointwise application of a predicate to a finite set — a standard characterization of a filterable set."
     :cs "The verb is a RD-kind (pure read) with a boolean return; the probe pattern uses it as a leaf inside a list-mapper. Because reads are safe to compose, the probe can be nested inside any larger diagnostic without risk of altering the system under observation."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape here is CURRENT-STATE-PREDICATE: a boolean read against a registered condition, answering 'is this condition asserted RIGHT NOW?' without touching or mutating the condition itself. That shape is not specific to floor problems."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "floor/status-check" :code "(floor/problem? 'shipping-delay)")
       (:domain "os/flag-probe" :code "(define (flag-set? name)\n  (member name '(read-only debug-mode maintenance)))\n(if (flag-set? 'debug-mode) 'yes 'no)")
       (:domain "logic/characteristic-function" :code "(define S '(2 4 6 8))\n(define (in-S? x) (if (member x S) #t #f))\n(list (in-S? 4) (in-S? 5))"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 is the verb in its own domain: is shipping-delay currently asserted in the floor system. Rung 2 is a metaphor from OS process flags: is the debug-mode flag currently set on this process; a boolean read against a small named set of flags. Rung 3 is math: the characteristic function of a set S is the function that returns true for members and false for non-members; the same shape as flag-set? and floor/problem?. All three answer the question 'is this named thing in the currently-asserted set?' with a plain boolean, with no effect on the set."
     :meta "The shape transfers because the underlying job in every case is the same: index a boolean-valued sparse map by a symbolic key. floor/problem? indexes the floor problem set; flag-set? indexes the process flag set; the characteristic function indexes any subset of any universe. Once you see that all three are the same query against different substrates, the mental model is portable — including the correctness discipline (the read is pure) and the failure mode (an unregistered key returns false, not error).")
    (:eng "Operators recognize this shape everywhere — feature flags, health probes, config gates. The audit rule is the same across all three: cache the result inside a decision only if you'll accept a stale answer; otherwise re-read at the decision point."
     :math "The pattern is the characteristic function χ_S : U → {0,1} of a subset S of a universe U; here U is the set of registered problem-kinds and S ⊆ U is the currently-active subset. book-of-math ch06 (algebra sets and relations) covers characteristic functions and their algebra."
     :cs "The pattern name is PREDICATE-OVER-A-REGISTERED-SET, the same shape as a feature-flag check in a running service. book-of-code ch08 (memory latches and flip-flops) describes the state-carrying substrate underneath; floor/problem? is the pure READ side of that substrate."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "floor/problem? is a PURE READ: for a given (kind, ctx) pair, and with no intervening escalate or floor mutation, the predicate returns the same value on every call. This is what makes the probe pattern above sound: mapping the predicate across a list gives a snapshot, and the snapshot is coherent because no probe call changes what the next probe call sees."
     :program "(define r1 (floor/problem? 'inventory-critical))\n(define r2 (floor/problem? 'inventory-critical))\n(display (equal? r1 r2))\n(newline)\n(define kinds '(inventory-critical shipping-delay fraud-alert))\n(define snap-a (map (lambda (k) (floor/problem? k)) kinds))\n(define snap-b (map (lambda (k) (floor/problem? k)) kinds))\n(display (equal? snap-a snap-b))\n(newline)"
     :invariant "∀ k. (no-mutation-between) → floor/problem?(k) = floor/problem?(k). ∀ K ⊆ Kinds. snapshot(K) = snapshot(K) under quiescence."
     :meta "The engineering consequence is that a diagnostic tool can call floor/problem? as many times as it likes during an incident without altering the very state under investigation — the read is Heisenberg-safe. In CS terms this is REFERENTIAL TRANSPARENCY for the predicate: no hidden state read (like wall-clock time), no hidden side effect (like a subscribe). What falsifies the claim is one kind whose floor/problem? call returns different booleans across two immediate consecutive calls with no escalate or mutate between; one such witness proves the predicate is reading a moving target (perhaps wall-clock-dependent) and every audit that relied on the read is invalidated. See book-of-code ch10 (state machines) for the theory of state-quiescence, and book-of-math ch06 for the algebra of characteristic functions.")
    (:eng "For SRE, a pure boolean read means the predicate can be sampled at any frequency without back-pressure on the floor system; the watchdog polling the predicate does not contribute to the incident it is observing. Any regression that makes the predicate write (e.g., log a hit counter) breaks the audit's assumption."
     :math "The claim is idempotence in the trivial sense of a pure function: repeated evaluation on the same input yields the same output. Combined with the map-preserves-purity property, snapshots are stable."
     :cs "The pattern is PURE PREDICATE OVER MUTABLE STATE: the state may change, but a read does not perturb it. Read/write separation is the CS discipline behind this; book-of-code ch08 (memory latches) covers the storage half, and floor/problem? is the read half."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "floor/problem? is a boolean predicate telling whether a given problem kind is currently active."
     :composition "(define (order-gate action-fn kinds)\n  (let ((tripped (filter (lambda (k) (floor/problem? k)) kinds)))\n    (if (null? tripped)\n        (action-fn)\n        (list 'blocked 'by tripped))))\n(define (place-order) 'order-placed)\n(display (order-gate place-order '(inventory-critical fraud-alert)))\n(newline)"
     :emergent "A CIRCUIT-BREAKER emerges from floor/problem? chained with a filter and a conditional call: given a list of problem kinds and an action, the gate runs the action only if none of the kinds is asserted, otherwise it returns a blocked-by report naming the tripped kinds.      :meta "The family here is the CIRCUIT BREAKER, the same family as the electrical breaker in the wall, as the circuit-breaker in a microservice mesh (Hystrix, resilience4j), as a rate-limit gate in a public API. book-of-composition ch16 (composing games) discusses gates at the game-state level; book-of-code ch08 (memory latches) and ch10 (state machines) describe the underlying state that a breaker reads. Adding more kinds to the gate's list widens the breaker; adding a rate window turns it into a throttle.")
    (:eng "The emergent breaker gives the operator a single, testable point where all floor conditions are consulted; failing kinds appear as the 'blocked by' payload so the on-call sees the specific cause without digging through the gate's implementation."
     :math "The chain is the composition (filter predicate kinds) then (null? tripped) then a two-arm conditional; the gate is total because filter is total and the conditional is total. Under the pure-predicate claim from Row 4, the gate's decision is a function of the current floor state alone."
     :cs "Circuit breaker is a canonical resilience pattern in distributed systems literature; here it is realized locally as a pure-predicate filter plus a conditional. book-of-composition ch16 (composing games) covers gates; the CS pattern is the same shape at a smaller scale.")))

;; ═══ 32 verbs in library game ═══

(verb
  :name "game/frame"
  :library "game"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(game/frame id) -> n"
  :summary "Return the frame counter of a specific game instance."
  :explanation "In Motoi Scheme, multiple independent games may be running in the same world via different cards or scenes. game/frame retrieves the frame count for a given game id. Unlike frame, which returns the global studio frame counter, game/frame is scoped to a single game instance. Use it when you need per-game timing (e.g. a card running its own logic independent of the world frame)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((g (big-bang 'my-game)))\n  (on-frame (lambda () (display (game/frame g)))))" :note "Create a game and periodically read its frame counter.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define g (big-bang 'scene-game))\n(on-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (when (game/running? g)\n      (let ((f (game/frame g)))\n        (when (= (modulo f 15) 0)\n          (display (list ':game-beat f)))))))" :note "Log the game frame only if the game is running and on a 15-frame boundary.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define games (list (big-bang 'game-a) (big-bang 'game-b)))\n(on-frame\n  (lambda ()\n    (for-each\n      (lambda (g)\n        (when (game/running? g)\n          (let ((f (game/frame g)))\n            (display (list (game/state g) f)))))\n      games)))" :note "Poll multiple game instances and log each one's frame and state, filtering out stopped games.")
  )
  :caveats ("game/frame requires a valid game id; passing an invalid id will escalate." "game/frame is only meaningful while the game is running; after game/stop, the frame value is stale." "Each game instance has its own independent frame counter; they do not sync with the studio frame or each other.")
  :drawbacks ("No direct way to reset a game's frame counter; create a new game instance if you need a fresh frame clock." "game/frame is read-only; use game/step or the game's on-tick handler to advance time.")
  :usecases ("Synchronize per-game logic to that game's timeline (e.g. a card's internal clock)." "Implement frame-rate-independent timing by comparing game/frame values across frames." "Debug multi-game scenarios by logging each game's frame independently.")
  :related ("big-bang" "game/running?" "game/state" "game/step" "frame" "on-frame")
  :learn (:concept "Scoped frame counters: each game world has its own time, independent of other games or the studio." :prerequisites ("big-bang" "frame") :progression "After querying game/frame, learn game/state and game/step to inspect and advance the game's full state.")
  :row-2-audit ((:problem "Two independent games run in parallel; the operator needs to log each one's own tick counter, not the shared studio frame."
                 :program "(define ga (big-bang 'a))\n(define gb (big-bang 'b))\n(list (game/frame ga) (game/frame gb))"
                 :explanation "Create two games. Query each one's frame counter. Independent numbers, one per world."
                 :meta "Reach for game/frame over the global frame primitive when per-game time matters; the global frame would give both games the same number.")
                (:eng "Per-game frames let the operator disambiguate logs of concurrent worlds."
                 :math "frame : id → ℕ, injective on ids."
                 :cs "Registry lookup by id; O(1)."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "per-instance counter scoped by id: same shape appears in games, in processes, in loggers with correlation ids"
                     :rungs ((:domain "game" :code "(let ((g (big-bang 'x))) (game/frame g))")
                             (:domain "process" :code "(define (proc-id pid) (list 'process pid 'ticks 0))\n(proc-id 42)")
                             (:domain "logger" :code "(define (with-cid cid msg) (list cid msg))\n(with-cid 'req-1 'saved)"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 reads per-game frame. Rung 2 tags per-process ticks. Rung 3 tags per-request logs. Each scopes a counter to an identifier."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'per-key counter' is one primitive across systems.")
                    (:eng "OS pids, request tracing, and per-game frames all instantiate 'scope by id'."
                     :math "counter : id × ℕ → ℕ."
                     :cs "Same registry pattern."))
  :row-4-proof ((:claim "game/frame is monotone: successive queries give non-decreasing values."
                 :program "(define g (big-bang 'x))\n(define f1 (game/frame g))\n(game/step g)\n(define f2 (game/frame g))\n(>= f2 f1)"
                 :invariant "∀ id t1<t2. frame(id, t1) ≤ frame(id, t2)"
                 :meta "Monotonicity is the defining property of a step counter. Falsified by any observed decrease. See book-of-code on monotone counters.")
                (:eng "Regression: frame never regresses across game/step."
                 :math "Non-decreasing sequence."
                 :cs "One assertion."))
  :row-5-emergence ((:base "game/frame reads the per-game tick counter."
                     :composition "(define g (big-bang 'x))\n(define (heartbeat g interval)\n  (when (= (modulo (game/frame g) interval) 0)\n    (list 'beat (game/frame g))))\n(heartbeat g 10)"
                     :emergent "A per-game heartbeat: chaining game/frame with modulo yields periodic-tick signals."
                     :meta "This is the same family as a cron/interval scheduler. Cross-ref book-of-composition on periodic triggers.")
                    (:eng "Heartbeats are how UIs animate spinners without global state."
                     :math "frame mod k = 0 defines a subsequence."
                     :cs "Composition = read + mod + guard.")))

(verb
  :name "game/grundy"
  :library "game"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(game/grundy state-set moves-fn) -> nimber"
  :summary "Compute the Grundy number (nimber) of an impartial game via mex-recursion."
  :explanation "In combinatorial game theory, the Grundy number of a position is the minimum excludant (mex) of the Grundy numbers of all positions reachable in one move. game/grundy automates this recursive computation with memoization: you provide a set of starting states and a function that generates the next states from a given state, and game/grundy returns the nimber. The nimber encodes the winning strategy of the game: a position with nimber 0 is a losing (second-player) position; any other nimber is a winning (first-player) position. This is the core engine for solving games like Nim, Wythoff's game, or custom rulesets."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(game/grundy '(3 5 7) (lambda (state) (list (- state 1))))" :note "Compute the Grundy number of a position where you can subtract 1 from any state.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (game-moves state)\n  (let ((valid '()))\n    (for-each\n      (lambda (subtract)\n        (when (>= state subtract)\n          (set! valid (cons (- state subtract) valid))))\n      '(1 2 3))\n    valid))\n(let ((nimber (game/grundy '(10) game-moves)))\n  (display (if (= nimber 0) 'losing 'winning)))" :note "Define a moves function that generates all reachable states, then classify a position as winning or losing.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (multi-heap-moves heaps)\n  (fold-left\n    (lambda (results i)\n      (let ((h (list-ref heaps i)))\n        (fold-left\n          (lambda (acc remove)\n            (when (> h remove)\n              (let ((new-heaps (map (lambda (j) (if (= j i) (- h remove) (list-ref heaps j)))\n                                     (range 0 (length heaps)))))\n                (cons new-heaps acc))))\n          results\n          '(1 2))))\n    '()\n    (range 0 (length heaps))))\n(game/grundy '((3 5 7)) multi-heap-moves)" :note "Solve a multi-heap game (like Nim) by recursively removing from each heap; the Grundy number predicts the winner.")
  )
  :caveats ("If the game tree is infinite or very large, memoization may exhaust the fuel budget and return 'fuel-budget instead of a nimber; check the result." "moves-fn must be deterministic; if the same state generates different successors on different calls, the memoization cache will give wrong answers." "The starting state-set should be a singleton list for most use cases; passing multiple states returns the mex of their nimbers (useful for parallel games)." "Nimbers are bitwise XOR-closed; combining independent games is done via game/nim-sum, not addition.")
  :drawbacks ("No way to extract the actual winning move; game/grundy only returns the nimber. Use game/ttt-best-move for tic-tac-toe or roll your own minimax for other games." "The memoization cache is global and not easily cleared; redefining moves-fn will not invalidate old cache entries (use for testing only)." "State representation matters: if two logically identical states have different representation, they will be cached separately, wasting memory.")
  :usecases ("Solve impartial games (both players have the same moves) by computing the winner from any position." "Analyze multi-heap games (Nim, Wythoff, etc.) without hardcoded lookup tables." "Build a game-playing AI that always makes optimal moves in a small game tree.")
  :related ("game/mex" "game/nim-sum" "game/nim-outcome" "game/ttt-best-move" "game/surreal")
  :learn (:concept "Grundy numbers: a numeric encoding of optimal play in impartial games. Compute via mex-recursion over all reachable states." :prerequisites ("game/mex" "lambda" "fold-left") :progression "After computing Grundy numbers, learn game/nim-outcome to apply the theory to Nim, and game/surreal for partisan (asymmetric) games.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A teacher needs to decide whether a custom subtraction game is a first-player win. What computes the answer for any move set?"
                 :program "(define moves (lambda (n) (filter (lambda (x) (>= x 0)) (map (lambda (k) (- n k)) '(1 2 3)))))\n(define g (game/grundy '(10) moves))\n(if (= g 0) 'second-player-wins 'first-player-wins)"
                 :explanation "Define the move-generator (subtract 1, 2, or 3 from the current heap). Compute the Grundy number from starting pile 10. Zero means the mover loses; non-zero, wins."
                 :meta "Reach for game/grundy over hand-rolled minimax when the game is impartial; nimbers collapse the tree to a scalar.")
                (:eng "Log the nimber; a change over game versions signals rule drift."
                 :math "G(s) = mex{G(s') : s' ∈ moves(s)}."
                 :cs "Memoized recursion; may hit fuel budget."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "recursive collapse to a fixed point via mex: same shape appears in games, in graph coloring, in constraint propagation"
                     :rungs ((:domain "game" :code "(game/grundy '(3) (lambda (n) (if (> n 0) (list (- n 1)) '())))")
                             (:domain "coloring" :code "(define (min-free-color used)\n  (let loop ((c 0)) (if (memv c used) (loop (+ c 1)) c)))\n(min-free-color '(0 1 3))")
                             (:domain "propagation" :code "(define (fixed-point f x) (let loop ((cur x)) (let ((nxt (f cur))) (if (equal? nxt cur) cur (loop nxt)))))\n(fixed-point (lambda (s) (map (lambda (x) (min x 3)) s)) '(5 2 4))"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 finds a game's nimber via mex-recursion. Rung 2 assigns the smallest free color. Rung 3 iterates to a fixed point. All three fold a graph of dependencies into a scalar or stable configuration."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'recursive collapse via mex/argmin' is one primitive.")
                    (:eng "Constraint solvers, game analyzers, and graph colorers share this pattern."
                     :math "Fixed-point of mex operator."
                     :cs "Memoization key; same solver kernel."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:claim "Two positions with the same Grundy number are equivalent under sum: their nim-sum is 0."
                 :program "(define a (game/grundy '(3) (lambda (n) (if (> n 0) (list (- n 1)) '()))))\n(define b (game/grundy '(3) (lambda (n) (if (> n 0) (list (- n 1)) '()))))\n(= (game/nim-sum (list a b)) 0)"
                 :invariant "∀ s. G(s) ⊕ G(s) = 0"
                 :meta "Self-XOR annihilation is the definition of nim-sum. Falsified by any nonzero result. See book-of-math on XOR.")
                (:eng "Regression: pair of identical games XOR to 0."
                 :math "a ⊕ a = 0."
                 :cs "One assertion."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:base "game/grundy returns the nimber of a game position."
                     :composition "(define moves (lambda (n) (filter positive? (map (lambda (k) (- n k)) '(1 2 3)))))\n(define positive? (lambda (x) (> x 0)))\n(define games '(5 8 11))\n(define nims (map (lambda (start) (game/grundy (list start) moves)) games))\n(fold-left (lambda (acc n) (game/nim-sum (list acc n))) 0 nims)"
                     :emergent "A multi-component solver: chaining game/grundy over independent games and combining with nim-sum yields the overall game value."
                     :meta "This is the same family as decomposing a big problem into independent sub-problems and XOR-combining. Cross-ref book-of-composition on component-wise solvers.")
                    (:eng "Complex tabletop games with independent parts use this decomposition."
                     :math "Sum-of-games: G(A + B) = G(A) ⊕ G(B)."
                     :cs "Map + reduce with XOR.")))

(verb
  :name "game/mex"
  :library "game"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(game/mex numbers-list) -> n"
  :summary "Return the minimum excludant (mex): the smallest non-negative integer not in the list."
  :explanation "The mex of a set of non-negative integers is the smallest natural number that is absent from the set. For example, the mex of (0 1 3) is 2; the mex of (1 2 3) is 0. In game theory, mex is the core operation for computing Grundy numbers: the nimber of a position is the mex of the nimbers of all positions reachable in one move. game/mex directly computes this; use it to implement game solvers or to reason about the structure of game trees."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(game/mex '(0 1 2))" :note "The smallest integer not in the list 0, 1, 2 is 3.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (nimber-of-position successors)\n  (game/mex (map nimber-of-position successors)))\n(nimber-of-position '((0) (1) (2)))" :note "Use mex to compute Grundy numbers recursively: the nimber is the mex of successors' nimbers.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (analyze-game-state state moves-fn)\n  (let ((successors (moves-fn state)))\n    (let ((successor-nimbers (map (lambda (s) (analyze-game-state s moves-fn)) successors)))\n      (game/mex successor-nimbers))))\n(analyze-game-state 'start (lambda (s) (list (list s 1) (list s 2))))" :note "Recursive game solver: compute the Grundy number of any state by mex-ing the nimbers of all successors (foundation for game/grundy).")
  )
  :caveats ("game/mex expects a list of non-negative integers; passing negative numbers, non-integers, or non-numeric values will produce unexpected results." "An empty list has mex 0 (since 0 is the smallest non-negative integer and is absent from the empty set)." "The list may be in any order; game/mex does not assume sorting.")
  :drawbacks ("O(n) scan for each call; if you need to compute mex many times, caching or bulk operations may be faster." "No built-in way to compute multiple mex queries on the same list; you must call game/mex once per query.")
  :usecases ("Compute Grundy numbers for impartial games by mex-ing successor nimbers." "Check whether a set of heap sizes (in Nim) is a losing position (nimber 0) via game/nim-sum." "Verify game-theoretic properties: positions with mex 0 are second-player wins.")
  :related ("game/grundy" "game/nim-sum" "game/nim-outcome" "list" "map")
  :learn (:concept "Mex (minimum excludant): the fundamental operation in Grundy-number arithmetic. Every position's nimber is the mex of its successors' nimbers." :prerequisites ("list" "map") :progression "Use game/mex in game/grundy; compose with game/nim-sum to analyze multi-component games.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A recursive solver needs the smallest non-negative integer absent from a set of successor nimbers."
                 :program "(define succs '(0 1 3 4))\n(game/mex succs)"
                 :explanation "Given the successors' nimbers, mex returns 2 — the smallest missing non-negative integer. This is the current node's Grundy number."
                 :meta "Reach for mex, not min or max; mex captures 'first gap in the coverage' which is what game-theoretic value assignment requires.")
                (:eng "Log the mex; a mex of 0 means the current position is losing."
                 :math "mex(S) = min(ℕ \\ S)."
                 :cs "O(n) scan; return first missing."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "smallest-absent-token in a set: same shape appears in game theory, in slot allocation, in generation of unique ids"
                     :rungs ((:domain "game" :code "(game/mex '(0 1 2 4))")
                             (:domain "slot-alloc" :code "(define (next-free used)\n  (let loop ((i 0)) (if (memv i used) (loop (+ i 1)) i)))\n(next-free '(0 1 3))")
                             (:domain "unique-id" :code "(define (next-id issued)\n  (let loop ((i 0)) (if (memv i issued) (loop (+ i 1)) i)))\n(next-id '(0 2))"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 finds the game-theoretic mex. Rung 2 allocates the next free slot. Rung 3 assigns the next unique id. All three scan a set for the smallest gap."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'smallest absent non-negative integer' is a substrate-neutral primitive.")

(verb
  :name "game/nim-sum"
  :library "game"

  :summary "Return the nim-sum (XOR) of a list of heap sizes, which is the Grundy value of a Nim position."

If nim-sum is 0, the position is a losing (second-player) win; otherwise it is a winning (first-player) win. game/nim-sum computes this XOR directly. In fact, nim-sum is the same as the Grundy number for Nim: it is the minimum excludant (mex) of all positions reachable in one move. Use game/nim-sum to reason about Nim, to find winning moves (reduce a heap so nim-sum becomes 0), or to compare Nim to other games."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(game/nim-sum '(3 5 6))" :note "Compute 3 ⊕ 5 ⊕ 6 = 0 (the heaps sum to a losing position).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (is-losing-position heaps)\n  (= (game/nim-sum heaps) 0))\n(display (is-losing-position '(3 5 6)))\n(display (is-losing-position '(1 2 3)))" :note "Test whether a position is a second-player win (nim-sum 0) or first-player win (nim-sum non-zero).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (bitwise-xor a b) (let loop ((a a) (b b) (out 0) (bit 1)) (if (and (= a 0) (= b 0)) out (loop (quotient a 2) (quotient b 2) (+ out (* bit (modulo (+ a b) 2))) (* bit 2)))))\n(define (fold-left f init xs)\n  (let loop ((xs xs) (acc init))\n    (if (null? xs) acc (loop (cdr xs) (f acc (car xs))))))\n(define (find-winning-moves heaps)\n  (let ((target (game/nim-sum heaps)))\n    (fold-left\n      (lambda (moves i)\n        (let ((h (list-ref heaps i))\n              (new-h (bitwise-xor (list-ref heaps i) target)))\n          (if (< new-h h)\n            (cons (list ':heap i ':remove (- h new-h)) moves)\n            moves)))\n      '()\n      (range 0 (length heaps)))))\n(find-winning-moves '(3 5 6))" :note "If nim-sum is non-zero, find all moves that reduce it to 0 by XORing each heap with the nim-sum.")
  )
  :caveats ("game/nim-sum is XOR, not addition; 3 + 5 ≠ 3 ⊕ 5. XOR is commutative and self-inverse: a ⊕ a = 0." "An empty heap list has nim-sum 0 (the empty XOR is the identity, 0)." "Heap sizes must be non-negative integers; passing negative or non-numeric values is undefined.")
  :drawbacks ("game/nim-sum only computes the value, not the strategy; you must use it as a building block (e.g., to find winning moves)." "Nim-sum is specific to Nim; other games use Grundy numbers or surreal numbers, which require game/grundy or game/surreal.")

(- a da) (- b db))) (list (- a da) (- b db)) (loop2 (+ db 1)))))) (if (game/wythoff-p? (- a da) b) (list (- a da) b) (loop (+ da 1)))))) (safe-move 5 8)" :note "Find a safe move from (a,b) by trying all successors and picking one that reaches a P-position")

(verb
  :name "geom/->degrees"
  :library "geom"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(geom/->degrees radians) -> float"
  :summary "Converts an angle from radians to degrees."
  :explanation "Angles in mathematical computation are often stored in radians (a pure ratio of arc length to radius). User-facing geometry and graphics sometimes use degrees (360 per circle). `geom/->degrees` multiplies the radian input by 180/π to convert to degrees. The result is a floating-point value, so conversion introduces device-level rounding; use it only when communicating with graphics or I/O."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(geom/->degrees const/pi)\n;; => 180.0" :note "π radians is 180 degrees; a half circle")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(geom/->degrees (/ const/pi 2))\n;; => 90.0" :note "π/2 radians is 90 degrees; a quarter circle")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (compass-bearing radians)\n  (let ((deg (geom/->degrees radians)))\n    (modulo deg 360.0)))\n(compass-bearing (/ const/pi 4))\n;; => 45.0" :note "Convert math radians to compass degrees (0–360); useful for graphics or UI display")
  )
  :caveats ("The result is a device-float, subject to floating-point rounding." "Negative radians produce negative degrees (no wrapping applied)." "Very large radian values may lose precision when converted to float.")
  :drawbacks ("One-way conversion; converting back with `geom/->radians` may not recover the original due to rounding." "Not suitable for high-precision scientific computation; exact rationals should be used if precision is critical.")
  :usecases ("Displaying angles in a user interface (protractor, compass, rotation widget)." "Converting math library output (often in radians) to graphics API angles (often in degrees)." "Angle arithmetic for UI animation (rotate a card by N degrees).")
  :related ("geom/->radians" "geom/sin" "geom/cos" "geom/tan" "geom/angle-between" "const/pi")
  :learn (:concept "Radians and degrees are two units for the same angular quantity; 180° = π rad. Conversion is a scalar multiplication." :prerequisites ("const/pi") :progression "Learn geom/->degrees and geom/->radians together for unit conversion, then geom/sin, geom/cos for trigonometry.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A UI needs to display a rotation angle in degrees but the game stores it in radians." :program "(define (display-angle rad) (string-append (number->string (geom/->degrees rad)) \" deg\"))
(display-angle (/ math/pi 2))" :explanation "Wrap the radian value in geom/->degrees so the UI layer sees degrees. Concat with a unit label. The math stays in radians internally; only the display crosses the boundary." :meta "geom/->degrees is the correct verb because degrees and radians are the same physical angle in different units. Using (* rad 57.2958) would work numerically but hides intent and the magic number is easy to typo. The named verb makes the conversion auditable.")
    (:eng "Log the operator's stated problem and the code path chosen; audits catch cases where a sibling verb would silently succeed with wrong answers." :math "The audit lens fixes the mathematical function class (unary, binary, inverse, aggregate) and gates on argument-domain checks stated in the caveats." :cs "Row 2 emphasizes single-call, single-effect: pure functions may be replaced by their memoized result; audits check that no impure sibling was substituted."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Same shape: unit conversion — a value stays semantically identical but changes the numeric label used to talk about it."
     :rungs (

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (paint-path points)\n  (for-each (lambda (p)\n    (let ((x (car p)) (y (cdr p)))\n      (grid/dot x y '#0099ff' 0.6)))\n    points))\n(paint-path '((5 . 10) (6 . 12) (8 . 13)))" :note "Iterate a list of (x . y) pairs and dot each; paints a visual breadcrumb trail.")

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let loop ((i 0))\n  (when (< i 8)\n    (grid/dot i i 'blue)\n    (loop (+ i 1))))" :note "Draw a blue diagonal from the top-left corner.")

;;;
;;; Every verb in this chapter has 5 rows. Each row does ONE job. Row
;;; contamination unbalances training data. If you author or edit a verb,
;;; STAY IN LANE.
;;;
;;;   Row 1 (HOW · Composition) — the verb written well; 1/3/5 module ladder
;;;   Row 2 (WHEN · Audit)      — operator's problem + this-verb-not-a-sibling
;;;   Row 3 (WHERE ELSE · Dim)  — same shape in 3 substrates (verb/metaphor/math)
;;;   Row 4 (WHY · Proof)       — claim + runnable test + ∀-invariant
;;;   Row 5 (WITH WHAT ELSE)    — chained verbs → named emergent pattern
