(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Library num — 2 verbs.")

(chapter :number "45" :library "num" :verb-count 2 :training-eligible #t)

;; ═══ 2 verbs in library num ═══

(verb
  :name "num/nintegrate-2d"
  :library "num"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(num/nintegrate-2d f x-bounds y-bounds [opts]) -> number"
  :summary "Compute a double integral over a rectangular region using Simpson's rule."
  :explanation "Evaluates the definite double integral ∫∫f(x,y) dx dy over a rectangle [x_min, x_max] × [y_min, y_max] using adaptive Simpson's rule. The function f is a Scheme closure that takes two arguments (x and y) and returns a number. This is a deterministic numerical method within a single device; results are reproducible across runs but subject to floating-point precision and the configured fuel budget. Over-cap (too many subdivisions) raises a 'fuel-budget error."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(num/nintegrate-2d (lambda (x y) 1) (list 0 1) (list 0 1))" :note "Integrates constant 1 over unit square → result ≈ 1 (area of square).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(num/nintegrate-2d\n  (lambda (x y) (+ x y))\n  (list 0 2)\n  (list 0 2))" :note "Integrates (x+y) over [0,2]×[0,2] → ∫∫(x+y)dxdy = 8.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (volume-under-paraboloid)\n  (num/nintegrate-2d\n    (lambda (x y) (- 4 (+ (* x x) (* y y))))\n    (list -1 1)\n    (list -1 1)))\n(volume-under-paraboloid)" :note "Computes volume under z = 4 - (x² + y²) over [-1,1]² as a named procedure; useful for caching or composition.")
  )
  :caveats ("The integrand f must be a procedure taking exactly two arguments (x, y)." "Bounds are given as lists [min, max]; reversed or inverted bounds will produce unexpected negative result." "Accuracy depends on function smoothness and fuel budget; pathological or highly oscillatory integrands may require tuning." "Over-cap (too fine a subdivision to fit in fuel budget) escalates; catch with (if (pair? result) ...).")
  :drawbacks ("Simpson's rule is O(h⁴) accurate but slow for very high precision; consider analytical solution if available." "Not suitable for unbounded integrals; must use change of variables to map to finite rectangle." "Discontinuous or singular integrands near boundaries may lose accuracy; pre-filter or split domain." "No adaptive mesh refinement per subregion; uniform Simpson may oversample flat regions.")
  :usecases ("Computing area or volume in physics/engineering simulations." "Evaluating probability distributions (integrating density functions)." "Curriculum demonstrations of numerical analysis." "Validating analytical integral solutions.")
  :related ("num/nintegrate-3d" "calc/line-integral" "calc/surface-integral")
  :learn (:concept "Deterministic numerical integration as a meta-verb; respecting fuel budgets." :prerequisites ("understanding of double integrals (calculus)" "familiarity with lambda expressions and closures") :progression "Learn num/nintegrate-3d for three dimensions, then calc/* for line and surface integrals.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "An engineer needs to compute the total mass of a flat plate whose density varies across a rectangular region — the mass is the integral of density over area. Analytical integration is possible for the toy case but the real density function comes from a lookup table and has no closed form. Symbolic integration (calc/integrate) will refuse; adaptive one-dimensional integration doesn't fit a two-variable domain. num/nintegrate-2d is the honest answer: give it the density function as a Scheme closure over (x,y), give it x and y bounds, and it returns a number with bounded error. The audit question is whether the operator picked the right integration verb for the shape of the domain."
     :program "(define (density x y) (+ 1 (* 0.5 x y)))\n(define mass (num/nintegrate-2d density (list 0 2) (list 0 3)))\n(display (list 'mass mass)) (newline)\n(display (< 0 mass)) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines the density function — a closure of two arguments returning a nonnegative number. Line 2 integrates the density over the rectangle [0,2] × [0,3]. The runtime evaluates the closure at a grid of points, applies Simpson's rule in both dimensions, and returns the numerical estimate. Line 3 prints the result; line 4 confirms the mass is strictly positive, which is a sanity check that follows from the density being nonnegative and the rectangle having nonzero area. The audit trail: closure defined, verb called with three arguments, result inspected against a physical constraint."
     :meta "Why num/nintegrate-2d and not a sibling: num/nintegrate-3d would work if the density were a function of three variables, but here the plate is flat and z-integration is nonsense. calc/line-integral is for one-dimensional path integrals — the domain shape is a curve, not a region. A hand-rolled Riemann sum would work but has no fuel-budget guard and no adaptive stopping. num/nintegrate-2d is honest: signature says (function-of-2, x-bounds, y-bounds), the runtime says Simpson's rule, and the result reports either a number or a fuel-budget failure. If num/nintegrate-3d had been used with a z-bound of [0,1], the result would be numerically the same but the signature would lie about the physical domain.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is bounded-cost numerical integration. The engineering rule: pick the integrator whose signature matches the domain shape (1D → adaptive quadrature, 2D → 2D Simpson, curve → line integral). Log the fuel budget alongside the result so an incident-review reader can tell whether the answer was truncated. See SRE Manual on 'name-your-numerical-method' — the shape of the integral must match the shape of the verb."
     :math "The claim is ∫∫_R f(x,y) dA where R is the rectangle [x0,x1]×[y0,y1]. Simpson's rule approximates this with error O(h^4) in the subdivision spacing h. The verb is a decision procedure for the definite integral over R, up to bounded error."
     :cs "The CS pattern is a numerical quadrature verb: a black-box function of a numerical recipe. Cost is polynomial in mesh fineness, output is a single number, side-effects are none (aside from possibly exhausting fuel). Contrast with symbolic integration (calc/*) which returns an exact expression when possible."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A summation over a bounded region: reduce a value-density defined at every point of a rectangle to a single scalar by aggregating over the whole domain. The shape is 'accumulate a function over a region.'"
     :rungs ((:domain "num (2D area integral)" :code "(num/nintegrate-2d f x-bnd y-bnd)")
             (:domain "grid of tiles" :code "(sum (map (lambda (tile) (score tile)) tiles-in-region))")
             (:domain "measure-theoretic integration" :code "∫_R f dμ ; the Lebesgue integral of f over region R"))
     :explanation "In the num domain a continuous density is aggregated over a rectangular region using Simpson's rule. On a discrete tile grid the same shape appears: sum a per-tile score over every tile inside a region, and you get the region-total. In measure theory the integral ∫_R f dμ is the abstraction that both cases specialize — a value-density is aggregated over the domain against a measure that says how much each infinitesimal piece counts. The three cases differ in whether the domain is continuous or discrete, but the shape — 'aggregate a function over a domain into a scalar' — is the same."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in each case there is a domain, a function of position on that domain, and a way to weight infinitesimal (or discrete) pieces. Any place you can name those three, the shape fits. The trick is picking the correct weighting: Simpson's rule for smooth functions on rectangles, a plain sum for uniform tiles, Lebesgue measure for pathological continuous cases.")
    (:eng "Engineering rule: match the integration method to the smoothness class of the integrand. Smooth on a rectangle → Simpson. Discontinuous or spiky → domain decomposition, then Simpson on smooth pieces. See book-of-motion ch09 for how the same choice appears in physics simulation."
     :math "The abstract object is a measure integral ∫_R f dμ. Riemann-Simpson is the special case where R is a box and μ is Lebesgue. Discrete summation is the special case where μ is counting measure on a lattice."
     :cs "The CS analog is a reduction over a rectangular domain. Related: NumPy's `np.sum(f(X, Y))` over a mesh grid, SQL's `SUM ... GROUP BY (x_bucket, y_bucket)`, MapReduce's cell-by-cell aggregate. All are 'accumulate a value over a region.'"))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "num/nintegrate-2d is linear in the integrand and additive in the domain: integrating a scalar multiple of f is that scalar times the integral of f, and integrating over a subdivided rectangle equals the sum of integrals over the pieces (up to numerical error)."
     :program "(define (f x y) (+ (* x x) (* y y)))\n(define c 3.5)\n(define whole (num/nintegrate-2d f (list 0 2) (list 0 2)))\n(define scaled (num/nintegrate-2d (lambda (x y) (* c (f x y))) (list 0 2) (list 0 2)))\n(display (< (abs (- scaled (* c whole))) 1e-6)) (newline)\n(define left (num/nintegrate-2d f (list 0 1) (list 0 2)))\n(define right (num/nintegrate-2d f (list 1 2) (list 0 2)))\n(display (< (abs (- whole (+ left right))) 1e-6)) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ c ∈ ℝ, f. ∫∫ cf = c·∫∫ f ; ∀ R = R₁ ∪ R₂ (disjoint). ∫∫_R f = ∫∫_{R₁} f + ∫∫_{R₂} f"
     :meta "The pattern is linearity plus additivity — the defining structural properties of an integral. See book-of-math ch11 (definite integral) for the mathematical grounding. What falsifies: any observed run where doubling the integrand does not double the result, or splitting the domain in half and summing does not recover the whole integral (both up to numerical tolerance). The runtime holds the invariant because Simpson's rule inherits linearity from the underlying weighted sum. Numerical tolerance means the check uses 1e-6, not exact equality."
     :eng "The engineering payoff is that you can compute an integral by decomposing the domain into pieces (e.g., to fit within a fuel budget) and summing the results, and you know the sum equals what a single call would have returned."
     :math "Linearity: ∫(αf + βg) = α∫f + β∫g. Domain additivity: ∫_A f + ∫_B f = ∫_{A∪B} f when A∩B has measure zero. These are the fundamental properties of the definite integral."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is a linear reduction. Related: parallel MapReduce works because linear reductions commute with domain partition; associative folds work for the same reason."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "num/nintegrate-2d aggregates a 2D density function over a rectangle."
     :composition "(define (density x y) (+ 1 (* 0.1 x y)))\n(define (mass-of-strip x0 x1)\n  (num/nintegrate-2d density (list x0 x1) (list 0 2)))\n(define strips (list (mass-of-strip 0 1) (mass-of-strip 1 2) (mass-of-strip 2 3)))\n(define total (apply + strips))\n(display strips) (newline)\n(display total) (newline)"
     :emergent "domain decomposition — a strategy where a large integral is split into subproblems, each cheap and independent, then recombined"
     :meta "The composition chains num/nintegrate-2d inside a per-strip helper and folds the results. What emerges is the domain-decomposition family: rather than integrating the whole thing at once, the caller partitions the domain, integrates each piece, and sums. The same family appears as tiled rendering in graphics, as MapReduce over spatial bins, as finite-element method (FEM) in engineering, as space-filling-curve traversal for parallel work. In book-of-composition ch14 this pattern is called out as one of the load-bearing shapes for making expensive computations fit in a fuel budget. What makes it a decomposition and not just a loop is that each PIECE could run independently — the composition trades sequential monoliths for parallelizable atoms."
     :eng "The operational win of decomposition is that fuel exhaustion in one strip does not lose the whole computation — you still have the strips that completed. Log per-strip cost and outcome so a re-run can retry only the failed pieces."
     :math "The composition is a monoid-fold under domain-additivity: (⊕ integrals-of-pieces) = integral-of-whole. The identity element is ∫_∅ f = 0."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is domain decomposition (or 'divide and conquer for numerical work'). Familiar analogs: MPI's domain decomposition, PyTorch's chunked matmul, PostgreSQL's parallel partition scans. Motoi's per-strip integration occupies the same slot for numerical quadrature.")))

(verb
  :name "num/nintegrate-3d"
  :library "num"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(num/nintegrate-3d f x-bounds y-bounds z-bounds [opts]) -> number"
  :summary "Compute a triple integral over a rectangular box using Simpson's rule."
  :explanation "Evaluates the definite triple integral ∫∫∫f(x,y,z) dx dy dz over a rectangular box [x_min, x_max] × [y_min, y_max] × [z_min, z_max] using tensor Simpson's rule. The function f is a Scheme closure taking three arguments (x, y, z) and returning a number. Like num/nintegrate-2d, this is deterministic within a single device and subject to fuel-budget limits; exhausting the budget escalates an error."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(num/nintegrate-3d (lambda (x y z) 1) (list 0 1) (list 0 1) (list 0 1))" :note "Integrates constant 1 over unit cube → result ≈ 1 (volume of cube).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(num/nintegrate-3d\n  (lambda (x y z) (+ x y z))\n  (list 0 2)\n  (list 0 2)\n  (list 0 2))" :note "Integrates (x+y+z) over [0,2]³ → ∫∫∫(x+y+z)dxdydz = 24.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (moment-of-inertia-z density)\n  (num/nintegrate-3d\n    (lambda (x y z) (* density (+ (* x x) (* y y))))\n    (list -1 1)\n    (list -1 1)\n    (list 0 2)))\n(moment-of-inertia-z 8.0)" :note "Computes rotational inertia about z-axis for a uniform box; density parameter allows reuse.")
  )
  :caveats ("The integrand f must be a procedure taking exactly three arguments (x, y, z)." "Bounds are given as lists [min, max]; reversed or inverted bounds will produce unexpected negative result." "Three-dimensional Simpson's rule is much slower than 2D; fuel budget will be tighter." "Over-cap escalates; catch result with (if (pair? result) ...).")
  :drawbacks ("O(h⁴) accuracy but prohibitively slow for very high precision or fine geometry." "Not suitable for unbounded integrals; must transform to finite box." "No adaptive mesh in subregions; uniform Simpson may waste fuel on flat zones." "Computational cost grows as O(n³) in mesh fineness; exponential in dimension makes higher-D integrals impractical.")
  :usecases ("Computing mass, center of mass, or moment of inertia in 3D rigid bodies." "Evaluating probability integrals in multivariate distributions." "Validating 3D simulations and CAD-derived volumes." "Curriculum work in multivariable calculus and physics.")
  :related ("num/nintegrate-2d" "calc/line-integral" "calc/surface-integral")
  :learn (:concept "Extension of 2D Simpson's rule to three dimensions; fuel cost and accuracy trade-off." :prerequisites ("understanding of triple integrals (multivariable calculus)" "familiarity with num/nintegrate-2d" "understanding of fuel budgets") :progression "Use for 3D physics/geometry; consider Monte Carlo integration or analytical methods for very high dimension.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "A physics engineer needs to compute the total mass of a solid block whose density varies through the interior. The block sits at rest on a table; density comes from a scan and has no closed form. calc/integrate refuses (no symbolic form); num/nintegrate-2d cannot represent depth. The engineer needs an integrator whose signature matches the domain shape: three variables of position (x,y,z), three sets of bounds, and a volumetric aggregation. The audit question is whether the engineer picked the verb whose shape matches the physical claim (mass = integral of density over volume)."
     :program "(define (density x y z) (+ 1.0 (* 0.1 (- z 1))))\n(define mass\n  (num/nintegrate-3d density (list 0 2) (list 0 3) (list 0 2)))\n(display (list 'mass mass)) (newline)\n(display (> mass 0)) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines density as a closure of three arguments returning a positive real (density with a small depth gradient). Lines 2-3 call the 3D quadrature verb with the density closure and three axis-aligned bounds. The runtime evaluates the closure on a 3D tensor grid, applies Simpson's rule in each direction, and returns the numerical estimate. Line 4 prints the result and line 5 confirms positivity — the sanity check that density > 0 and volume > 0 implies mass > 0. The audit trail: closure defined, verb called with four arguments (function + three bounds), result inspected against a physical invariant."
     :meta "Why num/nintegrate-3d and not a sibling: num/nintegrate-2d cannot express the third dimension — the depth integral would be missing and the reported mass would understate the physical mass by a factor of the depth. calc/line-integral is for one-dimensional curve integrals — the domain is a curve, not a box. Monte Carlo integration is possible for very high dimensions but is stochastic; the audit would need to include an error-bar analysis. num/nintegrate-3d is the honest, deterministic verb for the shape 'aggregate a function over a rectangular box.' Using num/nintegrate-2d and multiplying by depth would give a lower bound for uniform depth density but would be wrong for the varying density here.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is 3D bounded-cost numerical integration. The engineering rule: pick the integration verb whose dimensional shape matches the physical shape of the domain. Log the verb chosen, the bounds, and the fuel budget consumed so a report reader can distinguish 'answer within budget' from 'answer truncated.'"
     :math "The claim is ∫∫∫_R f(x,y,z) dV where R is the box [x0,x1]×[y0,y1]×[z0,z1]. Tensor Simpson approximates this with error O(h^4) per axis. Cost scales as O(N^3) where N is per-axis subdivision."
     :cs "The CS pattern is 3D numerical quadrature. Cost is polynomial in mesh fineness per axis but multiplicative across axes, so 3D is much more expensive than 2D. Fuel budgets exist to bound the multiplicative blowup."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A summation over a bounded 3D region: reduce a value-density defined at every point of a box to a single scalar by aggregating over the volume. The shape is 'aggregate a function over a volume.'"
     :rungs ((:domain "num (3D volume integral)" :code "(num/nintegrate-3d f x-bnd y-bnd z-bnd)")
             (:domain "voxel grid" :code "(sum (map (lambda (voxel) (density voxel)) voxels-in-box))")
             (:domain "measure theory in 3D" :code "∫_R f dμ ; the Lebesgue integral of f over a 3D box R"))
     :explanation "In the num domain a continuous density is aggregated over a rectangular box using tensor Simpson. On a voxel grid the same shape appears: sum a per-voxel density over every voxel inside the region, and you get the region-total. In measure theory the integral ∫_R f dμ where μ is 3D Lebesgue measure is the abstraction both cases specialize. The three cases differ in discretization strategy, but the shape — 'aggregate a function over a volumetric domain' — is the same."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in each case there is a 3D domain, a function of position on that domain, and a way to weight infinitesimal (or discrete) pieces. Any place you can name those three, the shape fits: MRI density integration, geological reservoir volume calculations, particle-in-cell simulation cell aggregation.")
    (:eng "Engineering rule: 3D integrals are dimensionally more expensive than 2D; budget accordingly. Log the mesh fineness used so a report reader can reason about the numerical error bar."
     :math "The abstract object is a 3D measure integral ∫_R f dμ. Tensor Simpson is the special case where R is a box and μ is Lebesgue in three dimensions."
     :cs "The CS analog is a 3D reduction. Related: NumPy's `np.sum(f(X, Y, Z))` over a mesh grid, SQL's `SUM ... GROUP BY (x_bucket, y_bucket, z_bucket)`, MapReduce with 3D spatial keys."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "num/nintegrate-3d is linear in the integrand and additive in the domain: integrating a scalar multiple of f is that scalar times the integral of f, and splitting a box into two boxes and summing equals the whole-box integral (up to numerical error)."
     :program "(define (f x y z) (+ (* x x) (* y y) (* z z)))\n(define c 2.5)\n(define whole (num/nintegrate-3d f (list 0 2) (list 0 2) (list 0 2)))\n(define scaled (num/nintegrate-3d (lambda (x y z) (* c (f x y z))) (list 0 2) (list 0 2) (list 0 2)))\n(display (< (abs (- scaled (* c whole))) 1e-4)) (newline)\n(define left (num/nintegrate-3d f (list 0 1) (list 0 2) (list 0 2)))\n(define right (num/nintegrate-3d f (list 1 2) (list 0 2) (list 0 2)))\n(display (< (abs (- whole (+ left right))) 1e-4)) (newline)"
     :invariant "∀ c ∈ ℝ, f. ∫∫∫ cf = c·∫∫∫ f ; ∀ R = R₁ ∪ R₂ (disjoint). ∫∫∫_R f = ∫∫∫_{R₁} f + ∫∫∫_{R₂} f"
     :meta "The pattern is linearity plus additivity — the same structural properties as any measure integral. See book-of-math ch11 for the definite-integral grounding. What falsifies: any observed run where doubling the integrand does not double the result, or splitting the box does not recover the whole integral (both up to numerical tolerance). The runtime holds the invariant because tensor Simpson inherits linearity from the underlying weighted sum. Tolerance is set at 1e-4 to reflect the coarser mesh implicit in 3D versus 2D at the same fuel budget.")
    (:eng "The engineering payoff is domain decomposition: a fuel-tight 3D integral can be computed by dividing the box into pieces that each fit the budget, and summing."
     :math "Linearity and additivity of the 3D Lebesgue integral. Both properties follow from the same axioms as in 2D."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is a 3D linear reduction. Related: parallel volumetric aggregation, tiled tensor operations."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "num/nintegrate-3d aggregates a 3D density function over a box."
     :composition "(define (density x y z) (+ 1.0 (* 0.05 (+ x y z))))\n(define (mass-of-slab z0 z1)\n  (num/nintegrate-3d density (list 0 2) (list 0 2) (list z0 z1)))\n(define slabs (list (mass-of-slab 0 1) (mass-of-slab 1 2) (mass-of-slab 2 3)))\n(define total (apply + slabs))\n(display slabs) (newline)\n(display total) (newline)"
     :emergent "layered aggregation — a strategy where a solid is analyzed as a stack of slabs each integrated independently, then summed"
     :meta "The composition chains num/nintegrate-3d inside a per-slab helper and folds the results. What emerges is the layered-aggregation family: analyze a 3D region as a stack of thin layers, each cheap and independent, then recombine. The same family appears as CT-scan slice reconstruction, as multi-layer PCB analysis, as pressure-per-layer atmospheric modeling. In book-of-composition ch14 this pattern is a sibling of domain decomposition, specialized to axis-aligned stacks. What makes it a layered aggregation rather than plain decomposition is that the SPLIT AXIS is chosen deliberately (usually the physical stacking axis) rather than arbitrarily."
     :eng "The operational win is that per-slab cost is bounded, so a memory-tight or fuel-tight run can stream results per slab rather than materializing a whole tensor grid."
     :math "The composition is a monoid-fold under domain additivity, specialized to a decomposition along one axis: ∫_R f = Σᵢ ∫_{R∩[zᵢ,zᵢ₊₁]} f."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is layered aggregation (or 'slab-wise reduction'). Familiar analogs: CT-scan reconstruction algorithms, streaming aggregation in database engines, per-layer feature computation in CNNs. Motoi's per-slab pattern occupies the same slot for 3D quadrature.")))

;; ═══ 2 verbs in library object ═══

(verb
  :name "object/fetch"
  :library "object"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(object/fetch [class: ...] [personality: ...] [at: ...] [scale: ...] [colour: ...]) -> 'ok | ['escalate code details]"
  :summary "Retrieve or instantiate an object from the scene, with optional personality and appearance parameters."
  :explanation "Fetches an object resource (likely a pre-defined character, prop, or entity) from the scene or asset library, optionally parameterized by personality vector, position, scale, and colour. Returns 'ok on success, or escalates with a structured error (code, reason, suggestion) if the object cannot be fetched or is not wired. This is a keyword-argument verb; all parameters are optional. Likely useful in imagination/scene-building workflows where you want to populate a scene with named objects on demand."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(object/fetch 'class: 'npc)" :note "Fetches an NPC object from the scene library with default appearance.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(object/fetch 'class: 'npc 'at: (list 10 20) 'scale: 2.0)" :note "Fetches NPC positioned at (10, 20) and scaled to 2× size.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (summon-companion charm wisdom-level)\n  (let ((personality (list charm 0.5 wisdom-level)))\n    (object/fetch 'class: 'companion 'personality: personality 'colour: 'gold)))\n(if (equal? (summon-companion 0.8 0.9) 'ok) (display \"companion ready\") (display \"fetch failed\"))" :note "Higher-order use: encapsulates object fetch with personality vector; checks result before continuing.")
  )
  :caveats ("If class is not registered or wired in the scene, returns escalate with 'not-wired status." "personality should be a list or vector of numeric traits; coercion to exact structure is undocumented." "at and colour parameters are validated but their exact formats are not documented; may require trial." "Success returns only 'ok, not the instantiated object; side effect is scene population.")
  :drawbacks ("No direct return of the spawned object ID; state must be queried separately via card-find-by-kind or card-list." "Requires scene to be pre-wired with object definitions; not suitable for dynamic asset loading." "Error details (reason, suggestion) are for debugging; not suitable for end-user error messages." "Keyword argument order is free but must use valid keys; typos silently become nil.")
  :usecases ("Populating an imagination scene with NPC characters on demand." "Spawning props or objects with custom personality traits (e.g., hostile/friendly)." "Narrative branching: conditionally fetch objects based on game state." "Testing: fetch objects to verify scene wiring and asset availability.")
  :related ("object/spawn" "scene/spawn-many" "scene/load" "card-find-by-kind" "card-list")
  :learn (:concept "Keyword-argument I/O verb for scene population; understanding escalation errors." :prerequisites ("understanding of keyword arguments in Motoi Scheme" "familiarity with escalate error pattern" "understanding of scene wiring and asset registration") :progression "Learn object/spawn to place a specific target; scene/load to pre-populate entire scenes.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A world-builder is prototyping and wants 'some NPC' at (30, 40) — any NPC. They do not have a concrete target ID yet; they only have a class in mind and a rough location. Committing to a specific ID up front is exactly what the prototype phase is trying to avoid."
     :program "(let ((r (object/fetch 'class: 'npc 'at: (list 30 40))))\n  (if (eq? r 'ok)\n    (display \"npc dropped in\")\n    (escalate 'fetch-failed r)))"
     :explanation "The verb accepts a class query rather than a concrete ID, chooses an appropriate object from the class, and drops it into the scene at the requested position. The return is 'ok on success or an escalation triple on failure. The prototype gets to move on with 'an npc is here' without ever naming a specific NPC prefab; the sceneship layer picks the concrete instance."
     :meta "object/spawn requires a concrete target ID and would have forced the world-builder to name a specific NPC prefab, which is the wrong shape for a prototype. scene/spawn-many is for batch stamping a known ID at many positions, not a class query. object/fetch is the query-by-class primitive; using either sibling forces the prototype phase to commit to an ID it does not yet want to pick.")
    (:eng "The audit lens is 'fetch returns 'ok, not an ID' — the operator does not get a handle to the spawned object and must query the scene separately if they need one; log-checking that a spawn happened requires reading the scene state, not the return value." :math "The verb is a class-indexed picker: fetch : Class → Instance, non-deterministic within the class; the operator receives a status, not the picked element." :cs "Non-deterministic constructor / factory-by-tag pattern; the same shape as 'give me any file from this directory' vs 'give me this specific file'."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Class-indexed acquisition: request 'one of these' rather than 'this specific one'."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "object"       :code "(object/fetch 'class: 'npc)")
       (:domain "worker-pool"  :code "(define (lease pool) (car pool))\n(lease '(worker-1 worker-2 worker-3))")
       (:domain "existential"  :code "(define (any-of xs pred) (cond ((null? xs) #f) ((pred (car xs)) (car xs)) (else (any-of (cdr xs) pred))))\n(any-of '(1 2 3 4) even?)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1: a scene is asked for an instance of a class rather than a specific object. Rung 2: a worker pool is asked to lease a worker, and the pool chooses any available one. Rung 3: an existential quantifier says 'there exists some x such that pred(x) holds'; the return is a witness, not a name the caller had to know. All three share the same shape — a request specifies a set, the substrate picks a member, and the picked member need not be named by the caller."
     :meta "The transfer works because 'class query' is really 'existential ask' — the caller does not know or care which instance answers, only that the set is non-empty and something in it works. Worker pools, DNS round-robin, and DHCP leases all use the shape; class-fetch is the same primitive in a scene substrate. Grounds in book-of-code ch 16 (cloud-llms-and-the-loop-that-closes) as the request-a-worker shape.")
     (:eng "The audit lens is 'the picked instance is not named in the return so the operator cannot log 'which one' from the call site' — every class-picker needs a companion introspection call if forensics is needed later." :math "Existential witness: ∃ x ∈ Class. spawn(x) holds; the substrate provides the witness but does not surface it in the return channel." :cs "Non-deterministic factory; classic pool-lease pattern where the caller has policy 'any member' and the pool has strategy 'pick something'."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "The picked instance carries the requested class: every successful fetch places an object whose class matches the query."
     :program "(define scene '())\n(define registry '((npc . (npc-warrior npc-scholar npc-child))\n                   (prop . (chair table lantern))))\n(define (fetch class-tag)\n  (let ((entries (assq class-tag registry)))\n    (if entries\n      (let ((pick (car (cdr entries))))\n        (set! scene (cons (list class-tag pick) scene))\n        'ok)\n      (escalate 'unknown-class class-tag))))\n(fetch 'npc)\n(fetch 'prop)\n(fetch 'npc)\n(define (every p xs) (cond ((null? xs) #t) ((p (car xs)) (every p (cdr xs))) (else #f)))\n(display (every (lambda (row) (assq (car row) registry)) scene))"
     :invariant "∀ class. fetch(class) succeeds ⇒ scene contains an object whose class = class  (soundness of the class-tag on the picked instance)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is soundness — the returned witness must actually satisfy the query. Falsified if a fetch for 'npc placed a chair — that would mean the picker is lying and the caller can no longer trust class as a contract. book-of-code ch 05 (logic-gates-in-scheme) grounds the every-predicate check; book-of-math ch-advanced-05 grounds the well-typed-picker shape.")
    (:eng "The engineering consequence is that a caller filtering the scene by class after a fetch will find at least one entry — 'I asked for an npc and I can find an npc' is the audit check that catches picker regressions." :math "The picker is a section of the class projection: pick : Class → Instance with class(pick(c)) = c." :cs "Well-typed factory; the type of the picked value is exactly the class-tag, and this is enforced structurally."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "object/fetch instantiates an object of a queried class at an optional position."
     :composition "(define (populate-market classes)\n  (for-each\n    (lambda (c)\n      (let ((r (object/fetch 'class: c 'at: (list (random-range 10 90)\n                                                   (random-range 10 90)))))\n        (if (not (eq? r 'ok))\n          (escalate 'populate-skip (list c r)))))\n    classes))\n(populate-market '(vendor customer guard child dog))\n(display (group/count 'npc))"
     :emergent "A crowd populator: a class list is walked, each class-fetch drops an instance at a random cell, and the aggregate scene has a distribution of NPC types matching the class list; together they are a distribution-generator, structurally the same as sampling from a categorical distribution."
     :meta "This is the population / sampler family — a class-tag list defines the distribution, and per-class fetch draws one sample per tag. Familiar analogs are Poisson process spawners in games, monte-carlo samplers in statistics, and the categorical sampler in a numpy simulation. The composition works because each fetch is a class-safe pick (Row 4) so the emergent distribution over the scene actually matches the intended distribution over classes. Grounds in book-of-math ch-advanced-07 (probability-random-processes) as the categorical-sampling shape.")
    (:eng "The audit lens: partial failure of any single class must not silently vanish; the escalate captures the class-and-reason so the operator can tell which classes were rejected by the picker and rebalance the target distribution." :math "The composition is a fold over the class list with each step being an existential-choice; the joint distribution factors as the product of per-tag choices when picks are independent." :cs "Categorical sampler; the same shape as populating a hash table from a list of keys with any-value-of-type semantics.")))

(verb
  :name "object/spawn"
  :library "object"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(object/spawn target [at: ...] [scale: ...] [colour: ...]) -> 'ok | ['escalate code details]"
  :summary "Instantiate a named object into the current scene at an optional position, scale, and colour."
  :explanation "Spawns a specific object (identified by the target symbol or identifier) into the scene with optional appearance and placement parameters. Like object/fetch, returns 'ok on success or escalates with code and details on failure (e.g., target not found or not wired). The key difference from object/fetch is that object/spawn takes a concrete target identifier rather than a class query. Useful for placing individual prefabs, enemies, or props in scene setup or dynamic game events."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(object/spawn 'sword-pickup)" :note "Spawns a named object 'sword-pickup' at default position.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(object/spawn 'enemy-guard 'at: (list 50 60) 'scale: 1.5)" :note "Spawns 'enemy-guard' at position (50, 60) scaled 1.5×.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (populate-treasure-room treasure-ids)\n  (for-each\n    (lambda (id)\n      (let ((result (object/spawn id 'at: (list (random-range 20 80) (random-range 20 80)))))\n        (if (pair? result) (escalate 'spawn-failed (list 'id id)))))\n    treasure-ids))\n(populate-treasure-room (list 'gold-coin 'gem 'potion))" :note "Batch spawn multiple objects at random positions; escalate if any fail.")
  )
  :caveats ("target must be a registered object ID; typos or non-existent IDs escalate with 'not-wired." "No return of instantiated object; must query separately via card-find-by-kind or card-list." "colour parameter format is undocumented; may be a symbol or hex string." "Spawning at out-of-bounds coordinates may cause undefined behavior.")
  :drawbacks ("Synchronous and blocking; no async spawn queue for many objects." "No way to configure post-spawn state (HP, team, etc.) directly; requires follow-up card-set! calls." "Error does not include spawned object ID on success; caller must track separately." "Repeated calls with same target/position may cause collision or overlap; no deduplication.")
  :usecases ("Procedural level generation: spawn enemies and props at computed positions." "Cutscene scripting: spawn characters or objects in narrative sequences." "Dynamic events: spawn rewards, hazards, or NPCs in response to player action." "Testing: verify that all registered objects can be instantiated.")
  :related ("object/fetch" "scene/spawn-many" "scene/load" "card-set!" "world/spawn")
  :learn (:concept "Direct object instantiation; keyword parameters for appearance; escalation error handling." :prerequisites ("understanding of keyword arguments" "understanding of escalate and error tuples" "familiarity with object/fetch") :progression "Learn scene/spawn-many for batch spawning; world/spawn for physics entities.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A level designer knows exactly which asset to place — 'enemy-guard-heavy' — and needs it at (50, 60) with 1.5× scale, not any old NPC. A class query would pick some enemy but the designer already picked; asking again would be redundant and possibly wrong."
     :program "(let ((r (object/spawn 'enemy-guard-heavy 'at: (list 50 60) 'scale: 1.5)))\n  (if (eq? r 'ok)\n    (display \"guard placed\")\n    (escalate 'guard-not-wired r)))"
     :explanation "The verb accepts a concrete target ID, positions the spawned instance at (50, 60), and scales it to 1.5×. 'ok on success; an escalation triple on failure. The designer's intent — 'this exact prefab, here, at this size' — is preserved end-to-end; no class picker gets a chance to substitute."
     :meta "object/fetch would let the scene pick some NPC and defeat the designer's specificity; scene/spawn-many is for stamping the same target at many positions, not a single-shot placement. object/spawn is the by-name primitive; picking either sibling either loses the designer's chosen ID or does the wrong quantity.")
    (:eng "The audit lens is 'the target ID appears verbatim in the escalation payload on failure' — if the ID is missing from the payload, the designer cannot tell whether they typoed the ID or the prefab is broken; the SRE check is grep-for-target-id in the log." :math "spawn is a total function from (target-id ∈ registry) × Position × Scale → SceneState, with domain guarded by the registry-membership predicate." :cs "Deterministic factory / by-name constructor; the same shape as new ClassName() in an OO language."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "By-name placement: request a specific member of a registry at a specific location."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "object"     :code "(object/spawn 'enemy-guard 'at: (list 50 60))")
       (:domain "process"    :code "(define (spawn cmd) (display cmd) 'started)\n(spawn \"nginx\")")
       (:domain "function-application" :code "(define (apply-at f x) (f x))\n(apply-at (lambda (v) (* 2 v)) 10)"))
     :explanation "Rung 1: a scene is asked to place a specifically-named prefab at a specific coordinate. Rung 2: a shell is asked to spawn a specifically-named binary; the OS looks up the name and executes it. Rung 3: a function is applied at a specific argument, producing a specific value. All three share the same shape — a named thing is invoked at a named place, and the substrate produces one concrete outcome; the caller specified everything and the substrate has no picking to do."
     :meta "The transfer works because 'by-name' is the total-function shape: given a legal name and its input, the output is uniquely determined. This is the shape of every deterministic factory and it stands in contrast to the class-picker of object/fetch. Grounds in book-of-code ch 12 (the-cpu-fetch-decode-execute) as the by-address fetch shape.")
     (:eng "Every by-name substrate has the same failure mode — 'name not in registry' — and the SRE fix is 'preflight the name against the registry before the call' so the substrate's error surface is bounded." :math "Function application at a specific argument; the caller lives in the domain and the substrate produces a value in the codomain, deterministically." :cs "Named-entity registry; the shape of DNS A-records, symbol tables, and prefab dictionaries."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "Spawn is location-honest: the spawned object's position equals the requested position."
     :program "(define scene '())\n(define registry '(chest coin gem))\n(define (spawn target at)\n  (if (memv target registry)\n    (begin (set! scene (cons (list target at) scene)) 'ok)\n    (list 'escalate 'not-wired target)))\n(spawn 'chest '(10 20))\n(spawn 'coin '(30 40))\n(define (every p xs) (cond ((null? xs) #t) ((p (car xs)) (every p (cdr xs))) (else #f)))\n(display (every (lambda (row) (equal? (cadr row) (cadr row))) scene)) (newline)\n(display (equal? (cadr (assq 'chest scene)) '(10 20)))"
     :invariant "∀ target position. spawn(target, position) = 'ok ⇒ scene contains (target, position)  (the position argument is preserved into the scene state)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is faithful storage — the caller's input coordinate must appear verbatim in the state, unaltered by the substrate. Falsified if the substrate rounded, clamped, or otherwise moved the coordinate silently — that would mean 'at:' is a suggestion, not a contract, and the designer's layout would drift under them. book-of-code ch 08 (memory-latches-and-flip-flops) grounds the faithful-write shape; book-of-math ch-advanced-04 grounds identity-preservation.")
    (:eng "The engineering consequence is that a designer inspecting the scene state after a spawn will see the same coordinate they typed; QA can round-trip a spec from JSON into the world without pixel drift." :math "The (target, position) argument tuple is preserved by the write — the substrate is a faithful embedding of the API call into the state graph." :cs "Faithful setter / write-through; the same shape as an in-memory store where set(k,v) then get(k) returns v exactly."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "object/spawn places a named target at a coordinate."
     :composition "(define (formation origin count spacing target)\n  (let loop ((i 0) (fails 0))\n    (if (>= i count)\n      (if (> fails 0) (escalate 'formation-partial fails) 'ok)\n      (let* ((x (+ (car origin) (* i spacing)))\n             (y (cadr origin))\n             (r (object/spawn target 'at: (list x y))))\n        (loop (+ i 1) (if (eq? r 'ok) fails (+ fails 1)))))))\n(formation '(20 40) 5 12 'grenadier)"
     :emergent "A formation composer: an origin and spacing plus a target ID plus a count generate a line-abreast of instances; together they are a placement pattern generator, structurally the same as a tile-map row-generator or a for-loop mail-merge that reuses a template."
     :meta "This is the templating / batch-instantiation family — one template, N derived placements, aggregated result. Familiar analogs are HTML template loops, DDL scripts that CREATE TABLE many times from a schema list, and Kubernetes replicasets that spawn N identical pods. The composition works because spawn is location-honest (Row 4) so the caller's arithmetic on x-positions arrives at the scene exactly — the formation looks like the math predicted. Grounds in book-of-sick-composition ch 4 (recursion) as the count-driven loop shape.")
    (:eng "Partial-failure aggregation is the SRE lens: the loop counts fails and returns an escalation summarizing them, so the operator learns that 3 of 5 spawns worked and can adjust the target inventory instead of chasing a single-shot error." :math "The composition is a fold over the position schedule; success count and fail count are the two accumulators tracked by the fold." :cs "Batch-with-partial-failure; the shape of every bulk-insert API that returns per-row status.")))

;; ═══ 35 verbs in library ops ═══

(verb
  :name "ops/absorbing-probs"
  :library "ops"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(ops/absorbing-probs transition-matrix) -> matrix"
  :summary "Absorption probabilities: for a Markov chain with transient and absorbing states, compute B = N·R, the probability of reaching each absorbing state from each transient state."
  :explanation "In a Markov chain, some states are absorbing (once entered, never left) and others are transient (temporary). This verb computes the absorption probabilities: a matrix B where B[i,j] = probability that starting from transient state i, the chain is absorbed into absorbing state j. The fundamental matrix N = (I − Q)⁻¹, where Q is the submatrix of transient-to-transient transitions; R is transient-to-absorbing. Essential for queuing, reliability, and stochastic optimization."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((P (matrix/make 3 3\n              (list 0.5 0.3 0.2\n                    0.0 1.0 0.0\n                    0.1 0.4 0.5))))\n  (ops/absorbing-probs P))" :note "State 1 is absorbing (all mass on self); compute absorption from states 0, 2")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (gambler-absorption p-win capital target)\n  (let ((P (list (list p-win (- 1 p-win) 0)\n                 (list 0 1 0)\n                 (list 0 0 1))))\n    (ops/absorbing-probs P)))\n(gambler-absorption 0.4 50 100)" :note "Gambler's ruin: states = current wealth; absorbing states = ruin or goal")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define my-chain 'my-chain)\n(define (multi-absorbing-analysis markov-chain start-state)\n  (let* ((B (ops/absorbing-probs markov-chain))\n         (absorb-dist (matrix/ref B start-state 0)))\n    (if (null? absorb-dist)\n      'no-absorbing-states\n      (list 'absorption-probability absorb-dist\n            'expected-steps (ops/absorbing-steps markov-chain)))))\n(multi-absorbing-analysis my-chain 0)" :note "Combine with absorbing-steps for full analysis: both probability and expected time to absorption")
  )
  :caveats ("Matrix must represent a valid stochastic (row-sum = 1) Markov chain." "If no absorbing states exist, result is undefined (may return error or matrix of zeros)." "Rows must sum to 1.0; rounding errors can accumulate in large matrices." "Transient states must be reachable from the starting distribution; unreachable states give degenerate rows.")
  :drawbacks ("Requires full transition matrix; dense representation is memory-heavy for large chains." "Computational cost O(t³) for t transient states; slow for t > 1000." "Requires inversion of (I − Q); numerical instability if Q is nearly singular." "Does not directly give expected hitting times; use ops/absorbing-steps for that.")
  :usecases ("Queuing theory: absorption into 'empty queue' or 'system failure' states." "Reliability: computing probability of eventual system failure from a healthy state." "Gambler's ruin and random walks: probability of reaching a target or losing all." "Inventory models: probability of stockout or overage after transient phase.")
  :related ("ops/absorbing-steps" "ops/markov" "ops/markov-step" "matrix/+" "matrix/*")
  :learn (:concept "Fundamental matrix and canonical form: decomposing a Markov chain into transient and absorbing structure." :prerequisites ("ops/markov" "matrix/*" "matrix/+") :progression "After absorption probabilities, pair with ops/absorbing-steps for expected hitting times; explore ops/pagerank for stationary distributions.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A gambler's-ruin analyst needs the probability that a random walk gets absorbed at each boundary."
                 :program "(define P '((0.5 0.5 0) (0 1 0) (0.5 0 0.5)))\n(ops/absorbing-probs P)"
                 :explanation "Compute B for the chain. Rows are transient states; columns are absorbing states. Entry B[i][j] is probability of ending at j starting from i."
                 :meta "Reach for absorbing-probs over hand-rolled simulation; the closed form is exact where simulation is only estimated.")
                (:eng "Log which rows sum to 1 (they must)."
                 :math "B = N R with N = (I - Q)⁻¹."
                 :cs "Matrix inversion; O(t³)."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "matrix inverse to sum over infinite paths: same shape in Markov chains, in DAG reachability, in game-tree evaluation"
                     :rungs ((:domain "ops" :code "(ops/absorbing-probs P)")
                             (:domain "reachability" :code "(define (reachable? g from to) #t)\n(reachable? '(g) 'a 'b)")
                             (:domain "game-eval" :code "(define (eval-tree t) 0)\n(eval-tree '(node))"))
                     :explanation "Rung 1 sums infinite absorption paths. Rung 2 checks reachability. Rung 3 evaluates a game tree. Each aggregates over an implicit infinite structure via a closed-form or fixed-point."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because 'infinite sum via closed form' is universal.")
                    (:eng "Reliability, network reach, and games share the shape."
                     :math "Σ Q^k = (I-Q)⁻¹."
                     :cs "Same linear-algebra kernel."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:claim "Rows of B sum to 1 (a transient state is absorbed with certainty)."

(verb
  :name "ops/bellman-ford"
  :library "ops"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(ops/bellman-ford graph source) -> (list distances predecessors)"
  :summary "Bellman–Ford shortest-path algorithm: find minimum-distance paths from a source to all nodes, even with negative edge weights (but no negative cycles)."
  :explanation "Unlike Dijkstra (which requires non-negative weights), Bellman–Ford works on graphs with negative edge weights. It relaxes all edges repeatedly: in each iteration, it updates distance[v] = min(distance[v], distance[u] + weight(u,v)) for every edge (u,v). If any distance changes after n−1 iterations (where n = node count), a negative cycle is detected and the function returns 'infeasible. Time: O(n·m) for n nodes and m edges."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((graph (list (list 0 1 4)\n                   (list 0 2 2)\n                   (list 1 2 -3)\n                   (list 2 1 1))))\n  (ops/bellman-ford graph 0))" :note "Returns shortest distances from node 0; handles negative edge 1→2")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define exchange-rates '())\n(define (arbitrage-detection rates)\n  (let* ((log-rates (map (lambda (r) (- (log r)))\n                         rates))\n         (result (ops/bellman-ford log-rates 0)))\n    (if (equal? result 'infeasible)\n      'profitable-cycle-exists\n      'no-arbitrage)))\n(arbitrage-detection exchange-rates)" :note "Convert currency exchange rates to log-costs; negative cycle = arbitrage opportunity")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define tasks '())\n(define edges 'edges)\n(define build-dag (lambda args (list \"build-dag\" args)))\n(define (critical-path-method tasks dependencies)\n  (let* ((neg-durations (map (lambda (t) (- (task-duration t)))\n                             tasks))\n         (graph (build-dag tasks dependencies neg-durations))\n         (result (ops/bellman-ford graph 'start)))\n    (if (equal? result 'infeasible)\n      'cycle-error\n      (let ((dists (car result)))\n        (map (lambda (task) (* -1 (assoc task dists))) tasks)))))\n(critical-path-method tasks edges)" :note "Negate task durations, find negative shortest paths = longest paths (critical path method)")
  )
  :caveats ("Returns 'infeasible if a negative cycle is reachable from the source." "Negative cycle detection is exact; if detected, distance/predecessor info is partial and unreliable." "For dense graphs (m ≈ n²), Bellman–Ford can be slower than repeated Dijkstra calls with potentials." "Weights must be real numbers; non-numeric edges produce errors.")
  :drawbacks ("O(n·m) time is slow for large graphs (n, m > 10k); Dijkstra is O((n + m) log n) for non-negative weights." "No pruning or early stopping if all nodes are finalized early." "Does not handle disconnected components well; returns ∞ for unreachable nodes." "If negative cycles are frequent, use a dedicated cycle-detection algorithm first.")
  :usecases ("Currency arbitrage detection: find negative cycles in exchange-rate graphs." "Critical path method: negate task durations and find 'longest paths'." "Shortest paths with time-dependent (negative) edge weights." "Constraint satisfaction: model constraints as weighted edges and check feasibility.")

                 :meta "Reach for bellman-ford over dijkstra when negative weights are possible; dijkstra silently gives wrong answers.")

  :signature "(ops/erlang-c intensity num-servers) -> queue-prob"
  :summary "Calculates the Erlang C formula: the probability an arriving customer must wait in queue."
  :explanation "Erlang C models an M/M/c queue (Poisson arrivals, exponential service, c identical servers) with unlimited queueing. Given traffic intensity (erlang) and number of servers, it returns the steady-state probability that an arriving customer finds all servers busy and must queue. (verb
  :name "ops/interior-point"
  :library "ops"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(ops/interior-point lp-instance) -> solution-or-escalation"
  :summary "Solves large-scale linear programming problems using interior-point methods via a backend solver."
  :explanation "Interior-point methods are algorithms that move through the interior of the feasible region (rather than along the boundary, as the simplex method does) to reach the optimal solution. They scale well to very large problems (thousands of variables and constraints) and often outperform simplex on real-world instances. This verb is BACKED, meaning it delegates to an external solver and may escalate special values like 'use-backend if the device solver is unavailable. Use ops/interior-point for large-scale LPs where ops/simplex would be slow or memory-constrained. For small problems, ops/simplex is usually faster."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((lp (ops/lp 'maximize\n                   (list 3 2 1)\n                   (list (list 1 1 1)\n                         (list 2 1 0))\n                   (list 10 8))))\n  (ops/interior-point lp))" :note "Builds a 2-constraint LP and solves it via interior-point; returns optimal value and decision variables")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((c (list 5 4 3 2 1))\n       (A (list (list 1 1 1 1 1)\n                (list 2 1 0 1 0)\n                (list 0 1 2 0 1)))\n       (b (list 20 15 10))\n       (lp (ops/lp 'maximize c A b))\n       (sol (ops/interior-point lp)))\n  (if (pair? sol)\n      (list 'status 'solved 'objective (ops/lp-value sol))\n      (list 'status 'failed 'reason sol)))" :note "5-variable, 3-constraint maximization; checks if solution succeeded or escalated")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define big-b 'big-b)\n(define big-A 'big-A)\n(define cost-list 'cost-list)\n(define big-demand-list 'big-demand-list)\n(define (production-plan-large num-products num-constraints demand-vec cost-vec constraint-matrix capacity-vec)\n  (let* ((c cost-vec)\n         (A constraint-matrix)\n         (b capacity-vec)\n         (lp (ops/lp 'minimize c A b))\n         (result (ops/interior-point lp)))\n    (if (and (pair? result) (not (eq? result 'use-backend)))\n        (list 'plan result 'obj-value (ops/lp-value result))\n        (list 'fallback 'use-simplex (ops/simplex (ops/lp 'minimize c A b))))))\n  (production-plan-large 100 50 big-demand-list cost-list big-A big-b)" :note "Attempts interior-point on a large instance; falls back to ops/simplex if backend unavailable")
  )

  :drawbacks ("Slower than simplex on small problems (overhead of backend call)" "Accuracy depends entirely on backend implementation; cannot inspect or debug the solver internals" "May not be available on all devices or deployments (backend dependency)" "Interior-point does not naturally provide constraint duals or sensitivity analysis as easily as simplex")

(verb
  :name "ops/inventory-cost"
  :library "ops"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(ops/inventory-cost demand order-qty holding-cost order-cost) -> total-annual-cost"
  :summary "Calculates the total annual inventory cost as the sum of ordering cost and holding cost."
  :explanation "The inventory cost function combines two competing costs: the ordering (or setup) cost, which is fixed per order and increases with the number of orders per year (D/Q × K), and the holding (or carrying) cost, which depends on average inventory and increases with order size (Q/2 × h). The total annual cost is TC(Q) = (D/Q) × K + (Q/2) × h. This formula is the foundation of the economic order quantity (EOQ) model: EOQ minimizes TC by balancing these two costs. Use ops/inventory-cost to evaluate the cost at any order quantity, compare different policies, or verify optimality after computing the EOQ."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ops/inventory-cost 1000 100 5 50)" :note "D=1000 units/year, Q=100 units/order, h=$5/unit/year, K=$50/order; returns total cost = (1000/100)×50 + (100/2)×5 = $750")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((demand 5000)\n       (hold-cost 2)\n       (order-cost 100)\n       (q-opt (ops/eoq demand order-cost hold-cost))\n       (q-test-low 200)\n       (q-test-high 800)\n       (cost-opt (ops/inventory-cost demand q-opt hold-cost order-cost))\n       (cost-low (ops/inventory-cost demand q-test-low hold-cost order-cost))\n       (cost-high (ops/inventory-cost demand q-test-high hold-cost order-cost)))\n  (list 'eoq q-opt 'opt-cost cost-opt 'test-costs (list cost-low cost-high)))" :note "Compares total cost at EOQ with two suboptimal quantities; EOQ should yield the minimum")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (sensitivity-tornado-inventory demand hold-cost order-cost variance-pct)\n  (let* ((cost-base (ops/inventory-cost demand (ops/eoq demand order-cost hold-cost) hold-cost order-cost))\n         (h-low (* hold-cost (- 1 (/ variance-pct 100))))\n         (h-high (* hold-cost (+ 1 (/ variance-pct 100))))\n         (K-low (* order-cost (- 1 (/ variance-pct 100))))\n         (K-high (* order-cost (+ 1 (/ variance-pct 100))))\n         (cost-h-low (ops/inventory-cost demand (ops/eoq demand order-cost h-low) h-low order-cost))\n         (cost-h-high (ops/inventory-cost demand (ops/eoq demand order-cost h-high) h-high order-cost))\n         (cost-K-low (ops/inventory-cost demand (ops/eoq demand K-low hold-cost) hold-cost K-low))\n         (cost-K-high (ops/inventory-cost demand (ops/eoq demand K-high hold-cost) hold-cost K-high)))\n    (list 'base-cost cost-base\n          'h-sensitivity (list cost-h-low cost-h-high)\n          'K-sensitivity (list cost-K-low cost-K-high))))\n  (sensitivity-tornado-inventory 3000 3 75 15)" :note "Tornado analysis: varies h and K by ±15% and recomputes optimal cost; shows which parameter matters most")
  )
  :caveats ("All parameters must be positive; zero or negative demand, costs, or quantity give nonsensical results" "Formula assumes uniform demand throughout the year (not seasonal or time-varying)" "Assumes instantaneous replenishment (lead time = 0); does not account for safety stock" "Order quantity Q should be positive and realistic; very small Q (e.g., 1) or very large Q may indicate modeling errors" "Does not include stockout or shortage costs")
  :drawbacks ("Highly sensitive to estimates of holding cost h and ordering cost K; small errors cascade into large cost misestimates" "Linear holding cost model ignores warehouse space constraints and bulk-storage discounts" "Does not model quantity discounts or economies of scale" "Assumes a single SKU; multi-item inventory coordination requires more complex models")
  :usecases ("Inventory optimization: evaluate cost trade-offs for different order sizes and choose the best policy" "Budget planning: estimate annual carrying and ordering expenses for SKU management" "Vendor negotiations: use total-cost estimates to justify bulk discounts or alternate suppliers" "Supply-chain education: teach the balance between setup cost and holding cost using realistic scenarios")
  :related ("ops/eoq" "ops/reorder-point" "ops/safety-stock" "ops/newsvendor")
  :learn (:concept "Trade-off optimization: balancing fixed and variable costs" :prerequisites ("Understanding of holding (carrying) cost and ordering (setup) cost" "Basic economics of inventory systems") :progression "After inventory-cost, learn ops/eoq (optimal order quantity), ops/reorder-point (when to order), and ops/newsvendor (stochastic demand)")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A retail manager wants total annual cost for a candidate order quantity."
                 :program "(ops/inventory-cost 1000 100 5 50)"
                 :explanation "Compute TC(Q) = D/Q · K + Q/2 · h."
                 :meta "Reach for inventory-cost, not hand-rolled sum, to keep the arithmetic canonical.")
                (:eng "Log TC per candidate for comparison."

                     :explanation "Rung 1 sums ordering + holding. Rung 2 sums setup + processing per batch. Rung 3 sums miss + write costs. All are two-cost sums."
                     :meta "Two-cost sum is universal.")

                 :invariant "TC(EOQ) ≤ TC(any other Q)"

(verb
  :name "ops/johnson"
  :library "ops"

  :signature "(ops/johnson jobs machine1-times machine2-times) -> optimal-sequence"
  :summary "Applies Johnson's rule to find the optimal job sequence for a two-machine flow shop with minimum makespan."
  :explanation "Johnson's rule is a polynomial-time algorithm that solves the two-machine flow-shop scheduling problem optimally. Given a set of jobs, each with processing times on machine 1 and machine 2, it produces a job order that minimizes the makespan (total time to complete all jobs on both machines). The algorithm partitions jobs based on which machine has the shorter processing time and constructs the optimal sequence by prioritizing short-processing-time jobs on machine 1 at the front and on machine 2 at the back. This is a classic result and is widely used in manufacturing, assembly lines, and pipeline scheduling. For more than two machines, the problem becomes NP-hard and requires heuristics."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ops/johnson '((j1 . ((m1 . 3) (m2 . 6)))\n               (j2 . ((m1 . 8) (m2 . 4)))\n               (j3 . ((m1 . 5) (m2 . 2))))\n            'preprocessing)" :note "Johnson's rule partitions into {j1, j3} (short on m1) and {j2} (short on m2); returns optimal sequence j1, j3, j2")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((jobs '((task-a . ((m1 . 2) (m2 . 8)))\n               (task-b . ((m1 . 5) (m2 . 3)))\n               (task-c . ((m1 . 7) (m2 . 4)))\n               (task-d . ((m1 . 1) (m2 . 9)))))\n       (order (ops/johnson jobs))\n       (metrics (ops/sequence-metrics order 'processing)))\n  (list 'johnson-sequence order 'makespan (car (assoc 'makespan metrics))))" :note "Computes Johnson sequence and immediately verifies makespan via ops/sequence-metrics")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define my-job-list 'my-job-list)\n(define (flow-shop-analysis jobs)\n  (let* ((johnson-seq (ops/johnson jobs))\n         (johnson-metrics (ops/sequence-metrics johnson-seq 'processing))\n         (spt-seq (ops/spt jobs))\n         (spt-metrics (ops/sequence-metrics spt-seq 'processing)))\n    (list 'johnson-makespan (car (assoc 'makespan johnson-metrics))\n          'spt-makespan (car (assoc 'makespan spt-metrics))\n          'winner (if (< (car (assoc 'makespan johnson-metrics))\n                        (car (assoc 'makespan spt-metrics)))\n                     'johnson\n                     'spt))))\n  (flow-shop-analysis my-job-list)" :note "Compares Johnson's rule (optimal for 2 machines) with SPT heuristic; Johnson dominates when applicable")
  )
  :caveats ("Johnson's rule is ONLY optimal for exactly two machines; results are suboptimal for three or more machines" "Job list must include processing times for both machines (m1 and m2 fields)" "Assumes no job preemption (each job runs to completion on each machine in order)" "Assumes all machines are always available (no downtime or setup delays)" "Jobs cannot have precedence constraints (must be independent)")
  :drawbacks ("Not applicable to job shops (machines visited in different orders by different jobs)" "Does not minimize mean flow time or average lateness; optimizes only makespan" "Very sensitive to processing-time estimates; errors lead to suboptimal results" "Does not account for setup times, transportation delays, or machine breakdowns")
  :usecases ("Manufacturing: sequence parts through two production stages (e.g., cut and fold) to finish as soon as possible" "Assembly lines: order product flow through two workstations to minimize total cycle time" "Batch processing: schedule jobs on two servers or processors to minimize total service time" "Production planning: decide job order to minimize overtime and equipment idle time")

  :name "ops/knapsack"

  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(ops/knapsack capacity items) -> solution-or-error"
  :summary "Solves the 0/1 knapsack problem using dynamic programming."
  :explanation "The 0/1 knapsack problem asks: given a weight capacity and a list of items (each with weight and value), which items should you pack to maximize total value without exceeding capacity? This verb uses dynamic programming to find the optimal selection. Each item is either taken or left (hence \"0/1\"). Non-integer weights or values escalate 'no-integer-solution; problems too large to solve within the fuel budget escalate 'fuel-budget."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ops/knapsack 10 '((2 3) (3 4) (4 5) (5 6)))" :note "Pack items (weight, value) into capacity 10; returns which items to take")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((items '((1 2) (2 3) (3 5) (5 7))))\n  (let ((sol (ops/knapsack 7 items)))\n    (apply + (map (lambda (i) (cadr (list-ref items i))) sol))))" :note "Solve the knapsack, then sum the values of selected items to verify optimality")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (filter pred xs)\n  (let loop ((xs xs) (acc '()))\n    (cond ((null? xs) (reverse acc))\n          ((pred (car xs)) (loop (cdr xs) (cons (car xs) acc)))\n          (else (loop (cdr xs) acc)))))\n(define (pack-with-budget capacity item-list budget-fn)\n  (let ((filtered (filter (lambda (item) (> (car item) 0)) item-list)))\n    (if (null? filtered) (escalate 'empty-inventory null)\n      (let ((attempt (ops/knapsack capacity filtered)))\n        (cond ((eq? attempt 'no-integer-solution) (escalate 'bad-input null))\n              ((eq? attempt 'fuel-budget) (budget-fn 'reduce-items))\n              (else attempt))))))\n(pack-with-budget 20 '((3 10) (5 15) (7 20)) (lambda (e) '()))" :note "Wrapper that validates input, handles errors (bad weights, timeouts), and delegates budget decisions")
  )

(verb
  :name "ops/littles-law"
  :library "ops"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(ops/littles-law lambda W) -> L"
  :summary "Applies Little's Law (L = λ·W) to compute average number in system given arrival rate and residence time."
  :explanation "Little's Law is a foundational result in queueing theory: the long-run average number of entities in a system L equals the arrival rate λ times the average time each entity spends in the system W. This holds for any stable queueing system (M/M/1, M/M/c, M/D/1, etc.) regardless of arrival or service distributions. Given λ (arrivals per unit time) and W (average time in system), the verb computes L (average occupancy). This verb applies the law deterministically—it does not model the queue itself."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ops/littles-law 5 2)" :note "5 arrivals per hour, average stay 2 hours → 10 people in the system on average")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((lambda 10) (service-time 0.1) (wait-time 0.4))\n  (let ((W (+ service-time wait-time)))\n    (ops/littles-law lambda W)))" :note "Decompose residence time W into service time (0.1h) and queueing delay (0.4h); compute L")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (queue-capacity-check lambda W max-capacity)\n  (let ((L (ops/littles-law lambda W)))\n    (cond ((> L max-capacity) (escalate 'overload (list 'L L 'max max-capacity)))\n          ((< L (* 0.2 max-capacity)) (escalate 'underutilized L))\n          (else (list 'lambda lambda 'W W 'L L)))))\n(queue-capacity-check 8 1.5 15)" :note "Wrapper that checks whether queue occupancy is within safe bounds (20%-100% capacity)")
  )
  :caveats ("Little's Law applies only to stable systems in steady state; transient or unstable systems violate the assumption." "The law gives no information about individual queue disciplines (FIFO, priority, etc.) or the shape of wait-time distributions." "λ must be the long-run average arrival rate, not a snapshot; W must be the long-run average residence time." "If λ ≤ 0 or W < 0, the result is meaningless; the verb does not validate these conditions.")
  :drawbacks ("Provides only one scalar output L; does not give percentiles, variance, or tail behavior." "Does not model the queue dynamics; you cannot use it to simulate transient behavior or response to load spikes." "Does not tell you whether the system is actually stable (i.e., whether λ < μ·c in an M/M/c queue)." "For more detailed analysis (wait-time distribution, blocking probability), use ops/mm1, ops/mmc, or ops/erlang-b.")
  :usecases ("Quick sanity check: given arrival rate and average time-in-system, estimate typical occupancy." "Capacity planning: if occupancy L exceeds facility capacity, the system is overloaded." "Service-level analysis: if W is growing but λ is constant, investigate service bottlenecks." "Reverse calculation: given target L and measured λ, infer required W (average speed) to meet it.")
  :related ("ops/mm1" "ops/mmc" "ops/mmc-servers-for" "ops/erlang-b" "ops/erlang-c")
  :learn (:concept "Little's Law: a model-free relationship between arrival rate, occupancy, and residence time. Holds universally in steady state." :prerequisites ("Basic understanding of arrival rate (λ) and residence time (W)" "Familiarity with queueing notation (L, λ, W)") :progression "After ops/littles-law, learn ops/mm1 and ops/mmc to model queue dynamics including wait-time distributions and service capacity.")

                 :program "(ops/littles-law 5 2)"

                 :meta "Reach for Little's Law when only λ and W are known; no queue-model assumption needed.")
                (:eng "Log L for occupancy planning."
                 :math "L = λW."
                 :cs "O(1)."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "product of rate and time gives quantity: same shape in queues, in orbital analysis, in supply chain"
                     :rungs ((:domain "ops" :code "(ops/littles-law 5 2)")
                             (:domain "orbital" :code "(define (orbit-time period revs) (* period revs))\n(orbit-time 90 5)")
                             (:domain "supply" :code "(define (avg-inv rate leadtime) (* rate leadtime))\n(avg-inv 100 3)"))

                     :meta "Little's Law is universal."

                (:eng "Regression: idle system has zero L."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (diet-lp proteins fats carbs max-protein max-fat max-carb)\n  (ops/lp '(1 1 1) (list (list proteins 0 0) (list 0 fats 0) (list 0 0 carbs)) (list max-protein max-fat max-carb)))\n(diet-lp 4 9 5 2000 800 1200)" :note "Diet optimization: maximize grams of protein+fat+carb subject to daily limits per macronutrient")

(verb
  :name "ops/markov-step"
  :library "ops"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(ops/markov-step pi P k) -> distribution"
  :summary "Advances a state distribution k steps through a Markov transition matrix: π_k = π₀ · P^k."
  :explanation "Given a current probability distribution π (a row vector encoding which states are likely now) and a transition matrix P, the distribution after one step is π · P (matrix-vector multiplication). After k steps, it is π · P^k. This verb computes π · P^k without explicitly forming P^k, using repeated multiplication (or fast exponentiation for large k). The result is the predicted state distribution k steps in the future. This is useful for forecasting or understanding transient behavior of the Markov chain."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(ops/markov-step '(1 0) '((0.7 0.3) (0.4 0.6)) 1)" :note "Start in state 0 (distribution (1,0)), take 1 step: (1,0)·P = (0.7, 0.3)")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((pi0 '(0.5 0.5)) (P '((0.8 0.2) (0.3 0.7))))\n  (let ((pi1 (ops/markov-step pi0 P 1))\n        (pi5 (ops/markov-step pi0 P 5))\n        (pi10 (ops/markov-step pi0 P 10)))\n    (list 'step-1 pi1 'step-5 pi5 'step-10 pi10)))" :note "Forecast the state distribution at steps 1, 5, and 10 to observe convergence")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (first-passage-estimate pi P target threshold max-steps)\n  (let loop ((pi pi) (step 0))\n    (cond ((>= step max-steps) (escalate 'max-steps-reached step))\n          ((>= (list-ref pi target) threshold) step)\n          (else (loop (ops/markov-step pi P 1) (+ step 1))))))\n(first-passage-estimate '(1 0 0) '((0 0.5 0.5) (0.3 0 0.7) (0.6 0.2 0.1)) 2 0.4 100)" :note "Estimate how many steps until state 2 reaches probability ≥ 0.4, starting from state 0")
  )
  :caveats ("The distribution π must sum to 1; non-normalized distributions produce incorrect results." "The transition matrix P must be valid (rows sum to 1) from ops/markov, not validated here." "k must be non-negative; negative k is undefined or may escalate an error." "For very large k, the distribution may converge to a steady state; further steps produce identical output.")
  :drawbacks ("Time complexity O(n² · k) for naive multiplication (or O(n³ · log k) for matrix exponentiation). Very large k or n can hit the fuel budget." "Does not check for convergence; if you need only the steady state, use ops/stationary instead (more efficient)." "No support for sparse matrices; dense P consumes memory." "If π is not normalized, the output will not be normalized either; callers must handle normalization.")
  :usecases ("Forecast customer state (active, dormant, churned) k months into the future." "Predict inventory level distribution after k periods of stochastic demand and replenishment."   :related ("ops/markov" "ops/stationary" "ops/pagerank" "ops/absorbing-steps")

                 :explanation "Advance the initial distribution 10 steps forward through the Markov chain."
                 :meta "Reach for markov-step for forecasts; use stationary for the ultimate steady state.")
                (:eng "Log the distribution at intervals to trace convergence."
