(verb
  :name "sym/->string"
  :library "sym"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(sym/->string poly) -> string"
  :summary "Convert a polynomial to a human-readable string with terms in descending degree order."
  :explanation "Renders a polynomial expression as a human-friendly string like \"2x^2 + 3x - 1\", ordering terms from highest degree to lowest. This is useful for display, logging, or feeding symbolic results back to a human reader. Non-polynomial inputs return the symbol 'nan to signal type mismatch gracefully."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(sym/->string (sym/poly '(1 2 3)))\n;; => \"3x^2 + 2x + 1\"" :note "poly with coefficients [1, 2, 3] (low-order-first) renders high-order-first")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((p (sym/add (sym/poly '(0 1)) (sym/poly '(5 0 1)))))\n  (display (sym/->string p)))\n;; => \"x^2 + x\"" :note "sum of two polynomials is rendered as a clean expression")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((f (sym/poly '(-1 3 2))))\n  (let ((f-deriv (sym/derivative f)))\n    (list (sym/->string f) (sym/->string f-deriv))))\n;; => (\"2x^2 + 3x - 1\" \"4x + 3\")" :note "chaining polynomial ops and rendering intermediate results for inspection")
  )
  :caveats ("Returns the symbol 'nan if the input is not a valid polynomial" "Output order is always high-degree-first, regardless of internal storage" "Omits zero coefficients automatically (no \"+ 0x^2\" terms)")
  :drawbacks ("sym/->string is for display only; use sym/= to check equality, not string comparison" "Very large degree polynomials may produce long strings; consider sym/degree to check structure first")
  :usecases ("Displaying symbolic results in a repl or debug log" "Building user-facing output from algebraic computations" "Verifying polynomial simplification by eye")
  :related ("sym/poly" "sym/degree" "sym/=" "sym/evaluate")
  :learn (:concept "Converting symbolic structures to human-readable text for inspection and communication" :prerequisites ("sym/poly") :progression "After printing a polynomial, move to sym/degree to query its structure, then sym/coeff to extract individual terms")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A cortex/tutor wants to display a polynomial after a step of algebra so the student sees the result in standard high-degree-first notation."
     :program "(define p (sym/mul (sym/poly '(1 1)) (sym/poly '(2 1))))\n(display (sym/->string p))"
     :explanation "Line 1 multiplies (1+x)(2+x) yielding 2+3x+x². Line 2 renders as \"x^2 + 3x + 2\". The tutor UI displays the string to the student."
     :meta "Reach for sym/->string and NOT display of the raw polynomial: raw display exposes internal coefficient-list representation, which is not standard math notation.")
    (:eng "The tutor log includes the rendered string for review." :math "sym/->string is a projection from Poly to String." :cs "Meta; O(degree)."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Structure-to-notation projection."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "sym"    :code "(sym/->string p)")
       (:domain "text (metaphor)" :code "(text/format-currency amount)")
       (:domain "type theory"  :code "show: A → String"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 poly to standard notation. Rung 2 amount to currency string. Rung 3 abstract show function. Same shape."
     :meta "Show functions transfer to any structure with a canonical rendering.")
    (:eng "Human-readable projections appear in every user-facing display." :math "Rendering function of an abstract type." :cs "The 'show' half of a serialize/display pair."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "sym/->string produces the same string for equal polynomials: sym/= implies string equality."
     :program "(define p1 (sym/poly '(2 3 1)))\n(define p2 (sym/add (sym/poly '(1 3)) (sym/poly '(1 0 1))))\n(and (sym/= p1 p2) (string=? (sym/->string p1) (sym/->string p2)))"
     :invariant "∀ p q. sym/=(p, q) → sym/->string(p) = sym/->string(q)"
     :meta "Pattern: rendering respects equality. Falsifies if two equal polys render differently. See book-of-code ch on canonical rendering.")
    (:eng "Rendering-equality is what makes visual comparison correct." :math "sym/->string factors through the polynomial quotient." :cs "The 'well-defined-on-quotient' property is a base of canonicalization."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "sym/->string renders polynomial as string."
     :composition "(define (trace-derivatives p n) (let loop ((cur p) (i 0) (acc '())) (if (>= i n) (reverse acc) (loop (sym/derivative cur) (+ i 1) (cons (list i (sym/->string cur)) acc)))))\n(trace-derivatives (sym/poly '(1 2 3 4)) 4)"
     :emergent "step-by-step derivative log — trace the derivative sequence with human-readable output at each step."
     :meta "Family: computation-trace. Same shape as Wolfram|Alpha's step-by-step display or a debugger watch expression. See book-of-composition ch on computation trace.")
    (:eng "The pattern gives ops human-readable audit trails for teaching contexts." :math "Realizes a fold-with-rendering over the derivative sequence." :cs "Trace-with-rendering is a base for teaching UIs."))

(verb
  :name "sym/="
  :library "sym"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(sym/= p1 p2) -> boolean"
  :summary "Test structural equality of two polynomials after canonicalization."
  :explanation "Two polynomials are equal if, after normalization (removing trailing zeros, sorting by degree), their coefficient lists match exactly. This is the canonical way to compare polynomial expressions in Motoi: it ignores surface-level representation and instead compares the true mathematical objects. Non-polynomial inputs return 'nan."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(sym/= (sym/poly '(1 2 3)) (sym/poly '(1 2 3)))\n;; => #t" :note "identical coefficient lists are equal")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((p1 (sym/add (sym/poly '(1 1)) (sym/poly '(2 0))))\n      (p2 (sym/poly '(3 1))))\n  (sym/= p1 p2))\n;; => #t" :note "canonicalization makes algebraically equivalent expressions equal")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((f (sym/poly '(-1 3 2))))\n  (let ((f-deriv-twice (sym/derivative (sym/derivative f))))\n    (sym/= f-deriv-twice (sym/const 4))))\n;; => #t" :note "second derivative of quadratic equals its leading coefficient × 2")
  )
  :caveats ("Returns 'nan if either argument is not a valid polynomial" "Trailing zero coefficients are stripped before comparison, so (sym/poly '(1 0 0)) equals (sym/poly '(1))" "Does not use string comparison; (sym/->string p1) = (sym/->string p2) is not equivalent")
  :drawbacks ("sym/= is strict: 2x and 2.0x are equal only if internal representation matches exactly" "Floating-point polynomials may have rounding artifacts; consider sym/evaluate to test sampled points")
  :usecases ("Verifying symbolic simplification matches an expected result" "Testing polynomial algebra in symbolic computations" "Asserting correct behavior after sym/add, sym/mul, sym/derivative")
  :related ("sym/->string" "sym/poly" "sym/add" "sym/mul" "sym/derivative")
  :learn (:concept "Canonical equality: two objects are equal when they reduce to the same normal form" :prerequisites ("sym/poly" "sym/degree") :progression "Use sym/= to verify algebra, then move to sym/evaluate to test values, and sym/derivative for calculus")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A math/homework auto-checker compares student input polynomial to the expected polynomial regardless of surface form."
     :program "(define expected (sym/poly '(2 3 1)))\n(define student (sym/add (sym/poly '(1 3)) (sym/poly '(1 0 1))))\n(sym/= expected student)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines expected. Line 2 defines what the student wrote. Line 3 returns #t: canonicalization makes different surface forms equal."
     :meta "Reach for sym/= and NOT (string=? (sym/->string a) (sym/->string b)): string comparison can fail on whitespace or ordering differences that don't matter mathematically.")
    (:eng "The auto-checker log names the answer as correct despite different surface form." :math "sym/= tests equality in the polynomial quotient." :cs "Canonical-form comparison; O(degree)."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Semantic equality: same object under a canonical projection."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "sym"    :code "(sym/= p1 p2)")
       (:domain "note (metaphor)" :code "(note/enharmonic? n1 n2)")
       (:domain "algebra"    :code "[a] = [b] in A/≡"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 polynomial equality. Rung 2 enharmonic note equality. Rung 3 quotient equality. Same shape."
     :meta "Semantic equality transfers wherever a canonical form exists.")
    (:eng "Enharmonic tests, polynomial tests, and canonical-form checks share a shape." :math "Equality on the quotient." :cs "Canonical-form equality is the base of memoization and deduplication."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "sym/= is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive — a proper equivalence."
     :program "(define p (sym/poly '(1 2 3)))\n(define q (sym/poly '(1 2 3)))\n(define r (sym/poly '(1 2 3)))\n(and (sym/= p p) (eq? (sym/= p q) (sym/= q p)) (if (and (sym/= p q) (sym/= q r)) (sym/= p r) #t))"
     :invariant "∀ p. sym/=(p,p) ∧ ∀ p q. sym/=(p,q) → sym/=(q,p) ∧ ∀ p q r. (sym/=(p,q) ∧ sym/=(q,r)) → sym/=(p,r)"
     :meta "Pattern: equivalence relation. Falsifies if any triple breaks. See book-of-math ch on equivalence relations.")
    (:eng "Equivalence guarantees the auto-checker is consistent." :math "The three equivalence axioms." :cs "Equivalence is the base of quotient-collection semantics."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "sym/= tests canonical polynomial equality."
     :composition "(define (verify-identity lhs rhs) (sym/= lhs rhs))\n(define (proof-fma-example)\n  (verify-identity (sym/mul (sym/poly '(1 1)) (sym/poly '(-1 1))) (sym/poly '(-1 0 1))))\n(proof-fma-example)"
     :emergent "algebraic-identity prover — verify that two algebraic expressions are the same polynomial."
     :meta "Family: identity-prover. Same shape as a CAS's Simplify/FullSimplify or a Coq tactic verifying an algebraic law. See book-of-composition ch on symbolic verification.")
    (:eng "The pattern lets ops verify algebra automatically." :math "Realizes decidability of polynomial equality." :cs "Automated identity-checking is a base for teaching tools."))

(verb
  :name "sym/add"
  :library "sym"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(sym/add p1 p2) -> polynomial"
  :summary "Polynomial sum: add two polynomials term by term."
  :explanation "Adds two polynomial expressions by aligning powers of x and summing coefficients. The result is a new polynomial with degree at most max(deg(p1), deg(p2)). Non-polynomial operands return 'nan. This is the foundation of symbolic polynomial arithmetic."
  :examples (

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((p (sym/poly '(0 1))))\n  (sym/add p (sym/add p p)))\n;; => polynomial with coefficients (0 3)" :note "successive addition: x + x + x = 3x")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((f (sym/poly '(-1 0 1)))\n      (g (sym/poly '(1 1))))\n  (let ((h (sym/add f g)))\n    (list (sym/degree h) (sym/->string h))))\n;; => (2 \"x^2 + x\")" :note "composing add with degree and display to inspect result structure")
  )
  :caveats ("Returns 'nan if either operand is not a polynomial" "Addition is commutative: sym/add is order-independent" "Cancellation may occur: (sym/add (sym/poly '(1 1)) (sym/poly '(-1 -1))) yields the zero polynomial with degree -1")

  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A phys/motion simulator combines two force polynomials — spring force and gravity — into a single net-force polynomial."
     :program "(define spring (sym/poly '(0 -1)))\n(define gravity (sym/poly '(-9.8)))\n(sym/->string (sym/add spring gravity))"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines -x for spring. Line 2 defines -9.8 constant for gravity. Line 3 renders as \"-x - 9.8\". Net force is the sum."
     :meta "Reach for sym/add and NOT sym/mul: forces combine by addition, not multiplication. Using mul would produce a different physics.")
    (:eng "The physics log records the combined force polynomial." :math "sym/add is the group operation of the polynomial abelian group." :cs "O(max degree); term-by-term."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Group-addition: combine two elements under an associative commutative operation."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "sym"     :code "(sym/add p q)")
       (:domain "vec (metaphor)" :code "(vec/add u v)")
       (:domain "algebra"    :code "a + b in (A, +)"))

  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "sym/add is commutative and associative — a proper abelian-group operation."
     :program "(define p (sym/poly '(1 2)))\n(define q (sym/poly '(3 -1)))\n(define r (sym/poly '(0 1 1)))\n(and (sym/= (sym/add p q) (sym/add q p)) (sym/= (sym/add (sym/add p q) r) (sym/add p (sym/add q r))))"
     :invariant "∀ p q. p + q = q + p ∧ ∀ p q r. (p + q) + r = p + (q + r)"
     :meta "Pattern: commutative-monoid laws. Falsifies if any triple breaks. See book-of-math ch on group axioms.")
    (:eng "Associativity/commutativity mean folded-additions produce the same result regardless of order." :math "Abelian-group axioms." :cs "Commutative-monoid laws enable parallel reduction."))
  :row-5-emergence (

     :emergent "polynomial sum reducer — fold sym/add over a list to accumulate an arbitrary polynomial."
     :meta "Family: monoid-fold. Same shape as summing a list of numbers, concatenating a list of strings, or unioning a list of sets. See book-of-composition ch on monoid folds.")
    (:eng "The pattern generalizes binary addition to n-ary via fold." :math "Realizes the free-monoid fold on the polynomial group." :cs "Monoid-fold is a canonical reduce shape."))

(verb
  :name "sym/coeff"
  :library "sym"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(sym/coeff poly k) -> number"
  :summary "Extract the coefficient of x^k from a polynomial."

If k is negative or not an integer, or the input is not a polynomial, returns 'nan. This is the inverse of sym/poly: you can reconstruct a polynomial from its coefficients by repeated calls to sym/coeff."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((p (sym/poly '(1 2 3))))\n  (sym/coeff p 2))\n;; => 3" :note "coefficient of x^2 in polynomial (1 + 2x + 3x^2) is 3")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((p (sym/poly '(5 0 -2 0 1))))\n  (list (sym/coeff p 0) (sym/coeff p 1) (sym/coeff p 4)))\n;; => (5 0 1)" :note "extracting multiple coefficients; absent terms return 0")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((f (sym/poly '(-1 3 2))))\n  (let ((df (sym/derivative f)))\n    (list (sym/coeff f 0) (sym/coeff df 1) (sym/->string df))))\n;; => (-1 4 \"4x + 3\")" :note "extracting coefficients from original and derivative to verify rule: d/dx(x^n) = n·x^(n-1)")

  :related ("sym/poly" "sym/degree" "sym/->string" "sym/derivative")
  :learn (:concept "Polynomial representation: a polynomial is a sequence of coefficients indexed by degree" :prerequisites ("sym/poly" "sym/degree") :progression "After extracting coefficients, use sym/add or sym/mul to perform arithmetic, then sym/derivative for calculus")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A calc/analyze routine wants only the leading coefficient of a polynomial to detect end-behavior."
     :program "(define p (sym/poly '(-1 3 2)))\n(sym/coeff p (sym/degree p))"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines 2x²+3x-1. Line 2 extracts the coefficient at degree 2 (the leading term): 2. The analyzer uses this to decide direction of end-behavior."
     :meta "Reach for sym/coeff and NOT parsing sym/->string: parsing the rendered string is fragile and O(degree). sym/coeff is direct.")
    (:eng "The analyzer log records the leading coefficient." :math "sym/coeff is a projection Poly × ℕ → ℝ." :cs "O(1) if the polynomial is stored as a coefficient vector."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Indexed lookup on a structured object."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "sym"     :code "(sym/coeff p k)")
       (:domain "vec (metaphor)" :code "(vec/nth v k)")
       (:domain "type theory" :code "π_k: Poly → ℝ (k-th projection)"))

  :row-4-proof (

     :program "(define lst '(-1 3 2))\n(define p (sym/poly lst))\n(and (= (sym/coeff p 0) -1) (= (sym/coeff p 1) 3) (= (sym/coeff p 2) 2))"
     :invariant "∀ lst k. 0 ≤ k < |lst| → sym/coeff(sym/poly(lst), k) = lst[k]"
     :meta "Pattern: constructor-projector identity. Falsifies if any index disagrees. See book-of-code ch on constructor-projector duality.")
    (:eng "The identity lets ops trust round-trips through the poly type." :math "Section of the constructor: coeff ∘ poly = id on valid indices." :cs "Constructor-projector duality is a base algebraic property."))
  :row-5-emergence (

     :composition "(define (evaluate-slow p x) (let loop ((k 0) (acc 0)) (if (> k (sym/degree p)) acc (loop (+ k 1) (+ acc (* (sym/coeff p k) (expt x k)))))))\n(evaluate-slow (sym/poly '(1 2 3)) 2)"
     :emergent "polynomial-evaluator by explicit index-and-sum — the pedagogical form of polynomial evaluation."
     :meta "Family: index-based reducer. Same shape as computing a dot product via indexed sum or matrix-vector product. See book-of-composition ch on indexed reduction.")
    (:eng "The pattern is the pedagogical evaluator, contrasted with Horner in sym/evaluate." :math "Realizes p(x) = Σ aₖ xᵏ directly." :cs "Index-and-accumulate is a base reducer shape."))

  :summary "Solve a linear inequality a·x ⧀ b where ⧀ is one of <, >, <=, >=; return interval as a-list."
  :explanation "sym/solve-ineq is a symbolic algebra verb that solves linear inequalities in one variable. If a = 0 and b ≠ 0, the inequality is unsolvable (inconsistent or always-false) and returns the symbol 'nan. If a = 0 and b = 0, all x satisfy it (or none, depending on the operator). The verb owns the \"flip rule\": when a < 0, the inequality direction reverses (x > b/a instead of x < b/a). This is a meta verb—it reasons about symbolic structure, not a concrete computation."

If the polynomial has degree > 1, a `'not-linear` escalation is raised. Use this when you know your polynomial is linear and want a quick, exact answer."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(sym/solve-linear (sym/poly '(3 2)))" :note "Solve 3+2x=0 → x=−3/2")

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (line-intercepts slope y-intercept axis)\n  (case axis\n    ((x) (sym/solve-linear (sym/poly (list y-intercept slope))))\n    ((y) y-intercept)\n    (else (escalate 'bad-axis))))\n(line-intercepts 3 -6 'x)" :note "Helper to find where y=3x−6 crosses the x-axis; returns 2")
  )

  )

(verb
  :name "synth/808"
  :library "synth"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(synth/808 part [tune [decay [accent]]]) -> handle | [status info-dict]"
  :summary "Trigger an 808 drum voice (kick, snare, tom, hihat, cowbell, clap, etc.) with optional tuning, decay, and accent."
  :explanation "synth/808 is a drum synthesizer interface that plays one of several pre-defined 808-style percussion voices. You specify the voice by name (a symbol like 'kick, 'snare, 'tom, etc.), and optionally tune the pitch, adjust decay time, and set the accent (loudness/velocity). The verb requires an active audio context (user must have gestured), and it returns either a playback handle or an error/pending status dict. Use it to build rhythm, layer beats, or respond to in-game events with synchronized drum sounds."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(on-tick (lambda ()\n  (synth/808 'kick)))" :note "Every tick, trigger a kick drum with default settings.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define on-beat (lambda args (list \"on-beat\" args)))\n(on-beat (lambda (beat)\n  (cond\n    ((= (modulo beat 4) 0) (synth/808 'kick 0 0.2))\n    ((= (modulo beat 2) 1) (synth/808 'snare 0 0.1))\n    (else (synth/808 'hihat 0 0.05)))))" :note "Kick on downbeats, snare on odd beats, hihat on off-beats; vary decay per voice.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (layer-kick-pattern bpm notes)\n  (let* ((spb (/ 60 bpm))\n         (tick-ms (* spb 1000)))\n    (define (play-seq seq idx)\n      (if (< idx (length seq))\n        (let ((note (list-ref seq idx)))\n          (when (car note)\n            (let ((res (synth/808 (cadr note) (caddr note) (cadddr note) (car (cddddr note)))))\n              (when (pair? res) (display (list 'drum-error res)))))\n          (time/when (+ (time/now) (* (car (cddddr (cdr note))) tick-ms))\n            (lambda () (play-seq seq (+ idx 1)))))))\n    (play-seq notes 0)))\n(layer-kick-pattern 120 '((#t kick 0 0.3 1) (#t snare 0 0.2 2) (#f hihat 0 0.05 0.5)))" :note "Schedule a drum sequence with absolute timing; each note specifies trigger, voice, tuning, decay, and beat offset.")
  )
  :caveats ("Requires an active audio context and user gesture (click/tap); returns pending status if audio not ready." "part must be a symbol matching one of the known drum voices; misspelled parts return 'unknown-drum-voice error." "tune, decay, accent are coerced to numbers; passing non-numeric values may silently use defaults or fail." "No guarantee the sound is audible; output routing (chainOutput) may fail if the audio chain is misconfigured." "Each call is independent; overlapping calls on the same voice may create phasing or clipping artifacts.")
  :drawbacks ("Limited to the preset 808 kit; no custom drum samples or synthesis parameters beyond tune/decay/accent." "Requires wrangling audio context and gesture state; beginners may struggle with pending audio errors." "No pattern sequencing built-in; you must manually schedule calls or integrate with a DAW/grid verb." "Polyphony and voice stealing are not exposed; too many simultaneous calls may truncate earlier voices.")
  :usecases ("Rhythm game: trigger drums on beat or on player input." "Procedural music: layer kick and snare patterns to build hypnotic loops." "Interactive audio: respond to game events (collisions, powerups) with percussion." "Educational tool: teach beat subdivision and drum kit layout.")
  :related ("synth/chord" "synth/kit" "synth/play" "audio/play" "on-beat" "on-tick" "time/when")
  :learn (:concept "Drum synthesis; sample-based wavetables with envelope control (pitch/decay/accent)." :prerequisites ("audio/play" "on-beat") :progression "After synth/808, layer with synth/chord and synth/kit to build full arrangements; then explore synth/load-score for pre-composed sequences.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "The operator wants a kick drum on the downbeat with tuning and decay control. The operator asks: which verb triggers an 808 kick with tuning? Not synth/kit (pattern-based), not synth/chord (harmonic)."
     :program "(synth/808 'kick 0 0.3 1.0)"
     :explanation "One call: 'kick voice, tuning 0, decay 0.3s, accent 1.0. synth/808 is the direct trigger for canonical 808 drum voices."
     :meta "Sibling synth/kit uses a pattern string; synth/808 is the single-hit trigger.")
    (:eng "Rhythm-game hits, per-beat SFX."
     :math "synth/808 : Symbol × ℝ × ℝ × ℝ → Handle."
     :cs "Voice trigger; mutation of the audio scheduler."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'parametric trigger — named voice, per-hit parameters.'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "synth/808" :code "(synth/808 'snare 2 0.1 0.8)")
       (:domain "audio/play with volume" :code "(audio/play 'jump 0.7)")
       (:domain "parametric function call" :code "(+ 1 2 3)"))
     :explanation "Each rung takes a name plus parameters and produces a specific instance."
     :meta "Parametric triggers are universal.")
    (:eng "Every synthesized hit is parametric."
     :math "A named function with numeric parameters."
     :cs "The base of parametric synthesis."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "Two calls with identical parameters produce two independent playbacks."
     :program "(define h1 (synth/808 'kick))\n(define h2 (synth/808 'kick))\n(not (equal? h1 h2))"
     :invariant "Each synth/808 call is a fresh event; handles are distinct."
     :meta "Instance uniqueness. See book-of-code ch on event uniqueness.")

     :composition "(define (backbeat)\n  (on-tick (lambda ()\n    (synth/808 'kick 0 0.3))))\n(backbeat)"
     :emergent "A tick-driven backbeat. The pattern is 'sequenced trigger.'"
     :meta "This is the sequencer family — same shape as MIDI clock, DAW step-programmer. See book-of-composition ch on sequencing.")

(verb
  :name "synth/chord"
  :library "synth"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(synth/chord section pitches [duration [dynamic [articulation]]]) -> handle | [status info-dict]"
  :summary "Trigger a chord (one or more pitches) on a named orchestra section (strings, brass, woodwinds, etc.) with optional duration, dynamic, and articulation."
  :explanation "synth/chord plays a simultaneous cluster of pitches on a given orchestral section. The section must be a recognized name (e.g., 'strings, 'brass, 'woodwinds); pitches can be a single pitch or a list of pitch symbols/numbers; duration specifies how long the chord sustains; dynamic controls loudness/intensity; articulation affects attack/release style (staccato, legato, etc.). Like synth/808, it requires an active audio context. The verb returns a playback handle or a status dict. Use it to compose harmonic sequences, underscore emotional moments, or layer chords over drums."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(synth/chord 'strings '(C4 E4 G4))" :note "Play a C major triad on strings section.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (play-progression changes)\n  (for-each (lambda (chord-data)\n    (let ((section (car chord-data))\n          (pitches (cadr chord-data))\n          (dur (caddr chord-data)))\n      (synth/chord section pitches dur)))\n    changes))\n(play-progression '((strings (C4 E4 G4) 2.0)\n                    (strings (D4 F4 A4) 2.0)\n                    (brass (G3 B3 D4) 1.5)))" :note "Play a sequence of chords; each waits or overlaps depending on the timeline.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (orchestrate-motif root chord-type sections durations)\n  (define (pitch-offset base semitones) base) ;; simplified pitch calc\n  (define (build-chord root type)\n    (cond\n      ((eq? type 'maj) (list root (pitch-offset root 4) (pitch-offset root 7)))\n      ((eq? type 'min) (list root (pitch-offset root 3) (pitch-offset root 7)))\n      ((eq? type 'dim) (list root (pitch-offset root 3) (pitch-offset root 6)))))\n  (let loop ((secs sections) (durs durations))\n    (when (and (pair? secs) (pair? durs))\n      (synth/chord (car secs) (build-chord root chord-type) (car durs))\n      (loop (cdr secs) (cdr durs)))))\n(orchestrate-motif 'C4 'maj '(strings brass woodwinds) '(2.0 1.5 1.0))" :note "Compose a motif across orchestral sections; chord shape is derived from root and type, then played on each section with a specific duration.")
  )
  :caveats ("section must match a known name (case-insensitive); unknown sections return 'unknown-section error." "pitches can be a list or a single value; empty or nil pitch list returns 'empty-chord error." "Requires active audio context and user gesture; returns pendingAudio('awaiting-gesture') until user interacts." "duration, dynamic, and articulation are optional; omitted arguments use instrument defaults." "No guarantee polyphony; too many simultaneous chords may truncate earlier voices or cause distortion.")
  :drawbacks ("Pitch notation is opaque (likely MIDI numbers or letter symbols); no standard conversion or validation exposed." "No built-in voice leading or voicing optimization; you must manually specify pitches to avoid awkward intervals." "Orchestral sections are fixed; no custom timbres or microtonal playback." "Returns a status dict on error; parsing errors and distinguishing from success requires careful pattern matching." "No query for current playing voices; cannot check which sections are busy before issuing new chords.")
  :usecases ("Compose underscores for story beats, victories, or defeats." "Create harmonic padding under gameplay sequences." "Teach music theory: visualize chord progressions and orchestration." "Respond to game state with thematic chords (e.g., minor on danger, major on success).")
  :related ("synth/808" "synth/kit" "synth/play" "synth/load-score" "audio/play" "on-tick")
  :learn (:concept "Harmonic synthesis; named orchestral sections as timbral/rhythmic units; simultaneous polyphony." :prerequisites ("pitch notation" "audio/play") :progression "After synth/chord, combine with synth/808 and synth/kit for full arrangements; then load pre-composed sequences with synth/load-score.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator wants a C-major triad on strings for two beats. The operator asks: which verb triggers a chord on a named section? Not synth/808 (drums), not synth/orch (single note)."
     :program "(synth/chord 'strings '(60 64 67) 2.0)"
     :explanation "One call plays middle C, E, G on the strings section for 2 seconds. synth/chord bundles simultaneity into one call."
     :meta "Sibling synth/orch requires N calls for N pitches. synth/chord is the polyphonic primitive.")
    (:eng "Harmonic underscores, chord stabs."
     :math "synth/chord : Section × [Pitch] × ℝ? × ℝ? × Sym? → Handle."
     :cs "Polyphonic voice allocation."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'simultaneous cluster — many voices, one trigger.'"
     :rungs (

       (:domain "fb/rect (many pixels one call)" :code "(fb/rect 0 0 10 10 'red)")
       (:domain "vector broadcast" :code "(map (lambda (x) (+ x 1)) (list 1 2 3))"))
     :explanation "Each rung applies one operation to many targets simultaneously."
     :meta "Bulk trigger vs single trigger — a scaling shape.")
    (:eng "Any bulk trigger."
     :math "Broadcast of an operation over a set."
     :cs "SIMD in miniature."))
  :row-4-proof (

(verb
  :name "synth/kit"
  :library "synth"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(synth/kit name pattern [voice]) -> handle | [status info-dict]"
  :summary "Trigger a drum kit (e.g., acoustic, electronic, live) with a pattern string and optional voice selection."

Returns a playback handle or status dict on error/pending."
  :examples (

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (evolve-pattern base-pat pressure-level swing)\n  (define (mutate-pattern pat mutation-rate)\n    (let loop ((i 0) (result \"\"))\n      (if (>= i (string-length pat))\n        result\n        (let* ((char (string-ref pat i))\n               (flip? (< (random) mutation-rate))\n               (new-char (if flip? (if (char=? char #\\0) #\\1 #\\0) char)))\n          (loop (+ i 1) (string-append result (string new-char)))))))\n  (let* ((mutated (mutate-pattern base-pat (* 0.1 pressure-level)))\n         (swung (if (> swing 0.5) mutated base-pat)))  ;; simplified swing\n    (synth/kit 'electronic swung 'kick)))\n(evolve-pattern \"1000100010001000\" 0.7 0.6)" :note "Dynamically mutate the drum pattern based on game pressure level; optionally apply swing feel.")

  :row-2-audit (

The handler receives the onset event; you get back an unsubscribe function so you can clean up the listener later."

(car result) 'ok)\n      (begin\n        (set! onset-listener (cadr result))\n        (next 'listening ctx))\n      (escalate 'onset-failed null))))\n(define (stop-tap ctx)\n  (if onset-listener\n    ((cadr (assoc 'unsubscribe onset-listener)) #t))\n  (next 'stopped ctx))" :note "Stateful subscription lifecycle: register listener on enter, clean up via unsubscribe on exit. (verb
  :name "system/cards"
  :library "system"
  :kind "rd"
  :signature "(system/cards) -> [{id kind x y k z focused} ...]"
  :summary "Return a list of all open cards with their position, size, z-order, and focus state."
  :explanation "A card is a UI container (window-like) on the Motoi surface. `system/cards` snapshots the entire card fleet: for each open card it reports the unique ID, the card kind (type/template), pixel position (x, y), size (k in pixels), z-depth (stacking order), and whether it has keyboard focus. This is introspection: you cannot modify cards with this verb, only read their state. Use it to query the layout, find cards by position, or monitor which card is active."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(display (system/cards))" :note "Print the current card roster: you'll see IDs, kinds, positions, and focus state for all open windows.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (filter pred xs)\n  (let loop ((xs xs) (acc '()))\n    (cond ((null? xs) (reverse acc))\n          ((pred (car xs)) (loop (cdr xs) (cons (car xs) acc)))\n          (else (loop (cdr xs) acc)))))\n(let ((cards (system/cards)))\n  (let ((focused (filter (lambda (c) (eq? (assoc 'focused c) #t)) cards)))\n    (if (not (null? focused))\n      (display (car focused)))))" :note "Find the focused card and display its data; pattern for locating the active window.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (find-card-at-xy x y)\n  (let ((cards (system/cards)))\n    (let loop ((cs cards))\n      (if (null? cs)\n        #f\n        (let* ((c (car cs))\n               (cx (assoc 'x c))\n               (cy (assoc 'y c))\n               (csize (assoc 'k c)))\n          (if (and (>= x cx) (< x (+ cx csize))\n                   (>= y cy) (< y (+ cy csize)))\n            c\n            (loop (cdr cs))))))))\n(find-card-at-xy 100 200)" :note "Spatial query: return the card at screen coordinates (100, 200) by iterating the roster and checking bounding boxes.")
  )
  :caveats ("This is a read-only snapshot; calling it twice in quick succession may return different results if cards open/close." "Position and size are in pixels; z-order is an integer (higher = on top)." "The 'position field may be an object with x/y keys or a 2-element array [x y]; code normalizes both." "Cards with missing data (e.g., a closed card that hasn't cleaned up) may have null values; check before dereferencing.")
  :drawbacks ("No card filtering by kind: you get the entire list; filter in Scheme if you want specific types." "No hierarchical or parent/child relationship info; all cards are treated as peers." "Continuous polling (calling repeatedly) is inefficient; consider caching or event subscription if available." "Does not report cards that are closed; only open cards appear in the list.")
  :usecases ("Layout introspection: query which windows are open to decide whether to spawn a new card or reuse an existing one." "Spatial hit-testing: find which card a mouse click or touch landed on." "Focus management: determine which card has keyboard input, used to decide message routing." "Telemetry: log the card state for debugging or analytics (e.g., how many cards did the user have open?).")
  :related ("card/list" "card/find-by-kind" "card/focus!" "card/unfocus!" "card/rect" "card/screen-rect" "system/health" "system/registry")
  :learn (:concept "System introspection: querying the runtime state of UI containers (cards) to inform control flow and spatial reasoning." :prerequisites ("(core)/let" "(core)/filter" "(core)/lambda" "(core)/null?" "card/list") :progression "Learn `system/cards` to understand the card roster, then use `card/focus!` or `card/emit` to interact with specific cards, then explore the card event system for reactive updates.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator's UI is doing hit-testing on mouse clicks. A click at (100,200) needs to find which card the click landed on. Hard-coding card positions would break as soon as the user moves a card. system/cards is the runtime's authoritative snapshot of the fleet. The audit question is whether the operator queried the snapshot correctly and matched the click against the reported bounds."
     :program "(define (card-at x y)\n  (let loop ((cs (system/cards)))\n    (cond ((null? cs) #f)\n          ((let ((c (car cs)))\n             (let ((cx (cdr (assoc 'x c)))\n                   (cy (cdr (assoc 'y c)))\n                   (k (cdr (assoc 'k c)))))\n               #f))\n           (car cs))\n          (else (loop (cdr cs))))))\n(display (system/cards)) (newline)"
     :explanation "The example iterates the snapshot and would compare click bounds against each card's rectangle. Line 8 displays the roster so the auditor can see the ground truth used for the search."
     :meta "Why system/cards and not hard-coded positions: cards move, get created, get closed. The runtime is authoritative.")
    (:eng "Operationally this is fleet-snapshot introspection. Log the snapshot at the moment of the click for later audit."
     :math "The verb returns a finite list of records — a snapshot of the current card fleet."
     :cs "The CS pattern is fleet introspection. Related: ps in Unix, docker ps, kubectl get pods."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A fleet snapshot: enumerate every live instance of a resource in one call, so the caller can search or aggregate."
     :rungs ((:domain "system (cards)" :code "(system/cards)")
             (:domain "process table" :code "ps -eo pid,cmd")
             (:domain "set of live objects" :code "'{ x : Card | live?(x) }'"))
     :explanation "In Motoi, system/cards enumerates cards. On Unix, ps enumerates processes. In set theory, a comprehension enumerates the live instances. All three cases share the shape of 'give me every live instance at this moment.'"
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever the caller needs to reason about the whole fleet.")
    (:eng "Log the snapshot length as a fleet-size signal."
     :math "The verb returns a finite subset of the potential-cards universe."
     :cs "The CS analog is process-table introspection."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "system/cards returns a list of card records with the fields id, kind, x, y, k, z, focused; and each id is unique in the returned list."
     :program "(define cards (system/cards))\n(display (list? cards)) (newline)\n(display (equal? (length cards) (length cards))) (newline)"
     :invariant "cards() ∈ List<CardRecord> ∧ ids in cards() are pairwise distinct"
     :meta "The pattern is fleet-record integrity. See book-of-code ch09 for record-list invariants. What falsifies: a run where two entries have the same id."
    :eng "Smoke test: length is stable across immediate re-reads."
     :math "The list is a subset of the CardRecord universe with a distinct-id constraint."
     :cs "The CS pattern is unique-id invariant."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "system/cards enumerates open cards."
     :composition "(define (count-focused)\n  (length (filter (lambda (c) (cdr (assoc 'focused c))) (system/cards))))\n(define (filter pred xs) (let loop ((xs xs) (acc '())) (cond ((null? xs) (reverse acc)) ((pred (car xs)) (loop (cdr xs) (cons (car xs) acc))) (else (loop (cdr xs) acc)))))\n(display (count-focused)) (newline)"
     :emergent "focus report — a summary of the fleet by a specific attribute, useful for dashboards showing which cards are active"
     :meta "The composition chains system/cards with filter and length. What emerges is the fleet-summary family: aggregate a snapshot by a predicate. The same family appears in monitoring systems (Prometheus counters), in SRE dashboards, in kubernetes get-pods filters."
     :eng "Log fleet aggregates on startup for capacity planning."
     :math "The composition is a filter-then-count reduction on a finite set."
     :cs "The CS pattern name is fleet aggregation. Familiar analogs: Prometheus counters, kubectl get filters.")))

(chapter :number "64" :library "text" :verb-count 9 :training-eligible #t)

;; ═══ 9 verbs in library text ═══

(verb
  :name "text/draw"
  :library "text"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(text/draw text [at: [x y]] [color: #xRRGGBB | color: symbol] [align: symbol] [font: symbol]) → 'ok | ['pending-visual info] | ['error reason]"
  :summary "Draw a text string to the surface with optional position, color, alignment, and font."
  :explanation "This verb rasterizes a text string and paints it onto the current drawing surface. Arguments are passed as keyword pairs: `at:` sets the (x, y) position; `color:` or `colour:` sets the color (hex or symbol); `align:` controls text anchor (left, center, right); `font:` specifies the typeface. Returns 'ok on success, ['pending-visual info] if rendering is deferred, or ['error reason] if invalid."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(text/draw \"Hello, world!\")" :note "Draw plain text at the default position (origin or cursor).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(text/draw \"Score: 42\"\n  'at: '(100 50)\n  'color: '#xFF0000\n  'align: 'center)" :note "Draw centered red text at (100, 50)—typical HUD label.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (score-label score x y)\n  (let ((result (text/draw (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score))\n                           'at: (list x y)\n                           'color: (if (> score 1000) '#00FF00 '#FFFFFF)\n                           'font: 'monospace)))\n    (cond ((eq? (car result) 'error) (display (cadr result)))\n          ((equal? result 'ok) (display \"text painted\"))\n          (else (display \"deferred\")))))\n(score-label 1500 100 50)" :note "Conditional color based on value; handle all return states.")
  )
  :caveats ("Text is painted to the surface, not to a card; it cannot be moved or edited after drawing." "If rendering is pending, the text may not be visible until the next frame." "Keywords `color` and `colour` are both valid (British/American spelling)." "If `align:` is invalid, the text defaults to left-alignment." "If `font:` is unknown, the system falls back to a default typeface.")
  :drawbacks ("Cannot be selectively erased; use surface/curtain to clear regions." "Expensive to call many times per frame; batch text draws when possible." "Pending-visual results delay visibility; use synchronously for critical HUD." "No support for multi-line text or text wrapping in a single call.")
  :usecases ("Draw score, timer, or debug info on the HUD." "Label cards or entities with names or descriptions." "Render dialogue or subtitle text." "Build a text-based menu or overlay.")
  :related ("rasterize-text" "surface/paint-text" "surface/curtain" "surface/dim" "fb/text" "text/measure" "text/wrap")
  :learn (:concept "Direct painting: how to render text to the surface with layout and styling control." :prerequisites ("(core)" "surface/paint-text") :progression "Learn rasterize-text to measure text before drawing; then surface/paint-text for lower-level control; then card/open for text inside interactive cards.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator is building a HUD that must show 'Score: 42' at the top of the surface, aligned to the center, in red. The operator asks: which verb draws a styled string to the surface with position and color keywords? Not fb/text (that targets the raw framebuffer, not the surface abstraction), not sprite composition (overkill for a label)."
     :program "(define (draw-hud score)\n  (text/draw (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score))\n             'at: '(160 20)\n             'color: '#xFF0000\n             'align: 'center))\n(draw-hud 42)"
     :explanation "The routine composes the label string, then paints it to the surface at coordinate (160,20), red, centered. text/draw handles the keyword-argument parsing, the color coercion, the alignment offset, and the rasterization. The return value is 'ok on success, an error tuple on failure — the caller can dispatch."
     :meta "Sibling fb/text writes to the pixel framebuffer directly and does not know about surface abstractions like curtains. Sibling surface/paint-text is the lower-level primitive; text/draw wraps it with the keyword sugar. For a HUD label, text/draw is the correct level of abstraction.")
    (:eng "HUD paints in a game loop. Audit: pending-visual returns mean the paint deferred; a critical HUD should be flushed via a followup surface flush."
     :math "text/draw : String × Kwargs → {ok, pending, error}."
     :cs "IO effect; state-changing on the surface buffer."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'render a symbolic value into its visual form on a target surface.'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "text draw" :code "(text/draw \"Hi\" 'at: '(10 10))")
       (:domain "sprite draw at position" :code "(fb/sprite 10 10 'hero)")
       (:domain "map projection — model to view" :code "(define (project x y camera-x camera-y) (list (- x camera-x) (- y camera-y)))\n(project 100 50 60 20)"))
     :explanation "In each rung a symbolic entity — a string, a sprite id, a world coordinate — is committed to a visual target at a chosen position. The shape 'symbol to pixels at coordinate' is universal in every rendering system."
     :meta "The shape transfers because every rendering pipeline has this render-and-place step. What differs is what's being drawn.")
    (:eng "The final render step in any UI or game loop."
     :math "A morphism from an abstract-representation space to a screen-coordinate space."
     :cs "This is the terminal step of a scene-graph traversal."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "text/draw called twice at the same position with the same string is idempotent on the output pixels."
     :program "(text/draw \"Hi\" 'at: '(10 10) 'color: '#xFFFFFF)\n(text/draw \"Hi\" 'at: '(10 10) 'color: '#xFFFFFF)\n'ok"
     :invariant "∀ s, at, color. draw(s,at,color); draw(s,at,color) ≡ draw(s,at,color) on the resulting pixel buffer."
     :meta "Idempotence on identical paints. See book-of-code ch on rendering idempotence.")
    (:eng "This is what makes 'always redraw the HUD from state' safe: doubling up the same paint doesn't produce visual doubling."
     :math "Idempotence: f(f(x)) = f(x)."
     :cs "Idempotent paint is what makes React-style whole-frame render safe."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "text/draw paints a styled string to the surface."
     :composition "(define (labeled-value label value x y)\n  (text/draw label 'at: (list x y))\n  (text/draw (number->string value) 'at: (list (+ x 60) y) 'align: 'right))\n(labeled-value \"score\" 42 10 10)"
     :emergent "A labeled-value pair widget: label on the left, right-aligned value on the right. The pattern is 'named field.'"
     :meta "This is the labeled-field family — same shape as CSS label+input pairs, gauge readouts, JSON key-value display. See book-of-composition ch on field widgets.")
    (:eng "Any dashboard row is a compose of labeled fields."
     :math "Composition of two positioned draws yields a compound widget."
     :cs "The base widget of every dashboard UI framework."))
)

(verb
  :name "fb/text"
  :library "text"
  :kind "io"
  :signature "(fb/text x y string [:font font] [:color color] [:scale n]) -> 'ok"
  :summary "Draw a string of characters or emoji directly onto the framebuffer at (x, y)."
  :explanation "fb/text is the framebuffer-native text verb: it takes a string (letters, digits, punctuation, or emoji — anything the current font can rasterize) and paints it pixel-by-pixel onto the framebuffer at position (x, y). Unlike text/draw, which targets the surface abstraction, fb/text writes into the raw framebuffer under the same coordinate system as fb/rect, fb/pixel, and fb/sprite. Emoji glyphs are drawn using the emoji font when :font is 'default; monospaced letters use the bitmap font in :font 'mono. The :scale keyword multiplies glyph pixel size (integer scaling). Returns 'ok."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(fb/text 10 10 \"hello\")" :note "Draw the word hello at pixel (10, 10) using the default font.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(fb/text 50 40 \"score: 42\" :font font/mono :color 'white)" :note "Draw a monospaced HUD label in white.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (draw-title s x y)\n  (fb/text x y s :font font/big :scale 2)\n  (fb/text x (+ y 30) \"press start\" :font font/tiny))\n(draw-title \"MOTOI\" 40 20)" :note "Compose two glyph sizes for a title screen; large title, small prompt.")
  )
  :caveats ("Emoji glyphs require the runtime's emoji font to be loaded; missing glyphs render as a placeholder tofu box." "Position (x, y) is the top-left corner of the first glyph's bounding box, not a baseline." ":scale must be a positive integer; fractional values are floored." "fb/text does not clip: strings that extend past the framebuffer edge are silently truncated at the boundary.")
  :drawbacks ("No word-wrapping; use text/wrap first, then fb/text on each line." "No kerning between glyphs; monospaced fonts look identical, proportional fonts may look loose." "Redrawing a moving string every frame is cheap for short strings, expensive for long ones (bounded by width * height * scale²).")
  :usecases ("HUD score, timer, lives display." "Speech bubbles above sprites and entities." "Emoji particles or reactive glyphs anchored to positions." "Title cards and menu labels.")
  :related ("text/draw" "text/measure" "text/wrap" "font/default" "font/mono" "font/big" "font/tiny" "fb/rect" "fb/pixel")
  :learn (:concept "Framebuffer text: same drawing surface as pixels and rectangles, but the atomic unit is a glyph." :prerequisites ("fb/rect" "fb/pixel") :progression "Learn text/measure to compute a string's width before drawing, then text/wrap to break long strings across lines, then compose with motion/move-to to animate glyphs.")

(verb
  :name "text/measure"
  :library "text"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(text/measure string [:font font] [:scale n]) -> (width height)"
  :summary "Measure the pixel width and height a string would occupy if drawn with the given font and scale."
  :explanation "text/measure is a pure, side-effect-free query: it takes a string and returns a two-element list (width height) in pixels, matching exactly what fb/text or text/draw would paint. Use it to position text (center a title, right-align a score, bound a speech bubble) or to decide when to wrap. The measurement respects the font's per-glyph advance widths (proportional fonts return exact widths; monospaced fonts return character-count × cell-width). Emoji glyphs measure at their bitmap size."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(text/measure \"hello\")" :note "Returns something like (30 8) — 30 pixels wide, 8 tall, in the default font.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (draw-centered s cx y)\n  (let ((wh (text/measure s)))\n    (fb/text (- cx (quotient (car wh) 2)) y s)))\n(draw-centered \"MOTOI\" 200 40)" :note "Center a string horizontally around cx by measuring first, then subtracting half the width.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (fit-in-box s box-w box-h)\n  (let loop ((scale 4))\n    (let ((wh (text/measure s :font font/big :scale scale)))\n      (if (or (> (car wh) box-w) (> (cadr wh) box-h))\n          (if (<= scale 1) 1 (loop (- scale 1)))\n          scale))))\n(fit-in-box \"long-title-text\" 120 40)" :note "Binary-friendly loop: find the largest integer scale that keeps the string inside a bounding box.")
  )
  :caveats ("Pure: does not draw; you must call fb/text or text/draw afterward." "Returns pixel counts, not character counts." "For proportional fonts the width depends on which glyphs are in the string; two strings of equal length can measure differently.")
  :drawbacks ("Measurements are per-string; no per-glyph decomposition is exposed." "Does not account for line wrapping; measure each line separately after text/wrap." "Assumes the font is already loaded; missing fonts fall back to defaults and measurements change.")
  :usecases ("Centering, right-aligning, or padding text." "Deciding whether a label fits in a UI slot before drawing." "Sizing speech bubbles or tooltip boxes around their content." "Choosing a font scale that fits inside a fixed region.")
  :related ("fb/text" "text/draw" "text/wrap" "font/default" "font/mono" "font/big" "font/tiny")
  :learn (:concept "Measurement before drawing — a general principle for laying out anything spatial." :prerequisites ("fb/text") :progression "Learn text/wrap to break long strings, then compose measure + wrap + draw for full layout control.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator needs to center a title horizontally on a 320-pixel-wide screen. The title's exact width depends on the font and the specific characters. The operator asks: which verb tells the pixel width without drawing? Not fb/text (that draws), not text/wrap (that reflows into a list)."
     :program "(define (draw-centered s y)\n  (let ((wh (text/measure s :font font/big)))\n    (fb/text (- 160 (quotient (car wh) 2)) y s :font font/big)))\n(draw-centered \"MOTOI\" 20)"
     :explanation "The routine measures the string, computes half the width, subtracts from screen center (160), and draws at the resulting x. text/measure returns (width height); the caller can use either. Because measure is pure, it can be called before or after any draw without side effects."
     :meta "Sibling fb/text draws — you'd have to draw offscreen and read pixels to measure indirectly, which is a hack. Sibling text/wrap breaks strings into lines but gives a list, not a pixel size. text/measure is the pure query.")
    (:eng "Any layout code that centers, right-aligns, or bounds text uses measure."
     :math "text/measure : String × Kwargs → (ℕ × ℕ)."
     :cs "Pure; O(n) in string length."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'query the size of a value without producing it.'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "text measurement" :code "(text/measure \"hello\")")
       (:domain "sprite bounding box" :code "(list 'sprite-w 32 'sprite-h 32)")
       (:domain "list length before allocation" :code "(length (list 1 2 3))"))
     :explanation "In each rung the caller wants the size of something in order to decide how to place or store it. Text width, sprite bounds, list length — all shape queries without side effect."
     :meta "The shape transfers because 'measure before commit' is universal in every layout system.")
    (:eng "Layout systems, memory allocators, capacity planners."
     :math "The size function is a homomorphism from container to natural numbers."
     :cs "Cheap pure size queries are what make lay-out algorithms feasible."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "text/measure is pure: same inputs produce same outputs, and the surface state is not observed."
     :program "(define first (text/measure \"hello\"))\n(fb/text 0 0 \"noise\")\n(define second (text/measure \"hello\"))\n(equal? first second)"
     :invariant "∀ s, kw. text/measure(s, kw) does not depend on framebuffer state and is deterministic on inputs."
     :meta "Purity of measure. See book-of-code ch on pure vs effectful verbs.")
    (:eng "This is what makes text/measure safe to call in any layout routine — its result cannot depend on when it's called."
     :math "Functions are deterministic (well-defined outputs)."
     :cs "Purity enables memoization and pre-computation."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "text/measure returns pixel dimensions."
     :composition "(define (fit-scale s box-w)\n  (let loop ((scale 4))\n    (let ((wh (text/measure s :font font/big :scale scale)))\n      (if (or (> (car wh) box-w) (= scale 1)) scale (loop (- scale 1))))))\n(fit-scale \"long title\" 100)"
     :emergent "A binary-search-like fit: find largest scale that fits. The pattern is 'iterative sizing to fit.'"
     :meta "This is the fitter family — same shape as CSS max-width sizing, auto-fit in spreadsheets. See book-of-composition ch on iterative sizing.")
    (:eng "Every 'scale text to fit box' UI stage."

(verb
  :name "text/wrap"
  :library "text"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(text/wrap string max-width [:font font] [:scale n]) -> (line1 line2 ...)"
  :summary "Break a long string into a list of lines that each fit within max-width pixels."
  :explanation "text/wrap takes a string and a maximum pixel width, and returns a list of strings — one per line — where each line's rendered width is guaranteed to be ≤ max-width. Wrapping happens at word boundaries when possible; words longer than max-width are broken mid-word as a fallback. The verb is pure: it computes the wrap plan but does not draw. Pair it with fb/text (once per returned line, incrementing y by line-height) to render wrapped paragraphs, dialogue, and long labels. Emoji glyphs are treated as single-word atoms and never split."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(text/wrap \"the quick brown fox\" 40)" :note "Returns something like (\"the quick\" \"brown fox\") for a narrow column.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (draw-paragraph s x y width line-height)\n  (let loop ((lines (text/wrap s width)) (dy 0))\n    (cond ((null? lines) 'ok)\n          (else (fb/text x (+ y dy) (car lines))\n                (loop (cdr lines) (+ dy line-height))))))\n(draw-paragraph \"once upon a time in a forest lived a small fox\" 20 20 120 10)" :note "Draw a wrapped paragraph starting at (20, 20), each line 10 pixels below the last.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (speech-bubble sprite s)\n  (let* ((lines (text/wrap s 100 :font font/tiny))\n         (h (* (length lines) 8))\n         (sx (entity/x sprite))\n         (sy (- (entity/y sprite) h 6)))\n    (fb/rect (- sx 2) (- sy 2) 104 (+ h 4) 'white)\n    (let loop ((ls lines) (dy 0))\n      (cond ((null? ls) 'ok)\n            (else (fb/text sx (+ sy dy) (car ls) :font font/tiny :color 'black)\n                  (loop (cdr ls) (+ dy 8)))))))\n(speech-bubble 'hero \"I found the flower you were looking for!\")" :note "Compose wrap + rect + text into a positioned speech bubble that hovers above an entity.")
  )
  :caveats ("Wrapping preserves whitespace between words but does not preserve embedded newlines; split on newline first if the source string has them." "Words longer than max-width are broken mid-word without hyphenation." "Emoji glyphs are atomic and are placed at the start of a new line if they don't fit on the current one.")
  :drawbacks ("Does not compute total pixel height; call (length result) * line-height yourself." "No indent or hanging-indent support; each line starts at the same x." "Not language-aware; wraps by ASCII whitespace and does not know about non-breaking spaces or hyphens.")
  :usecases ("Speech bubbles and dialogue boxes." "Long tooltips or help text in a bounded column." "Book-page rendering — long prose broken into scroll-friendly lines." "Chat log rendering.")
  :related ("fb/text" "text/measure" "text/draw" "font/tiny" "font/default")
  :learn (:concept "Wrapping is a plan; drawing is the execution. Separate the two so you can inspect or transform the plan." :prerequisites ("text/measure" "fb/text") :progression "Compose wrap + measure + draw into paragraph, bubble, and page layouts; then animate line-by-line reveal with motion/with-pace.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator needs to display dialogue text inside a fixed-width speech bubble. The text may be longer than the bubble. The operator asks: which verb breaks the string at word boundaries into a list of lines that fit? Not text/measure (returns size only), not string-split (splits on a character, not on width)."
     :program "(define (bubble x y w text)\n  (let ((lines (text/wrap text w)))\n    (for-each (lambda (i) (fb/text x (+ y (* i 10)) (list-ref lines i)))\n              (iota (length lines)))))\n(bubble 10 10 60 \"the quick brown fox jumps\")"
     :explanation "The routine wraps the text to width w, then draws each line offset by 10 pixels. text/wrap does the width-aware line breaking; the routine handles positioning. The two responsibilities are cleanly separated."
     :meta "Sibling string-split on space would need the caller to measure and rebuild lines manually. Sibling text/measure alone doesn't wrap. text/wrap is the width-aware breaker.")
    (:eng "Speech bubbles, tooltips, paragraph text."
     :math "text/wrap : String × ℕ × Kwargs → [String]. Each line's measured width ≤ max-width."
     :cs "O(n) in string length; pure."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'break a linear input into chunks that each satisfy a size constraint.'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "text wrap" :code "(text/wrap \"the quick brown\" 40)")
       (:domain "audio buffer chunking" :code "(list 'chunk-1 'chunk-2 'chunk-3)")
       (:domain "MTU packet fragmentation" :code "(define (fragment data mtu) (if (<= (length data) mtu) (list data) (list (list-head data mtu) (list-tail data mtu))))\n(fragment (list 1 2 3 4 5) 3)"))
     :explanation "In each rung the caller has a stream too large to send/display in one piece, and needs to break it into constraint-satisfying chunks. Text lines, audio buffers, network packets — same shape."
     :meta "The shape transfers because 'break to satisfy a size constraint' is the shape of every chunking/fragmentation problem.")
    (:eng "Chunking pipelines in networking, storage, and rendering."
     :math "A partition of the input into ordered chunks each within a bound."
     :cs "Fragmentation is a fundamental storage/transport concern."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "Each output line's measured width is ≤ max-width, unless the line consists of a single unbreakable word."

     :emergent "A page renderer: wrap plus per-line draw. The pattern is 'reflow then paint.'"

(verb
  :name "text/rasterize"
  :library "text"
  :kind "pure"
  :signature "(text/rasterize str [font] [color]) -> raster"
  :summary "Turn a string into a pixel raster — mirror of sprite/rasterize for text. Returns a record with width, height, font, color, and a sparse list of (x y color) cells."
  :explanation "`text/rasterize` is the text counterpart to sprite/rasterize: it takes a string and produces a raster in the same record shape a sprite would produce, so callers can compose text and sprites uniformly through one pipeline. The raster is an alist with keys :width, :height, :font, :color, and :cells; :cells is a list of (x y color) triples, sparse (only opaque cells present). The actual glyph pixel data routes through the adapter seam — the browser adapter can ship real Canvas bitmaps, the terminal adapter can ship cell-grid glyphs, and the default no-op adapter produces a plausibly-shaped solid rectangle (using measureText for dimensions) so headless tests still work. Empty string returns a zero-sized raster with an empty cell list."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(text/rasterize \"hi\")" :note "Rasterize the string \"hi\" using the default font and color. Returns an alist ((:width W) (:height H) (:font default) (:color \"#14\") (:cells (...)))")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((raster (text/rasterize \"WIN!\" font/big 'gold)))\n  (list (cadr (assq ':width raster))\n        (cadr (assq ':height raster))\n        (length (cadr (assq ':cells raster)))))" :note "Rasterize with a font and color, then extract width, height, and cell count from the raster. Useful for pre-computing layout before you stamp.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (paint-raster raster ox oy)\n  (let ((cells (cadr (assq ':cells raster))))\n    (for-each (lambda (cell)\n                (let ((x (+ ox (car cell)))\n                      (y (+ oy (cadr cell)))\n                      (c (caddr cell)))\n                  (fb/pixel x y c)))\n              cells)))\n(paint-raster (text/rasterize \"score\" font/tiny 'white) 10 10)" :note "Stamp a text raster at (10, 10) by iterating its cells and painting one pixel each. Same shape as stamping a sprite raster.")
  )
  :caveats ("Pure: does not draw. Call fb/text or paint the cells yourself if you need pixels on the framebuffer." "The default adapter produces a SOLID BLOCK raster (dimensions from measureText, no glyph shape). Real hosts override via setAdapters to ship exact bitmaps." "Cell list can be large for long strings at big fonts (width * height cells for the default stub). Prefer caching if you rasterize repeatedly." "Emoji glyphs measure via the adapter's measureText; without a real host they occupy the default 6px cell width like ASCII.")
  :drawbacks ("Does not expose per-glyph decomposition; only the whole-string raster." "Cell list is dense in the fallback (every pixel in the bounding box); real host overrides can be sparse (only opaque glyph pixels), so cell count is implementation-dependent." "No cross-frame animation seam; if you want a text raster to animate, re-call each frame or wrap in a tween.")
  :usecases ("Compose text and sprites into one pipeline: rasterize a label the same way you'd rasterize a sprite, then stamp both through the same code path." "Pre-compute layout: measure the raster once, then stamp many copies at different positions." "Custom effects: iterate over the raster's cells and modify color per-cell before stamping (e.g. rainbow text)." "Snapshot text for tests: the raster is a plain data record, easy to assert against.")
  :related ("sprite/rasterize" "fb/text" "text/measure" "text/wrap" "font/default")
  :learn (:concept "Text and sprites as the same data shape: a raster is a bag of (x y color) cells, regardless of whether it came from glyphs or hand-drawn art." :prerequisites ("text/measure" "sprite/rasterize" "fb/pixel") :progression "Learn text/rasterize; then compose it with sprite/rasterize into a single stamping loop; then layer effects (per-cell color transforms, alpha, rotation) uniformly.")
  :library "core"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :any
  :content-rating :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :provenance :added-2026-07-16-from-mapping-approval
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "The operator wants to compose text and sprites through one uniform pipeline — same code path for both. The operator asks: which verb produces a raster from a string in the same shape sprite/rasterize produces from a sprite? Not text/draw (draws directly), not text/measure (returns only dimensions)."
     :program "(define raster (text/rasterize \"HI\" font/big 'yellow))\n(define cells (cadr (assq ':cells raster)))\n(length cells)"
     :explanation "Line 1 rasterizes 'HI' into a record with :width, :height, :font, :color, and :cells. Line 2 extracts the cells (a list of (x y color) triples). Line 3 counts them. The record shape matches sprite/rasterize's output, so downstream code can process both."
     :meta "Sibling text/draw draws directly, no data. Sibling text/measure only returns size. Sibling would be a manual glyph iteration — but that requires reimplementing font raster logic. text/rasterize is the data-shape-uniform primitive.")
    (:eng "Any pipeline where text and sprite share code — for example, effect layers that stamp both — uses this."
     :math "text/rasterize : String × Font × Color → Raster."
     :cs "Pure; returns a data record."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape being demonstrated is 'reification — turning what would be a draw side-effect into a data value.'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "text rasterize" :code "(text/rasterize \"hi\" font/default 'white)")
       (:domain "sprite rasterize" :code "(sprite/rasterize 'hero)")
       (:domain "computation as a data structure" :code "(list 'add 1 2)"))
     :explanation "In each rung a would-be action is turned into a data value. Text pixels, sprite pixels, computation — all reified into inspectable data before the action is committed."
     :meta "The shape transfers because reification is the shape of every 'plan then commit' architecture.")
    (:eng "Any pipeline that wants to inspect or transform before committing."
     :math "Reification is the isomorphism between actions and their descriptions."
     :cs "Same shape as JSX (UI as data), AST (code as data)."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "text/rasterize is pure: same inputs give same output, and no side effect is observable."
     :program "(define a (text/rasterize \"hi\" font/default 'white))\n(define b (text/rasterize \"hi\" font/default 'white))\n(equal? a b)"
     :invariant "∀ s, f, c. text/rasterize(s, f, c) is deterministic."
     :meta "Purity of rasterize. See book-of-code ch on pure rasterizers.")
    (:eng "The audit: rasterize must be memoizable — same string, same result."
     :math "Determinism means it's a proper function."
     :cs "Purity enables caching; expensive rasterizations can be precomputed."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "text/rasterize turns a string into a raster record."
     :composition "(define (stamp-raster raster ox oy)\n  (for-each (lambda (cell) (fb/pixel (+ ox (car cell)) (+ oy (cadr cell)) (caddr cell)))\n            (cadr (assq ':cells raster))))\n(stamp-raster (text/rasterize \"HI\" font/big 'gold) 10 10)"
     :emergent "A uniform stamp pipeline: rasterize once, iterate cells, stamp pixels. Same code works for sprite rasters. The pattern is 'reified compositor.'"
     :meta "This is the immediate-mode-rendering family — same shape as GPU vertex buffers. See book-of-composition ch on immediate mode.")
    (:eng "Any rendering system that uniformly handles text and sprite."
     :math "Cells are a sparse-matrix representation."
     :cs "Uniform data means uniform code paths downstream.")))

(verb
  :name "tick/ease"
  :library "tick"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(tick/ease name t) → scalar | 'nan"
  :summary "Apply a named Penner easing function to t ∈ [0, 1]; unknown name yields 'nan."
  :explanation "Penner easing functions smooth time-based animations. Given a name (symbol) and a normalized time `t` between 0 and 1, this verb returns the eased value. Common names: 'linear, 'ease-in-quad, 'ease-out-quad, 'ease-in-out-cubic, etc. Unknown names return the symbol 'nan; invalid `t` also yields 'nan. Use this to control animation curves in motion, morphs, and choreography."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(tick/ease 'linear 0.5)" :note "Linear easing at 50% progress returns 0.5.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (ease-card-in frame duration easing-name)\n  (let ((t (/ frame duration)))\n    (if (<= t 1.0)\n      (tick/ease easing-name t)\n      1.0)))\n(ease-card-in 30 60 'ease-out-quad)" :note "Compute eased progress over a 60-frame duration with ease-out-quad.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (morph-position t easing-name start end)\n  (let ((eased-t (tick/ease easing-name t)))\n    (if (eq? eased-t 'nan)\n      start\n      (+ start (* eased-t (- end start))))))\n(morph-position 0.3 'ease-in-out-cubic 100 200)" :note "Interpolate between two values using an eased time; fallback to start on invalid easing.")
  )
  :caveats ("Named easing functions are case-insensitive symbols." "`t` should be in [0, 1]; values outside this range return 'nan." "Unknown easing name returns 'nan, not an error; check result before using." "Easing names are registered by the system; custom easing is not (yet) supported.")
  :drawbacks ("Only works with `t` normalized to [0, 1]; you must handle time rescaling." "No support for easing vectors or colors directly; use for each dimension or channel separately." "Limited easing library; if a specific curve is needed, may need to interpolate or combine.")
  :usecases ("Smooth card transitions and morphs." "Create expressive motion timing (ease-in-out for natural acceleration)." "Animate HUD elements with polish." "Build dialogue or narrative sequences with paced reveals.")
  :related ("tick/osc" "tick/sine" "tick/phase" "motion/with-feel" "motion/with-pace")
  :learn (:concept "Easing curves: how to map linear time into nonlinear (perceptually smoother) motion." :prerequisites ("(core)" "tick/phase") :progression "Learn tick/sine and tick/osc to generate periodic motion; then motion/with-feel to apply easing to card transitions.")
  :row-2-audit ((:problem "A card fades in and looks robotic. The design brief says the fade should feel like a hand placing something down. The operator has a normalized progress value t and needs to shape it so early t moves fast and late t decelerates."
                 :program "(define (fade-alpha t) (tick/ease 'ease-out-cubic t))\n(fade-alpha 0.25)\n(fade-alpha 0.75)"
                 :explanation "Line 1 defines a helper that takes a linear progress t in [0,1] and returns an eased value. Line 2 samples the curve at 25% — with ease-out-cubic this returns ~0.578, so the card is already more than half faded in at a quarter of the duration. Line 3 samples at 75% and returns ~0.984, so the last quarter of time barely moves alpha — that is the deceleration. The perceived effect is that the card lands soft."
                 :meta "Reaching for tick/sine or tick/phase instead would give a linear ramp or a sinusoidal wobble. Neither shapes the arrival. tick/ease is the honest answer because it consults a named Penner curve library, which is the vocabulary designers already share for arrival shape. Choosing linear would falsify the design brief; choosing sine would introduce a wobble the operator did not ask for.")
                (:eng "The operator can log the eased value each frame and see the deceleration in the numbers. If a stakeholder complains the fade feels wrong, the fix is a single symbol swap: 'ease-out-cubic' → 'ease-in-out-sine'. That is a one-line audit trail." :math "The eased function e:[0,1]→[0,1] must be surjective and (for arrival) satisfy e'(0) large, e'(1) small. Named Penner curves are chosen precisely so their derivatives at endpoints match perceptual intent." :cs "tick/ease is a table lookup keyed by symbol; the effect kind is pure computation on a scalar, O(1) per frame."))
  :row-3-dimension ((:setup "Mapping progress-in-time through a shaping function is a shape that shows up in many substrates. It is time-remapping."
                     :rungs ((:domain "tick" :code "(tick/ease 'ease-out-cubic 0.5)")
                             (:domain "audio envelope" :code "(let ((t 0.5)) (* t t (- 3 (* 2 t))))")
                             (:domain "monotone lattice" :code "(define (mono f x) (f x))\n(mono (lambda (t) (- 1 (expt (- 1 t) 3))) 0.5)"))
                     :explanation "In tick's rung, a symbol names a curve and the verb evaluates it at t=0.5. In audio, an ADSR envelope segment is exactly the same shape — a monotonically-increasing map from normalized time to normalized level. In the lattice rung, a monotone function on [0,1] preserves order: if a≤b then f(a)≤f(b). All three read the same input and shape it, keeping the endpoints pinned."
                     :meta "The shape transfers because each rung asks the same question: 'given a normalized progress, how much of the effect has happened by now?' The verb name changes; the shape does not. That is why an animator, an audio engineer, and a mathematician can look at these three lines and see the same thing.")
                    (:eng "One tool (a shaping function) covers three surfaces (motion, audio, order theory). Ship-time consequence: an on-call engineer who knows animation can debug an audio envelope." :math "Monotonicity + boundary conditions f(0)=0, f(1)=1 is the essential frame; the specific polynomial or trig form is decoration." :cs "The function is a pure map with O(1) evaluation; whether the closure holds a cubic or a sine, the interface contract is identical."))
  :row-4-proof ((:claim "For any registered Penner curve, evaluating at the two boundary points returns those exact boundaries: e(0)=0 and e(1)=1. This is the endpoint-pinning invariant, and it is what makes easing safe to compose with an interval [lo,hi] via lo + e(t)·(hi−lo)."
                 :program "(define (check-endpoints name)\n  (let ((a (tick/ease name 0))\n        (b (tick/ease name 1)))\n    (and (= a 0) (= b 1))))\n(and (check-endpoints 'linear)\n     (check-endpoints 'ease-in-quad)\n     (check-endpoints 'ease-out-cubic)\n     (check-endpoints 'ease-in-out-sine))"
                 :invariant "∀ name ∈ registered-Penner-names . e_name(0) = 0 ∧ e_name(1) = 1"
                 :meta "A curve that violates this invariant would break the remap formula lo + e·(hi−lo). Falsification is one counter-example: a curve that returns 0.02 at t=0 would leak into the target range and every animation starting from that curve would jump. The CS pattern name is 'boundary-preserving monotone map'. Book-of-motion ch 4 covers named Penner easings and their boundary conditions.")
                (:eng "A regression test on this invariant catches any registry corruption; add it to CI as a smoke test." :math "Boundary conditions plus monotonicity define the class; specific coefficients do not matter for the invariant." :cs "Table-driven lookup + pure evaluation; the invariant is preserved by construction if the table is built correctly."))
  :row-5-emergence ((:base "tick/ease shapes a normalized progress via a named curve."
                     :composition "(define (fade-in-then-out entity total-frames)\n  (lambda (f)\n    (let* ((t (tick/phase f total-frames))\n           (up (tick/ease 'ease-out-cubic (min 1 (* 2 t))))\n           (down (tick/ease 'ease-in-cubic (max 0 (- (* 2 t) 1)))))\n      (- up down))))\n((fade-in-then-out 'ghost 120) 90)"
                     :emergent "A staged envelope — the composition of tick/phase (linear clock), tick/ease (up-shape), and tick/ease again (down-shape) produces an attack-and-release envelope that neither verb carries alone."
                     :meta "This is the same family as an ADSR envelope, or in animation a lift-and-place gesture. Cross-reference book-of-composition ch 7 (envelope shapes from primitive oscillators). Familiar analog: an audio ADSR patch cable in a modular synth.")
                    (:eng "The engineer gets a reusable envelope generator by chaining three primitives; the shape is transparent in the code." :math "The result is a composition e_down ∘ φ − e_up ∘ φ where φ is the phase function; the two easings must share boundary conditions." :cs "Higher-order: fade-in-then-out returns a closure; each verb in the chain is O(1) so the closure is O(1) per frame.")))

(verb
  :name "tick/lissajous"
  :library "tick"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(tick/lissajous freq-x freq-y phase-x phase-y t) → [x y] | 'nan"
  :summary "Compute a 2-D Lissajous orbit at time `t`; any bad numeric yields 'nan."
  :explanation "A Lissajous curve is traced by two independent sinusoidal oscillators with different frequencies and phases. Given frequencies, phases, and a time `t`, this verb returns the [x, y] point on the curve. Use it for orbital motion, decorative paths, or parametric animation. If any input is non-numeric or invalid, returns 'nan."
  :examples (
