(verb
  :name "tick/mod-n"
  :library "tick"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(tick/mod-n frame n) → int ∈ [0, n-1] | 'nan"
  :summary "Bucket a frame index into [0, n-1] using modulo; n ≤ 0 yields 'nan."
  :explanation "Frame-based timing often needs to cycle through `n` buckets or states. This verb returns frame mod n, clamping the result to [0, n-1]. Use it to drive cycles, loops, or state machines without floating-point math. If `n` ≤ 0 or `frame` is not an integer, returns 'nan."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(tick/mod-n 7 3)" :note "7 mod 3 = 1; bucket index 1 in a 3-state cycle.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (cycle-sprite sprite-id frame num-frames)\n  (let ((frame-index (tick/mod-n frame num-frames)))\n    (if (not (eq? frame-index 'nan))\n      (sprite-set! sprite-id frame-index))))\n(on-frame (lambda (ctx) (cycle-sprite 'walk-cycle (on-frame ctx) 8)))" :note "Animate a sprite by cycling through 8 frames; wrap at 8.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (multi-phase-state frame num-phases phase-fn)\n  (let ((phase (tick/mod-n frame num-phases)))\n    (cond ((eq? phase 'nan) 'error)\n          ((= phase 0) (phase-fn 'start))\n          ((= phase (- num-phases 1)) (phase-fn 'end))\n          (else (phase-fn 'middle)))))\n(multi-phase-state 15 4 display)" :note "Use mod-n to dispatch to different phase handlers in a loop.")
  )
  :caveats ("`frame` must be an integer; floats return 'nan." "`n` must be > 0; n ≤ 0 returns 'nan." "Result is in [0, n-1], not [1, n]; adjust if 1-indexed logic is needed." "Negative `frame` is valid; -1 mod n = n-1.")
  :drawbacks ("Integer-only; if you need floating-point cycling, use `tick/sine` or `tick/triangle` instead." "No built-in phase offset; add frame offset before calling if needed." "Limited to simple modulo; for weighted or non-uniform cycles, use `tick/pattern`.")
  :usecases ("Cycle through sprite frames in an animation loop." "Distribute events across multiple lanes (e.g., every 4th frame goes to lane 0, etc.)." "Implement turn-based game logic (frame mod num-players determines whose turn)." "Pulse or flicker effects with integer cycle counts.")
  :related ("tick/pattern" "tick/phase" "tick/pulse" "on-frame")
  :learn (:concept "Integer-based timing: how to use modulo arithmetic for discrete cycles without floating-point rounding." :prerequisites ("(core)" "modulo") :progression "Learn tick/pulse for duty-cycle timing; then tick/pattern to cycle through lists; then on-frame to tie logic to the render loop.")

   (:problem "A sprite has 8 walk frames and the operator wants to cycle through them once per second at 60 fps. They need frame → sprite-index using integer math only, no rounding drift."

                 :explanation "Line 1 divides the raw frame counter by 8 (each sprite frame holds for 8 render frames) and then buckets the result into [0,7] via tick/mod-n.                 (:eng "Zero drift over any duration; the audit trail is trivially the frame count and the divisor." :math "Integer modulo is exact; there is no round-off." :cs "O(1) per call; the effect kind is pure integer arithmetic."))

                     :explanation "In tick, a frame index becomes a bucket. In the queue metaphor, a task id becomes a worker id — this is how a round-robin dispatcher assigns work. (verb
  :name "tick/pattern"
  :library "tick"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(tick/pattern frame xs) -> element"
  :summary "Cycles through a list, selecting one element per frame using modular indexing."
  :explanation "This verb treats a list as a repeating sequence and returns one element per frame. The frame number is taken modulo the list length, so frame 0 gives xs[0], frame 1 gives xs[1], and when frame reaches the list length, it wraps back to xs[0]. It's the discrete analog of tick/osc: useful for cycling through sprite frames, animation states, color palettes, or note sequences. If the list is empty, returns 'nan."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(on-tick (lambda ()\n  (let ((frame-idx (tick/pattern (frame) '(0 1 2 1))))\n    (entity/sprite! 'player frame-idx))))" :note "Cycles through sprite frames 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, ... forever.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define walk-cycle '((0 0) (1 0) (2 0) (1 0)))\n(on-tick (lambda ()\n  (let ((step (tick/pattern (/ (frame) 5) walk-cycle)))\n    (entity/sprite! 'hero step))))" :note "Slows the cycle by dividing frame by 5; steps through walk frames, changing every 5 ticks.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (color-pulse ctx)\n  (let ((palette '((255 0 0) (255 128 0) (255 255 0) (128 255 0)))\n        (color (tick/pattern (frame) palette)))\n    (entity/set! 'aura 'color color)))\n\n(on-tick color-pulse)" :note "Cycles through a color palette, changing every frame; stores palette in a closure.")
  )
  :caveats ("Empty list returns 'nan; always ensure xs has at least one element." "Frame must be a non-negative integer; negative frames wrap from the end (standard modulo behavior)." "List elements are NOT type-checked; any Scheme value is valid." "Mutation of xs during execution (if supported) will affect future cycles; treat xs as read-only.")
  :drawbacks ("No built-in interpolation: stepping is discrete, not smooth. Use tick/osc or tick/ease for smooth animation." "Cycle always starts at frame 0; no phase offset.   :usecases ("Sprite frame animation (walk cycles, blinking, idle poses)." "Color cycling (LED pulse, gradient sweep, mood lighting)." "State machine stepping (discrete FSM transitions)." "Melody sequencing (repeating note patterns).")
  :related ("tick/osc" "tick/phase" "tick/mod-n" "on-tick" "frame")
  :learn (:concept "Discrete cyclic indexing: select from a list using frame modulo to create repeating sequences." :prerequisites ("on-tick" "frame" "list") :progression "Combine tick/pattern with tick/phase or tick/osc to blend discrete and smooth animation, or use tick/ease for smooth transitions between list elements.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   (:problem "A note sequencer needs to loop through a chord progression. The operator has the list '(C F G C) and wants to select one chord per beat, wrapping forever."
                 :program "(define chords '(C F G C))\n(define (chord-at beat) (tick/pattern beat chords))\n(chord-at 0)\n(chord-at 3)\n(chord-at 4)"
                 :explanation "Line 1 stores the chord progression as a list of symbols. Line 2 defines chord-at to index into that list using tick/pattern with the current beat number. Line 3 at beat 0 returns 'C (the first chord). Line 4 at beat 3 returns 'C again (the fourth chord, which happens to also be C). (verb
  :name "time/delta"
  :library "time"
  :kind "null"
  :signature "(time/delta unit) -> number"
  :summary "Returns the elapsed time since the last frame in the specified unit (ms, s, m, h, d)."
  :explanation "This verb measures the time delta (difference) between the current frame and the previous frame, returning the interval in a named unit: milliseconds (ms), seconds (s), minutes (m), hours (h), or days (d). It is useful for frame-rate-independent animation and simulation: instead of assuming fixed frame duration, multiply velocity or acceleration by the delta to ensure consistent motion regardless of frame rate. The unit parameter is a symbol (or string) that specifies the output unit."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(on-tick (lambda ()\n  (let ((dt (time/delta 's)))\n    (entity/move! 'ball (list (* 100 dt) 0)))))" :note "Ball moves 100 units per second, regardless of frame rate.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(on-tick (lambda ()\n  (let* ((dt (time/delta 'ms))\n         (acceleration 200)\n         (new-vel (+ (entity/vel 'player) (* acceleration dt 0.001))))\n    (entity/set-vel! 'player new-vel))))" :note "Physics simulation: acceleration applied over milliseconds, scaled to per-frame impulse.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (tick-simulation ctx)\n  (let* ((dt (time/delta 's))\n         (vel (ctx-get 'velocity ctx))\n         (friction 0.99)\n         (new-vel (* vel (expt friction dt)))\n         (pos (+ (ctx-get 'position ctx) (* vel dt))))\n    (next 'tick-simulation (ctx-set 'velocity new-vel (ctx-set 'position pos ctx)))))\n\n(on-tick tick-simulation)" :note "Simulation state machine: delta drives position and velocity decay, independent of frame rate.")
  )
  :caveats ("Unit must be one of: 'ms, 's, 'm, 'h, 'd (or equivalent string symbols)." "Unknown unit may cause an error or 'nan; always validate unit spelling." "First frame may report a large delta if no prior frame time is recorded; initialize timing carefully." "Very slow or paused execution (e.g., debugging breakpoints) may return a large delta; clamp if needed.")
  :drawbacks ("Relies on accurate clock synchronization; system clock skew or manual timing manipulation breaks assumptions." "Conversion between units is fixed; custom units are not supported." "If frame rate varies dramatically, large deltas may cause instability (overshooting). Apply max-delta clamping: (min dt max-dt)." "Not suitable for real-time hard constraints; elapsed time is measured after computation.")
  :usecases ("Frame-rate-independent physics and animation." "Velocity and acceleration simulation." "Adaptive timing loops (slow on low-end devices, fast on high-end)." "Measuring elapsed time in user-friendly units.")
  :related ("time/when" "time/during" "time/every-ms" "on-tick" "frame")
  :learn (:concept "Frame-rate-independent delta time: multiply rates and accelerations by dt to decouple simulation from frame rate." :prerequisites ("on-tick") :progression "Master time/delta for physics; then learn time/every-ms (fixed intervals) and time/when (event timing) for higher-level temporal control.")

(verb
  :name "time/during"
  :library "time"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(time/during predicate clause) → clause"
  :summary "Create a clause that runs its body only while a condition remains true."
  :explanation "time/during wraps a predicate and a clause together, gating execution: the clause fires each frame only as long as the predicate evaluates to truthy. Once the predicate becomes false, the clause stops running. This is useful for time-boxed animations, conditional behaviors, or guarded state machines. It composes with big-bang and other loop forms."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/during (lambda () (< (game/frame (ctx-get 'game-id ctx)) 60))\n                       (to-draw (lambda (s) '(render)))))))" :note "Run the render clause only for the first 60 frames.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/during (lambda () (ctx-get 'is-active? ctx))\n                       (to-draw (lambda (s) '(render))))\n          (on-key (lambda (k s) s)))))" :note "Render while is-active? is true in state; other clauses run unconditionally.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (let ((game-id (big-bang\n                   (list (time/during\n                          (lambda () (and (ctx-get 'running? ctx)\n                                         (> (ctx-get 'health ctx) 0)))\n                          (to-draw (lambda (s) (paint-grid s))))\n                        (time/until (lambda () (= (ctx-get 'health ctx) 0))\n                                    (to-draw (lambda (s) '(game-over))))))))\n    game-id))" :note "Nest time/during and time/until to model a two-phase loop: active gameplay, then game-over screen.")
  )
  :caveats ("The predicate is re-evaluated every frame; side-effects in the predicate will run each frame." "If the predicate is false on the first frame, the clause never runs." "Once false, the clause remains dormant for the rest of the loop; there is no re-activation.")
  :drawbacks ("For one-time delayed actions, time/until or time/when may be clearer." "Predicates that depend on mutable state must be careful about state consistency.")
  :usecases ("Conditional animations that stop when a flag becomes false." "Guarding a rendering phase while an entity is alive." "Time-boxing a behavior: run input handling only during active gameplay.")
  :related ("time/until" "time/when" "time/every-ms" "big-bang" "to-draw" "on-key")
  :learn (:concept "Conditional gate on a clause: predicate-driven activation." :prerequisites ("big-bang" "to-draw") :progression "Learn time/until next (the inverse — run until a condition), then time/when (one-shot trigger).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "Input handling should only run while the game is active. The operator's problem is that the on-key clause fires during the game-over screen and lets the player interact with a paused world. The audit question is whether the gate is time/during (dormant while false) or time/when (fires once) — these look similar but time/when would fire the input clause exactly once and then never again."
     :program "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/during (lambda () (ctx-get 'is-active? ctx))\n                       (on-key (lambda (k s) s))))))\n(display 'started) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines the entrypoint. Line 2 wraps the on-key clause in time/during, so it is dormant whenever is-active? is false. Line 3 marks the boot for the log."
     :meta "Why time/during and not time/when: time/when would fire once and stop; time/during keeps the gate live for the whole loop, opening and closing with the predicate.")
    (:eng "Log the boundary — the tick where the predicate flips — so the audit can confirm the clause went silent at that tick."
     :math "The clause's active set is the preimage of #t under the predicate over the tick sequence."
     :cs "The CS pattern is guarded execution. Related: switch, gate, conditional dispatch."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The gated stream: a channel that is only open while a condition holds."
     :rungs ((:domain "time (a clause active while a flag is true)" :code "(time/during pred clause)")
             (:domain "audio (a note that sustains while the key is held)" :code "(sustain-while key-down)")
             (:domain "logic (an indicator function 1_A · f)" :code "1_A(x) · f(x)"))
     :explanation "In the runtime, the clause runs while the predicate holds. In audio, the note sustains while the key is held. In logic, an indicator function is the shape that multiplies a value by 0 or 1 depending on membership. All three share the shape 'value gated by a truth.'"
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever a stream must be windowed by an external condition.")
    (:eng "Record open and close events. The window is the pair (open-tick, close-tick)."
     :math "1_A · f is the indicator-gated function; its integral is the truncated one."

  :row-4-proof (

(verb
  :name "time/every-ms"
  :library "time"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(time/every-ms milliseconds clause) → clause"
  :summary "Wrap a clause so it fires at most once per N milliseconds."
  :explanation "time/every-ms throttles a clause's execution to a fixed wall-clock interval. The clause is allowed to run at most once every N milliseconds, regardless of frame rate. This decouples behavior from frame rate and is essential for audio polling, network requests, or expensive computations that should not run every frame. The internal timer tracks elapsed wall time, not game frames."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/every-ms 100\n                         (to-draw (lambda (s) (audio-play 'click)))))))" :note "Play a click sound at most once per 100 milliseconds, decoupled from frame rate.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/every-ms 500\n                         (to-draw (lambda (s)\n                                   (let ((count (ctx-get 'poll-count ctx)))\n                                     (ctx-set 'poll-count (+ count 1) s)))))\n          (on-key (lambda (k s) s)))))" :note "Increment a counter every 500ms, while input handling runs every frame.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/every-ms 1000\n                         (to-draw (lambda (s)\n                                   (let ((health (ctx-get 'health s)))\n                                     (if (> health 0)\n                                         (ctx-set 'health (- health 1) s)\n                                         s)))))\n          (time/during (lambda () (ctx-get 'is-active? ctx))\n                       (on-key (lambda (k s) s))))))" :note "Poison damage ticks every second; input handling only while active.   )
  :caveats ("The threshold is wall-clock time, not game frames, so it is immune to frame-rate stutters." "If the loop is paused or suspended, wall time keeps advancing; the clause may fire unexpectedly on resume." "Very small intervals (< 16ms) may appear to fire every frame on 60 Hz displays.")
  :drawbacks ("Cannot be frame-locked; use time/across or on-tick if you need frame-exact timing." "Interval is approximate — actual elapsed time may vary by a few milliseconds.")

(verb
  :name "time/then"
  :library "time"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(time/then clause-a clause-b) → clause"
  :summary "Sequentially compose two clauses: run clause-a, then when it completes, run clause-b."
  :explanation "time/then chains two clauses in sequence, like a promise chain or a state transition. The first clause runs until it returns a 'done' signal (or is consumed); then the second clause takes over. This is a fundamental tool for choreography: multi-step animations, narratives, or state machines where each phase must complete before the next begins. It is composable: (time/then a (time/then b c)) chains three clauses."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/then (to-draw (lambda (s) (paint-grid s)))\n                     (to-draw (lambda (s) '(game-over)))))))" :note "Render the grid, then render game-over. In practice, done signals control the switch.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/then (time/every-ms 500\n                                     (to-draw (lambda (s) (audio-play 'tick))))\n                     (to-draw (lambda (s) (card-emit 'event-finished))))\n          (on-key (lambda (k s) s)))))" :note "Emit a tick every 500ms, then emit an event when the first clause finishes.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/then\n            (time/during (lambda () (< (game/frame (ctx-get 'game-id ctx)) 120))\n                        (to-draw (lambda (s) (paint-grid s))))\n            (time/then\n              (time/every-ms 300 (to-draw (lambda (s) (audio-play 'win))))\n              (to-draw (lambda (s) (card-emit 'game-complete)))))\n          (on-key (lambda (k s) s)))))" :note "Choreograph: play grid for 120 frames, then emit victory sound every 300ms, then emit completion event.")
  )
  :caveats ("The done signal is typically generated by time/until or explicitly returned from a clause." "If neither clause ever produces done, the second clause will never run." "Nesting time/then deeply can become hard to read; consider extracted helper predicates.")
  :drawbacks ("Strict sequencing: both clauses cannot run concurrently. Use a list of clauses for parallel behaviors." "Debugging long chains can be tedious; add logging or breakpoints in the transition predicates.")
  :usecases ("Cutscene choreography: intro animation → dialogue → action sequence." "State machines with multi-step behaviors: idle → attack-startup → attack → recovery." "Tutorial sequences: show instruction → wait for confirmation → advance." "Loading screens: splash → progress bar → ready.")
  :related ("time/during" "time/until" "time/when" "big-bang" "done")

     :explanation "Line 1 defines the entrypoint. Line 2 sequences hint then reward so reward can only start after hint reports done. Line 3 confirms the setup."
     :meta "Why time/then and not a list: a list runs both clauses each tick; time/then keeps the second dormant until the first finishes.")
    (:eng "Log the transition tick. Without a transition, the sequence is stuck on step A forever."
     :math "The composition is a total order on two clauses; length of the schedule is length(A) + length(B)."
     :cs "The CS pattern is sequencing — the semicolon of scheduling."))

(verb
  :name "time/until"
  :library "time"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(time/until predicate clause) → clause"
  :summary "Run a clause, and signal done once a condition becomes true."
  :explanation "time/until is the complement of time/during: the clause runs freely until the predicate flips true, at which point the clause signals completion. Use this to gate a behavior until an end condition is met (e.g., \"run this animation until the health reaches zero\"). Unlike time/during, which keeps a clause dormant while the predicate is false, time/until keeps the clause active and checks for an end condition. It pairs naturally with time/then to chain behaviors."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/until (lambda () (= (ctx-get 'health ctx) 0))\n                      (to-draw (lambda (s) (paint-grid s)))))))" :note "Render the grid until health reaches zero, then stop.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/until (lambda () (> (game/frame (ctx-get 'game-id ctx)) 300))\n                      (to-draw (lambda (s) (card-emit 'frame s))))\n          (on-key (lambda (k s) s)))))" :note "Emit a frame event every frame, until we've run for 300 frames.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/then\n            (time/until (lambda () (>= (ctx-get 'score ctx) 100))\n                       (to-draw (lambda (s) (paint-grid s))))\n            (time/every-ms 100\n                          (to-draw (lambda (s) (audio-play 'victory)))))\n          (on-key (lambda (k s) s)))))" :note "Play the grid until score hits 100, then play victory sound every 100ms.")
  )
  :caveats ("The predicate is checked after the clause executes, so the clause runs at least once even if the predicate is true on frame 0." "Once the condition is true, the clause is done and does not re-activate." "The state must be updated externally (via ctx-set or other mutations) for the predicate to change.")
  :drawbacks ("For conditions that should prevent the clause from running at all, use time/during instead." "Predicates that depend on external state (e.g., a flag set by another system) can be fragile.")
  :usecases ("Play an animation until a timer expires." "Render a scene until the player health reaches zero." "Accumulate score or resources until a threshold is met." "Run a loop body until an invariant is violated or a goal is reached.")
  :related ("time/during" "time/when" "time/then" "big-bang" "stop-when")
  :learn (:concept "End-condition gating: run until a flag, then hand off." :prerequisites ("big-bang" "to-draw" "ctx-get" "ctx-set") :progression "Combine with time/then to build multi-phase loops; compare with time/during for the dual pattern.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A boss fight should stay active until the boss's health hits zero, then hand off to the victory screen. The operator's problem is choosing between time/during (which goes dormant when the predicate is false) and time/until (which stays active until the predicate becomes true, then signals done). The audit question is which one composes with time/then for the handoff."
     :program "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/then\n            (time/until (lambda () (= (ctx-get 'boss-hp ctx) 0))\n                        (to-draw (lambda (s) (paint 'boss))))\n            (to-draw (lambda (s) (paint 'victory)))))))\n(display 'wired) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 defines the entrypoint. Line 2 wraps the boss render in time/until so it stops when boss-hp hits zero. Line 3 chains victory after done. Line 4 confirms."
     :meta "Why time/until and not time/during: time/during would render dormant while the predicate is false — never; time/until produces a done signal that time/then can hook on to.")
    (:eng "Log the boss-hp value and the emitted done event. The audit needs the tick where done fired."
     :math "The active set is a prefix of ticks up to the first t with predicate true."
     :cs "The CS pattern is until-loop with promotion — the loop runs and then emits a completion signal."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The until-and-done: run until a condition, then hand off."
     :rungs ((:domain "time (a clause active until predicate true)" :code "(time/until pred clause)")
             (:domain "boiler (heat until temperature reached, then stop)" :code "(heat-until 'temp 100)")
             (:domain "search (iterate until a solution is found)" :code "loop { if goal? break; else step! }"))
     :explanation "In the runtime, a clause runs until a flag flips. A boiler heats until the target temperature. A search loop iterates until the goal is found. All three share the shape 'iterate until predicate, then done.'"
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever a workflow needs a completion condition rather than a completion count.")
    (:eng "Log the flip event; the flip is what upstream stages consume."

(verb
  :name "time/when"
  :library "time"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(time/when predicate clause) → clause"
  :summary "Create a one-shot clause that fires once, the first time a condition becomes true."
  :explanation "time/when is a one-time trigger: the wrapped clause runs exactly once, the first frame the predicate evaluates to true. On all other frames, it is inert. This is distinct from time/during (which keeps running while true) and time/until (which runs until true). Use time/when for single-fire events: a doorway opening when the player arrives, a sound cue on a specific beat, or a transition at the exact moment a condition flips."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/when (lambda () (> (ctx-get 'health ctx) 50))\n                     (to-draw (lambda (s) (audio-play 'alarm)))))))" :note "Play the alarm sound once, the first frame health exceeds 50.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/when (lambda () (audio-beat? (ctx-get 'beat-id ctx)))\n                     (to-draw (lambda (s) (sprite-address 'pulse))))\n          (on-key (lambda (k s) s)))))" :note "Trigger a visual pulse exactly once when the audio beat arrives.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (start ctx)\n  (big-bang\n    (list (time/when (lambda () (= (ctx-get 'phase ctx) 'boss-enter))\n                     (to-draw (lambda (s) (card-emit 'boss-dialogue))))\n          (time/during (lambda () (ctx-get 'is-running? ctx))\n                       (on-key (lambda (k s) s))))))" :note "Emit a dialogue event exactly once when the boss-enter phase begins, while input runs continuously.")
  )

"The predicate is re-evaluated every frame, so side-effects in the predicate will run until it is true.")
  :drawbacks ("Cannot be re-triggered; for repeating events on a condition, use time/during." "If the condition is false for the entire loop, the clause never runs (which is silent — no error).")
  :usecases ("Play a doorway-open sound the first time the player enters a region." "Emit a tutorial hint the moment the player's score hits a milestone." "Trigger a cutscene the first time a boss is encountered." "Sync a visual effect to the first beat of a song.")

     :explanation "Line 1 defines the entrypoint. Line 2 wires the doorway sound to fire exactly once at the first tick that crossed-threshold? returns true. Line 3 confirms."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (log-line level msg)\n  (list (time/iso) level msg))\n(log-line 'info \"card opened\")" :note "Simple structured log entry.")
  )
  :related ("time/now" "time/today" "time/from-ms")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "An operator wants to tag a card-open event with a timestamp that survives copy-paste across time zones. The problem is that time/now returns an integer that requires context to interpret; the audit needs a self-describing string with a Z suffix. The audit question is whether the record uses time/iso (UTC, explicit) or a local-time formatter (which loses the zone)."
     :program "(define event (list 'card-opened (time/iso) 'card-id 'main))\n(display event) (newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 constructs the event record with an ISO timestamp. Line 2 prints the record. The Z suffix in the timestamp is what makes the record portable."
     :meta "Why time/iso and not time/now: two operators reading the log across time zones can each compute their local interpretation from the Z-suffixed UTC string; an integer requires a shared decoder.")
    (:eng "Log the string. It is self-describing: no unit column needed."
     :math "The mapping from wall time to ISO string is injective on ms precision."
     :cs "The CS pattern is self-describing timestamp — RFC 3339."))

     :rungs ((:domain "time (ISO 8601 UTC string)" :code "(time/iso)")
             (:domain "shipping (label with unit and value)" :code "(label 'weight 'kg 5)")
             (:domain "physics (dimensional quantity)" :code "5 kg · m / s²"))

     :meta "The shape transfers wherever a datum crosses a boundary and must be self-interpreting on the other side.")
    (:eng "Prefer self-describing values across boundaries. Loss of context is loss of meaning."

  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "time/iso and time/from-ms are mutually round-tripping to millisecond precision: time/from-ms(time/to-ms(iso)) = iso for any iso produced by time/iso in this build."

    (:eng "Smoke test: round equals now-iso."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (age-ms iso-string)\n  (let ((then (time/to-ms iso-string)))\n    (if then (- (time/now) then) #f)))\n(age-ms \"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z\")" :note "Milliseconds since a stored timestamp; #f if the input can't be parsed.")
  )
  :related ("time/from-ms" "time/iso" "time/now")

The audit question is whether the parse uses time/to-ms with a #f guard, or trusts the string blindly."

    (:eng "Smoke test: equality holds."

(verb
  :name "topo/ball"
  :library "topo"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(topo/ball center radius metric-space) -> set"
  :summary "Compute the closed metric ball {j : d(center,j)≤radius} in a metric space."
  :explanation "topo/ball constructs the closed ball centered at a point, containing all points within a given distance (including the boundary). It is a fundamental topological object: neighborhoods, open covers, and filtrations all build on metric balls. The operation takes a center point, a radius, and a metric space object, and returns the set of all points satisfying the distance constraint. This is deterministic within a given device/precision context. Balls form the basis for Vietoris–Rips complexes and persistent homology computations."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((ms (topo/metric-space '((0 0) (1 0) (0 1) (1 1)))))\n  (topo/ball '(0 0) 1.5 ms))" :note "Find all points within distance 1.5 of the origin in a 2×2 grid.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((pts (list '(0 0) '(1 0) '(2 0) '(3 0))))\n  (let ((ms (topo/metric-space pts)))\n    (length (topo/ball '(1.5 0) 1.0 ms))))" :note "Count points in a 1D line segment within distance 1 of x=1.5.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (topo/metric-space->points ms) (list (list 0 0)))\n(let ((evolve-cover (lambda (ms scales)\n                      (map (lambda (eps)\n                            (topo/ball (car (topo/metric-space->points ms))\n                                      eps\n                                      ms))\n                          scales))))\n  (let ((ms (topo/metric-space (list '(0 0) '(1 1) '(2 0)))))\n    (map length (evolve-cover ms '(0 1.0 2.0)))))" :note "Track how the ball size grows over a sequence of scales, showing nested filtration structure.")
  )
  :caveats ("The result includes the boundary (≤, not <); this is the closed ball." "Distance is computed according to the metric in the space object; changing the metric changes the ball." "Computation time grows with the number of points in the metric space.")
  :drawbacks ("topo/ball is a local operation; computing many balls (as in topo/vietoris-rips) may be expensive." "No caching of distances; repeated ball computations recompute all distances." "Limited to finite metric spaces; infinite or continuous spaces require discretization.")
  :usecases ("Building neighborhoods in topology or differential geometry." "Constructing Vietoris–Rips complexes for persistent homology." "Studying how topological features persist as a scale parameter varies.")
  :related ("topo/vietoris-rips" "topo/rips-filtration" "topo/metric-space" "topo/persistence")
  :learn (:concept "Metric balls as the fundamental building block of topology; filtrations parameterized by radius." :prerequisites ("topo/metric-space") :progression "After topo/ball, learn topo/vietoris-rips to build complexes, then topo/persistence for barcode analysis.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "The operator is analyzing whether a point cloud from a sensor reading has clusters. Candidates: topo/ball (neighborhood at a radius), topo/vietoris-rips (whole complex at once), a raw list-of-distances (unstructured). For a single-scale neighborhood probe, topo/ball is the honest verb."
     :program "(define ms (topo/metric-space '((0 0) (0.1 0) (1 0) (1.1 0))))\n(display (length (topo/ball '(0 0) 0.5 ms)))\n(newline)"

The Euler–Poincaré formula relates χ to Betti numbers: χ = Σ(−1)ᵏβₖ, giving a strong consistency check. The Euler characteristic is invariant under continuous deformations (homeomorphisms), making it a robust topological fingerprint."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code ";; A single edge has χ = 2 − 1 = 1\n(let ((c (topo/close (topo/complex '((0 1))))))\n  (topo/euler-char c))" :note "f_0 = 2 (vertices 0,1), f_1 = 1 (edge); χ = 2−1 = 1.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code ";; A triangle has χ = 3 − 3 + 1 = 1\n(let ((c (topo/close (topo/complex '((0 1 2))))))\n  (list 'face-vector (topo/f-vector c)\n        'euler (topo/euler-char c)))" :note "f_0=3 vertices, f_1=3 edges, f_2=1 triangle; χ = 3−3+1 = 1.")

  :name "topo/persistence"

  :explanation "Persistent homology tracks how topology evolves as you build a complex scale by scale. The barcode is a list of intervals [birth, death], with infinite bars for features that never die. This verb is central to topological data analysis: it reveals the structure of data at all scales. Use it when you want to understand which features are real (persistent) vs. noise (short-lived)."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((filt (topo/rips-filtration (topo/metric-space (list (list 0 0) (list 1 0) (list 0 1)) (lambda (p q) (apply + (map (lambda (a b) (abs (- a b))) p q)))) 0 2.0 0.5)))\n  (topo/persistence filt 0))" :note "Persistence barcode in dimension 0 (connected components) for a Rips filtration.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let* ((pts (list (list 0 0) (list 1 0) (list 1 1) (list 0 1)))\n       (ms (topo/metric-space pts (lambda (p q) (sqrt (apply + (map (lambda (a b) (expt (- a b) 2)) p q))))))\n       (filt (topo/rips-filtration ms 0 2.5 0.25))\n       (b0 (topo/persistence filt 0))\n       (b1 (topo/persistence filt 1)))\n  (list 'h0 b0 'h1 b1))" :note "Compare persistence in dimensions 0 and 1 for a square point cloud.")

(verb
  :name "topo/persistence-entropy"
  :library "topo"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(topo/persistence-entropy barcode) -> number"
  :summary "Computes the Shannon entropy of the finite persistence bar lengths in a barcode, measuring the disorder or spread of feature lifetimes."
  :explanation "In a persistent homology barcode, each bar has a length (death − birth); entropy quantifies how spread out these lengths are. High entropy means bar lengths vary widely (diverse features); low entropy means most bars have similar lengths (homogeneous structure). Entropy is a single-number summary useful for comparing datasets. A barcode with one very long bar and many short ones has low entropy; a barcode with evenly distributed bar lengths has high entropy. Use this when you want a scalar measure of topological diversity."

    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((barcode (list (list 0 1.0) (list 0 1.0) (list 0 1.0))))\n  (topo/persistence-entropy barcode))" :note "Three bars of equal length (1.0): entropy is maximal (≈1.58 for 3 equal bars in bits).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((barcode1 (list (list 0 1.0) (list 0 0.1) (list 0 0.05)))\n      (barcode2 (list (list 0 0.5) (list 0 0.5))))\n  (list 'barcode1-entropy (topo/persistence-entropy barcode1)\n        'barcode2-entropy (topo/persistence-entropy barcode2)))" :note "Compare entropy of a heterogeneous barcode vs. a homogeneous one.")

  )
  :caveats ("Entropy is defined only for non-empty barcodes with at least one finite bar; empty or all-infinite barcodes return 0 or undefined." "The logarithm base matters: using log₂ (bits) vs. natural log (nats) changes the scale; both are valid." "Bars of length 0 (birth = death, birth point) are degenerate; filter them out before computing entropy." "Small numerical errors in bar lengths can distort entropy; use rounded or binned lengths if needed.")

  :learn (:concept "Persistence entropy is a single-number summary of how spread out the lifetimes of topological features are; it captures topological diversity." :prerequisites ("topo/persistence" "topo/total-persistence") :progression "After topo/persistence-entropy, use topo/bottleneck to compare barcodes from different datasets.")

  :library "topo"
  :kind "meta"

  :summary "Constructs the Vietoris–Rips complex at scale ε: a simplicial complex with all cliques of points within pairwise distance ε."
  :explanation "The Vietoris–Rips complex is a fundamental construction in topological data analysis. At scale ε, include a vertex for each point, an edge between any two points within distance ε, and a k-simplex (face) for any (k+1)-clique of edges. Unlike the Čech complex, it does not require circumradius checks—only pairwise distances. This makes it fast and widely used. The result is a simplicial complex suitable for computing homology and Betti numbers. Fuel (computation budget) prevents runaway on dense point clouds."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((pts '((0 0) (1 0) (0.5 0.866))))\n  (topo/vietoris-rips pts 1.5))" :note "Three points of a triangle; at ε=1.5, all edges form and the 2-simplex (triangle face) is included.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((pts '((0 0) (1 0) (2 0) (1 1))))\n  (let ((cpx (topo/vietoris-rips pts 1.1)))\n    (list (topo/betti cpx)\n          (topo/euler-char cpx))))" :note "Four points in a rough square; compute Betti numbers and Euler characteristic of the resulting complex.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((circle-pts (map (lambda (t) (list (cos (* 6.28 t)) (sin (* 6.28 t))))\n                        (map (lambda (i) (/ i 16.0)) (range 0 16)))))\n  (let ((cpx (topo/vietoris-rips circle-pts 0.8 10000)))\n    (cond ((eq? cpx 'too-many-simplices)\n           (display \"Fuel exceeded; reduce epsilon or point count\"))\n          (else\n           (list 'betti (topo/betti cpx)\n                 'homology (topo/homology-gf2 cpx))))))" :note "16 points on a circle; construct complex and check for robust 1-hole (β₁=1).")
  )

"For non-Euclidean metrics, use topo/metric-space to define distance; vietoris-rips assumes the metric is available.")
  :drawbacks ("Clique enumeration is NP-hard; computation time grows rapidly with epsilon and point density." "Unlike Čech, Rips over-approximates (includes simplices not in Čech); good for speed, less accurate topologically."   :usecases ("Building simplicial complexes for persistent homology (input to topo/rips-filtration)." "Computing Betti numbers and Euler characteristic of point clouds."      :program "(define c (topo/vietoris-rips '((0 0) (1 0) (0.5 0.866)) 1.5))\n(display (topo/betti c))\n(newline)"

(verb
  :name "topo/writhe"
  :library "topo"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(topo/writhe knot-diagram) -> number"
  :summary "Computes the writhe: the algebraic sum of crossing signs in a knot diagram."
  :explanation "In a knot diagram, each crossing is labeled with a sign: +1 for a right-handed crossing (the over-strand goes right relative to the under-strand) and −1 for left-handed. The writhe is the sum of all crossing signs. It is an invariant under the first Reidemeister move (which changes writhe) and the second and third moves (which preserve it). Writhe is useful for knot analysis, classification, and as input to other invariants. Unlike the crossing number, writhe is signed and can be 0 even for knotted diagrams."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(let ((unknot (topo/knot '())))\n  (topo/writhe unknot))" :note "The unknot has no crossings; writhe is 0.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((right-trefoil (topo/knot '((1 2 3 4 2 1 4 3))))\n      (left-trefoil (topo/knot '((1 4 3 2 4 1 2 3)))))\n  (list (topo/writhe right-trefoil)\n        (topo/writhe left-trefoil)))" :note "Right and left trefoils have opposite writhe (±3), reflecting chirality.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(let ((diagrams (map topo/knot\n                   '(() ((1 2 3 4 2 1 4 3)) ((1 2 3 4 5 6 2 3 1 4 5 6))))))\n  (map (lambda (d) (list (topo/writhe d)\n                        (topo/crossing-number d)))\n       diagrams))" :note "Compare writhe and crossing number; writhe is signed, crossing number is absolute.")
  )
  :caveats ("Writhe depends on the diagram orientation; reversing the knot's direction flips the sign of all crossings." "Writhe is not a complete knot invariant; two different knots can have the same writhe." "Changing a crossing via a Reidemeister I move changes writhe by ±2; moves II and III preserve it." "Malformed diagrams may cause 'diagram-invalid error; validate with topo/knot first.")
  :drawbacks ("Does not uniquely identify knots; useful in combination with other invariants (e.g., crossing number, Jones polynomial)." "Sensitive to diagram choice; different projections of the same knot can have different writhe." "For full knot classification, writhe alone is insufficient; use external tools (SnapPea, KnotTheory).")
  :usecases ("Detecting chirality: knots with opposite writhe are mirror images." "Analyzing Reidemeister moves: tracking writhe change under diagram manipulation." "Comparing diagram families: understanding how writhe varies across the same knot type." "Education: teaching knot invariants and their geometric meaning.")
  :related ("topo/knot" "topo/crossing-number" "topo/unknot?")
  :learn (:concept "Writhe as a signed sum of crossing orientations; an invariant under certain diagram moves" :prerequisites ("topo/knot" "topo/crossing-number") :progression "Understand writhe as an algebraic invariant, then study how it relates to crossing number, then combine with other invariants for knot classification.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "The operator wants to distinguish a right-handed trefoil from a left-handed one. Candidates: topo/writhe (signed), topo/crossing-number (unsigned). For chirality, topo/writhe is honest."
     :program "(define k (topo/knot '((1 2 3 4))))\n(display (topo/writhe k))\n(newline)"
     :explanation "Line 1 builds a diagram. Lines 2-3 report the writhe."
     :meta "Why topo/writhe and not crossing-number: writhe is signed and captures chirality; crossings don't.")
    (:eng "Writhe is the sign discriminator for mirror-image knots."
     :math "Signed sum of ±1 over crossings."
     :cs "Constant time per crossing."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "A signed count: aggregate signed items to produce a net magnitude."
     :rungs ((:domain "topo" :code "(topo/writhe k)")
             (:domain "net panning of a stereo mix (signed L/R sum)" :code "(mix/net-pan mix)")
             (:domain "signed sum over a finite set" :code "(define (signed-sum items sign-fn) (apply + (map sign-fn items)))"))
     :explanation "Each rung aggregates signed contributions. Crossings, pan positions, arbitrary signed items."
     :meta "The shape transfers wherever direction or polarity accumulates."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "The empty diagram (unknot) has writhe 0."
     :program "(display (= 0 (topo/writhe (topo/knot '()))))\n(newline)"
     :invariant "topo/writhe(topo/knot([])) = 0"
     :meta "The pattern is boundary-case correctness. CS pattern: base case. Falsifier: non-zero writhe on empty. See book-of-math ch14."
     :eng "Base case gate on the invariant."
     :math "Empty sum is 0."
     :cs "Constant time."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "topo/writhe returns signed crossing sum."
     :composition "(define k (topo/knot '((1 2 3 4))))\n(display (list 'writhe (topo/writhe k) 'crossings (topo/crossing-number k)))\n(newline)"
     :emergent "chirality report — signed writhe alongside unsigned count"
     :meta "Chaining topo/writhe with topo/crossing-number yields a chirality report. Same family as sign+magnitude readouts. See book-of-composition ch14.")))

When you call transport/tempo with a numeric BPM, you return a control descriptor (not an immediate side effect) that the runtime interprets to resynchronize all beat-dependent verbs (audio/play, synth/play, on-frame, across-beats, etc.) to the new tempo. Use this when you need to lock multiple subsystems to a single rhythmic pulse."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(transport/tempo 120)" :note "Set the shared clock to 120 BPM; all beat-synchronized verbs will retune to this pulse.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(define (tempo-shift ctx)\n  (let ((new-bpm (+ (audio-bpm) 10)))\n    (act 'transport/tempo (list new-bpm) 'tempo-set)))" :note "Read the current BPM, increment it, and issue a tempo shift; the act descriptor queues the change.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (sync-to-track ctx)\n  (let* ((track-meta (ctx-result ctx))\n         (track-bpm (ctx-get 'bpm track-meta)))\n    (next 'playing (act 'transport/tempo (list track-bpm) 'tempo-locked))))" :note "Extract BPM from a fetched track metadata object and lock the global tempo to it before transitioning to playback state.")
  )
  :caveats ("Tempo changes take effect on the next frame boundary; rapid consecutive calls may coalesce." "Does not affect already-scheduled notes or audio samples mid-playback; only applies to newly initiated playback." "The BPM must be a positive number; zero or negative values are rejected silently.")
  :drawbacks ("Global tempo changes affect all synchronized subsystems simultaneously—use with care in multi-track or multi-agent scenarios." "No gradual tempo ramp; transitions are instantaneous at frame boundary.")
  :usecases ("Synchronizing a multi-track composition to a master metronome." "Matching playback tempo to detected audio onset or live tap input." "Coordinating dance choreography, animation loops, and beat-locked state transitions.")
  :related ("audio/tempo" "audio/bpm" "on-beat" "synth/play" "audio/play")
  :learn (:concept "Global tempo as a control descriptor; the separation between descriptor (what to do) and effect (when it happens)." :prerequisites ("audio/bpm" "act") :progression "After understanding transport/tempo, learn audio/tempo for per-channel tempo control, then explore across-beats and on-beat for beat-aligned choreography.")
  :row-2-audit (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:problem "Two subsystems fell out of sync. The drum loop is playing at 128 BPM (set at track load) but the animation choreography was authored at 120 BPM. Dancers hit the floor a beat late every measure."
     :program "(define (retune-to-track track-bpm)\n  (transport/tempo track-bpm)\n  (display (list 'retuned-to track-bpm)))\n(retune-to-track 128)"
     :explanation "The operator's incident: sync drift between drums and dancers. The fix is to name the single truth (transport tempo) and force everything downstream to inherit it. The program pulls the track's declared BPM and calls transport/tempo once; the runtime propagates the pulse to every beat-locked subsystem at the next frame boundary. One line, one truth, one propagation event."
     :meta "The wrong sibling here is audio/tempo. audio/tempo only retunes the audio channel; the animation subsystem would keep running at 120 BPM and the drift persists silently. transport/tempo is the shared clock; audio/tempo is a per-channel override. Under audit, using audio/tempo would leave the log clean but the visible symptom unfixed — the exact fingerprint of a wrong-sibling call.")
    (:eng "Operator symptom is a phase drift log line: 'anim-frame N expected beat B, got beat B-1'. Setting transport/tempo resets both clocks at the next frame boundary; the drift shows one delta then goes flat. Audit trail: one transport/tempo call, timestamped."
     :math "Tempo is a positive-real scalar in beats-per-minute. The propagation is a broadcast — one write, many reads. If tempo drift is measured as ΔBPM = |declared − actual|, then transport/tempo drives ΔBPM to 0 at the next frame."
     :cs "This is a global mutable state write with coalesced-write semantics: repeated calls within one frame collapse to the last-wins value. The descriptor is not the effect; the effect is deferred to the frame-boundary applicator. Think of it as a config-registered singleton reload."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "The shape is master-clock-broadcast: one authoritative source publishes a rate, and every subscriber retunes to it."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "motoi transport" :code "(transport/tempo 120)")
       (:domain "wall clock in an operating system" :code "(define (settime-simulation new-secs)\n  (list 'settimeofday new-secs 'broadcasts-to 'ntp-daemon 'kernel-hrtimer))\n(display (settime-simulation 1700000000))")
       (:domain "least common multiple as a shared period" :code "(define (lcm-two a b)\n  (/ (* a b) (gcd a b)))\n(display (lcm-two 3 4))"))
     :explanation "In the motoi rung, transport/tempo publishes a BPM; every beat-locked verb reads it on the next frame. In the OS rung, a settimeofday broadcast retunes every subscribed daemon at once. In the math rung, the least common multiple names the shared period at which two rhythms realign — the algebraic essence of 'the tempo everyone agrees on'. Same shape: one canonical rate, many followers."
     :meta "The shape transfers because in all three cases the followers do not carry their own truth — they defer to a broadcast. Nothing survives a rate change without re-reading the canonical value. That property is what makes tempo 'master' rather than 'suggested'.")
    (:eng "In systems terms, this is a config-hot-reload shape: one source of truth, many refreshers. The engineering value is that debugging a phase-drift bug means checking exactly one variable."
     :math "The LCM rung captures why beat-alignment feels natural at rational tempo ratios: the shared period is finite and small. Irrational ratios produce polyrhythms that never realign, which is a different useful shape (see pattern/clave)."
     :cs "Broadcast semantics vs. per-channel semantics is the key CS distinction; broadcast is O(1) for the writer and O(k) for k subscribers on next tick. The alternative is per-channel writes which are O(k) at write time and O(1) per read."))
  :row-4-proof (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:claim "Setting the tempo is idempotent: calling transport/tempo with the same BPM twice in a row has the same visible effect as calling it once."
     :program "(define (assert-eq a b label)\n  (if (equal? a b)\n    (begin (display label) (display \": #t\\n\"))\n    (begin (display label) (display \": FAIL got \") (display a) (display \" want \") (display b) (newline))))\n(transport/tempo 120)\n(define after-one 120)\n(transport/tempo 120)\n(transport/tempo 120)\n(define after-three 120)\n(assert-eq after-one after-three 'idempotent-tempo)"
     :invariant "∀ b > 0. tempo(tempo(state, b), b) = tempo(state, b)"
     :meta "The CS pattern is idempotence, the same shape carried by HTTP PUT, kubectl apply, and any set!-with-single-value operation. Idempotence is what makes retries safe: if the frame-boundary applicator drops or duplicates a message, the visible tempo is unchanged. Falsification would be a hidden counter — e.g., if each call incremented a phase-offset in addition to setting the BPM, then double-set would drift. It does not. Cite book-of-code ch 5 (state machines) for the general theory of idempotent state operations.")
    (:eng "Idempotence in the operational sense means 'safe to retry'. If the transport network drops the descriptor and it is re-sent, the tempo is not double-applied. Log line count may double; visible pulse does not."
     :math "In semigroup notation: tempo-set is a constant function on its second argument — f(x, b) = b regardless of x. Constant functions are idempotent by definition (f ∘ f = f)."
     :cs "Contrast with tempo/nudge or tempo/ramp, which would be non-idempotent (each call shifts phase). transport/tempo is deliberately the absolute-set variant so retries are safe."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    :runs "spec-only"
   
    (:base "transport/tempo sets the shared BPM."
     :composition "(define (metronome-with-visual-flash bpm)\n  (transport/tempo bpm)\n  (on-beat (lambda ()\n    (surface/spotlight 'stage)\n    (audio/play 'tick))))\n(metronome-with-visual-flash 96)"
     :emergent "A metronome. The composition of transport/tempo + on-beat + a paired audio-and-visual pulse verb produces the recognizable metronome pattern: audible tick, visible flash, both locked to the same rate."
     :meta "The family is 'shared-clock pattern' — the same family as the cron daemon (shared time drives many jobs), the game-tick loop (one dt drives many updates), and the Redux store (one action drives many reducers). Cross-ref book-of-composition ch 8 (Timeline) — the timeline widget in that chapter is built on exactly this composition.")
    (:eng "Operationally, metronome is the smallest useful emergent pattern for a live-coding session: change one number, everything retunes. The engineering value is that the coupling is by-clock, not by-message."
     :math "The chained composition is a fanout: one rate becomes many synchronized outputs. In graph terms, transport/tempo is the root of a star topology where the leaves are the beat-locked verbs."
     :cs "Metronome emerges from shared-clock + subscriber pattern. The same emergence appears in publish-subscribe systems (Kafka topics, Redis pub/sub) where a single write fans out to many subscribers.")))

;;; 69-vec.slat — Motoi Scheme Reference · Chapter 69 · library vec
;;;
;;; 18 verbs in this library. Read chapter 00-intro.slat first.

;;;
;;; ─── THE ROW RULES (summary — full doctrine in 00-intro.slat) ───
;;;
;;; Every verb in this chapter has 5 rows. Each row does ONE job. Row
;;; contamination unbalances training data. If you author or edit a verb,
;;; STAY IN LANE.
;;;
;;;   Row 1 (HOW · Composition) — the verb written well; 1/3/5 module ladder
;;;   Row 2 (WHEN · Audit)      — operator's problem + this-verb-not-a-sibling
;;;   Row 3 (WHERE ELSE · Dim)  — same shape in 3 substrates (verb/metaphor/math)
;;;   Row 4 (WHY · Proof)       — claim + runnable test + ∀-invariant
;;;   Row 5 (WITH WHAT ELSE)    — chained verbs → named emergent pattern
;;;
;;; Every row carries the three-discipline lens: :eng · :math · :cs.
;;; No philosopher names in entries (they live in 00-intro.slat).
;;; Real Motoi domains only (no card/*, shop/*, cine/*, flower/*).

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Library vec — 18 verbs.")

(chapter :number "69" :library "vec" :verb-count 18 :training-eligible #t)

;; ═══ 18 verbs in library vec ═══

(verb
  :name "vec/+"
  :library "vec"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(vec/+ v1 v2 ...) -> vector"
  :summary "Element-wise addition of vectors; all must have the same dimension."
  :impl-status "wired"
  :impl-file "src/wired-verbs.js"
  :impl-notes "Variadic component-wise sum over an arbitrary number of vectors. Missing components are treated as 0, so vectors of different length are padded rather than raised — a design choice that lets 2D vectors freely embed into 3D contexts. Empty arg list returns ()."
  :explanation "Vector addition is the fundamental linear algebra operation: add corresponding components. If v1 = [a, b, c] and v2 = [d, e, f], then v1 + v2 = [a+d, b+e, c+f]. This is exact arithmetic (no floating-point error beyond Scheme's native number operations). Variadic: vec/+ can add 2 or more vectors in sequence, walking through them position by position."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(vec/+ '(1 2 3) '(4 5 6))" :note "3-dimensional vector addition. Returns (5 7 9) — each position summed independently.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "apprentice" :code "(define player-pos '(100 200))\n(define delta '(3 -1))\n(vec/+ player-pos delta)" :note "The classic 'move by a delta' pattern. New position (103 199). Move north-east by (3, -1) — the -1 means down one because screen Y grows downward.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((v1 '(1 0 -1))\n      (v2 '(2 3 4))\n      (v3 '(-3 2 0)))\n  (vec/+ v1 v2 v3))" :note "Variadic: add three vectors in one call. Returns (0 5 3).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(define (fold-left f init xs)\n  (let loop ((xs xs) (acc init))\n    (if (null? xs) acc (loop (cdr xs) (f acc (car xs))))))\n(let* ((forces (list '(10 0) '(0 15) '(-5 3)))\n       (net-force (fold-left vec/+ '(0 0) forces)))\n  net-force)" :note "Sum a list of force vectors via fold. Net force = (5 18). This is the standard physics pattern for accumulating impulses in a frame.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "master" :code "(define (path->positions origin steps)\n  ;; Given a starting position and a list of step vectors,\n  ;; return the visited positions including the origin.\n  (let loop ((cur origin) (rest steps) (acc (list origin)))\n    (if (null? rest)\n        (reverse acc)\n        (let ((next (vec/+ cur (car rest))))\n          (loop next (cdr rest) (cons next acc))))))\n(path->positions '(0 0) '((1 0) (0 1) (1 0) (0 -1)))" :note "Cumulative fold builds a path from step-deltas. Returns ((0 0) (1 0) (1 1) (2 1) (2 0)) — a square-like walk that ends one right of the start.")
  )
  :caveats ("Component-count mismatch does not raise; shorter vectors are zero-padded up to the longest. Callers who need strict equality should validate first." "Exact arithmetic is preserved; 1/2 + 1/3 yields 5/6, not a float approximation." "vec/+ is variadic; (vec/+ v1 v2 v3) adds all three in one call, not sequential nesting.")
  :drawbacks ("No in-place operation; creates a new vector (functional programming style)." "Variadic unpacking may be slower than binary + for very long chains." "Exact rationals in each component can grow in numerator/denominator size; simplification is not automatic.")
  :usecases ("Physics: summing forces, velocities, or displacements." "Computer graphics: adding translation or offset vectors." "Linear algebra: assembling linear combinations (paired with vec/scale)." "Data science: element-wise merging of numerical features.")
  :related ("vec/-" "vec/scale" "vec/dot" "vec/norm")
  :learn (:concept "Vector addition as component-wise operation preserving exact arithmetic" :prerequisites ("vec/make") :progression "Master vec/+, then combine with vec/scale to build linear combinations, then use vec/dot for projections, then study matrix operations.")
  :math (:algebra ("associative" "commutative" "identity: zero-vector") :total #t :domain "n vectors of equal dimension d" :codomain "vector of dimension d")
  :cs (:complexity "time O(k·d), space O(d) for k vectors of dimension d" :effects (none) :pure #t)
  :ai (:deterministic #t :cacheable #t :cardinality one :common-mistakes "Assuming vec/+ raises on dim mismatch; it zero-pads instead. If you need strict dim checking, use (vec/dim v) yourself first.")
  :hacker (:primitive #f :kin ("R7RS: no built-in; Clojure: (mapv + v1 v2); NumPy: v1 + v2") :history "Standard linear algebra since Grassmann (1844). Our impl is a straightforward variadic component-wise fold.")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "A physics tick accumulates forces from gravity, wind, and drag on an entity; the operator wants one net-force vector to feed entity/set-vel!."
     :program "(define forces (list '(0 -9.8) '(2 0) '(-0.3 0.1)))\n(define (fold-left f init xs) (if (null? xs) init (fold-left f (f init (car xs)) (cdr xs))))\n(define net-force (fold-left vec/+ '(0 0) forces))\nnet-force"
     :explanation "Three 2-D force vectors are folded left-to-right into a zero-vector seed. Each fold step calls vec/+ once, adding the running total to the next force. The final value is (1.7 -9.7) — gravity dominates the y axis, wind and drag mostly cancel on x."
     :meta "vec/+ is the honest verb because we are combining SAME-KIND quantities (forces on the same body in the same frame). A sibling like vec/lerp would blend two forces halfway — wrong semantics. vec/scale would multiply by a scalar — wrong shape. Under audit, vec/+ documents that we accumulated; that intent survives into logs. See SRE Manual ch on 'the verb names the intent'.")
    (:eng "Operators grep logs for '(vec/+ ...)' to prove force accumulation happened; if the code used raw map+ zip, the audit trail vanishes."
     :math "Vector addition in R^n is closed, associative, and commutative — the fold order does not affect the answer, so parallel workers can partial-sum safely."
     :cs "O(k·d) time; folded via left-fold to keep intermediate allocations linear in k. The variadic surface is a thin wrapper over binary +."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Same-shape combine: two things of the same kind get merged into one thing of that kind, preserving totals."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "vec" :code "(vec/+ '(3 4) '(1 2))  ;; (4 6)")
       (:domain "audio/mix" :code "(audio/mix track-a track-b)  ;; two waveforms superposed sample-by-sample")
       (:domain "monoid ⟨R^n, +, 0⟩" :code "(fold-left + 0 (map car pairs))  ;; the underlying monoid operation on any component"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 sums two vectors component-wise. Rung 2 superposes two audio buffers sample-by-sample — the SAME shape: two signals combine into one by pointwise addition. Rung 3 is the underlying algebraic structure: a commutative monoid where the identity is the zero element and the operation is closed. All three rungs are the same aspect wearing three costumes."
     :meta "The shape transfers because each substrate has an identity element and a closed, associative binary op. Any domain with those two properties supports the same 'accumulate-a-batch-into-a-running-total' idiom.")
    (:eng "Mixing consoles physically implement the audio rung with resistor summing junctions — engineering realizes the same shape."
     :math "The abstract structure is a commutative monoid; see book-of-math ch on abelian groups and monoids."
     :cs "Any monoid supports MapReduce-style parallel summation because associativity lets us re-parenthesize freely."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "vec/+ is commutative: adding a to b gives the same vector as adding b to a."
     :program "(define a '(3 -1 2))\n(define b '(0 5 7))\n(equal? (vec/+ a b) (vec/+ b a))"
     :invariant "∀ a b ∈ R^d.  vec/+(a, b) = vec/+(b, a)"
     :meta "Commutativity is inherited from + on numbers component-by-component. What would falsify: any pair where left and right disagree — e.g., a floating-point non-associativity artifact showing up in a triple sum. See book-of-math ch on abelian groups; the pattern-name is 'commutative binary operation'.")
    (:eng "Order-independent combine means a load balancer can shard force-accumulation across workers and reduce with matrix/+ later without deterministic-ordering constraints."
     :math "Commutativity + associativity = the vector monoid is abelian; this is what lets us re-order fold sequences."
     :cs "For high-dimensional float vectors, commutativity holds bitwise per pair, but ASSOCIATIVITY of a longer chain can drift by ULPs — a different invariant with a different test."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "vec/+ adds two vectors component-wise."
     :composition "(define positions (list '(0 0) '(1 0) '(1 1) '(0 1)))\n(define (fold-left f init xs) (if (null? xs) init (fold-left f (f init (car xs)) (cdr xs))))\n(define n (length positions))\n(define centroid\n  (let ((sum (fold-left vec/+ '(0 0) positions)))\n    (list (/ (car sum) n) (/ (cadr sum) n))))\ncentroid"
     :emergent "centroid / average-of-points — a summary statistic emerges from (repeated vec/+) + (division by count). Neither verb alone is a centroid; their composition is."
     :meta "Family: reduction-then-scale, the same pattern as arithmetic mean, center-of-mass, and running-average. Analog: SQL AVG() = SUM()/COUNT(). See book-of-composition ch on fold-and-normalize.")
    (:eng "Every game that computes 'party center point' or 'average enemy position' composes exactly this chain — vec/+ over a list, then scale by 1/n."
     :math "This is the arithmetic mean of a set of points in R^d."
     :cs "Two-pass fold: first accumulate, then normalize. Streaming variants (running mean) fuse into one pass with a counter.")))

(verb
  :name "vec/-"
  :library "vec"
  :kind "meta"
  :signature "(vec/- v1 [v2 ...]) -> vector"
  :summary "Element-wise subtraction of vectors; single-arg negates, N-ary subtracts left-to-right."
  :impl-status "wired"
  :impl-file "src/wired-verbs.js"
  :impl-notes "Variadic component-wise subtraction. One arg negates. Two args = v1-v2. N-ary = (((v1-v2)-v3)-v4). Missing components zero-pad rather than raise — see vec/+ for the matching design."
  :explanation "Vector subtraction is addition of the negated vector: v1 − v2 = v1 + (−v2). If v1 = [a, b, c] and v2 = [d, e, f], then v1 − v2 = [a−d, b−e, c−f]. Exact arithmetic is preserved. With one argument, returns the negation. With 2+ arguments, subtracts left-to-right: vec/- v1 v2 v3 = (v1 − v2) − v3."
  :examples (
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(vec/- '(5 7 9) '(1 2 3))" :note "3-D subtraction. Returns (4 5 6).")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "apprentice" :code "(vec/- '(1 2 3))" :note "One-arg negates every component. Returns (-1 -2 -3) — cleaner than writing (vec/- '(0 0 0) v) for the same effect.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "intermediate" :code "(let ((start '(3 4))\n      (end '(7 1)))\n  (vec/- end start))" :note "Displacement vector (end − start) from two positions. Returns (4 -3) — four right, three up in screen space where Y grows downward.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "expert" :code "(vec/- '(10 10 10) '(1 2 3) '(1 1 1))" :note "N-ary left-to-right subtraction. (10-1-1, 10-2-1, 10-3-1) = (8 7 6). Handy for subtracting several offsets in one call.")
    (:dialect "motoi" :tier "master" :code "(define (velocity from to dt)\n  ;; Given two positions and a time delta, return the average\n  ;; velocity vector: displacement / dt applied component-wise.\n  (map (lambda (x) (/ x dt)) (vec/- to from)))\n(velocity '(0 0) '(6 8) 2)" :note "Compose vec/- with map to compute a velocity. From (0,0) to (6,8) over 2 seconds: (3 4). Magnitude 5 — the 3-4-5 triangle appearing in kinematics.")
  )
  :caveats ("Component-count mismatch does not raise; shorter vectors are zero-padded." "Left-associative: vec/- a b c = (a − b) − c, not a − (b − c)." "Single-argument form returns negation." "Exact arithmetic is preserved; 1/2 − 1/3 yields 1/6 exactly.")
  :drawbacks ("Variadic left-associativity can be counterintuitive; use parentheses to clarify intent." "No in-place operation; creates a fresh vector each time." "Exact rationals can accumulate large numerators/denominators over many operations.")
  :usecases ("Physics: computing relative velocity or displacement between two points." "Graphics: computing edge vectors from vertex pairs." "Linear algebra: forming differences for numerical methods (e.g. gradient descent)." "Signal processing: computing deltas or differences in time series.")
  :related ("vec/+" "vec/scale" "vec/norm" "vec/dot")
  :learn (:concept "Vector subtraction as component-wise negation and addition; left-to-right evaluation" :prerequisites ("vec/+" "vec/make") :progression "Use vec/- to compute displacements, then combine with vec/norm to compute distances, then study vec/angle-between for relative orientation.")
  :math (:algebra ("not-commutative" "identity: zero-vector on the right") :total #t :domain "one or more vectors" :codomain "vector of the largest input dimension")
  :cs (:complexity "time O(k·d), space O(d)" :effects (none) :pure #t)
  :ai (:deterministic #t :cacheable #t :cardinality one :common-mistakes "Expecting right-associative evaluation. (vec/- a b c) subtracts BOTH b and c from a, not (a - (b-c)).")
  :hacker (:primitive #f :kin ("NumPy: v1 - v2 - v3; Clojure: (mapv - v1 v2 v3)") :history "Follows Grassmann's vector algebra; the negation-of-one-arg convention echoes Scheme's numeric (-).")
  :row-2-audit (
    (:problem "An entity at position P wants to know the direction and magnitude to a target T so the AI planner can decide whether to pursue or ignore."
     :program "(define P '(3 4))\n(define T '(10 9))\n(define delta (vec/- T P))\n(define dist (sqrt (+ (* (car delta) (car delta)) (* (cadr delta) (cadr delta)))))\n(list 'delta delta 'dist dist)"
     :explanation "vec/- with two args returns the displacement vector T − P. We then compute Euclidean magnitude by hand from delta. Result: displacement (7 5), distance sqrt(74) ≈ 8.60."
     :meta "vec/- is the audit answer because 'displacement' has a signed direction. A sibling like vec/distance collapses direction to a scalar — losing the pursuit-vector the planner needs. Order matters: (vec/- T P) points FROM P TO T; reversed operands would send the entity backward.")
    (:eng "Operational logs show 'delta = (7 5)' when pursuit begins; if we had used a scalar distance verb, the log would say only '8.60' and later replay would not tell us which direction the entity was moving."
     :math "T − P is the vector from P to T; this is the coordinate-free definition of displacement in an affine space."
     :cs "Two-arg call is O(d); we manually re-square components rather than call vec/norm to show the shape."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "Directed difference: taking one state and asking 'what's the arrow to another state?'"
     :rungs (
       (:domain "vec" :code "(vec/- '(10 9) '(3 4))  ;; (7 5) — displacement")
       (:domain "time/deltas" :code "(- t-now t-then)  ;; elapsed time between two clock reads")
       (:domain "affine space P^n" :code "(sub P T)  ;; the tangent vector such that T + v = P"))
     :explanation "Rung 1 subtracts vector positions. Rung 2 subtracts scalar timestamps to get a duration. Rung 3 is the general affine principle: subtracting two POINTS gives a VECTOR — the tangent that connects them. All three share the shape 'two states → the arrow between them.'"
     :meta "The shape transfers because in any affine structure, the difference of points is a vector — a group-theoretic complement to a torsor.")
    (:eng "Both a game engine tracking positions and a distributed system tracking clocks use exactly this shape to reason about relative offsets."
     :math "In an affine space, subtraction of points yields the associated vector-space element; see book-of-math ch on affine geometry."
     :cs "The tangent-vs-point distinction shows up as separate types in type-safe geometry libs; Motoi keeps them as lists for brevity."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "vec/- is the inverse of vec/+ in the second argument: (vec/+ a (vec/- b a)) recovers b."
     :program "(define a '(3 -1 2))\n(define b '(0 5 7))\n(equal? (vec/+ a (vec/- b a)) b)"
     :invariant "∀ a b ∈ R^d.  vec/+(a, vec/-(b, a)) = b"
     :meta "This is the affine reconstruction identity: from a base point and the displacement to another, we recover the other.     (:dialect "motoi" :tier "novice" :code "(define u (vec/make (list 1 2)))\n(define v (vec/make (list 3 4)))\n(vec/dot u v)" :note "Computes 1*3 + 2*4 = 11.")

    (:claim "vec/add is associative when combined into a fold: order of pairwise adds does not affect the final sum."
     :program "(define a '(1 0)) (define b '(0 1)) (define c '(1 1))\n(equal? (vec/add (vec/add a b) c) (vec/add a (vec/add b c)))"
     :invariant "∀ a b c ∈ R^d.  vec/add(vec/add(a, b), c) = vec/add(a, vec/add(b, c))"
     :meta "Associativity is inherited from + on numbers. Falsifier: any triple where reparenthesization changes result beyond ULP. Pattern-name: associative binary op. See book-of-math ch on semigroups.")
    (:eng "Associativity means fold-left and fold-right yield the same result — parallel workers can shard freely."
     :math "Vector addition forms an associative monoid."
     :cs "Under exact rationals, bit-exact; under floats, ULP-level drift possible."))
  :row-5-emergence (
    (:base "vec/add takes two vectors and returns their component-wise sum."
     :composition "(define (fold-left f init xs) (if (null? xs) init (fold-left f (f init (car xs)) (cdr xs))))\n(define (centroid pts)\n  (let ((sum (fold-left vec/add '(0 0) pts))\n        (n (length pts)))\n    (list (/ (car sum) n) (/ (cadr sum) n))))\n(centroid '((0 0) (2 0) (2 2) (0 2)))"
     :emergent "centroid computation — same pattern as vec/+, showing that the alias participates in the same emergent behaviors."
     :meta "Family: fold-reduce-then-scale, the mean/centroid family. See book-of-composition ch on aggregators.")
    (:eng "Centroids power camera-follow logic (average of party positions)."
     :math "Arithmetic mean in R^d."
     :cs "One O(n·d) fold plus O(d) scale.")))

  :name "vec/sub"

  :related ("vec/add" "vec/distance" "vec/norm")
  :row-2-audit (

     :explanation "vec/sub returns leader − follower = (10 5). This is the 'toward-leader' vector; normalizing it gives a heading direction."
     :meta "vec/sub is honest for 'directed difference'. A sibling like vec/distance would collapse to a scalar, losing direction.")
    (:eng "Log 'to-leader = (10 5)' documents follower AI decisions."

     :cs "O(d); binary form of vec/-."))
  :row-3-dimension (
    (:setup "State-to-state arrow: given two states, produce the vector connecting them."
     :rungs (
       (:domain "vec" :code "(vec/sub b a)  ;; the vector from a to b")
       (:domain "time" :code "(- t-end t-start)  ;; duration between events")
       (:domain "affine space" :code "b − a = tangent vector"))
     :explanation "Rung 1: geometric arrow. Rung 2: elapsed time. Rung 3: general affine subtraction."
     :meta "Same as vec/-; this alias-family shares the shape.")
    (:eng "State-arrows appear in every distributed system tracking events between states."
     :math "Affine subtraction; see book-of-math ch on affine spaces."
     :cs "The tangent-vs-point distinction is what makes affine typing possible."))
  :row-4-proof (
    (:claim "vec/sub is the inverse of vec/add on the second slot: (vec/add a (vec/sub b a)) = b."
     :program "(define a '(1 2)) (define b '(4 6))\n(equal? (vec/add a (vec/sub b a)) b)"
     :invariant "∀ a b ∈ R^d.  vec/add(a, vec/sub(b, a)) = b"
     :meta "Round-trip identity — same as vec/-. Falsifier: any pair where the identity fails. Pattern: group inverse. See book-of-math ch on abelian groups.")
    (:eng "Delta-encoding (send only b − a and reconstruct at destination) relies on this identity."
